content_blocks.text: This path is here to make you effective with AI at work, fast and without the guesswork. By the end you will know what to hand off, what to check, and what to keep for yourself.

Most people meet AI through trial and error. A few results that genuinely impress, a few that quietly embarrass, and no reliable sense of when to trust the thing. That is a slow and inefficient way to learn. This path swaps that guesswork for judgment, so you can direct AI on purpose and help set the tone for how the people around you use it.
What this path is

A structured route from "I have heard AI is useful" to "I know where it pays off and where it does not." It is built for anyone who wants to use AI well at work, whether that means leading a team's decisions or simply doing your own job better with AI in it.

It is not a tour of buttons and menus, and that is on purpose. Tools get renamed and rebuilt every few months; the judgment about when to trust them lasts a lot longer. So the focus stays on what holds steady: what these systems are good at, how they fail, how to steer them, and where the responsibility stays with you.
What you will be able to do
By the end, none of the choices that actually matter will be a guess.

cards.body: Brief AI the way you would brief a capable but very literal new hire, clearly enough to get useful work back on the first or second try.
cards.title: Direct with intent

cards.body: Tell the difference between work that is ready to send and work that only looks finished, and know what to verify before you rely on any of it.
cards.title: Judge the output

cards.body: Know what is worth handing off, what to keep for yourself, and what should never go near an AI tool at all.
cards.title: Draw the lines

content_blocks.text: How it is structured

Short lessons, grouped into modules, in a deliberate order. The early modules build a working picture of what AI is and how it behaves. The middle ones teach you to steer it and catch it when it goes wrong. The last modules turn that into a way of working: deciding what to delegate, building your own instincts, and putting it all to work on a task you do again and again. This General track is the foundation — once it's done, the tool-specific tracks (Copilot, Claude, and others) build the same judgment into the tools you actually use.
Lessons build on each other. Skipping ahead is the fastest way to end up confused about something a two-minute earlier lesson would have made obvious.
How to use it

Read actively rather than passively. The lessons only pay off when they change how you handle a real task afterwards. Keep something concrete in mind as you go: a customer complaint you want to answer well, a budget review before a decision meeting, the release notes nobody has had time to write yet. Those are the kinds of jobs the later lessons work through, and every idea sticks better once you have tested it against work you actually own.

Short lessons, a little practice in between, and some honesty with yourself about what worked will take you further than reading straight through in one sitting.

questions.q: Why does this path focus on judgment rather than the specific features of AI tools?
options: Features are too fiddly to explain inside short lessons
Tools change quickly, but the judgment about when to trust AI and how to steer it holds up
The tools on the market are all much the same underneath
Feature knowledge matters mainly to technical staff
questions.explanation: Specific buttons and menus get redesigned every few months. What lasts is knowing what AI is good at, how it fails, and where responsibility stays with you, so that is what the path builds.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to work through the path?
options: Skip ahead to the lessons that sound most relevant to save time
Read every lesson in one sitting to keep your momentum up
Follow the order and test each idea against a real task you own
Memorise the key terms before you move on from each lesson
questions.explanation: Lessons build in a deliberate order, and the value comes from applying each idea to real work you own, not from finishing quickly or memorising terms.

questions.q: By the end of the path, what should you be able to decide?
options: Which AI vendor offers the best pricing
How to build and train a model of your own
What to hand off to AI, what to keep, and what should never go near it
How to write software that calls AI systems
questions.explanation: The path is about direction and judgment: briefing AI well, judging what it returns, and drawing clear lines around what to delegate, keep, or avoid entirely.

title: What this learning path is and how to use it

content_blocks.text: You hand AI the all-hands script, skim the first paragraph, and it sounds like you on a good day. The reflex is to forward it and get on with something else. That reflex is what this lesson is about.

Before deciding where AI fits into your work, it helps to set aside two common reactions:

- **Over-enthusiasm:** assuming AI is close to replacing entire functions, so the safest move is to hand it everything.
- **Dismissal:** assuming it is unreliable and not worth trusting with anything that matters.

Both reactions make the same mistake: treating AI as a single verdict rather than a tool that is strong in some areas and weak in others.
Why the extremes both mislead

The hype misleads because fluent output is not the same as sound output. AI writes text that reads as confident and finished whether or not it is correct. That polish is persuasive, and persuasive-but-wrong costs you more than obviously-wrong, because it is the version that slips through unread and surfaces later.

The dismissal misleads because the same tool, pointed at the right work, is genuinely fast and good. Someone who tried it once, got a bad answer, and wrote the whole thing off has judged it on a single sample. That is the standard they would never accept from a colleague.
The stance that pays

What works instead is calibration. You walk in expecting AI to be strong at some things and weak at others, and you read every output as a draft you are accountable for rather than a result you can forward unread.

It is a simple idea to state and an easy one to abandon once you are busy.

This changes the question you ask. The useful question is which parts of a job you can hand off and which you have to keep. Take the all-hands script. AI can give you a structure and a serviceable first draft in a minute, and on a routine quarter that gets you perhaps 70 to 80 percent of the way there. The rest is the part that was always yours: what the message should say, whether the tone fits a room that has just heard about a hiring freeze, which figures are safe to commit to out loud. If you do not run an all-hands, the same split turns up in the update you post to your team channel or the note you send round after a decision.
What "realistic" looks like day to day

Being realistic here means knowing roughly what to expect before you ask. You are then neither surprised when AI delivers nor caught out when it does not, and your attention goes to the parts that need it.

cards.body: Ask once, forward the answer, trust it because it sounds right. The problem surfaces later, usually in front of the people you least wanted to see it.
cards.title: Unrealistic optimism

cards.body: Refuse to touch it because it got something wrong once. You keep doing by hand the drafting it could have done in seconds, and you fall behind the people who learned the tool.
cards.title: Unrealistic dismissal

cards.body: Point it at drafting, structure, and synthesis. Read what comes back the way a sharp, fast, sometimes-wrong colleague would want you to read theirs, and keep the judgment calls for yourself.
cards.title: Calibrated use

content_blocks.text: The rest of this track is about where that line sits: which tasks reward handing off, how AI fails, and how to direct it well. You do not need any of that yet. You only need to walk in expecting a capable, fallible instrument that still needs your judgment.

questions.q: What is the shared flaw in both hyping AI and dismissing it?
options: Both underestimate how quickly the technology is improving
Both treat AI as a single verdict instead of a tool that is strong at some tasks and weak at others
Both put too little money into the software
Both assume AI behaves the same way for every kind of task
questions.explanation: Hype and dismissal reach for the same kind of answer: one blanket judgment. The workable stance is calibration, expecting AI to be strong in some areas and weak in others.

questions.q: Why is fluent, confident-sounding AI output a particular trap?
options: It usually takes longer to read than writing the draft from scratch would
Polish reads as correctness, so a wrong answer is persuasive and can be passed on unchecked
It tends to produce very short outputs that miss the detail
It avoids questions that call for judgment
questions.explanation: AI produces finished-sounding text whether or not it is right. Persuasive-but-wrong costs more than obviously-wrong, because it is the error that slips through and surfaces in front of the wrong audience.

questions.q: In a calibrated approach to the all-hands script, which part stays with you rather than the AI?
options: Producing the first rough draft of the script
Laying the script out into clear sections
Judging what the message should say and which figures are safe to commit to out loud
Summarising last quarter results into a short recap
questions.explanation: Drafting, structuring, and summarising are strong candidates to hand off. The judgment about what to say and what you can stand behind stays with you.

title: What to realistically expect from AI

content_blocks.text: Older software could only find, sort, and count what already existed. Generative AI writes something new on demand: a draft, a summary, a plan that did not exist a moment ago.

Artificial intelligence has meant many different things over the decades, but the branch that actually changed how work gets done is generative AI: models that produce new text, drafts, and summaries on demand, rather than retrieving something that was already stored. Whether you lead a team or just do your own job, that shift lands the same way and works the same way.
What "generative" actually means

Traditional software follows rules a person wrote in advance. A spreadsheet adds the numbers you type in. A search engine returns pages that already exist somewhere. A database hands back the record you asked for. In every case the output was already there in some form, waiting to be retrieved or calculated, and the same input gives the same result every time because someone specified exactly what to do.

Generative AI works from patterns instead of fixed rules. Hand it your scattered notes on how your team runs its release process and it can draft a clean wiki entry that existed nowhere until you asked. Nobody wrote a rule for your particular request. The model produces a response that fits the shape of what you asked for, assembled fresh.
Why this is a different category, not just better software

The distinction has real consequences. It changes both what you can safely hand off and what you have to watch for.

Because the output is generated rather than retrieved, it comes back fluent, fast, and shaped to your request. That is exactly why it helps with drafting that wiki entry, turning a long recorded meeting into a short list of decisions, or putting a dense policy clause into plain language. Work that used to mean sitting down and producing prose from a blank page can now start from a draft.

That same quality creates the risk. Retrieved information is either in the system or it is not. Generated content always comes back looking complete and confident, whether or not it is correct. You are no longer running arithmetic you can trust by default. You are reading something that has to be judged on its merits before you rely on it.

cards.body: **Deterministic.** Finds, sorts, or calculates what already exists. Fixed rules, and the same input gives the same output every time. You can trust it to do exactly what it was told.
cards.title: Traditional software

cards.body: **Probabilistic.** Produces new content that fits your request. Fast and flexible, but the output is written fresh each time and has to be judged before you rely on it.
cards.title: Generative AI

content_blocks.text: What this means for how you use it

Two habits follow from how the technology works: reach for it where producing a first version is the slow part: drafting, summarising, restructuring, reformatting, and treat what comes back as a capable draft rather than a finished answer, since it is written to look right, which is a different thing from being right. A later lesson, "What AI is good at, and where it falls short," goes into exactly where that line sits in practice.

questions.q: What is the core difference between generative AI and traditional software like a database or search engine?
options: Generative AI is faster at retrieving stored records
Generative AI produces new content rather than retrieving or calculating what already exists
Generative AI keeps a much larger database of records to search through
Generative AI can only work with numbers, not text
questions.explanation: Traditional software returns what is already there through fixed rules. Generative AI writes a fresh response that fits your request, which is why it can draft a wiki entry or a summary but also why the result has to be judged rather than trusted by default.

questions.q: Why does the fluent, confident quality of generative output call for judgment?
options: Because the model is slower than a search engine
Because generated content always looks complete and confident whether or not it is correct
Because the output changes only when the rules are rewritten
Because it can only produce short answers
questions.explanation: Retrieved data is either present or absent. Generated content comes back looking finished no matter how accurate it is, so a polished response is not proof that it is right.

questions.q: Where does generative AI help most?
options: Tasks where a fixed, guaranteed-identical result is required every time
Tasks where producing a first version from scratch is the slow part, such as drafting or summarising
Tasks that involve only exact arithmetic
Tasks where no human review is possible
questions.explanation: The technology is at its best generating a first version you then refine: a wiki entry, a summary, a restructured set of notes, instead of starting from a blank page. A fixed, guaranteed-identical result is what traditional software is for.

title: What is generative AI

content_blocks.text: When someone asks "can AI do this?", the honest answer is another question: which model, and how capable is it?

In most workplace conversations, "AI" is shorthand for a large language model, an LLM, running behind a chat window. Knowing what that actually is, and how one model differs from the next, changes how you brief it, what you trust it with, and where your budget goes.
What a large language model is

An LLM is trained on huge amounts of text to do one thing: predict what text should plausibly come next, given what came before. That sounds narrow, but in practice it covers a lot of ground. The same trained system can draft a stakeholder update, pull a batch of open-ended survey comments into a themed summary, rewrite a dense clause in plain language, or turn scribbled notes into a clean action list.

The reach is genuinely wide, but so are the limits. The model has no memory of your last conversation unless the tool feeds it back in, and it does not see live information unless something connects it to a source that does. As covered in the previous lesson, it produces plausible text rather than looked-up facts: that is why it is usually right and occasionally, confidently, wrong.
Model versus tool

A model is the specific trained system that does the predicting. It has a name and a version. The tool is the product you open to reach it: the chat window, the app in your browser. When you type into that window, the tool hands your prompt to a model and passes the answer back. Keep the tool the same, swap the model behind it, and the result changes.

That matters because providers do not ship a single model. They ship a family, each member tuned to a different balance of speed, cost, and reasoning power.
Capability tiers

Within a family, models come in tiers. Each tier trades speed and cost against raw capability, and most providers follow the same shape: a fast, cheap model for high-volume routine work, a balanced model for everyday tasks, and a top model built for hard reasoning.

cards.body: Quick and low cost, made for simple high-volume work: short summaries, quick rewrites, routine drafting. Capable enough for most everyday asks.
cards.title: Fast and economical

cards.body: The sensible default for real work. Strong on drafting, synthesis, and structured tasks, without the cost or lag of the top tier.
cards.title: Balanced

cards.body: Built for hard reasoning, such as pressure-testing an argument or working through a layered problem. Slower and pricier, and worth it when the task is genuinely difficult.
cards.title: Most capable

content_blocks.text: The Claude family is a clear example. Haiku is the fast, economical tier, Sonnet the balanced one, and Opus the most capable. Other providers sell the same range under their own names. A model name points to a specific version, and newer versions are usually better across the board. The fast tier is a different point on the curve, not a cheaper knock-off of the good one.
Why the choice matters

Picking a model is a design decision. Say you have a few hundred free-text responses from a customer survey to summarise before a review meeting. If you just want the recurring themes grouped and counted, the fast tier does it well, and running the top model over the same batch buys you nothing but a longer wait and a bigger bill. But if you need it to weigh contradictory feedback, catch the quiet complaint that signals a real problem, and tell you which themes actually matter, that is reasoning work, and the fast tier will hand you a smooth summary that misses the point. Reach for the top tier on the hard read. Keep the fast tier for the routine roll-up.

Turn every vague "can AI do this?" into something you can act on: which tool, which model, how capable, and where does it fall short? That question is what separates deliberate use from hoping for the best.

questions.q: A colleague asks whether AI can review a complex proposal for weak arguments before it goes up. What is the most useful way to think about the question?
options: AI can either do it or it cannot, because it is one fixed capability
Which model, running in which tool, and how capable it is for this task
Whichever tool is cheapest will give much the same result
Only the newest product on the market could attempt it
questions.explanation: AI is not one thing. A flat yes or no hides the real variables: the specific tool, the model behind it, and whether that model tier is capable enough for the task in front of you.

questions.q: You need to summarise a large batch of routine customer survey comments into a themed roll-up, and you do this every month. Which tier fits best?
options: The most capable tier, so the summary comes out as thorough as possible
The fast, economical tier, since the task is straightforward and high in volume
The tier makes no difference to the result, so pick by habit
A different model for each batch, to compare how they read
questions.explanation: Routine, high-volume summarising is what the fast tier is built for. Sending it to the top tier burns cost and time for no real gain in quality.

questions.q: Why can the same LLM give you a confident answer that turns out to be wrong?
options: It looks the answer up and the source it found was out of date
It predicts plausible next text rather than retrieving verified facts
It holds the correct answer back to keep costs down
It only slips up when you pick the cheapest tier
questions.explanation: An LLM produces text that plausibly follows your input. Plausible and true usually line up, but not reliably, which is why fluent output still needs checking whatever tier produced it.

title: LLMs and models

content_blocks.text: Where AI earns its keep

AI is strongest when the work is open-ended language and weakest when it turns on facts, figures, or judgment only you can supply. Turning a page of messy meeting notes into a clean list of decisions and owners sits right on the strong side of that line: it is language work, and AI is fast at it. Deciding what those notes actually mean for the project, and what your team should do next, stays with you.

The distinction that matters is the kind of task, not the tool. The same model that turns scattered notes into a clean list in seconds will also name a wrong cause or decision with total confidence if you ask it to judge instead of restructure. What changes between those two results is the kind of task you handed it.
The four things it does well
Most of what AI genuinely accelerates falls into four buckets. They share a trait: the value is in producing fluent language or structure, and a human still owns the final call.

cards.body: Open-ended work with words: writing, summarising, reasoning through a problem out loud. Hand it a page of scattered meeting notes and it returns a first-pass list of decisions, owners, and open questions. What comes back is a rough document you then shape further.
cards.title: Thinking and drafting

cards.body: Turning information from one form into another: a requirements list into a table, a dense policy clause into plain language, raw notes into a slide outline. Reliable, because the source material sits right in front of it.
cards.title: Structured transformation

cards.body: Emails, summaries, the opening draft of a write-up you'll refine. You get something usable in seconds and spend your time refining instead of staring at a blank page.
cards.title: First-draft generation

cards.body: Pulling together what is generally known about a topic into a starting map: a quick primer on how other teams run blameless retros, say, that you then check and sharpen against your own situation.
cards.title: Broad synthesis

content_blocks.text: The pattern across all four: AI is fast at the first 80 percent of language work. The last 20 percent stays with you: the accuracy, the judgment, the sign-off.
The four places it falls short

The limits are just as predictable. They cluster where the task stops being about producing plausible language and starts being about something the model cannot reliably do.

**Calculation and live facts.** On its own, a language model does not calculate. It produces text that looks like a computed answer, and it has no live data unless a tool feeds it some. So when a summary says a project is three weeks behind or that costs have doubled, treat those as text shaped like numbers until you check them against the actual source. Both limits lift when the tool is wired for it, since some now run real code or reach a live source. Unless you know that is happening, a figure it hands you is a claim to verify rather than one it worked out.

**Novel judgment with no clear right answer.** Deciding what a set of meeting notes actually means for the project, and what to do about it, is the part that matters most. When that call turns on competing accounts of what happened, or on which risk is worth carrying, AI gives you something generic and reasonable-sounding. It cannot make the trade-off for you, because the trade-off depends on what you know and value, not on what plausibly comes next.

**Anything needing context it does not have.** The model has what you told it and what it absorbed in training. The real reason a decision stalled is often the thing nobody wrote down: the objection raised off the record, the constraint nobody mentioned in the meeting, the history between two people in the room. None of that reached the model. Missing context does not stop it from answering: it answers as if the gap were not there.

**High-stakes precision work.** Financial modelling, regulatory decisions, anything carrying legal or safety weight. The task itself demands an exactness the model does not guarantee, so it sits outside what you can hand over and accept as-is.
Across every category, one rule holds: AI output is a starting point a human checks, never a finished product you forward untouched.
Ask whether it needs AI at all

Part of the skill is knowing when not to reach for it. A recurring email wants a saved template. A known process wants a checklist. A single fact wants an ordinary search. Pointing a language model at work that a plain search or a saved template would handle faster and more reliably is its own small mistake. What you are after is the outcome, and often the older tool gets you there sooner.
The instinct to build

Before you hand off a piece of work, run one quick test: is this mostly about producing language and structure, or does it turn on a number, a fact, or a judgment about what really happened? The first kind AI does well and fast. The second it will answer anyway, confidently and often wrong. Learning to feel that difference before you delegate is most of what separates the people who get real value from AI from the people who do not.

items.text: Turning a page of messy meeting notes into a clean list of decisions and owners
items.reason: Structured transformation: reshaping information that is already there, not inventing or judging.

items.text: Finalising the wording of a regulatory compliance filing
items.reason: High-stakes precision work carries legal weight the model does not guarantee.

items.text: Drafting the first pass of an email you will edit before sending
items.reason: First-draft generation: fast and usable, and you spend your time refining rather than starting blank.

items.text: Deciding whether to renew a vendor contract given mixed feedback from three teams
items.reason: Novel judgment with no clear right answer depends on what you know and value, not on what plausibly comes next.

content_blocks.prompt: Sort each task into the right bucket.

questions.q: You need to turn a page of messy meeting notes into a clean list of decisions, owners, and open questions. Why is this a good fit for AI?
options: It depends on tallying how many action items each person owns, which is where models are most reliable
Structured transformation: reshaping information the model can already see
It hinges on judgment calls that only the model is positioned to make
It needs live data that the model quietly pulls in on its own
questions.explanation: Turning information from one form into another is one of the most reliable uses of AI, because the source material is present and the task is about restructuring rather than inventing or judging.

questions.q: Someone asks AI to decide what actually went wrong on the project and what the team should change, weighing competing accounts from the people involved. What is the honest limitation here?
options: AI cannot produce any text on the topic
The decision hinges on weighing competing values and what you know, so AI produces a generic answer rather than the real judgment
AI will refuse to comment on a project that failed
The task is too small for AI to be worth using
questions.explanation: Novel judgment with no clear right answer depends on what you know and value, not on what plausibly follows next. AI can lay out the considerations, but the call itself stays with you.

questions.q: Which task is the weakest fit for a language model working on its own?
options: Drafting a first pass of the post-mortem writeup
Rewriting a dense policy clause into plain language
Working out the total cost of the outage from the raw system logs
Turning scattered incident notes into a structured timeline
questions.explanation: A language model does not calculate; it produces text that looks like a computed answer. Working out a total cost from raw logs turns on arithmetic the model does not actually perform, which makes it the poorest fit of the four.

title: What AI is good at, and where it falls short

content_blocks.text: Every AI tool works inside two hard limits: how it chops your text into pieces, and how much of it the model can hold at once. Knowing where those limits sit helps you get a reliable answer instead of one built on material the model can no longer see.

The model does not read your input the way you do. Where you see words, paragraphs, and pages, it sees tokens, and it can only hold so many of them at once. Those two facts govern what you can hand a model and what comes back. This lesson covers both.
Tokens: the unit the model reads

A token is a chunk of text, usually a few characters, roughly three-quarters of a word on average. The word "board" is one token. A longer or unusual word might run to two or three. The conversion worth keeping in your head is simple. 1,000 tokens is about 750 words, or a page or two of dense text.

The exact conversion matters less than a rough sense of scale. Everything you send and everything the model returns is measured in tokens, and there is a ceiling on how many it can work with at once. A one-line question is a handful of tokens. A spreadsheet export with a few thousand rows, pasted in whole, is tens of thousands. That gap is why the limit turns real on exactly the tasks where AI is most useful, the long and information-dense ones.
The context window: everything the model can see at once

The context window is the total pool of tokens the model can hold in a single conversation. It covers everything in play: the background instructions it starts with, every message you have sent, every reply it has given, and any document or spreadsheet you have pasted or attached. If it is not in the window, the model cannot use it.
What gets cut, and why long chats "forget"

When a conversation or a set of documents outgrows the window, something has to give, and the oldest material falls out of view first. The model does not warn you and does not stop responding. It carries on with less to work from.

This is why a long working session can feel as though the model is forgetting what you told it at the start. It is not a glitch. The detail you set out early has dropped outside the window, and the model is now answering from what remains. The same effect explains why a summary of a very long document can quietly miss what sat on page one, because not all of it was in view when the answer was produced.

If you are not sure how much room is left, you can simply ask the model how full its context window feels and whether starting a fresh session would help. Some tools also **compact** a long conversation behind the scenes, quietly summarising older messages to free up room: worth knowing so you are not surprised when older detail gets fuzzier even though you never cleared the chat.

A long conversation does not preserve everything you have said. When an early instruction or figure stops being honoured, assume it has fallen out of the window and restate it rather than trusting the model to still hold it.
What this changes about how you hand over work

Modern models have large context windows, hundreds of thousands of tokens, enough to take a full contract, a long email thread, or several files at once, and these windows have grown enormously over the past few years and keep expanding with each new generation. But "much bigger" is not the same as "unlimited," and that ceiling still matters for the tasks that push against it. Cleaning up a big spreadsheet export, reformatting a few thousand rows into one consistent structure, is exactly the kind of task that can still reach the edge, and the failure is silent.

The practical moves are straightforward. For a large clean-up, the more you narrow what you hand over to what the task actually needs, the more reliable the result: send the columns that matter, not the whole export, when you can. When you must supply a lot, structure it, because clear headings and labels help the model find what counts inside the pool. And when precision on a specific detail matters, put that detail late and state it plainly rather than assuming an instruction from twenty exchanges ago is still in view.

cards.body: A large window lets you paste a full contract or a long thread and still leave the model room to answer questions about it. Most single documents fit comfortably.
cards.title: What fits

cards.body: Once the window is full, the oldest material drops out of view first, and it goes silently. The model keeps answering from whatever remains.
cards.title: What gets cut

questions.q: Why can a model seem to forget details you gave it earlier in a long conversation?
options: The model deletes old messages to save cost
The earliest material has fallen outside the context window, so the model can no longer see it
The model decides some of your instructions are not worth keeping
A bug corrupted the conversation history
questions.explanation: The context window is finite. When a conversation grows past it, the oldest tokens drop out of view and the model answers from what remains. It is a structural limit rather than a malfunction, which is why restating a key instruction works.

questions.q: You need to clean up and reformat a large spreadsheet export, and every row has to be accounted for. What do the token and context-window limits tell you to do?
options: Paste the whole export at once and trust the large window to handle it
Hand over only the columns the task needs, structure the input clearly, and stay alert that hitting the edge fails silently
Break every row into a separate message before pasting
Assume the model will flag you if anything overflows the window
questions.explanation: Large windows are not unlimited, and overflowing one degrades the result with no warning. Handing over only what the task needs, labelling it clearly, and watching for silent edge cases is the reliable approach.

questions.q: Roughly how much text is 1,000 tokens?
options: About 10 words
About 750 words, or a page or two of dense text
Exactly 1,000 words
About 50 pages
questions.explanation: A useful rule of thumb is that 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words. Knowing the rough conversion helps you judge when a long document or a big spreadsheet is nearing the limit of what the model can hold at once.

title: How models read your input

content_blocks.text: The previous lesson covered what goes into a model: tokens and the context window. This one covers what comes out, because the same mechanism that reads your input this way also explains two things people notice quickly: why the same prompt can give two different answers, and why AI can hand you a confident, well-formed fact that is simply untrue.
Prediction, not retrieval

As covered earlier in this track, the model builds each answer by predicting the next plausible chunk of text rather than retrieving a stored fact. Two consequences follow directly from that, and this lesson covers both: why identical prompts can produce different answers, and why a fluent answer is not proof that it is correct.
Why the same prompt varies

Ask the same question twice and you can get two different answers. That is by design, not a fault.

At each step the model does not lock onto one guaranteed next word. It weighs many candidates, each with its own probability, and picks from among them. A setting called **temperature** controls how much freedom it has in that choice. Turn it low and the model stays close to the single most likely path: steady and repeatable, the right setting for pulling figures out of a report or forcing messy notes into a fixed structure. Turn it up and the model ranges into less likely paths, which reads as more varied and more creative.

Temperature is not a quality dial. A higher setting produces more variation and more drift; it does not produce a better answer. Most tools run at a moderate default you never see, which is why the same prompt rarely comes back the same way twice.

So whether that variability helps or hurts comes down entirely to what you asked for. When you need one exact result every time, it is a liability. When you want options, it is an asset: ask for three ways to open a difficult message to your team, or a few different angles on a recommendation you are about to send up, and the spread is the point. Same mechanism, opposite value.

content_blocks.task: Run both prompts below, each as a separate, brand-new conversation. Compare what comes back.

steps.text:
Context: You're naming a new internal newsletter that shares AI tips with non-technical staff.
Task: Suggest a name for the newsletter.
steps.label: Prompt 1 (vague task)

steps.text:
Context: You're naming a new internal newsletter that shares AI tips with non-technical staff.
Task: Suggest three name options, each 2–4 words, that sound approachable rather than corporate. For each, add one sentence on why it fits a non-technical audience.
steps.label: Prompt 2 (detailed task)

content_blocks.material: A made-up scenario: you're naming a new internal newsletter that shares AI tips with non-technical staff.
content_blocks.whatToNotice: The vague task leaves the model free to invent its own criteria, so two runs produce two unrelated, incomparable lists. The detailed task pins down count, tone, and reasoning, so the output is more consistent between runs. That's the same mechanism (the model filling gaps you left open) that also explains why a vague prompt is more likely to hand you a confident, ungrounded answer.

content_blocks.text: Why it can be confidently wrong

The same mechanism produces the failure that catches people off guard: a **hallucination**, where the model states something plausible-sounding that is simply false.

Ask for a citation, a figure, or a name the model was not well trained on, and it does the only thing it can: it produces the text that most plausibly fits. A convincing reference to a paper that was never published. A precise-looking number with nothing behind it. It arrives in the same fluent tone as everything else it gets right, with no signal that this particular answer was invented.

Hallucinations cluster exactly where the mechanism predicts: on specific facts the model has little exposure to, like names, dates, figures, technical specs, and references to real documents. They are far rarer when the model works from material you supplied, such as rewriting a clause in plain language, restructuring notes, or reasoning over a document you pasted in. Take a competitor brief you are building from your own scattered notes. Pulling those notes into a clean structure is low-risk. The moment the model volunteers a market-share figure you never gave it, the risk climbs.
Two behaviours, one cause

cards.body: The model chooses among several probable next words rather than one fixed answer, and temperature sets how freely it strays. Same prompt, different output: an asset when you want options, a liability when you need consistency.
cards.title: Variation

cards.body: Asked for facts it does not reliably hold, the model produces the most plausible-looking text anyway. It arrives in the same fluent tone as everything it gets right, with no signal that it was invented.
cards.title: Confident fabrication

content_blocks.text: Both come from one root: prediction. The model generates plausible text and calls nothing up from a verified store. Understanding that is not the same as knowing what to do about it; checking output and judging where the real risk sits come later in the track. For now, form one instinct: the more a task turns on specific facts, figures, or names, the less the model's confidence is worth.

questions.q: Why can the same prompt produce two different answers on two tries?
options: The model looks the answer up and the source changed between tries
At each step the model selects among several probable next tokens, and temperature governs how freely it strays from the most likely one
The context window emptied between the two attempts
The model corrects its earlier answer because it detected a mistake
questions.explanation: Output is generated by selecting among probable next tokens, not retrieved. Temperature controls how much the model strays from the single most likely path, so identical prompts can yield different results by design.

questions.q: A model returns a precise, professional-sounding statistic with a named source. What does its confident tone tell you about whether the number is correct?
options: Nothing, because fluency is produced regardless of accuracy, so tone is no signal of truth
The confident tone means the model verified it against its training data
A named source means the figure was retrieved rather than generated
The precision of the number indicates it is reliable
questions.explanation: The model produces authoritative-sounding text as a matter of course. A fabricated figure and a correct one arrive in the same even voice, so confidence carries no information about accuracy.

questions.q: In which task is hallucination LEAST likely?
options: Supplying the publication dates of three named industry reports
Recalling a competitor market-share figure from memory
Rewriting a policy clause you pasted in into plain language
Naming the authors of a specific academic paper
questions.explanation: Working from source material you supplied keeps the model on ground it can see. Requests for specific facts it must produce from thin training exposure, things like dates, figures, names, and references, are where fabrication clusters.

title: Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong

content_blocks.text: Every response a model produces is shaped by two layers of instruction: the prompt you send, and a standing set of instructions set before you ever arrived. Knowing both exist changes how you read what comes back, and how much of a tool's behaviour you can actually change.
The prompt: what you send

A prompt is any input you give the model: a question, an instruction, a document to summarise, a set of notes to turn into a task list. The model takes your prompt, adds whatever else is already sitting in the context window, and builds a response out of all of it.

The term gets used loosely. Sometimes it means a single message; sometimes it means the whole approach to phrasing a request well. Either way the principle holds: what you put in shapes what you get back. Ask a support tool to "reply to this complaint" and you get something generic and cautious. Tell it the customer has been waiting nine days, that you want an apology without admitting fault, and that a goodwill credit should be offered in the last line, and you get a reply you can almost send as it stands.

You don't need the full craft yet; that comes in the next module. One instinct is enough for now: the model fills gaps with assumptions, and its assumptions are not always yours.
The system prompt: what was set before you arrived

Before your first message, the model has already been handed a set of standing instructions. This is the system prompt. It runs behind the interface, never shows up in the chat thread, and shapes how the model behaves across the whole conversation: what role to play, what tone to strike, what to focus on, what to refuse.

Every AI tool you open already has one, and some of it is safety-related: a model's own system prompt is often what makes it refuse a request for racial slurs or instructions to build a weapon, regardless of how the conversation is worded. That refusal isn't the model spontaneously deciding what's off-limits; it's a standing instruction set before you ever typed a word.

The same layer also shapes ordinary behaviour, not just safety. Take the customer support assistant behind a company's help chat: its system prompt is what turns a general model into that assistant, fixing the tone, the policies it can quote, the refunds it is allowed to mention, and the topics it must hand to a human.

You can write a version of this yourself. When you set a persona or global custom instructions in a tool that offers them (most chat tools have a settings menu for this), you are writing your own system prompt: telling the model to always answer concisely with bullet points, to adopt a particular tone, or to never use em dashes. It runs quietly in the background of every conversation you start from then on, the same way the builder's system prompt does for everyone else using that tool.
Builders use a system prompt to configure a model once, for everyone who touches the tool. You use prompts to steer it in the moment, for the task in front of you.
Why the difference matters to you

You may never write a system prompt. Knowing one is always running still changes how you read what you see.

When a model refuses a reasonable request, softens an answer, or keeps forcing a format you didn't ask for, consider that a system prompt may be shaping that behaviour, rather than assuming your own wording is at fault. A standing rule you cannot see is often the thing steering the model, and once you spot that, you either work around it or move to a tool configured for what you actually need.

It also sets your expectations about control. The system prompt sets the stage; your prompt directs the scene inside it. You have real influence over the second layer and none over the first, which is why the tool you pick matters as much as the wording of any single request.

cards.body: Written by you, during the conversation, and visible in the chat. It directs the task in front of you right now. This is the layer you control.
cards.title: Prompt

cards.body: Written by the builder or admin before the conversation, and never shown to you. It shapes the role, tone, and limits the model follows across the whole session. You inherit it rather than set it.
cards.title: System prompt

content_blocks.text: What this buys you

Two takeaways carry into the rest of the track. Output quality tracks input quality: the sharper and more specific your prompt, the more usable the result, and that skill is entirely yours to build. And when a tool behaves in a way your prompt never asked for, look past your own wording to the instructions you cannot see. Both come down to the same recognition. You are always working inside a frame someone else set, and you steer with the one layer that belongs to you.

questions.q: A support tool keeps refusing to mention refunds and forces every reply into the same rigid template, no matter how you word the request. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is broken and needs to be restarted
A system prompt is imposing rules and behaviour you cannot see or edit
Your prompt contains a technical error
The model has run out of context window
questions.explanation: Restrictive behaviour that holds across a whole conversation usually traces to the system prompt: standing instructions set by the builder that you cannot see. Recognising this points you to work around it or switch tools rather than blame your own wording.

questions.q: What is the core practical difference between a prompt and a system prompt?
options: A prompt is written by you in the moment; a system prompt is set by the builder before the conversation and shapes overall behaviour
A prompt is for questions and a system prompt is for commands
A system prompt is simply a longer, more detailed prompt
There is no real difference; the terms mean the same thing
questions.explanation: The prompt is the layer you control turn by turn. The system prompt is a standing configuration set by whoever built the tool, invisible to you and applied across the whole session.

questions.q: Why does a vague prompt often produce a poor result rather than an obvious error?
options: The model deliberately holds back effort until you are specific
The model fills the gaps with its own assumptions and returns a confident answer to a slightly different question
Vague prompts push the request past the context window
The system prompt blocks any request it judges to be vague
questions.explanation: Faced with ambiguity the model does not stall. It fills the gaps with assumptions that may not match yours and returns a plausible, confident answer, which is why a vague prompt fails quietly rather than loudly.

title: Prompts and system prompts

content_blocks.text: Say you ask an AI to update the risk register for a project you run. One version drafts from the notes you paste in. Another opens the tracker itself, reads the past fortnight, spots a supplier delay slipping from amber to red, and flags two mitigations already overdue. Same request, very different reach.

So far you have met AI as something you talk to. You send a prompt, get text back, take it from there. That is the base case, and it is where most people stay. Two developments push past it:

- **AI that takes actions instead of only answering** (agents).
- **AI that plugs into the tools and data where your work already lives** (connectors).

You will not build either yourself, but anyone deciding where AI fits needs to recognise what they are and where the risk moves.
The versions of AI that actually change how work gets done go further than chat: they can act on your behalf and reach into the systems where that work already lives.
From answering to acting: agents

A standard chat model responds one message at a time, and you stay in the loop for every step. It drafts, you read, you decide what comes next. An agent works differently: you define the goal or outcome, and it plans its own steps to reach it, running a search, reading a file, drafting a result, checking its own work, using whatever tools it has access to along the way. Your input along the way is far lighter.

Take the risk-register example from the start of this lesson: ask a chat model, and it structures whatever you handed it. An agent could instead go and find the material itself, pull the recent status updates, cross-reference them against last quarter's entries, and hand back a marked-up draft.

That autonomy is where the value sits, and where the risk sits with it. More unsupervised steps mean more places a wrong turn goes unseen. A single confident-but-wrong answer is easy to catch when you read every reply. A wrong step buried three actions deep in an agent run is not: the overdue mitigation it quietly dropped, or the risk it rated low because it never saw the email that would have raised the flag. Two things reduce that risk: giving the agent a clear goal and enough context to work from, and building in checkpoints along the way, so you can course-correct partway through a run rather than only judging the finished result.
The more steps an AI takes without you, the more the job shifts from checking the reply to verifying the outcome. Autonomy raises the value and the stakes at the same time.
Reaching your systems: connectors and MCP

An agent still needs a way to reach beyond the chat window. That link is called a connector: a pre-built connection between an AI tool and an outside system, whether that is your files, an email thread, a document store, or the tracker holding your risk register. Point the tool at that tracker through a connector and it can read what is there.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the open standard most connectors are now built on. Rather than every AI tool needing a custom-built connector for every system, MCP gives them a shared format to speak, so a connector built once works across any tool that supports MCP. Think of a universal plug instead of a drawer full of mismatched adapters: MCP is the plug standard, and a connector is a specific plug built to it.

Connectors turn AI from a writing partner into something wired into where your work already sits. That is what makes it useful, and it is also why access, permissions, and oversight are worth asking about before you switch one on.

cards.body: Responds to one input at a time. You stay in the loop and decide each next step. The safe default for most work.
cards.title: Chat model

cards.body: Given a goal, it takes several steps toward it with limited supervision. More capable, and more able to go wrong where you cannot see it.
cards.title: Agent

cards.body: A pre-built link from an AI tool to an outside system: files, email, a tracker, a database. How AI reaches your real work.
cards.title: Connector

cards.body: The shared standard behind connectors, so one link works across tools. A universal plug, not a fresh custom build each time.
cards.title: MCP

content_blocks.text: What to take from this

You are not being asked to set any of this up. What matters now is recognition. When someone says an AI can just handle a multi-step job, hear agent, and ask how the outcome gets checked. When a tool offers to connect to your inbox, your files, or that project tracker, hear connector, and ask who approved the access and what it can see.

MCP is the general, cross-vendor standard behind the idea, and support for it is still spreading unevenly across products. Some tools already connect through it directly, others still rely on their own older connector systems. Rather than tracking which is which today, the tool-specific track you're using will tell you where things stand for that product; what carries across all of them is recognising the pattern itself.

questions.q: What is the core difference between a chat model and an agent?
options: An agent is simply a newer and larger model than a chat model
A chat model answers one message at a time, while an agent pursues a goal across several steps with limited supervision
An agent runs at a higher temperature, so its answers come out more creative
A chat model needs a prompt, while an agent needs no instruction at all
questions.explanation: The distinction is acting versus responding. A chat model answers each message and waits for you. An agent pursues a goal across several steps on its own, which makes it more capable and also more able to err before you notice.

questions.q: What does a connector do?
options: It makes the model produce more varied output
It links an AI tool to an outside system such as your files, email, or a project tracker
It speeds up how fast the model generates text
It removes the need to write a prompt at all
questions.explanation: A connector is a pre-built link between an AI tool and an external service or data source. It is how AI reaches past the chat window into the systems where your work actually lives.

questions.q: Why should a leader care about the difference between reviewing a chat reply and overseeing an agent?
options: An agent finishes faster, so there is less time pressure to review its work
The more steps an AI takes on its own, the harder a wrong step is to catch, so oversight moves to verifying the outcome
An agent keeps its own audit log, so reviewing the final result is optional
There is no practical difference in how you check the work
questions.explanation: Autonomy raises both value and stakes. A wrong answer is easy to spot when you read every reply, but a wrong step buried inside a multi-step run is not, so the burden moves to checking the final outcome rather than just the last message.

title: Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do

content_blocks.text:
Most disappointing AI output traces back to a vague request that got a vague answer. The model filled the gaps you left with the most generic, plausible thing it could reach for. Prompting is a skill you can improve quickly, using a handful of rules of thumb rather than months of practice: a sharper instruction can turn a throwaway draft into something you can forward or decide from with only light edits.

This lesson covers the four things that make a prompt good in the first place: specificity, audience, format, and constraints. Whether you are prepping talking points for a vendor negotiation or getting a usable draft of an everyday email, the same four decisions do most of the work.
Specificity: say what you actually want

The most common mistake is asking for too little. **"Summarise this document"** is a prompt, but it forces the model to guess how long, for whom, and to what end. Now compare that against a fuller version: **"Summarise this vendor contract in five bullet points for a non-technical colleague, focusing only on the clauses that carry a cost or a deadline."** The second gets you something usable on the first pass. The first gets you a coin flip.

Every guess you leave in a prompt is a decision you have handed to the model, and it will make that decision generically, with no idea what you had in mind. Cutting those guesses is all that specificity means. The extra words are just what it takes to get there.
When the output feels generic, the prompt is the first place to look: most of the time, an important choice was left unspecified rather than decided.
The four levers
For anything you intend to use directly, four decisions carry most of the weight. You will not need all four every time, but deciding them upfront is quick and saves a round trip of edits later.

cards.body: Who is this for? Notes for your own prep read nothing like a message you send to the vendor. State it: **for my own use**, **for a colleague who was not in the room**, or **for a new hire**. The model calibrates vocabulary, depth, and what it assumes they already know.
cards.title: Audience

cards.body: What should the output look like? Bullet points, three short paragraphs, a table with named columns, a one-line answer. If you have a shape in mind and do not say so, you get whatever the model defaults to.
cards.title: Format

cards.body: What stance should it take? Neutral analysis, a clear recommendation, or a list of risks only. Asking the model to frame a problem is a different request from asking it to solve one. Decide which you want.
cards.title: Angle

cards.body: What are the hard limits? A word cap, a tone to hold, jargon to avoid. Constraints keep the output inside the box you need it to fit.
cards.title: Constraints

content_blocks.text: Take a real case. You are preparing talking points for a contract renewal with a software vendor who has just proposed a double-digit price increase. **"Help me prepare for this negotiation"** leaves everything open. Instead: **"Draft talking points for our renewal call. We have used this vendor for three years and rely on it daily. They want a large annual increase, and I want to hold it near inflation and add two user seats. Give me three opening positions and the likely pushback on each. Direct, businesslike tone, no filler, one page."** Audience, format, angle, and constraints, all decided by you rather than left to the model.
Constraints work in the negative, too

Telling the model what to avoid works as well as telling it what to do, and it's an easy step to skip. If the output keeps coming back with the same flaw, name the flaw directly.

Common examples: **"Do not open with a preamble. Start with the first point."** **"Do not suggest fixes; I only want the problem framed."** **"Do not use corporate filler like leverage, synergy, or holistic."** **"Do not exceed 200 words."** None of these is a nitpick: a recurring annoyance you keep editing out by hand is a one-line instruction you have not written yet.
If you find yourself deleting the same thing from every output, stop deleting and start excluding. Name it in the prompt.
Anatomy of a strong prompt

The difference is intention, not creativity. Watch what happens when the four levers meet a weak request.

- **Prompt 1 (weak):** "Write talking points for my vendor call."
- **Prompt 2 (strong):** "Write talking points for a 30-minute renewal call with our IT vendor. Open with the value we have had from them, then make the case that their proposed increase runs above market, and close with the two concessions I need to walk away satisfied. Firm but friendly tone, under 250 words, no header."

The strong version came from decisions made up front rather than a better imagination. It said who it is for, what shape it takes, what it should do, and what it must not do. That is all it comes down to. Worth knowing too: today's models have advanced enough that even a simpler, reasonably well-rounded prompt usually gets you most of the way there. The four levers just make that outcome reliable instead of lucky.
A note on where this goes next

You can push quality further with heavier techniques, such as showing the model a worked example of what good looks like, or giving it a role to shift its perspective, like asking it to pressure-test your talking points the way the vendor account manager would. Those are genuine multipliers, and the next lesson is dedicated to them. For now, the four levers plus a clear statement of what to avoid will handle most of your work. Master the baseline before reaching for the extras.
The habit worth building

Before you send a prompt for anything that matters, run a two-second check: have I said who it is for, what it should look like, what stance to take, and what to avoid? You will skip some of those on purpose, and that is fine. The point is that you decided, instead of leaving the model to guess.

content_blocks.task: Run both prompts below in your own AI tool, using the sample project in place of specifics.

steps.text: Write a status update email about the reporting dashboard refresh project.
steps.label: Prompt A

steps.text: Write a status update email to my manager about the reporting dashboard refresh. Cover what shipped this week, the one blocker, and what's next. Keep it under 150 words, plain and direct, no corporate filler.
steps.label: Prompt B

content_blocks.material: A made-up project called the reporting dashboard refresh. This week: migrated the backend, fixed two bugs, still waiting on design sign-off for the new charts. Blocker: the design sign-off. Next: user testing starts Monday.
content_blocks.whatToNotice: Prompt A likely comes back generic and padded, since it has to guess at tone, length, and what matters. Prompt B should come back close to sendable on the first try, because you made the decisions instead of leaving them to the model.

questions.q: You need talking points you can actually walk into the call with. Which prompt is most likely to deliver them?
options: Help me prepare for the vendor renewal call.
Give me some good talking points for the vendor call, and make them professional.
Draft five talking points for a renewal call with our analytics vendor, aimed at holding their proposed increase near inflation, in a firm but friendly tone.
Can you help me think through this vendor negotiation?
questions.explanation: The third names the format (five talking points), the context and goal (hold the increase near inflation), and the tone. Those decisions are what turn a coin-flip response into something usable. Professional is too vague to act on.

questions.q: Every draft the model gives you opens with a paragraph of throat-clearing before the real content. What is the fix?
options: Regenerate until one comes back without the preamble.
Add an explicit exclusion: do not open with a preamble, start with the first point.
Switch to a more capable model.
Accept it and delete the opening each time.
questions.explanation: A recurring flaw is usually a missing instruction. Naming what you do not want works as well as naming what you do, and it fixes the problem at the source instead of every single time.

questions.q: What actually separates a weak prompt from a strong one, in most cases?
options: The strong one is longer and uses more advanced vocabulary.
The strong one makes the decisions, audience, format, angle, and constraints, instead of leaving them to the model.
The strong one asks the model to be creative.
The strong one uses a special role or worked example, which is what makes any prompt good.
questions.explanation: Strength comes from intention, not word count or creativity. Every choice you do not make, the model makes for you, usually generically. Roles and worked examples help, but they are not what makes a baseline prompt good.

title: How to write a good prompt

content_blocks.text: It starts before the model writes

You have your monthly one-on-one with your manager on Thursday, and a month of scattered work to turn into three things worth actually raising. You could open a model and ask for help. What you get back depends less on how you word the request and more on what you put in front of it first.

A good prompt tells the model what to do. Context is the raw material it works with: the project updates you are pulling from, the manager you are writing for, the constraints you already know apply. Get the context right and the difference in output is larger than any clever phrasing. Most people bring an instinct from search: that more input means a better result, and that instinct works against you here: the model responds to relevance, not volume.
What context actually is

Everything the model can see in one conversation counts as context: your instructions, the files you attach, the data you paste, and the whole back-and-forth up to that point. All of it shapes the answer. So the question that matters is what the task needs.

Think about how you would brief a capable new colleague. You would not drop every document the company owns on their desk and ask for a summary. You would give them the two or three things that matter, tell them who it is for, and flag the one constraint they could not have guessed. The model rewards the same discipline.
What to include
The context worth giving usually comes down to four things. Give the model the ones the task turns on and leave the rest out.

cards.body: The actual thing the task works on: the project updates you are pulling from, the thread you need to reply to, the notes you want turned into actions. Paste the relevant parts and leave the surrounding archive out.
cards.title: The source material

cards.body: Who reads the output and what it is for. A talking-points list for your own one-on-one reads nothing like a summary for the whole team. Say it, because the model cannot guess your reader.
cards.title: The audience and purpose

cards.body: The boundaries the model could not infer: length, tone, what to leave out, a format you must match, a decision already taken. These are what keep a usable draft from going off the rails.
cards.title: The constraints

cards.body: What good looks like. A short example of the tone or structure you want, or one line on what a strong answer covers, sharpens the output more than another paragraph of instruction.
cards.title: The standard to hit

content_blocks.text: Back to the Thursday one-on-one from the start of this lesson: the context that matters is the handful of projects you want to raise, where each stands, and what you want from your manager on each: a decision, cover for a delay, a heads-up. Your whole task list for the quarter, every thread the projects touched, or the org chart does not sharpen the talking points; it just gives the model more to wade through before it reaches anything useful.
More is not necessarily better

This cuts against instinct, though it isn't an absolute rule: if a bigger document genuinely holds the context a complex or iterative task needs, upload it: the cost is just that it fills more of the context window, not that it is automatically wrong. The problem is unfiltered volume, not size itself. Overload the context with material that is not actually needed and the model has to reason across all of it to find the few things that matter, and the signal you care about gets diluted by everything sitting around it. The usual culprits are familiar:

- A 60-page contract pasted whole when the question is about one clause
- A raw data export dropped in instead of the relevant rows
- A long conversation that began on one thing and wandered through five others

That last one is easy to miss. In a long, drifting thread, an instruction you gave near the start, keep this under a page, write it for someone non-technical, gets buried under everything that came after and quietly stops being honoured. The model is weighing the whole conversation, and your early steer has become a small voice in a crowded room.

A couple of habits keep it clean, and which one applies depends on the kind of work. For a single, one-off chat, paste the minimum that does the job: the relevant clause rather than the whole contract, a filtered subset rather than the full export. For work you come back to repeatedly, a project or an ongoing piece of work, uploading a larger reference document into a persistent memory or project space (see the Claude track, or your tool's equivalent, for how that works in practice) is exactly what those features are built for: reusable standing context you set once, like who the work is for, the format you always use, and the constraints that keep recurring, instead of re-explaining it every time or re-pasting it into every new chat.

One more rule belongs here, briefly: do not paste confidential, personal, or regulated information into an AI tool that has not been approved for it: customer records, employee data, unreleased financials, a colleague's performance notes, anything covered by a contract or a regulation. The full picture on data, approved tools, and where the real risks sit gets its own lesson later in this track; for now, the short version is enough to keep you out of trouble: relevant beats plentiful, and confidential stays out.
If you would not put it in an email to someone outside the company, do not paste it into an unapproved AI tool. When in doubt, leave it out, or use only a tool that has been approved for it.

questions.q: You want the model to help you prep talking points for one project ahead of your one-on-one. What should you give it as context?
options: Your full task list and every project you touched this quarter, for complete background
The status of that one project and what you want from your manager on it
Every thread and email the project generated, so nothing is missed
A summary you already wrote, plus the entire project archive as well
questions.explanation: The task turns on one project. Giving the model that project status and your goal for the conversation is a clean signal. The rest is noise it has to wade through, which usually makes the output worse.

questions.q: A chat you started an hour ago has wandered from your one-on-one prep through formatting, wording, and two side questions. The model has started ignoring your early instruction to keep things under a page. What is the most likely cause?
options: The prompt was not detailed enough to begin with
The model has hit the limit of what it can do on this task
The early instruction has been diluted by a long, noisy conversation
The model needs the instruction repeated in firmer language
questions.explanation: In a long, drifting thread the model weighs the whole history, and an early steer gets buried under everything that followed. The fix is usually a cleaner context, and often a fresh start.

questions.q: Your AI tool offers a persistent project space that carries context across conversations. What belongs there?
options: Every document related to the work, so nothing is ever lost
Stable context that rarely changes: who the work is for, the standing format, the recurring constraints
Confidential personnel notes, so you do not have to paste them each time
The full transcript of every previous conversation
questions.explanation: Persistent spaces hold the standing context you would otherwise re-explain in every conversation. An archive of everything, or confidential data in a tool that has not been approved, does not belong there.

title: Providing context, and what never to include

content_blocks.text:
A lot of weak AI output comes from treating each prompt as a single shot: you fire off one instruction, judge whatever comes back, and move on unimpressed. The more reliable pattern is a loop: get a draft, work out what is wrong with it, correct that one thing specifically, and go again. Two or three exchanges routinely land somewhere a single prompt never would.

Say a vendor has gone quiet on a deliverable, and you ask the model for a follow-up email. React to the draft the way you would react to anyone else's rough first attempt: cut the throat-clearing, lead with the overdue item, soften the closing line. The second version is better because your feedback was concrete: the tool works the same way, only faster.
Reacting is faster than specifying

This is not a contradiction of writing a clear prompt upfront: both matter, and which one to lean on depends on the task. For anything you can specify well in advance (the four levers from the last lesson), do that. But for anything fuzzier, trying to anticipate every requirement in one enormous prompt often costs more time than it saves. It is usually quicker to say roughly what you want, look at what comes back, and redirect from there. Seeing a draft you dislike tells you what you actually want far more precisely than staring at a blank page trying to predict it: one look at a message that reads too aggressively tells you the tone you need better than any adjective you could have supplied up front.
Expect to iterate. A near-miss you can react to is often the quickest route to the version you need.
Make corrections specific

Everything in the loop depends on how you give feedback. Ask the model to make it better and it learns nothing useful; it reshuffles the words and hands you something equally off. Name the actual problem, and name what right looks like.

Compare the two registers. Vague: improve this, make it more professional, not quite right. Specific, on that vendor email: the opening is too soft, so lead with the deliverable and the date it was promised; the second paragraph repeats the first, so cut it; the tone reads irritated, and we want to keep this supplier, so make it firm but neutral. Each of those names what is wrong and what right would look like. That is the difference between a correction that sticks and one that spins the model in circles without moving it forward.
Build long outputs in stages

Not everything is a short email. For something substantial and complex, a full vendor evaluation or a multi-section supplier review, asking for the whole finished document in one go can still drift, even though today's models handle long single-shot requests better than they used to.

The safer pattern for complex documents is still to ask for the structure first. An outline is fast to produce and fast to correct, and approving the shape before any real content means a wrong frame gets caught while it is still cheap to change. Then fill it in section by section, leaving tone, word choice, and formatting until the end, once the substance is settled. For simpler or shorter documents, asking for the whole thing at once and then iterating is often just as fast.
Know when to start fresh

Sometimes the loop stops paying off. The model repeats a mistake you have already corrected twice. Each turn drifts further from what you want. Corrections stop sticking. Those are the signals to stop iterating and open a fresh conversation.

Starting fresh consolidates what you have. You take the parts that work, write a cleaner and sharper prompt, and begin again with the accumulated noise stripped out.

cards.body: The history is actively helping. A shared frame is in place, the format is agreed, an output is mid-refinement, or you are asking a direct follow-up. The conversation is carrying useful weight.
cards.title: Keep going when

cards.body: The topic has shifted, quality has drifted over several turns, the model keeps dragging in irrelevant earlier context, or you want an unanchored view that the thread so far has not coloured.
cards.title: Start fresh when

content_blocks.text: The reset has a technique of its own. Before you close the thread, ask the model to summarise what's useful so far into a short handoff you can paste into the new conversation, rather than retyping from memory. Paste that summary into the fresh chat and give sharper instructions around it. You drop what was dragging the thread down and keep the part worth keeping. If your AI tool lets you store stable background, the standing facts about a project or a supplier, starting fresh drops the noise without losing that foundation.
Where this sits

Everything above is the mechanic: instruct, review, refine, and know when to reset. It says nothing yet about the specific moves that make any single turn land harder, things like worked examples, role framing, or asking the model to critique its own draft. Those levers come next.

For now, the loop itself is the skill: expect to iterate, react precisely, build in stages, and reset when the thread stops helping.

content_blocks.task: Run both prompts below, each as a separate, brand-new conversation. Compare what comes back.

steps.text:
Context: A vendor was due to deliver a piece of work last week and has gone quiet since. You still need it and want to keep the relationship workable.
Task: Write a follow-up email to the vendor.
steps.label: Prompt 1 (vague task)

steps.text:
Context: A vendor was due to deliver a piece of work last week and has gone quiet since. You still need it and want to keep the relationship workable.
Task: Write a follow-up email to the vendor. Open by referencing the missed deadline directly, keep the tone firm but not hostile, ask for a specific new delivery date, and keep it under 120 words.
steps.label: Prompt 2 (detailed task)

content_blocks.material: A made-up scenario: a vendor was due to deliver last week and has gone quiet since. You need the deliverable and want to keep the relationship workable.
content_blocks.whatToNotice: The vague version usually comes back polite but toothless, easy to imagine burying the missed deadline or softening the ask past the point of being useful. That's normally the moment you'd iterate: read it, name the one thing wrong, and ask again. The detailed version shows what happens when you already know that fix and write it into the task the first time, skipping the round trip. In practice you won't always know the right fix in advance, which is exactly why iterating a rough first draft, rather than trying to front-load every constraint, is usually the faster path.

questions.q: The model drafts your vendor follow-up, but the opening buries the overdue deliverable and one paragraph runs too long. What is the most effective next move?
options: Tell it to make the whole email better and more professional
Name the fixes: lead with the overdue deliverable, and cut the long paragraph to two sentences
Start a brand new conversation and write the prompt again from scratch
Accept it and rewrite the whole thing yourself by hand
questions.explanation: Iteration works when feedback is specific. Naming the exact problem and the exact fix produces a correction that sticks, while a vague instruction like make it better only reshuffles the same flawed output.

questions.q: You need a long, multi-section supplier review drafted end to end. What is the best way to build it with the AI tool?
options: Ask for the entire finished document in one carefully detailed prompt so nothing is missed
