Get an outline first, approve the shape, then fill in section by section
Write it yourself and use the tool only to check spelling at the very end
Settle the final tone and formatting before deciding what the sections are
questions.explanation: Long outputs drift when demanded all at once. Approving the structure before the content means a wrong shape is caught early and cheaply, and the substance is settled before you spend effort on polish.

questions.q: You have corrected the same mistake three times and the output keeps drifting further off. What should you do?
options: Keep correcting in the same thread until it finally sticks
Retype your original prompt into a blank conversation unchanged
Open a fresh conversation, paste in the useful draft, and give sharper instructions
Lower your expectations and accept the drifting output
questions.explanation: When corrections stop sticking and quality drifts, the thread itself has become the problem. A reset consolidates progress: you carry the good draft into a clean conversation and drop the accumulated noise.

title: Working iteratively

content_blocks.text: You have hired someone who starts in two weeks, and you want a real onboarding plan: week one, who they meet, what good looks like by month one. A model gives you a usable first pass in about a minute. Whether you bin that pass or send it comes down to a handful of deliberate moves in the prompt.

By now you can write a clear prompt and run the review-and-refine loop. This lesson is the toolkit you reach for inside that loop: specific levers that lift output from acceptable to good, each taking seconds, used dozens of times a week. The onboarding plan is a good place to watch them work one at a time, and the same moves apply just as well to any structured document you own: a runbook, a wiki page, or the checklist you run through whenever a new project starts.
Show an example, do not just describe one

The fastest way to tell a model what you want is to show it. Describing a style in adjectives, "concise, warm, practical", leaves the model guessing at what those words mean to you; one concrete example removes the guesswork.

Write a single onboarding item the way you want the rest to read: owner, task, and the week it falls in, in that order. The model matches a visible pattern far more reliably than a described one, and one task written your way sets the shape for the twenty that follow.
One good example is worth ten adjectives. When you catch yourself piling up describing words, stop and paste a sample instead.
Assign a role to shift the lens

Assigning the model a role changes what it pays attention to. Ask it to review your onboarding plan plainly and you get a flat, generic once-over. Ask it to review the plan as a brand-new joiner reading it on day one, someone who knows none of your systems or shorthand, and it starts flagging the jargon, the login nobody requested, and the week-one task that quietly assumes a fortnight of context.

A role sets a lens for a particular kind of scrutiny or reader: a finance reviewer hunting for soft numbers, a sceptical peer poking holes in a timeline, a non-technical reader tripping over jargon. For an onboarding plan, the most useful reviewer is often the new hire themselves: the one person who will hit every gap left in it. Reviewing it through that lens before it reaches them catches the gaps while they are still easy to fix.
Specify the format, not just the content

You can dictate the exact shape of the output: how many sections, what each one covers, a length ceiling, the columns of a table. You met format as one of the baseline levers already. What matters here is that a tight format spec compounds with the others and cuts a whole round off the refine loop.

Take the plan again. "Build me an onboarding plan" hands you prose you then have to carve into a schedule. "Organise the first month into four weekly blocks, each a table with columns for task, owner, and what done looks like, plus one line on the goal for that week" hands you something already shaped like a document you can send. The specified version asks no more of the model, only more intention from you about the shape.

There is a negative half you already know from the constraints lever: naming what to leave out. A format spec is as much about what you exclude, no filler, no motivational preamble, as what you put in, and it combines cleanly with a role or a self-critique instruction layered on top.
Make the model critique itself

Here is the lever most people never touch. Once the model has produced the plan, ask it to turn on its own work, for example: **"List the three weakest points in this onboarding plan."** **"Where would a new joiner get stuck in week one?"** **"What did I leave out that a real first week needs?"**

With nothing to defend, the model will often name genuine gaps: the access request nobody kicked off, the introduction you skipped, the first task that assumes context the new person has not been handed yet. You stay the judge of which flags are fair. A self-critique pass in the same conversation surfaces candidates for revision faster than reading the draft cold, and it costs you a single line.

An even stronger version: paste the finished draft into a brand-new conversation with no earlier context, and ask that fresh session to critique it. Without the history that shaped how the first session wrote it, a fresh set of eyes tends to catch different gaps than a self-critique in the same thread: worth doing for anything a person will actually live by, like the plan a new hire follows through week one.
A self-critique pass finds weak spots; it does not fix them. It will list problems and then, if you let it, paper over them with confident filler. You decide which gaps matter and how to close them.
Combining levers

The levers stack. A strong onboarding prompt might set a role, fix the format, and end with a self-critique all at once:

**"As an experienced manager onboarding a new team member, draft a four-week plan as weekly tables, then list the two things a first-timer would still find confusing."**

You won't need all four every time. For anything you will send onward, or that a new hire will lean on, layering two or three of them is the cheapest quality gain you have.

cards.body: Show one line, row, or task written exactly the way you want the rest to read. The model copies a visible pattern better than a described one. Best for locking format and tone fast.
cards.title: Example

cards.body: Tell the model whose eyes to read through: a brand-new joiner, a sceptical peer, a non-technical reader. Best for a specific kind of scrutiny, especially before a tough or unfamiliar reader sees it.
cards.title: Role

cards.body: Dictate structure, length, and what to exclude. Naming what you do not want matters as much as naming what you do. Best for getting close to final on the first pass.
cards.title: Format spec

cards.body: Ask the model to attack its own draft and name the weak spots. Best for high-stakes work someone will actually rely on.
cards.title: Self-critique

content_blocks.prompt: Which lever is missing from this prompt?
content_blocks.example:
Draft the onboarding plan.

Here's how I wrote the first week's task, in the style and order I want:
- Owner: Jamie
- Task: set up laptop and accounts
- Week: 1

Write it as if you are the new hire seeing it on day one. Once you're done, list the two things a first-timer would still find confusing.

candidates.text: Example
candidates.reason: Present already: it shows one task written exactly the way the author wants.

candidates.text: Role
candidates.reason: Present already: it asks the model to write it as the new hire would read it.

candidates.text: Format spec
candidates.reason: Missing: nothing dictates the shape of the rest of the plan, no weekly blocks, no table columns, no length ceiling. Without it you get prose you still have to carve into a schedule yourself.

candidates.text: Self-critique
candidates.reason: Present already: it asks what a first-timer would still find confusing.

content_blocks.task: Run both prompts below, each as a separate, brand-new conversation. Compare what comes back.

steps.text:
Context: Your team just wrapped a two-week sprint. You shipped three planned features and slipped one deadline.
Task: Summarise this sprint for the retro doc.
steps.label: Prompt 1 (vague task)

steps.text:
Context: Your team just wrapped a two-week sprint. You shipped three planned features and slipped one deadline.
Task: Summarise this sprint for the retro doc as a sceptical peer would read it, in three sections (wins, the slipped deadline and why, one thing to change next sprint), under 150 words.
steps.label: Prompt 2 (detailed task)

content_blocks.material: A made-up scenario: your team just wrapped a two-week sprint that shipped three features but slipped one deadline.
content_blocks.whatToNotice: The vague task produces a smooth, generic summary that glosses over the slipped deadline. The detailed task adds a role (sceptical peer), a format (three named sections), and a length constraint, the same three levers covered earlier in this lesson, and the model's output shifts to actually confront the miss instead of gliding past it.

questions.q: You want a structured onboarding plan and keep getting long paragraphs you have to carve into a schedule yourself. Which lever fixes this fastest?
options: Ask the model to be more concise
Specify the exact format: weekly blocks, a table with named columns, and a one-line goal for each week
Regenerate until the shape improves on its own
Give the model more background on the role
questions.explanation: A tight format spec dictates the shape up front, the blocks, the columns, the goal lines, so you get something you can send on the first pass instead of prose you then have to reshape.

questions.q: Why does showing one onboarding task written your way usually beat describing the style you want in adjectives?
options: Examples use fewer tokens than descriptions
The model can match a concrete visible pattern more reliably than an abstract description
Adjectives confuse the model into refusing the task
Examples force the model to be more creative
questions.explanation: One good example is worth ten adjectives. A visible pattern gives the model something exact to copy, where words like concise or practical leave room to guess.

questions.q: You want to find the gaps in your onboarding plan before the new hire hits them. Which lever fits best?
options: Ask for the plan in a shorter format
Assign a new-joiner reviewer role and ask the model to critique the plan
Provide more background documents
Lower the temperature setting
questions.explanation: A role sets the lens and a self-critique pass surfaces the holes. Together they give you the problems a new joiner would hit in week one, while you stay the judge of which are worth fixing.

title: Specific levers for better output

content_blocks.text:
Plain text has no built-in way to show a heading, a bold word, or a list. Markdown is the fix: a lightweight way to add that structure using ordinary characters you can type on any keyboard, a hash for a heading, asterisks for bold, a hyphen for a bullet. That is all it is: punctuation for structure rather than a coding skill, and it takes about two minutes to learn to read.

It has become the default way AI tools format text for a practical reason: it adds structure using only a few extra characters, which keeps documents compact and easy for a model to read back, an efficient use of the context window covered earlier in this track. Most AI models both read and write it fluently as a result. That is also why it turns up everywhere AI touches: when your tool hands back an answer with headings, bold key terms, and neat bullets, it's writing Markdown, and documentation, notes apps, and plenty of editors use the same conventions.
Using it in your own prompts

The same efficiency runs the other way: a prompt you organise with a heading and a few bullets is easier for the model to follow than one long paragraph. Say you're turning a sprint's worth of changes into release notes: give it the fixes, the new features, and the breaking changes as three separate points, and it tracks each one instead of losing them mid-sentence. You already do this when you write a good prompt; Markdown is just the tidy way to lay it out.
The handful of patterns worth recognising
You will never need most of the syntax. These few cover almost everything you will meet.

cards.body: A hash then a space makes a heading; two hashes make a smaller sub-heading. Text wrapped in double asterisks is bold; single asterisks is italic.
cards.title: Headings and emphasis

cards.body: A hyphen and a space starts a bullet. A number, a dot, and a space starts a numbered list. This is what turns a set of points into a scannable list.
cards.title: Lists

cards.body: A greater-than sign and a space marks a quoted block. Text wrapped in backticks shows as monospace, used for things like file names or a single command.
cards.title: Quotes and code

content_blocks.text: The one thing that trips people up

Markdown only becomes clean formatting when something renders it. A chat window renders it, so you see tidy headings and bullets. A plain email field or a basic text box usually does not, so you get the raw symbols instead.

Say AI drafts a short update for you with headings and bullet points, and you paste it straight into an email: if it arrives cluttered with hashes, double asterisks, and stray hyphens, nothing has gone wrong: you are looking at unrendered Markdown. Paste it somewhere that renders it, since most modern document and mail editors do, or ask the tool for plain text with no formatting. For anything going out to the whole team or to a customer, that quick check is worth making before you hit send.

questions.q: You paste AI-drafted release notes into a plain email field and they are full of ## symbols, double asterisks, and hyphens. What has happened?
options: The AI tool made an error and corrupted the text
It is unrendered Markdown, and the email field is showing the raw symbols instead of formatting them
The output was too long and got garbled
The model used a broken template
questions.explanation: Those symbols are Markdown. The chat window rendered them as headings and bold text, but a plain email field does not render Markdown, so you see the raw characters. Paste it somewhere that renders it, or ask for plain text.

questions.q: Why is it worth organising a long prompt with headings and bullet points?
options: It makes the prompt look more professional to colleagues
It forces the model to answer faster
Structured input is easier for the model to follow than one long block of text, so you tend to get a more complete response
It reduces the cost of the prompt
questions.explanation: Structure helps the model track distinct instructions. Laying out separate points as a short list makes each one harder to overlook than when they are buried in a single paragraph.

questions.q: How much Markdown syntax do you actually need to master to work well with AI?
options: All of it, since models rely on the full specification
None at all, because it never appears in practice
Just enough to recognise the common patterns and know how to get plain text when a destination does not render it
Only the code-related syntax
questions.explanation: This is a recognition skill, not a writing skill. Knowing headings, bold, and lists on sight, and knowing how to get clean text when you need it, covers virtually every situation you will meet.

title: Markdown

content_blocks.text: Picture the budget you are pulling together ahead of a decision meeting: last quarter's actuals, a couple of forecasts, and a recommendation on where the money should go next. A model can draft most of that in minutes. It can also get four specific things wrong, in ways that survive a quick read and land in the room looking finished. This lesson walks through those four failure points: the same mechanism you have already met, plausible text rather than looked-up fact, is behind all of them, and what each one actually costs you.
Stale information

The underlying model's own knowledge is genuinely frozen at its training cutoff. Ask it about a tax threshold that changed last quarter, a supplier that raised its rates in March, or a regulation amended since its training, and it can only answer from what it learned before that date, with the same steady confidence it uses for facts that have held for a decade.

But most AI tools people actually use pair the model with retrieval: web search, connectors, or documents you supply. When one of those is active, the answer can be genuinely current: the risk isn't "AI is always out of date," it's knowing whether your current tool or session actually has a live source, or is answering from memory alone. If nothing shows it's grounded (a citation, a connector indicator, a visible search step), that is the moment to check it yourself. A budget built on last year's rates, a pricing recommendation resting on market conditions that have since moved, a cost line that misses a supplier increase half the room already knows about: each reads perfectly, and each is quietly out of date if nothing refreshed the model's view.
Weak arithmetic and quantitative reasoning

Numbers are where AI's fluency is most likely to mislead you: on its own, a model writes the text of a calculation. It does not run the calculation. It generates the digits that most plausibly follow the words "the total is", which is a different act from adding the numbers up. Some tools now run real code and compute exactly, and where that happens the maths is genuine. Until you know a real calculation ran, treat every figure as text shaped like a number.

It often lands close, and close is the tricky part: a total that is off by a little slips past review in a way a wildly absurd number would not. This shows up most in the work you would most want to hand off: summing the columns in a budget, working out a percentage change on a forecast, reconciling two totals that should agree. Multi-step reasoning follows the same pattern: each step can read as sound while a small slip compounds along the way, arriving at a confident but wrong conclusion. Whenever you know the tool actually ran a calculation rather than predicted one, that risk drops substantially: the caution here is for the more common case where you don't know which happened.

The more a task turns on numbers or a chain of logical steps, the less its answer is worth at face value. And the more it looks like the model just saved you the effort, the more of that effort has simply moved to checking it.
Bias

A model learned from an enormous body of human writing, and it absorbed the patterns there, including the skewed ones. Ask it to sketch a candidate for a senior role, name a typical customer, or describe who does what on a team, and its defaults track the majority patterns in its training data rather than the people actually in front of you.

This surfaces in two places. In anything that touches people, such as hiring language, performance notes, or assumptions about an audience, the model can dress a stereotype up as professional-sounding prose. And when you ask it to weigh options, it leans toward the conventional, mainstream take, which makes it a poor source of real contrarian challenge. Left unchecked, it narrows your thinking at the exact moment you wanted it widened, whether that shortlist or those survey comments are shaping a team decision or just your own work, they inherit the model's defaults, not your read of the situation.

content_blocks.prompt: Spot the planted problem in this draft vendor recommendation.
content_blocks.example: Vendor A is the market leader and most companies our size use it. Vendor A also costs 20% more, and in our trial the team found its search feature slower than Vendor B's. Vendor B scored higher on every trial criterion the team logged. Given Vendor A's market position, we recommend proceeding with Vendor A.

candidates.text: Vendor A costs 20% more and tested slower in the trial
candidates.reason: Plain reporting of the trial data, not the problem.

candidates.text: Vendor B scored higher on every trial criterion the team logged
candidates.reason: Plain reporting of the trial data, not the problem.

candidates.text: Recommending Vendor A given its market position
candidates.reason: This defaults to the safe, conventional choice despite the team's own evidence pointing the other way, exactly the lesson's point that AI leans toward the mainstream take rather than genuinely weighing what is in front of it.

content_blocks.text: Reasoning gaps

The model is fluent, and fluency reads as competence, but it does not always hold a complex argument together as reliably as the polish suggests. It can miss a load-bearing assumption in a proposal, accept a flawed premise you hand it, or contradict something it claimed three paragraphs earlier, none of it flagged. This has improved with newer models, but it is still worth watching for.

A related risk is agreeableness. Push back on its answer and it will sometimes fold and reverse, whether or not you had a point; frame a question so it implies the answer you are hoping for and it can hand that answer straight back. The upside is that you are always free to challenge it directly and ask it to argue the other side, but left unchallenged, that agreeableness can turn into an echo chamber that just confirms what you already believed. So when you ask it to stress-test the case for a budget before the meeting, ask it explicitly to argue against you, rather than trusting a first pass that simply agrees.
What this costs, in one line

None of these failures announces itself: the output comes back equally fluent, formatted, and confident whether it's right or wrong. An error you catch costs you almost nothing: you fix it and move on. The one worth guarding against is the plausible mistake that reads perfectly and gets forwarded: a stale rate in the budget, a total that does not add up, a stereotype in a job description, an assumption nobody challenged sitting under a recommendation. None of that is a reason to avoid AI: the checks in this lesson are exactly how you catch them before they go out under your name, which is what turns speed into something you can trust.

cards.body: The model's own knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, but many tools pair it with search or connectors that add live information. If a task turns on a recent change or a live figure, check whether your tool is actually grounded in a current source before you trust it.
cards.title: Stale by default

cards.body: Arithmetic and multi-step reasoning are close-but-wrong territory unless the tool is actually running a calculation rather than predicting one. When you're not sure which is happening, the more the answer rests on numbers or a chain of steps, the more it needs an independent check.
cards.title: Numbers and logic

cards.body: Ask about people or audiences and the model reaches for the majority pattern in its training data, not the situation in front of you. It can turn a stereotype into clean prose.
cards.title: Bias in the defaults

cards.body: Push back and the model can fold, or hand back the answer your framing implied. Ask it explicitly to challenge you rather than just agree, especially for any decision that needs honest friction.
cards.title: A weak challenger

questions.q: You ask the model to total the columns in a budget headed for a decision meeting. Why is this a risky thing to trust?
options: The model will not attempt sums, so there is nothing there to check
It writes the text of a calculation rather than performing it, and often lands close enough that the error slips through
Errors in model arithmetic are usually large and obvious, so a quick glance catches them
Arithmetic mistakes tend to appear only in long documents, so a short budget is safe
questions.explanation: The model generates plausible-looking digits rather than computing them. It frequently lands close to the right figure, and a close-but-wrong total is far harder to catch than an obvious blunder, which is why any number headed for a decision needs an independent check.

questions.q: You ask the model to stress-test the case for a budget before you carry it into the meeting. What is the specific risk?
options: It will refuse, because genuine critique sits outside what these models can do
It leans toward agreeableness and the conventional view, so it makes a weak challenger and may fold the moment you push back
It can only summarise text and cannot offer any critique at all
It will quietly invent a stronger case and hide your original from you
questions.explanation: The model leans toward mainstream takes and often reverses under pushback whether or not you had a point. That makes it a poor source of honest friction for a decision. Use it to generate a first pass, but do not read its agreement as validation.

questions.q: What makes these failures costly at work, beyond the mistakes themselves?
options: They crash the tool, so the work is lost and has to be redone
The output looks equally fluent, formatted, and confident whether it is right or wrong, so a plausible mistake gets forwarded as your own work
They show up only with older models
The tool flags each one clearly before you send anything
questions.explanation: Not one of these failures raises a flag on its own. Because the output looks just as polished when it is wrong, the real cost is the confident, well-dressed mistake that slips through review and travels forward as your work.

title: What AI consistently gets wrong

content_blocks.text:
Verification is a habit you run before output leaves your hands: a short, repeatable check that turns a plausible draft into something you can defend. Take the competitive scan you pull together before a strategy session: the model hands you a tidy page on three rivals, with pricing tiers, headcount, a recent funding round, a couple of product claims. It looks finished. Whether it is actually right is a separate question, and you are the only one who can answer it.

The reason to bother is ownership: once a figure shapes a decision, or you repeat it in a meeting or paste it into a shared doc, it becomes your claim rather than the model's, and "the AI said so" is not a defence anyone accepts. Verification is how you turn speed into something you can stand behind.
Match the check to the risk

Not every output needs the same scrutiny. A rough brainstorm you plan to rework barely needs a look. A competitor price that decides how you position your own is worth getting right. Calibrate the effort to two things: how much the task turns on specific facts, and how costly a wrong one would be.
The more an output turns on specific facts, figures, names, or quotes, the more the responsibility sits with you to check it before you forward it, cite it, or act on it.

A quick reflex helps: ask what happens if this is wrong. If the honest answer is that someone places a bet on bad information or the team loses credibility with the board, the output has bought itself a real check. If the answer is nothing much, move on.
What to check

Verification is not rereading until it feels right. It is checking named claims against a source you trust, one at a time. Fluent prose reads as correct whether or not it is, so a general sense that something seems solid tells you very little. Check specific things instead, each tied to a failure mode you already know.

cards.body: Every number, date, name, and quote is a place the model may have produced something plausible and invented. Trace each one back to a source you trust. A competitor funding round stated with full confidence is not proof the round happened.
cards.title: Facts and figures

cards.body: Ask whether the claim depends on recent events or changed circumstances. The model's own training has a cutoff, though a connected or search-enabled tool may have current data. Check which applies. A rival price or a headcount can be out of date if nothing refreshed the model's view.
cards.title: Currency

cards.body: Follow the logic step by step. Output can reach a wrong conclusion through fluent, confident steps that skip a link. Check the chain, not just the answer at the end.
cards.title: Reasoning

cards.body: Ask what is missing, not only whether what is present is true. A scan can be accurate on every line and still leave out the competitor who matters most, or the caveat that would change the decision.
cards.title: Omission and slant

content_blocks.text: Three moves that make checking faster

You do not have to verify everything by hand from a blank slate. A few habits cut the cost.

First, make the claims traceable. When you prompt, ask the model to mark which parts rest on the material you gave it and which come from its own general knowledge. The second kind is where invented detail hides. This does not prove the source-backed claims are right, but it tells you where to look hardest.

Second, check against the source, not against the model. If you handed it a set of analyst notes to condense, verify the summary against those notes: the ground truth is the input you provided, not a second answer from the AI, which will revise a correct answer or defend a wrong one with equal confidence either way.

Third, take anything about the outside world to the outside world. For a market-share figure, a regulation, a rival funding round, confirm it in a real source. Treat the model as a fast way to draft and structure, and go elsewhere for facts about the world. Keeping those two jobs separate is most of the discipline.
Where it goes wrong in practice

The first common failure is checking the wrong thing: polishing tone and flow while the numbers go unexamined. Polish is not accuracy. The second is anchoring. Once you have read a confident, well-formed answer, it is hard to see what is missing, because the draft has already framed the problem for you. Guard against it by deciding what a good answer must contain before you read the model version. For the competitive scan, write down the questions the strategy session has to answer, then check whether each one is genuinely covered and sourced, rather than being led by whatever the model chose to include.
The workflow in one pass

For any output that carries real weight: decide up front what a good answer must contain; separate the model claims from what your source actually supports; check every fact, figure, and date against a trusted source rather than against the AI; follow the reasoning a step at a time; and ask what has been left out. It takes minutes. Skipping it can cost far more than the minutes it saved.

questions.q: You asked an AI tool to condense a stack of analyst notes into a short competitive brief. What is the right way to verify the figures in the brief?
options: Ask the model whether it is sure the figures are correct
Reread the brief carefully to see whether the figures feel consistent
Check each figure against the analyst notes you provided
Regenerate the brief and compare the two versions
questions.explanation: The notes you supplied are the ground truth. Checking against that input catches both invention and misreading. Asking the model or regenerating just produces more model output, which is not evidence of anything.

questions.q: Why is checking an output for tone and flow a weak form of verification?
options: Tone does not matter in business writing
Fluent, well-formed prose reads as correct whether or not the facts behind it are right
Models handle facts reliably and mainly struggle with tone
Tone is the only thing worth checking
questions.explanation: Producing authoritative-sounding text is exactly what the model is built to do, so polish is no signal of accuracy. Verification has to target facts, figures, reasoning, and omissions on their own terms.

questions.q: How much verification should a given AI output get?
options: The same thorough process for every output, to be safe
As much as the task turns on specific facts and how costly a mistake would be
More when the output runs longer
Less when the output sounds confident and more when it does not
questions.explanation: Calibrate effort to risk. A disposable brainstorm barely needs a look; a competitor figure headed into a strategy decision does. Length and confidence are not reliable guides to how much scrutiny is warranted.

title: How to verify AI output

content_blocks.text: So far the track has been about getting more out of the tool: sharper prompts, closer verification, a clear read on where it fails. This lesson is about the opposite discipline, the one that says leave it shut. Some tasks fail the test before verification even comes up, because AI never belonged in them. For those, no prompt and no amount of checking helps. The right move is to not open the tool at all.
The line is about stakes, not difficulty

A task lands off-limits for one of two reasons: a confident wrong answer would cost more than you can absorb, or using the tool breaks a duty you hold no matter how the answer turns out, not because the task itself is technically difficult.

A model produces plausible text. It does not know what is true, and nothing holds it accountable when it gets things wrong. Set those two facts against high stakes and the tool becomes a real liability. So the question worth asking before you hand something over is a plain one: if it is confidently wrong here, what happens, and can you live with it?

None of this argues for caution everywhere. Most day-to-day work carries low stakes and easy checking, and AI belongs there: cleaning up a spreadsheet export, turning a batch of survey comments into themes, drafting the first pass of release notes. The point is narrower: a small set of tasks should never touch the tool, and a slightly larger set earns a deliberate pause before it does. Treating AI as something that makes getting to a draft fast and easy is exactly why the thinking has to come from you first on anything that matters: sorting one from the other is the skill the rest of this lesson builds.
The hard stops

Some categories stay off the table for the tool making the actual call, however convenient AI would be. That doesn't mean AI is banned from touching them at all, only that it cannot be the thing deciding. Treat these as defaults, not suggestions.

cards.body: Anything where a wrong output causes damage you cannot undo: legal filings, medical or safety calls, financial commitments, hiring or firing on the say-so of a model. AI can inform the thinking. It must not make the call.
cards.title: Irreversible or high-harm decisions

cards.body: If the input holds data you are not permitted to share outside the company, the answer quality is beside the point. The only question is whether the tool is allowed to see that input at all. The next lesson covers this in full.
cards.title: Confidential or regulated information you cannot expose

cards.body: If you lack the knowledge, time, or source material to check the output, you cannot use it responsibly. Unverifiable plus consequential is the worst combination. If you cannot check it and it matters, do not ship it.
cards.title: Anything you cannot verify

cards.body: A performance review, a condolence note, a personal recommendation, a hard judgment call your role exists to make. Handing these to a model gives away the very thing your job is there to do, however polished the result comes back.
cards.title: Work that must be genuinely yours

content_blocks.text: The pull of convenience

The dangerous cases are rarely the obvious ones. Nobody sets out to file a fabricated legal citation: it happens because the tool was fast, the output looked right, and the stakes weren't felt until later.

Speed is exactly what makes a tool tempting in the moments it should stay shut. AI makes getting to a draft very easy and fast, but for some tasks the thinking has to happen first: work out your own position or read of the situation before you bring AI in, rather than outsourcing that reasoning to it from the start. A confident, well-formatted answer to a question you haven't thought through yourself is easy to mistake for progress, particularly under deadline pressure.
Trusting AI's answer because checking it would be inconvenient is a signal worth pausing on, not a green light to carry on anyway.
When it is a judgment call

Most work is not a hard stop. The grey zone is wider, and it is where the real call sits: AI is allowed, but is using it wise?

Take a message announcing a reorg to your team, or a note where you're owning a mistake to a customer, or raising a hard concern with your own manager. Nothing forbids having a model draft any of these, and it would hand you something clean and calm in seconds. But the lines that land are the ones that show you understand what the other person is about to feel, and that read is yours to bring: work out the substance yourself first, then let the tool tidy the phrasing once it's written.

The test is ownership: whose name sits on it, and what are they answerable for? If AI helped with the draft and you still stand fully behind every line because you supplied the judgment, the tool did its job. If you would be using it to stand in for judgment that is yours to bring, keep the work yourself, even when nothing formally forbids it: your credibility is what carries it, and no model can supply that.

questions.q: What is the primary factor that makes a task a no-go zone for AI?
options: The task is technically complex
A confident wrong answer would cost more than you can absorb, or using AI breaks a duty you hold
The task would take a long time to do by hand
The AI tool is slow at that kind of work
questions.explanation: The line is about stakes and duty, not difficulty. AI is off-limits when a wrong output causes harm you cannot undo, or when using it breaks an obligation regardless of how good the output is.

questions.q: Under deadline pressure you get a confident, well-formatted answer to a question you do not have time to verify. What does the lesson say this situation is?
options: A green light, since the output looks correct and time is short
A sign the tool is working well, so you should move on
A warning sign: the temptation to skip the check because you are busy often marks a task where skipping it is what hurts you
Fine as long as you add a disclaimer
questions.explanation: When checking is inconvenient and you feel the pull to trust the output anyway, treat that pull as a stop signal rather than a green light.

questions.q: AI is allowed on the task and nothing formally forbids it, but it is the message announcing a reorg to your team. What is the right call?
options: Use AI fully, since it is allowed and saves time
Keep the work yourself: reading what your team is about to feel is a judgment your role exists to bring, and a model cannot supply it
Let AI write it, then change a few words so it sounds like you
Use AI only if you are short on time
questions.explanation: Some work has to be yours. When the task turns on a judgment your role exists to exercise, using AI to stand in for it gives away the thing you are there to do, even when it is permitted.

title: When not to use AI

content_blocks.text:
Paste text into a consumer AI tool and that text leaves your building. It travels to a model running on someone else's servers, where, depending on the tool and its settings, it might be retained, logged, reviewed by a person checking quality, or used to train the next version of the model. Some tools promise none of that; others do all of it by default and let you opt out. Few people check which kind they are using before they paste something sensitive in.

The mechanics take a sentence to explain. Deciding what is safe to paste is the part that takes attention, every time you open a chat window with real work in front of you, and if you manage people, the norm you set here is the one your team will copy too.
What happens to what you type

The question worth asking is a concrete one. Where does your input go, who can see it, and what are they allowed to do with it? A tool your organisation has vetted and licensed answers those questions in your favour. A free account someone signed up for on their own does not.
What counts as sensitive
Passwords and credit card numbers are the obvious cases, but the real exposure at work is broader and a good deal more mundane than that.

cards.body: Names, contact details, salaries, performance notes, health or HR matters. Anything that identifies a person carries legal obligations, however harmless it feels in the moment.
cards.title: Personal data

cards.body: Unreleased financials, pricing strategy, deal terms, roadmaps, merger and acquisition discussions. The budget you assemble before a decision meeting is exactly this.
cards.title: Commercial secrets

cards.body: Anything shared with you under an agreement: partner data, customer records, supplier terms. It is not yours to expose, and the obligation is often written into a contract.
cards.title: Third-party confidential

cards.body: Board material, legal advice, security details, anything covered by confidentiality. Fluent output is worthless if the input should never have left the room.
cards.title: Internal and privileged

content_blocks.text: A useful test before you paste: if this text turned up in a competitor's inbox or on a news site, would it cause a problem? If the answer is yes, it does not go into an unapproved tool.

items.text: A public product blurb already on your website
items.reason: If it turned up in a competitor's inbox tomorrow, it would not matter. It is already public.

items.text: This quarter's unreleased financial results ahead of the earnings call
items.reason: A commercial secret, the exact budget-before-a-decision-meeting case this lesson uses.

items.text: A colleague's performance review notes
items.reason: Personal data carrying legal obligations, however routine it feels to write.

items.text: The agenda for tomorrow's all-hands, already shared company-wide
items.reason: Already visible to everyone it could reach. The competitor-inbox test comes back clean.

content_blocks.prompt: Sort each item using the competitor-inbox test.

buckets.label: Approved tool only, or strip first

content_blocks.text: Concrete behaviours

A few concrete habits:

- **Default to the approved tool for anything real**, even when it is marginally less convenient than the alternative.
- **When you are unsure whether something is sensitive, treat it as if it is.**
- **If you must work in an unapproved tool for some reason, strip the specifics first**: remove names, figures, and identifiers while keeping the structure, so you'd ask the model to pressure-test the shape of a budget case with the real numbers pulled out rather than left in.
- **Set the expectation with your team plainly**: they will match what you actually do, not what the policy says.
Approved tools, in practice

"Approved" means your organisation has done the diligence: checked where the data goes, signed terms that forbid training on your input, and confirmed the tool meets the standards your sector requires. It can look identical to the free version. The difference lives in the contract and the configuration, well out of sight of the interface.
The same brand name can be safe or unsafe depending on the account. A licensed enterprise tenant and a personal free login are different tools wearing the same logo.

The practical move is narrow: know which tools your organisation has sanctioned for which kinds of data, and make that answer easy for your team to find. When the answer is ambiguous, people improvise rather than pause.
Unsanctioned tool use is the real risk

"Shadow AI" is the term for using unapproved tools for real work: a marketing manager drafting on a personal account, an analyst pasting next quarter's budget into whatever tool ranked first in a search. It rarely comes from bad intent: usually the unsanctioned tool was just easier to reach than the approved one.

This is where leadership matters more than IT. If the approved path is slow, hidden, or worse than the free alternative, people will route around it, and policing alone won't hold that line. Closing the gap means making the sanctioned tool the path of least resistance, and being clear out loud about what belongs where.

questions.q: A manager wants AI help pressure-testing the budget case before a decision meeting but only has a personal free AI account. What is the sound move?
options: Paste the full budget case, since it is just internal analysis and not customer data
Use the approved organisational tool, or strip the confidential figures and work with the structure only
Avoid AI entirely for anything work-related
Turn off chat history in the free tool and carry on
questions.explanation: Budget and pricing figures are a commercial secret. Keep AI in play by using a vetted tool or by removing the sensitive specifics before you paste. Turning history off does not change where an unapproved tool sends your input or what its terms permit.

questions.q: Why is shadow AI primarily a leadership concern rather than a technical one?
options: Because employees who use unapproved tools are acting maliciously
Because IT can block every unapproved tool at the network level
Because people route around the approved path when it is slower or harder to reach, so the fix is making the sanctioned tool the easy default
Because free tools tend to be more capable than licensed ones
questions.explanation: Shadow AI usually comes from convenience rather than malice, and blocking rarely holds for long. The durable fix is making the approved tool the path of least resistance and setting a clear norm, both of which are leadership levers.

questions.q: What best describes the difference between an approved and unapproved version of the same AI brand?
options: The approved version has a different user interface
The approved version is governed by vetted terms and configuration that control where data goes and whether it trains the model
There is no real difference once you turn off history
The approved version uses a more capable model
questions.explanation: The interface can be identical. What matters is the contract and configuration behind the account, meaning whether your input is retained, reviewed, or used for training. Same logo, different guarantees.

title: Data, privacy, confidentiality, and approved tools at work

content_blocks.text: You feed the model your rough notes from a performance review and it hands back a clean, confident write-up in seconds. That fluency is why accountability is where this module ends: the easier the output is to accept, the easier it is to pass on something you never actually checked. The tool does not sign the review. You do.
Delegation moves the work, not the responsibility

You can hand the write-up to a model the way you would hand it to someone on your team. What you cannot hand over is ownership of the result. When that review lands in the record, or goes up to an HR partner who trusts your read, the model's part in it is invisible, and your decision to send it is not. If you manage no one, the same thing holds for the customer reply or the wiki entry you draft with AI and put out as your own work: you are still the one who chose to release it.

None of this is new. You were always answerable for work done in your name by other people. AI just makes the review step easier to skip, because the draft arrives polished and instant. A thin draft from a colleague looks thin. A hallucinated figure inside a fluent summary looks fine right up until someone acts on it.

A confident tone on the page tells you nothing about whether the facts behind it hold. Output earns exactly as much trust as the checking you have put into it, and it goes out as your work, not the tool's.
Where the accountability bites

The consequences land in specific places. A performance summary that overstates a target someone actually hit can sink a promotion case. The model can also attribute a quote to a colleague who never said it, and that line then sits in a record people will read for years. A single reworded policy sentence can change what the policy permits, with the exposure surfacing only once someone relies on it.

In each case the model did nothing unusual. It predicted plausible text, which is all it ever does. The failure was that a person forwarded that text without owning it.
Attribution and intellectual property
Attribution is yours to sort out before you rely on the output. Look at what went into the draft, and at what comes out of it.

cards.body: A model can reproduce text close to what it was trained on, and it will echo whatever you fed it, including material you had no right to reuse. Paste in a competitor document or a copyrighted source, pass the result along, and the provenance problem is now yours.
cards.title: What went in

cards.body: AI output generally cannot be claimed as original authored work the way human writing can, and the rules vary by jurisdiction and context. When originality or attribution carries weight, such as external publication or anything legal or contractual, treat provenance as something you must be able to account for.
cards.title: What comes out

content_blocks.text: For most internal work the bar is simple: you should be able to say where a claim came from and stand behind it. If you cannot, it is not ready to leave your hands.
What owning it looks like in practice

Owning the output is what lets you use AI with confidence rather than caution. When you verify, check provenance, and stand behind the result, you can move fast, because you are not gambling on something you never read.

Set the tone for the people around you. If leaders forward unchecked AI output, the lesson everyone absorbs is that fluent equals finished. If they visibly own what they send, checking the figures and questioning the sources, that becomes the standard others copy.

questions.q: A manager runs their performance-review notes through AI, forwards the write-up with a fabricated figure in it, and a promotion decision is made on that basis. Where does accountability sit?
options: With the AI tool, since it produced the error
With the manager, who sent it as their own judgement
Nowhere, because hallucinations cannot be prevented
With the team that built the model
questions.explanation: Handing a task to AI does not hand over responsibility for the result. The person who chose to forward the write-up owns the outcome, the same as they would for work a colleague produced in their name.

questions.q: Why does fluent AI output carry a sharper accountability risk than a weak human draft?
options: It tends to be less accurate than a human draft
Its polish hides the gaps, so it invites being passed on unchecked
It cannot be edited before it is sent
It becomes the property of the sender automatically
questions.explanation: A thin draft signals that it needs work. Confident, finished-looking output can carry a hallucination and still look ready, which is how it slips past review.

questions.q: When does provenance and attribution of AI output most need your attention?
options: Only when the AI tool you used was free rather than paid
For routine internal notes with no external reach
For external publication or anything legal or contractual
As long as you rewrote most of the wording yourself
questions.explanation: The bar rises when output leaves your control or carries legal weight. There you have to be able to account for where the content came from and whether it can stand as original or properly attributed.

title: You're accountable for what AI produces

content_blocks.text: *Typing the first draft yourself matters less now. Making sure what goes out is actually right is what matters more.*

This is a shift you already recognise in some form: briefing the work, reviewing what comes back, adding context that wasn't there, and putting your name on the result before it goes anywhere, whether that work used to go to someone else, or you produced it yourself, start to finish.
The bottleneck moved

The old limit on knowledge work was time: hours spent drafting, summarising, formatting, moving information from one shape into another. Much of that can now be handed off. What's left is what was never actually the bottleneck: judgment, context, and the read on what matters and who's in the room. AI didn't change what good work looks like. It just moved the constraint away from the mechanical steps and onto your judgment.

This lands harder for people who manage others, because you've spent your career being judged on outcomes you didn't personally produce. The habit of directing rather than doing is already there. What's new is that it now reaches into the drafting and the synthesis too, the parts you might have kept doing yourself out of habit, or because handing them to a person cost more than just doing it. If you've never had anyone to delegate to before, this is that experience for the first time, just aimed at a model instead of a person.
What your contribution becomes

You move from producing to directing. Instead of writing the first draft of a stakeholder update yourself, you write the brief and review what comes back. Instead of reading through a stack of interview notes and building the hiring recommendation single-handed, you direct the first pass and then interrogate it: what did it flatten, what did it miss, what would the hiring committee push back on. Instead of building structure from a blank page, you steer it and sharpen the language.

This sounds like less work. It isn't: directing well takes more clarity than doing, not less. You have to know what good looks like before you ask for it, catch a plausible-looking error before it goes out, and supply the judgment the model can't reach: the history, the politics, the thing that can't go in the recommendation for reasons no prompt would ever surface.
Directing takes more upfront clarity than doing does: vague direction produces vague work, whether it comes from a model or a person.
Three habits that make it work

cards.body: Say what good looks like before you ask for it. One sentence on the goal, the audience, and the shape you want forces enough clarity to get a usable first pass instead of a generic one.
cards.title: Brief before you build

cards.body: Your job is to review and refine, not rewrite from scratch. If you catch yourself rewriting everything by hand, that's a signal the brief was the problem, not the output. Fix the instruction and run it again, rather than grinding through a manual rewrite.
cards.title: Review, do not redo

cards.body: The model does not know your context, your history, or the politics in the room. Every output needs your read on what matters before it leaves your hands. That layer is the part only you can add.
cards.title: Own the judgment layer

content_blocks.text: What this is not

This is not permission to **route everything through AI**, **replace thinking with prompting**, or **trade accuracy for speed**. Hand off the production work and keep the judgment: that is the whole shift. Do it right and the hours you free up go toward the read only you can supply, the part nobody and nothing else can do for you.
The move in one line
Hand off the production work. Keep the judgment. Brief clearly, review honestly, add the context the model cannot see, and own what goes out as your work.

questions.q: Which best describes the directing mindset in practice?
options: Write a detailed prompt, then send the output as-is to save time
Brief the key points, review what comes back, and apply your own context before it goes out
Write the whole thing yourself and use AI only to check spelling
Ask the model to make every judgment call so the work is consistent
questions.explanation: Directing means steering the assembly and keeping the judgment: a clear brief, an honest review, and your own context added before anything leaves your hands.

questions.q: You keep having to rewrite the output almost entirely. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model is not capable enough for the task
Your brief was too vague about what good output looks like
You should always write the first draft yourself
The task cannot be done with AI at all
questions.explanation: Heavy rewriting is usually a symptom of a weak brief, not a weak model. Fix the instruction before concluding the task is not suited to AI.

questions.q: Building a hiring recommendation from a stack of interview notes, which part should you keep rather than delegate?
options: Merging the interview notes into one structured summary
Reformatting the notes into a consistent table
Deciding which concerns matter enough to flag to the hiring committee
Drafting the opening paragraph in a neutral tone
questions.explanation: Merging, reformatting, and drafting are assembly, exactly what to hand off. Deciding what matters enough to flag is the judgment call, and the part your name is on.

title: From doing to directing

content_blocks.text: A colleague hands you a dense clause, on data residency, say, and asks you to make it readable for the whole company. Stripping the jargon is a clean hand-off to a model. Deciding which caveat cannot be simplified away without making the result quietly wrong is not.

The last lesson made the case for directing rather than doing everything yourself. This one is about the judgment call underneath that shift: what actually to hand off, and what to keep. You already run this calculation whenever you pass a task to someone else, weighing what it costs to brief and check them against what it costs to just do it yourself. Handing work to AI takes the same discipline, applied to your own work if you've never delegated to a person before: which parts to hand off, and which to keep because only you can do them right. The one real difference is that the model is fast and never tires, but it arrives with none of your context, and it carries none of the accountability when the call turns out wrong.
The two questions that decide it

Before you hand anything off, check one thing first, then ask two questions.

**First, is the data itself allowed near AI at all?** If it's confidential, personal, or regulated, that's a separate gate covered in the safety module later in this track: settle that before anything below applies. What follows assumes the answer is yes.

- **How much task-specific context does this need?** Context the model cannot pull from the words in front of it: who is in the room, why a timeline really slipped, which stakeholder is privately opposed. For the plain-language rewrite, the context that matters is narrow: which regulatory detail is load-bearing and which is decoration, and you can hand that over in a sentence. When a task turns on context you cannot supply that cheaply, either keep it or brief the model properly first. When it needs little, it is a strong candidate to pass on.
- **What does a subtle error cost, and how easily would you catch one?** A mistake that jumps out on a quick read is cheap, because you see it, you fix it, you move on. A mistake only an insider would notice is expensive, because it can pass review and reach a decision-maker intact. In this kind of rewrite, a dropped qualifier that changes what the clause actually permits is that kind of quiet, costly error. The harder a mistake is to catch, the more the task belongs with you.

The dangerous combination is high context plus errors that are hard to catch: fluent, confident output that looks right and is wrong in a way only you would spot. That is where the time AI saved comes back to cost you, with interest.
Where the time saving is real

AI pays off on structured, repetitive work, and on moving information from one shape into another: the same territory covered in "What AI is good at, and where it falls short." The quality bar is clear enough for the model to hit, the time saved is genuine, and mistakes tend to surface on review.

Underneath most good delegation sits a split you can make on almost any task: separate the judgment from the assembly. Deciding which findings belong in a report is judgment, so keep it. Writing those findings up once you have chosen them is assembly, so pass it on. Deciding which technical nuance must survive a rewrite is judgment. Producing the clean plain-language draft around that decision is assembly.

That split is why so much real work is neither fully kept nor fully handed off. You do the thinking; the model does the production.
What to keep

Keep the work whose value lives in the parts a model cannot supply. Novel judgment calls with no obvious right answer and competing risks. Anything that depends on having been in the room. Anything where the output has to reflect your read of the politics, the history, or the people involved.

The model will always give you an answer, which is worth keeping in mind: ask it to recommend a pricing change and it will recommend one, fluently, drawing on nothing about your market, your margins, or your competitors. The answer comes out generic, and your value on that task was the non-generic part. When a task turns on knowing something the model cannot know, holding onto it is exactly where you add value.
A working map

cards.body: Summarising an interview or a long thread. Rewriting a dense clause in plain language. Drafting a standard status update. Writing up findings you have already chosen. Clear quality bar, visible errors, real time saved.
cards.title: Delegate

cards.body: Deciding what goes in the report. Recommending an approach. Choosing which nuance a translation cannot lose. Any call that turns on context the model cannot have: the room, the history, the politics. Generic is not good enough here.
cards.title: Keep

cards.body: Most real work. You supply the judgment, then hand over the assembly. Decide the risks, then let the model draft the write-up. Spot-check and prioritise what comes back.
cards.title: Split

content_blocks.text: One caution: handing the model a task that needs context you never gave it does not make the task easier, it just makes the output confidently generic. Splitting well depends on doing the judgment part yourself first: delegate the decision along with the drafting, and the effort you thought you saved is gone, because you've handed away the part that was yours to own.

questions.q: You have decided which technical caveat in a clause must survive the rewrite into plain language. What is the sound way to use AI here?
options: Ask it to decide which caveats matter and rewrite the clause for you
Ask it to draft the plain-language version around the caveat you have already flagged, then check it
Keep the whole task, since anything with legal nuance should stay with you
Ask it to suggest an entirely different set of caveats as a cross-check
questions.explanation: The judgment, choosing the caveat that has to survive, is already done and is yours to own. Rewriting the clause in plain words around that decision is assembly, which is what the model is good at. Hand over the drafting, keep the decision.

questions.q: What is the primary filter for deciding whether to hand a task to AI?
options: How long the task would take you to do by hand
How much task-specific context it needs that the model cannot get from your words
Whether the task is technically complex
Whether other people on your team already use AI for it
questions.explanation: Context is the first filter. If the task turns on things the model cannot know, either keep it or supply that context first. Time saved and complexity matter, but they come after this question.

questions.q: Why is asking AI to recommend a strategic approach usually a keep, not a delegate?
options: Models are not allowed to give recommendations
It will refuse without a system prompt
It will produce a fluent answer, but a generic one that ignores your market, history, and constraints
A recommendation takes longer to review than to write
questions.explanation: The model will always produce an answer. On a judgment call, that answer is generic because it lacks your specific context, and the value of the task lived in the non-generic part. That is what makes it a keep.

title: What to delegate and what to keep

content_blocks.text: You do not build good AI instincts by reading about them. You build them by noticing what happened after each round, and why.

You already have the frame: the shift from doing to directing, and the judgement call about what to hand off and what to keep. This lesson turns that frame into something faster than working it out step by step each time. A well-calibrated user knows within seconds whether a task is worth handing over, writes a usable brief without labouring over it, and reads the output already knowing what to fix. None of this needs a team: if you turn the same messy meeting notes into a task list most weeks, the calibration happens on your own desk, one round at a time.
What miscalibration looks like
Most people go wrong in a handful of predictable ways. Naming them is the fastest route to catching yourself in the act.

cards.body: The context question from the last lesson, missed: you hand over a task without the background it needs, and the output comes back polished and confidently wrong in ways that matter. The fix: supply that context before you ask for output.
cards.title: Over-delegating without context

cards.body: You do a structured, low-stakes task by hand because that is how you have always done it. The fix: when you finish one of these without AI, ask whether that was the right call.
cards.title: Under-delegating out of habit

cards.body: You treat the first output as finished and ship something generic that needed one more pass. The fix: assume the first output needs at least one round of refinement.
cards.title: Accepting the first draft

cards.body: The highest-risk mistake. The fix: read every output asking whether anything in it would embarrass you if you sent it as your own work.
cards.title: Copying without reading

content_blocks.text: How the read gets faster

Calibration is pattern recognition, and every delegation is a data point. Take a recurring task like turning meeting notes into a task list: did it come back usable, or did it invent an owner nobody agreed to and miss the one action that actually mattered? If it missed, ask why: thin context, the wrong task for a model, or a first draft that needed another turn. Over enough rounds you build a mental map of what this kind of work does well and where it slips, until the judgment becomes a fast read instead of a step-by-step process.

The problem is that most people use AI and move straight on, registering nothing. The output was fine, or it was not, and the moment passes either way. You do not need a log or a system for this. You need the habit of pausing for five seconds after each round to ask what you learned. Calibration costs you almost nothing extra. It is attention, paid to the rounds you are already running.
Repeated disappointment with a task usually means too few reps to calibrate your brief yet, rarely proof the task can't be delegated at all. Give it enough rounds before writing it off.
Narrow beats broad

Here's a practical way to train that instinct: calibrating across everything at once is slow and muddy, so pick one recurring task and use AI for it consistently for two weeks. Your weekly meeting notes are a good candidate: the same shape every time, low stakes, and frequent enough to give you real repetitions.

Watch three things as you go: what it reliably gets right, where it consistently misses, and which adjustments to your brief move the needle most. Focusing on one task teaches you faster than spreading the same attention across many. That single repeated task is exactly the kind of work the next module puts into practice, start to finish.

questions.q: You have tried turning your messy meeting notes into a task list with AI three times and been disappointed each time. What is the most likely reading?
options: The task cannot be delegated and you should go back to doing it by hand
You have too few repetitions to have calibrated the task and your brief yet
AI is the wrong tool for any note-processing work
The model is not capable enough for the task
questions.explanation: Three rounds is rarely enough to learn where a task misses and how to adjust the brief. Repeated disappointment usually signals too little practice, not a task that cannot be delegated. Give it enough reps before writing it off.

questions.q: Which best describes a well-calibrated AI user?
options: Someone who uses AI for as many tasks as possible
Someone who classifies tasks fast, briefs efficiently, and reviews output knowing what to look for
Someone who no longer needs to review AI output
Someone who writes long, detailed briefs for every task
questions.explanation: Calibration is a matter of judgement, not sheer volume. It shows up as quick task classification, efficient briefs, and targeted review of what comes back.

questions.q: Of the common calibration mistakes, which carries the highest risk?
options: Doing a simple task by hand out of habit
Accepting a first draft that needed one more pass
Copying output into your work without a critical read
Giving slightly too much context in a brief
questions.explanation: Using output without reviewing it is the mistake that puts wrong or embarrassing content into work that goes out as yours. The others cost you efficiency or polish. This one costs you credibility.

title: Building reliable instincts through use

content_blocks.text: Take a recurring task you actually own this week: a folder of raw meeting notes, a report you rewrite every month, a draft you always end up untangling. This lesson is not a demonstration. You run your own task through it, start to finish, right now.

Everything so far has built toward one ability: taking work you actually own, putting an AI tool to it, and keeping enough judgement in the loop to trust what comes out. This lesson is where you do it, not read about it. Have your task in mind, and your AI tool open, before you go further.
Choose the right task to start with

The best first task is one you do often, that eats real time, and where you can tell good output from bad because you know the subject. That last point matters most: judging the result is what lets you catch what AI gets wrong, so this lesson is as much about building that eye as it is about saving time.

Skip anything that touches a hard no-go zone: final decisions that carry legal or personal weight, confidential material that cannot go into your tool, work where a plausible-but-wrong answer would slip through unnoticed. You already hold those judgements: apply them before you start, not after.

If nothing comes to mind immediately, a few good candidates:

- Turning a pile of messy meeting notes into a clean list of decisions, owners, and open questions
- Drafting the status update or report you rewrite every week
- Turning a stack of feedback or survey comments into themes
- Cleaning up a rough set of notes into a structured document

Pick your task now. This lesson uses the messy meeting notes example throughout to keep things concrete, but that's just this path's chosen stand-in: if a different task from the list above (or something else entirely) is the thing you actually rewrite every week, use that instead. You'll just need to write your own Step 1 prompt to match whatever you picked, rather than following the meeting-notes prompt below verbatim. Whatever you choose, it should be real work with a deadline you already have.
Run your task through, step by step
Step 1: frame what it needs

Write the prompt now, covering the four things every prompt needs: the task, the audience, the format you want, and any constraints. If you have a strong example of what good looks like, paste it in: a model matches a shown standard far better than a described one.

Then give it the context it cannot see on its own: the actual source material. If you're using the meeting-notes example, a prompt like this covers the basics, adapt it to your own task and notes:

**"Turn these meeting notes into a task list for my team. Separate firm decisions from open questions rather than blurring the two, and attach an owner to every action where one was named. Format as a short table: task, owner, status. [paste your notes below]"**
Step 2: read the draft like an editor, not a reader

Read your draft the way you would review a colleague's proposal before it goes up: look for gaps, weak claims, and anything that sounds right but might not be. Check anything factual against your source material: a figure, a name, or a date the model produced on its own is exactly where a hallucination hides. If your task list names a deadline or an owner that appears nowhere in your notes, that is your signal to check it before you send it on.
Step 3: refine, or reset

If your draft lands close but wrong in a specific way: too long, the wrong emphasis, a section that missed the point. Name the fix and ask again. For a task this size, staying in the same conversation and refining is usually all you need; starting fresh matters more on longer or more complex work, where a thread can drift far enough that correcting it costs more than a clean prompt would. Knowing which situation you're in is the instinct you've been building all along, and this is where you use it for real.

cards.body: Each turn gets closer. Your corrections land, and the model holds the context and builds on it. When that is happening, keep steering from inside the same conversation.
cards.title: Stay in the thread

cards.body: Corrections stop sticking, the output contradicts an earlier turn, or you are spending more effort patching than a clean prompt would take. When that is the pattern, reset with a sharper opening prompt.
cards.title: Start fresh

content_blocks.text: Step 4: verify before it leaves your hands

Once the output is good enough, it is still yours. Do the final read now: confirm the facts hold, the tone fits the audience, and nothing confidential slipped in along the way. Then send it, file it, or carry it into the meeting as your own work.
Verification is what makes the speed safe to rely on: a quick final check turns a fast draft into something you can stand behind.

Running this once with a real task turns the earlier advice into something concrete: you can now feel where AI saved you real time, where your judgement was the thing that mattered, and what you'd push harder on next time. That's what lets you take on the next task with confidence, already knowing what to check.
Reflect on what just happened

You moved from doing the task to directing it. You framed it, supplied the context it could not see, judged the drafts, refined or reset, and verified before anything left your hands. That is the whole track in one pass, and it repeats on the next task, and the one after that.

content_blocks.prompt: Where did AI save you real time on this task, and where did your own judgement do the work the tool could not? A couple of sentences is enough.

title: Work through a real recurring task with AI

content_blocks.text: You started this track knowing how to use AI. You're finishing it knowing how to direct it: what to hand over, what to check, and when to keep your hands on the work yourself.
That shift is what carries. The mechanics of any single tool will change within a year. The judgment you have built will not.
What you now know

Seven things, each building on the last:

- **What generative AI really is**: a model that predicts text rather than a system that looks up facts, though many tools now pair it with search or connectors that add current information on top of that.
- **Enough about how it works to have good instincts**: tokens and context, why the same prompt gives different answers, why it can hand you a fluent but confidently wrong answer.
- **How to write a prompt that gets a usable result.**
- **How to supply the context the model cannot see on its own.**
- **The instruct-review-refine loop**, instead of taking the first draft as final.
- **Where it fails and what those failures cost**: bias, stale information, gaps in reasoning, the tasks that are simply off-limits.
- **How to verify before you forward or decide**, what should never be pasted into a tool, and that whatever goes out is yours to stand behind.

And you have seen the move from doing the work to directing it, choosing what is worth handing off and what needs your own hand, whether that applies to work you used to hand to other people, or work you used to grind out yourself from start to finish.
The core skill is a way of thinking, not a tool. You start from a plain question, what is this task really asking for, then choose the method to fit, including the decision to use no AI at all.
What comes next

The three categories below (conversational, agentic and connected, specialist) are the lens worth carrying forward, even though the tracks you'll meet from here aren't organized by them. Each track instead goes deep on one product (Copilot, Claude, Lovable, and so on), and a single product often mixes capabilities from more than one category depending on what it actually offers. What holds across all of them is the lens itself: it's how you recognise what a given feature inside any of those tracks is actually doing, even as the specific products around it get renamed and replaced.

cards.body: The chat-style tools you already know. Drafting a reply to a customer complaint, turning two hours of messy notes into a task list, putting a technical clause into plain language. Broad, flexible, and the default for most knowledge work.
cards.title: Conversational tools

cards.body: Tools that take several steps on their own and reach into your files, inbox, or systems through connectors. More capable, and more to keep an eye on, because they act rather than only answer.
cards.title: Agentic and connected tools

cards.body: Built for one kind of work: writing code, automating a business process without code, running a personal knowledge base. Deeper inside their lane, weaker outside it.
cards.title: Specialist tools

content_blocks.text: Most individual features land cleanly in one of these categories, even when the product they live in spans more than one. The tool tracks that follow go deep on a single product at a time, into the practical detail of getting real work done with it. You already have the foundation they build on. You will judge a new tool by what it does and where it breaks, not by how it is sold.
Where to point it first

You've already run this once, on the task you worked through a couple of lessons ago: the same approach carries forward as your parting advice: pick one recurring task you already own, the weekly report you always rewrite, the inbox thread that eats an hour, the write-up nobody enjoys drafting, and refine your approach over a few real repetitions. Calibration comes from reps on work you can already judge; experiments on unfamiliar, high-stakes work teach you far less.

questions.q: Why does this track teach categories of AI tools rather than specific products?
options: Specific products cost too much to cover in a course
