Products change quickly, while the categories and the judgment for choosing between them stay stable
There is only one tool worth using in each category
Category names are easier to memorise than product names
questions.explanation: Individual products come and go. The kinds of work they support, and the skill of matching a task to the right approach, carry forward. That judgment is what the foundation was built for.

questions.q: What does this foundation call the core skill for working with AI?
options: Memorising the strengths of every major AI product
Writing the longest, most detailed prompt you can
Starting from what the task actually needs, then choosing the method, including no AI at all
Reaching for the most powerful or most agentic tool on hand
questions.explanation: The judgment is task-first, not tool-first. Sometimes the right call is a simple method or no AI at all. Choosing well beats grabbing the flashiest option.

questions.q: What is the best way to build real skill with a new tool from here?
options: Experiment on unfamiliar, high-stakes work so you learn under pressure
Point it at a recurring task you already own and can judge, then refine over a few repetitions
Read every product review before you touch the tool
Skip verifying the output so you can move faster
questions.explanation: Calibration comes from repetitions on work you can already evaluate. That is what lets you tell when the output is right or wrong and adjust your direction accordingly.

title: You're ready: here's what comes next

content_blocks.text: You are three messages deep in an Outlook thread and you need to reply. You could open a separate AI chat, paste the whole thread in, and explain the situation from scratch. Or you could ask the assistant that is already sitting inside that email, looking at the same thread you are. That second option is the point of Copilot: it lives inside M365, so it can work with the content you already have open instead of asking you to carry it somewhere else.
The two places you meet Copilot

Copilot shows up in two forms. There is the standalone chat at copilot.microsoft.com, where you type a prompt and get a response, much like any other AI chat. And there is Copilot embedded in the M365 apps you already use: Word, Outlook, Teams, PowerPoint. The embedded version is the one with reach. It can see the document, the email thread, or the meeting you are working in, so it acts on your real content rather than a copy you pasted in.
What makes it Copilot and not just another chat

Underneath, Copilot runs on the same kind of prediction engine you met in the general track's "What is generative AI" (What AI is). What sets it apart in the Microsoft setting is access. It can draw on the emails, files, chats, and meetings you already have permission to open, and it stays inside your organisation while it does. It only ever sees what you could reach yourself, and in the M365 version your content is not used to train the model.

That protection applies to the M365-embedded Copilot, not the public chat. Before pasting anything confidential into copilot.microsoft.com, remember it is a different environment with different data handling. For sensitive material, use Copilot inside M365.
Which assistant for which job

If your organisation has given you both Copilot and Claude, the useful question is not which one is better. They are built for different moments. Reach for Copilot when the work is anchored in M365 content: summarising that Outlook thread, catching up on a Teams meeting you missed, turning your rough bullets into a first draft in Word. The value is that the content is already there and the result lands back where you need it.

Reach for Claude when the job is open-ended thinking: working through a hard problem, weighing options, reasoning across a long document where you want room to iterate on ideas.

Back in that Outlook thread, the split gets concrete. If you just need a clean, polished reply to what was said, Copilot drafts it in place. If the reply hinges on a decision you have not actually made yet, that thinking is where Claude fits. You reason it through there, then bring the conclusion back to the email and let Copilot help you word it.

cards.body: Copilot. It can read the thread you are in directly, so you do not paste anything.
cards.title: Summarise a long email thread

cards.body: Copilot. A fast starting point you then edit to add the specifics that make it land.
cards.title: Draft a reply in Outlook

cards.body: Copilot, if the meeting was recorded or transcribed. Otherwise there is nothing for it to work from.
cards.title: Catch up on a Teams meeting

cards.body: Claude. Deep reasoning and iterating on ideas is where it gives you more room than Copilot.
cards.title: Think through a complex, open-ended problem

content_blocks.text: Whichever you use, read the output before you act on it. Copilot produces fluent, confident text, and as the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong" put it, fluent is not the same as accurate. It does not know the history behind the thread or what actually matters to the person you are replying to. You bring that.
Building the habit

The people who get the most from Copilot do not reach for it constantly. They know its sweet spots and use them deliberately. A thread got complicated, so you ask Copilot to orient you. A meeting finished, so you pull the action items. A draft needs a first pass, so you get something on the page. Those small, deliberate moments are where the time adds up, and knowing when to reach for something else is part of the same skill.

questions.q: You are several messages into an Outlook thread and need to write a reply that pulls together what was agreed. What is the most direct approach?
options: Open the standalone chat, paste the thread in, and describe the situation from scratch
Ask Copilot inside Outlook, which can already read the thread you are working in
Forward the thread to yourself first so it is easier to copy
Write the reply by hand, since Copilot cannot see email content
questions.explanation: Copilot embedded in Outlook works with the thread directly, so you do not need to move the content into a separate tool.

questions.q: Your organisation has both Copilot and Claude. You need to think through a difficult trade-off before you can write a decision email. Which tool fits the thinking part?
options: Copilot, because the email will live in Outlook anyway
Claude, because open-ended reasoning is where it gives you room to iterate
Neither, because reasoning is better done away from any AI tool
Whichever one opens faster on the day
questions.explanation: Copilot is strongest transforming M365 content you already have. Open-ended reasoning is where Claude fits, and you then bring the conclusion back to the email.

questions.q: A colleague is about to paste a confidential document into the public chat at copilot.microsoft.com to summarise it. What is the better move?
options: Leave them to it, since both versions handle data identically
Suggest Copilot inside M365, where the content stays within your organisation
Tell them to disconnect from the internet first
Tell them to summarise it by hand, since Copilot cannot be trusted with documents
questions.explanation: The M365-embedded Copilot keeps content within your organisation. The public chat is a different environment, so use the embedded version for confidential material.

title: Where Copilot fits and when to use it

content_blocks.text: This lesson takes you from nothing to your first useful result in Copilot chat. It assumes you already decided, in the previous lesson, "Where Copilot fits and when to use it," when a job is worth handing to Copilot.
Where Copilot chat lives

Copilot chat is the prompt-and-response window where you type a request and Copilot replies. You reach it in a few places you already work, all signed in with your work account rather than a personal one:

cards.body: The standalone chat, on the web and as a desktop and mobile app. This is your home base for a full conversation that is not tied to one document.
cards.title: The Copilot app

cards.body: Copilot chat is available in Teams, where it can also work with your meetings and channel conversations.
cards.title: Inside Teams

cards.body: Copilot chat sits alongside your mail, so you can ask about a thread without copying it out.
cards.title: Inside Outlook

cards.body: A chat pane in the Microsoft Edge browser, so you can ask a question without leaving the page you are on.
cards.title: In the Edge sidebar

content_blocks.text: Which account you sign in with matters. A personal Microsoft account gives you a chat grounded only on the web, one that cannot see any of your work content. Only the work experience, signed in with your organisation account, can reach your emails, chats, and files.
Your first task: catching up after leave

Say you are back from a week away and a busy Teams channel has kept moving without you. Instead of scrolling a week of messages, ask Copilot to do the reading.

Open Copilot inside Teams, or open the Copilot app while signed in with your work account. In the chat box, describe the task in plain language: ask it to summarise what was discussed in the named channel over the past week and to list anything still waiting on a decision from you. Copilot reads the recent messages and returns a short write-up covering the main threads, what was decided, and the open questions.

Reaching into your Teams channels, mail, and files is the work-grounded experience, and whether you have it depends on the licence and settings your organisation has enabled. If Copilot only answers from the web and cannot see your channel, check with IT before assuming the feature is broken or missing.
What to expect from the answer

Two things are worth knowing before you act on the result. First, the summary is only as good as what Copilot can see: a side conversation in a private chat, or a thread in a team you do not belong to, will not show up. Second, a fluent summary is not a verified one. Copilot can state something with real confidence and still be wrong, so for anything that leads to a decision, open the original message and check it yourself.

That habit is what turns Copilot from a party trick into something you trust with your Monday morning. The tool does the reading; you keep the judgment.
Turning a Monday habit into a scheduled prompt

If catching up on that channel becomes something you do every Monday, you do not have to keep typing the same request each week. Copilot chat lets you save a prompt to run on a schedule, daily, midweek, or end of day, so the summary is waiting for you instead of something you have to remember to ask for. Set it once, on the same catch-up prompt you used above, and Copilot delivers a fresh answer on that cadence without you opening the chat.

Manage these the same way you manage any other conversation: open your list of scheduled prompts to see what is running, edit the wording if the ask changes, or delete one once it stops being useful. Like the rest of Copilot chat, whether you see this option at all depends on what your organisation has switched on.

A scheduled prompt is still reading only what your account can already reach, and it can still be confidently wrong. Automating the question does not automate the judgment, so the same check from the last section applies: read what comes back before you act on it, every time, not just the first time.

questions.q: You are back from leave and want Copilot to summarise a busy Teams channel. What does it need in order to do this?
options: It can summarise any channel in your organisation, whether or not you are a member
It can only work with content your work account can already reach, through the work-grounded experience your organisation has enabled
It needs you to paste every message into the chat box first
It behaves the same whether you sign in with a personal or a work account
questions.explanation: Copilot reasons over content your account can already open, through the work experience. A personal account, or a channel you cannot reach yourself, will not work.

questions.q: Copilot returns a clear, confident summary of the channel. What is the right next step before you act on it?
options: Forward it to your team as the official record of what was decided
Treat it as a starting point and check the original messages for anything that drives a decision
Assume it is complete because it reads well
Ask Copilot to confirm that it is correct
questions.explanation: A fluent answer can still be wrong or incomplete, and asking the model to check itself does not fix that. Verify against the source before acting, especially where a decision is involved.

questions.q: Which is a fair description of where Copilot chat lives?
options: At a single website you have to bookmark
In several places you already work, including the Copilot app, Teams, and Outlook, all signed in with your work account
Only inside Word documents
Only on a mobile phone
questions.explanation: Copilot chat appears across the tools you already use, and signing in with your work account is what lets it reach your own content.

questions.q: You find yourself asking Copilot the same Monday catch-up question every week. What is the better long-term approach?
options: Keep typing the same prompt manually each week, since automation is not available in Copilot chat
Save it as a scheduled prompt so it runs on a cadence and delivers the answer without you asking
Ask a colleague to forward you a summary instead
Switch to a personal Microsoft account so the chat remembers your questions automatically
questions.explanation: Copilot chat supports scheduled prompts: the same request run on a cadence (daily, midweek, end of day) so you get the answer without repeating yourself.

title: Getting started with Copilot chat

content_blocks.text: The prompt box looks the same wherever you meet Copilot, but what it can reach differs by where you open it. This lesson covers the mechanics: where Copilot lives in each app, and the two typed gestures that let you point it at a specific file or a specific agent. It does not cover how to word a prompt well. That craft you already have from the general track's "How to write a good prompt" (How to prompt well).

The gestures below assume a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence is assigned to your account. Which entry points you see depends on what your organisation has switched on. If a button or feature is missing, check your licence with IT before assuming it does not exist.
Where Copilot lives

Copilot shows up in two shapes. There is the standalone chat, opened from the Microsoft 365 Copilot app or its web version, where you start with a blank prompt. And there is embedded Copilot, reached from a Copilot button inside Word, Outlook, Teams, PowerPoint, and Excel, which already has the document or conversation you are working in within view.

That difference matters in practice. In the standalone chat, Copilot sees nothing of your work until you point it at something. Inside a Word document or an Outlook thread, it can already act on what is open, so you do not have to hand it the file.

cards.body: The Microsoft 365 Copilot app and its web version. You open a blank prompt and bring in files, emails, or meetings yourself. Best when the job spans several sources.
cards.title: Standalone chat

cards.body: Reached from a Copilot control in the app. It works on the open document, so drafting and rewriting happen in place.
cards.title: In Word, PowerPoint, Excel

cards.body: A Copilot control on the message or thread. It can summarise what you are reading or draft a reply without you copying anything out.
cards.title: In Outlook

cards.body: In a meeting (if recording or transcription is on) and in chat threads. It works on that meeting or that conversation.
cards.title: In Teams

content_blocks.text: Pointing Copilot at a specific file: the forward slash

Say you are in the standalone chat and want Copilot to work from one particular Word document, the project brief you finished last week. You could paste the whole thing in or describe it from memory. You do not have to. Type a forward slash in the prompt box, start typing the document name, and pick it from the list that appears. Copilot then reads that file directly as part of your request.

The forward slash is the reference gesture. It pulls a specific file into your request so you can ground a prompt in it rather than re-explaining it. Depending on where you are, the same picker may also let you reference other items you can already open, such as a recent email or meeting. In Word, referencing lets you point Copilot at several source files to draft from.

Referencing beats pasting for a reason beyond convenience: a pasted copy is a snapshot, while a referenced file is the live document. If the brief changes after you paste it, Copilot is working from the stale version and will not tell you.
Calling a specific agent: the at-sign

The at-sign does a different job. Type `@` in Copilot chat to summon a specific agent into the conversation, so your request goes to that agent rather than to general Copilot. Agents themselves are covered elsewhere in this track, in "What Copilot Studio is and when to build an agent." Here the point is only the mechanic: `@` chooses who answers, the forward slash chooses what they read.

This trips people up, so it is worth fixing now. If you `@` a document expecting Copilot to open it, nothing useful happens, because the at-sign is not the file gesture. Reach for the forward slash when you want a file in view, and the at-sign when you want a particular agent on the job.
The prebuilt agents behind the at-sign

Type `@` and Copilot chat does not only offer up your organisation's own custom agents, the leave-policy or onboarding kind covered in "What Copilot Studio is and when to build an agent." It also offers a handful of agents Microsoft has already built and configured, ready to summon the moment you need them, no setup required.

cards.body: Works with data you attach or reference, spots patterns, and can write and run its own analysis to answer a question like "what changed in this dataset and why." Reach for it over general Copilot when the job is genuinely numeric.
cards.title: Analyst

cards.body: Takes a broad question and does the multi-step digging for you, pulling from your files, the web, and your other Microsoft 365 content, then writes up a structured answer. Suited to something you would otherwise spend an afternoon researching by hand.
cards.title: Researcher

cards.body: Turns prompt-writing into a conversation. Describe roughly what you want, and it asks follow-up questions to sharpen the prompt with you before you send it on to general Copilot.
cards.title: Prompt Coach

cards.body: A brainstorming partner that pushes back and asks questions rather than handing you a finished list, useful when you want to think something through rather than get an instant answer.
cards.title: Idea Coach

cards.body: Reviews a piece of writing you give it and gives feedback on tone, clarity, and structure, closer to an editor than a ghostwriter.
cards.title: Writing Coach

content_blocks.text: Summon any of them the same way you would summon a custom agent: type `@`, start typing the agent's name, and pick it from the list. Which of these you see, and whether more appear over time, can depend on your organisation's settings, same as everything else in this lesson.
Reaching Copilot inside the apps

Embedded Copilot is opened from a Copilot control in each app, and because it already holds the open item, you rarely need the forward slash there. In Outlook you open Copilot on the thread you are reading. In Teams you open it inside the meeting or on the chat. In Word, PowerPoint, and Excel you open it on the document you have in front of you.

Exact positions shift between releases, so treat "the Copilot button" as the thing to look for rather than memorising a menu path. If you cannot see it, that usually points back to the licence, not to you missing a click.

Copilot in a Teams meeting has nothing to work with unless recording or transcription was on for that meeting. If transcription was off, there is no transcript to summarise, and no setting will recover it afterwards.
Keeping an answer you want to reuse

When a standalone chat produces something you will build on, a plan or a table, you can send that response to a Page. That turns the answer into an editable document stored in your OneDrive, which you can keep working on and share, instead of leaving it to scroll away in the chat. It is the mechanic for getting output out of the conversation and into something durable. For a one-off answer you will not return to, leave it in the chat.

questions.q: You are in the standalone Copilot chat and want it to work from one specific Word document you already have, without pasting the text in. What is the quickest way to bring that file in?
options: Type a forward slash, start typing the file name, and select it from the list so Copilot reads the file directly
Describe the document from memory and hope Copilot finds it
Attach the document to an email to yourself first, then forward it to Copilot
Paste the entire document into the prompt box every time you ask about it
questions.explanation: The forward slash is the reference gesture. It points Copilot at the live file, so you do not have to paste or re-describe it.

questions.q: In Copilot chat, what does typing the at-sign do?
options: It attaches the file you are viewing
It summons a specific agent to handle your request
It formats your prompt as a list
It saves the conversation to a Page
questions.explanation: The at-sign chooses who answers by calling a specific agent. The forward slash is the separate gesture for choosing what content Copilot reads.

questions.q: Why does Copilot in Outlook usually not need you to reference the email thread with a forward slash?
options: Outlook does not support the forward slash gesture at all
Embedded Copilot already has the open thread in view, so it can act on it without you pointing at it
Referencing is disabled unless an administrator turns it on for each mailbox
Outlook Copilot can only work with attachments, not the thread itself
questions.explanation: Embedded Copilot works on whatever is open, which is why you point at files mainly in the standalone chat, where it starts with nothing in view.

questions.q: You get a useful table back from a standalone Copilot chat and know you'll want to keep editing and sharing it later. What should you do with it?
options: Leave it in the chat, since Copilot chats never expire
Send it to a Page, turning it into an editable document stored in your OneDrive
Copy it into an email draft so it is not lost
Start the same request again in a new chat each time you need it
questions.explanation: Sending a response to a Page turns it into a durable, editable document in your OneDrive. A one-off answer you will not return to can just stay in the chat.

questions.q: You need to pull together research from several files and the web on a topic, a job that would normally take you an afternoon. Which prebuilt Copilot agent is built for this?
options: Writing Coach
Researcher
Prompt Coach
Analyst
questions.explanation: Researcher does multi-step digging across your files, the web, and other Microsoft 365 content and writes up a structured answer, suited to open-ended research questions.

title: Copilot's commands and app entry points

content_blocks.text: The same assistant, four different jobs

Copilot is the same assistant in every M365 app, but the experience is not. What changes from app to app is the content Copilot can see and the kind of output it gives you back. In Outlook it works on a mail thread, in Teams on a meeting transcript, in Word on the document open in front of you, in PowerPoint on slides. Knowing what each one does well is the difference between reaching for it at the right moment and fighting it at the wrong one.

This lesson walks through the four core apps and where each earns its place. Whatever Copilot produces in any of them is a draft to check, not a finished answer.
Copilot in Word

Copilot in Word works on the document you have open. You can open the side panel to ask about the whole document, or use the inline Copilot prompt to draft or rewrite at your cursor.

Its strongest work is on content that already exists. Tighten a paragraph, rewrite a technical section for a non-technical reader, or turn a fifteen-page document into a short executive summary. Give it a specific target and it does well. Ask it to "improve this document" and you get something polished but generic, because it does not know the constraints and history you are carrying in your head. The pattern that works: you supply the substance in rough notes or bullets, Copilot supplies the structure and language, and you edit the result.
Copilot in Outlook

Copilot in Outlook does two jobs: it helps you read, and it helps you write.

On a long thread it will summarise what was said and flag what action is expected of you. On a forty-message chain about a single decision, that is a real time saver. On the writing side, you describe the reply you want and Copilot drafts a starting point you then edit. The draft gives you a foundation to build on. The specific detail that makes an email actually land is still yours to add.
Copilot in Teams

Copilot in Teams works on conversations rather than documents. After a meeting it can produce a recap, list the decisions, and pull out action items. In chat it can summarise a busy channel or a thread you missed, which helps when you come back from leave or join a project midway.

Copilot in Teams has nothing to work with unless the meeting was recorded or transcribed. Transcription is often off by default, and some organisations restrict it for privacy reasons. Confirm it was on before you rely on a recap.
Copilot in PowerPoint

PowerPoint is where the experience differs most from Word, and the example for this lesson shows why. Say you have an approved project brief in Word and need a first-draft deck from it.

In Word, Copilot edits and drafts inside the document you already have open. In PowerPoint, it can do something Word cannot: build a brand-new deck from a separate file. You start a new presentation with Copilot, point it at the Word brief, and it generates a slide structure from the document headings. Because it reads those headings, a well-organised brief produces a better deck.

What you get back is a scaffold: plausible structure, placeholder content, and functional formatting. It is far faster than staring at a blank deck, but you will reshape almost every slide. If your organisation has set a template, Copilot uses it; otherwise it applies its own default styling. Either way the design is functional and no more, so the polish is yours to add. The content engine is the useful part.

That is the shift from Word to PowerPoint. Word Copilot refines content you are already sitting in. PowerPoint Copilot can construct a new object from a source you hand it, then leaves you a draft to rework. Once the deck exists, the reliable asks are the contained ones: add a summary slide, rewrite a dense slide into bullets, or generate speaker notes for a slide.
Copilot in Excel

Excel is the odd one out in this lineup: instead of prose, Copilot is working with a table, and its job shifts from drafting to explaining what the numbers say. Say you have a spreadsheet of regional sales figures for the quarter, updated an hour ago by finance. Open Copilot in Excel and ask it to summarise the sheet: which regions came in over target, which fell short, and how this quarter compares with the last one. Copilot reads the structure of the table, headers, ranges, formulas, and answers in a short write-up, sometimes with a suggested chart alongside it.

It does not stop at a summary. Ask it to break the data down by region in a PivotTable, add a calculated column for percentage change, or chart the trend over the last four quarters, and it will build the object for you rather than just describing what one would look like. That is the same shift you saw with the Word brief becoming a PowerPoint deck: give Copilot a well-structured source, in this case clean rows and columns with headers that mean something, and it will construct real analysis on top of it rather than a page of text about your data.

A confident number is not a checked number. Copilot in Excel can misread a range, miscount a filter, or summarise a column you did not mean to include, especially if the sheet has hidden rows, merged cells, or a header row that is not quite where it expects. Before a figure from Copilot goes into a report or a decision, trace it back to the cells it came from.

cards.body: Works on the document you have open. Best at refining what exists: tighten, rewrite for a new audience, summarise. Give it a specific target, not improve this.
cards.title: Word

cards.body: Summarises long threads and flags the action expected of you, and drafts replies you then edit. Treat the draft as a starting point and add the detail yourself.
cards.title: Outlook

cards.body: Recaps meetings and lists decisions and action items, but only if the meeting was recorded or transcribed. In chat it summarises busy channels and threads you missed.
cards.title: Teams

cards.body: Can build a new deck from a file such as a Word brief, using its headings for structure. The result is a scaffold to rework, with functional design you refine yourself.
cards.title: PowerPoint

cards.body: Summarises and analyses the table you point it at, and can build a PivotTable, chart, or calculated column instead of just describing one. Best on a clean, well-headed sheet. Check any figure against the source cells before you rely on it.
cards.title: Excel

content_blocks.text: These features need a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence, and exact entry points shift with app updates and with what your organisation has enabled. If a feature is not where this lesson says it should be, check your licence and your app version before assuming it is missing.
Check your understanding

questions.q: You have an approved project brief in Word and need a first-draft slide deck quickly. What is the most effective way to use Copilot in PowerPoint?
options: Retype the brief into slides, then ask Copilot to format them
Start a new presentation with Copilot and point it at the Word brief so it builds slides from the document structure
Ask Copilot in Word to convert the document into slides in place
Ask Copilot for a deck on the topic without referencing the brief
questions.explanation: Copilot in PowerPoint can generate a deck from a file. Pointing it at a well-structured brief gives it headings to build from, which produces a stronger scaffold than a topic-only prompt.

questions.q: You missed a two-hour Teams meeting and want to know what was decided. When can Copilot give you a reliable recap?
options: Whenever the meeting was in your calendar
Only if the meeting was recorded or transcribed
Only if you attended the first ten minutes
Whenever the organiser used Copilot themselves
questions.explanation: Copilot in Teams reads the transcript or recording. If transcription was off there is nothing for it to summarise, so confirm it was on before relying on a recap.

questions.q: Copilot in Word returns polished but generic text when you ask it to improve your document. Why?
options: Word Copilot cannot handle business documents
It does not know the constraints, history, and audience you have in mind, so a vague prompt produces generic output
The document is too long to process
You need to switch to the standalone chat at copilot.microsoft.com
questions.explanation: Copilot works from what is in the document and the direction you give it. A vague ask leaves the specifics to guesswork, so name the audience, goal, and format.

questions.q: You ask Copilot in Excel to summarise a sheet of quarterly regional sales and it returns a confident figure for the top-performing region. What should you do before using that figure in a report?
options: Nothing, Copilot's numeric answers in Excel are pulled directly from formulas so they cannot be wrong
Trace the figure back to the cells it came from, since Copilot can misread a range or an unexpected hidden row
Ask Copilot a second time and use whichever answer sounds more confident
Switch to Copilot in Word, which is more reliable with numbers
questions.explanation: Copilot in Excel can misread ranges, filters, or hidden structure in a sheet. A fluent, confident number is still worth tracing back to its source cells before it goes into a report.

title: Copilot across the M365 apps (Word, Outlook, Teams, PowerPoint)

content_blocks.text: You already know Copilot can read the email thread you are in or the document open in front of you. This lesson is about the bigger move: asking Copilot a question and having it search across everything your organisation has stored in Microsoft 365 to answer it. That is grounding, and it is what separates Copilot from a general chatbot that only knows what you paste into it.
What grounding means here

Grounding is the general-track idea of pointing a model at your own trusted data instead of relying on its general training. You have met the concept. What matters now is the specific machinery Copilot uses, because that machinery decides which answers you can trust and which ones quietly go wrong.

When you type a prompt into Microsoft 365 Chat, Copilot does not send it straight to the model. It first runs a grounding step. It queries Microsoft Graph and the semantic index for content relevant to your question, adds what it finds to your prompt, and only then sends that enriched prompt to the model. After the model replies, Copilot runs the answer back through Graph for post-processing, adds citations, and applies its security and compliance checks before you ever see it.

Microsoft Graph is the layer that already knows the relationships between your people, files, meetings, and messages in M365. The semantic index sits on top of it and lets Copilot match on meaning, not just exact keywords, so a question about "travel costs" can surface a document titled "Expense reimbursement".
The permission boundary

The single most important fact about grounding is what Copilot is allowed to reach. The grounding step only ever accesses content you are already authorised to open. It uses the same access controls as the rest of M365, so it cannot surface a file, an email, or a SharePoint page you could not already open yourself.

This holds even for an individual contributor with no team and no admin rights. Two colleagues asking Copilot the exact same question can get different answers, because they can see different things. Grounding does not widen your access. It searches within it.
What this looks like in practice

Suppose you ask Microsoft 365 Chat: "What is our travel-expense policy, and what is the daily meal allowance?" Copilot searches your SharePoint and OneDrive content through the index, finds the policy document, and returns an answer that quotes the allowance with a citation linking back to the source file. You did not need to know where the document lived or what it was called. That retrieval is the whole value of grounding.

The tenant-level index is built from text-based SharePoint files, so an organisation-wide policy stored there is exactly the kind of content grounding handles well. Your own mailbox and documents feed a separate user-level index, which is why Copilot can also answer questions about your own emails and files.
Where the answer quality breaks down

Grounding is retrieval, and retrieval can pull the wrong thing while sounding completely sure of itself. The travel-expense question is a good stress test, because policies are exactly the kind of content that drifts out of date and exists in several versions.

cards.body: If a 2019 policy and the current one both sit in SharePoint, Copilot may quote whichever the index ranks highest, which is not always the current one. Check the citation date before trusting the number.
cards.title: More than one version

cards.body: A scanned policy saved as an image-only PDF has no text layer, and a SharePoint site can be set to be non-searchable. Copilot cannot read what the index never captured.
cards.title: Not in the index

cards.body: If the authoritative policy lives in a site you cannot access, Copilot will not surface it for you. It may fall back to a weaker source that you can see, without telling you it did.
cards.title: Behind a permission wall

cards.body: A policy that lives only in a separate HR system is invisible to grounding unless that system is connected to Graph through a Copilot connector, Microsoft's own term and a different thing from the MCP connector from the general track.
cards.title: Outside Microsoft 365

content_blocks.text: The failure mode to watch for is a confident, fluent answer built on the wrong source. You met this in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong" as the reason fluency is not evidence. That risk still applies here, only from a different origin: the error now comes from the retrieval step pulling the wrong document rather than from the model inventing something. The citation is your check. Open it, confirm it is the current document, and confirm the number Copilot quoted actually appears there.

A missing citation is a signal. If Copilot answers a policy question with no source link, treat the answer as ungrounded, closer to a general guess than a retrieved fact, and verify it before you act on it or forward it.
What you need for any of this to work

Grounding on organisational data requires a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence assigned to your account. The tenant-level index is enabled by Microsoft automatically and needs no setup from you. If Copilot can answer general questions but cannot find your organisation's documents, the likely causes are a licence that is not active, content sitting in a site that is not searchable, or a source system that is not connected to Graph. Check the licence with your IT administrator before assuming the feature is missing.

One thing you never have to configure is the safety of your data. Prompts, responses, and the content Copilot retrieves stay inside your organisation's tenant and are not used to train the underlying model. That boundary, and what it means for the content you put into a prompt, is the subject of the next lesson.

questions.q: You and a colleague ask Copilot the same question about a project document and get different answers. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Copilot gives randomised answers to reduce bias
Grounding only retrieves content each of you is already authorised to open, so you may be searching different sets of files
One of you has a faster internet connection
Copilot caches the first answer and reuses it for everyone
questions.explanation: Grounding respects your existing M365 permissions. If you can each access different content, Copilot can surface different sources, so the answers differ.

questions.q: Copilot quotes a daily meal allowance from your travel-expense policy, but you suspect the figure is out of date. What is the best next step?
options: Trust it, because a grounded answer draws from your own data
Open the citation and confirm it points to the current policy document and that the figure appears there
Ask Copilot to confirm whether it is correct
Re-run the prompt until you get a consistent number
questions.explanation: Grounding can retrieve an older version that still sits in SharePoint. The citation lets you verify the source and its date rather than trusting a fluent answer.

questions.q: Your organisation stores its travel-expense policy only in a third-party HR system, not in SharePoint or M365. What should you expect when you ask Copilot about it?
options: Copilot will find it, because grounding reaches any system in your organisation
Copilot cannot ground on it unless that system is connected to Graph through a connector
Copilot will download the policy from the web instead
Copilot will ask you to paste the policy first, every time
questions.explanation: Grounding works over Microsoft Graph. Content in an external system is invisible to it unless a Copilot connector brings that source into Graph.

content_blocks.text: Where this leaves you

You can now explain why Copilot sometimes nails a question about your organisation and sometimes confidently misses. The answer is almost never the model itself. It is what the grounding step could reach, which version it ranked first, and whether you had permission to see the real source. Treat the citation as the thing you verify, and grounding becomes a genuine shortcut rather than a source of quiet errors.

title: Grounding Copilot on your organisation's data

content_blocks.text:
You ask Copilot a broad question about pay bands for a planning exercise, and its answer quotes a specific figure from a spreadsheet that holds a colleague's salary. You were never meant to see that file. Copilot did not break in or bypass anything. It surfaced a document your account could already open, which nobody had realised was shared that widely.

That scenario is the whole point of this lesson. Copilot in M365 introduces a genuinely new risk surface, and it is not the one people expect. The risk is not that Copilot leaks data outside your organisation. It is that Copilot makes whatever is already overshared inside your organisation far easier to stumble into.
The rule Copilot follows

Copilot only ever reaches content you could already open yourself. It works strictly within your existing M365 permissions, using the same identity-based access controls as the rest of Microsoft 365. If you do not have access to a file, an email, or a Teams message, Copilot cannot read it for you or quote it back to you. It grants no new access.

Your data also stays inside your organisation's Microsoft tenant, and your prompts and files are not used to train the underlying model. Where a document is protected with a Purview sensitivity label that restricts access, Copilot honours those usage rights too.
Copilot changes nothing about who can access what. Every permission is exactly as it was before Copilot arrived. What changes is how quickly the content behind those permissions can be found.
Why discoverability is the real risk

Before Copilot, an overshared salary file could sit in a SharePoint site nobody browsed. It was technically open to more people than intended, but finding it meant knowing the link or digging through folders by hand, so in practice it stayed buried. Copilot reads across everything your account can reach and answers in seconds. Content that was exposed on paper but hidden in practice is now one plain-language prompt away.

So Copilot behaves like an honesty test for your permissions. The exposure was already there; Copilot simply makes it easy to find. An answer that surfaces something you did not expect is usually a signal that a file, folder, or site is shared more broadly than its owner assumed.

cards.body: Anything your account already has permission to open: your emails, your chats, files shared with you, and documents on sites you can access. If a permission is looser than intended, that content is in scope.
cards.title: What Copilot can surface

cards.body: Files, sites, and messages you have no access to. Content locked down by a Purview sensitivity label you are not entitled to. Anything outside your organisation tenant.
cards.title: What Copilot cannot reach

content_blocks.text: M365 Copilot versus public web chat

There is a difference between Copilot working inside your licensed M365 experience and a general web chat interface. The M365 experience keeps your content within your organisation's tenant and does not use it to train the model. A general-purpose public chat that is not covered by your organisation's enterprise data protection is a different environment with different handling.

The practical rule is simple. If you are working with anything confidential, keep it inside the M365-embedded Copilot rather than pasting it into a public chat window. Pasting a confidential document into an unmanaged tool takes it outside the boundary that protects it.
For managers: govern the sharing behind Copilot

Rolling out Copilot makes the state of your sharing hygiene suddenly visible to every licensed user at once. The governance work happens before and around the tool, in how your content is shared, not inside Copilot itself.

The priorities are the familiar ones, now more urgent: make sure every SharePoint site has an accountable owner, tighten default sharing links so new content is not open to everyone by default, and run an assessment to find sites and files that are overshared or ownerless. Microsoft provides controls to keep sensitive sites out of Copilot's reach while you remediate, and Purview sensitivity labels let you classify and protect content so Copilot respects those limits.

The exact names and locations of these admin controls, and which require additional licensing such as SharePoint Advanced Management or Purview, shift over time and depend on what your organisation has enabled. Confirm the current settings and licence requirements with your M365 administrator before relying on any specific control.

An individual contributor has a role here too. If you own or manage a SharePoint site, a shared folder, or a Team, you are the person who decides how widely its content is shared. Reviewing your own sharing links before a Copilot rollout is one of the most useful things you can do, and it needs no authority over anyone else.
For an individual: check before you trust the answer

Two habits keep you safe when you are the one using Copilot day to day.

First, if an answer quotes something that surprises you, pause. That content is technically accessible to your account, but seeing it does not mean it was meant for you. Do not forward it, repeat it, or paste it into a message. Flag it to the file owner or your administrator so the permission can be corrected.

Second, remember that anything you move out of Copilot carries the same weight as anything else you send. Once a Copilot answer goes into an email, a shared document, or a Teams post, it is your communication and your responsibility. And because a fluent answer can still be wrong, as you saw in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong," read what Copilot produces before you act on it.

content_blocks.prompt: Spot the planted problem in how this colleague handles a surprising Copilot answer.
content_blocks.example: Copilot's answer includes salary figures you did not expect to see. You paste the figures into a Teams message to a colleague, joking that Copilot "knows everything," then continue with your original planning question.

candidates.text: Asking Copilot the original planning question
candidates.reason: A normal question. Copilot only surfaces what your account can already open.

candidates.text: Pasting the surprising figures into a Teams message
candidates.reason: The rule is to flag a surprising answer to the file owner, not forward or repeat it. Seeing it does not mean it was meant for you.

candidates.text: Continuing with the original planning question afterward
candidates.reason: The original question itself was fine. The problem was what happened to the unexpected content, not the question.

questions.q: You ask Copilot a general question and its answer quotes salary figures from a document you did not know existed. What has most likely happened?
options: Copilot bypassed the file permissions to give you a complete answer
The document was shared more broadly than intended, and your account already had access to it
Copilot invented the figures because it could not find real data
Your organisation tenant has been breached by an external party
questions.explanation: Copilot only surfaces content your account can already open. A surprising result usually means the file was overshared, not that Copilot broke any boundary.

questions.q: A manager says Copilot is dangerous because it gives everyone access to sensitive files. What is the most accurate correction?
options: They are right, so Copilot should not be deployed until Microsoft fixes it
Copilot grants no new access; it only makes content that is already overshared easier to find, so the fix is to tighten sharing
Copilot only reads files stored in the users own OneDrive, so there is no risk
Sensitivity labels have no effect on what Copilot can surface
questions.explanation: Copilot respects existing permissions and adds no access. The real exposure is pre-existing oversharing, which Copilot makes discoverable, so remediation belongs in sharing settings and labels.

questions.q: You need Copilot to summarise a confidential contract. Which choice best protects the content?
options: Paste the contract into a public web chat interface so it processes faster
Use the M365-embedded Copilot, where the content stays inside your organisation tenant
Email the contract to yourself first, then summarise the email in any tool
Remove the confidential clauses before pasting it anywhere
questions.explanation: The M365-embedded Copilot keeps data within your organisation tenant and does not use it to train the model. A public, unmanaged chat is a different environment with weaker protection for confidential content.

title: Using Copilot safely, data boundaries in M365

content_blocks.text: Your HR team answers the same handful of questions every week. How much leave do I have left, how do I book it, what happens to unused days at year end. The answers already live in a policy document on SharePoint. Copilot Studio is the tool that lets you turn that repeated answering into something people can just ask, without writing a line of code. The harder skill is not building the thing. It is knowing which repeated questions are worth building an agent for in the first place.
What Copilot Studio is

Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code platform for building conversational agents: things people talk to, in Teams or on a web page, to get an answer or complete a task. You point one at a knowledge source, like your leave-policy library, and it answers questions from that source. You can also give it a set of structured steps for a defined process, or have it call a Power Automate flow to actually do something, such as logging a leave request. It sits inside the Power Platform family and connects natively to Microsoft 365, so an agent can draw on the documents and data your organisation already holds.

You do not need to run a team to see where it fits. If you are the person who answers the same question for colleagues every week, that repetition is the signal.

Copilot Studio agents can now also reach an outside MCP server directly, the general cross-vendor standard from the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do" (How AI works). That connection runs through the same Power Platform connectors and data policies covered in "Governed, safe use, DLP and connectors" (Power Platform track), so it does not bypass the guardrails you will meet there.
Two ways to build: Agent Builder and Copilot Studio

"Building an agent" does not always mean opening Copilot Studio. Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat has its own lightweight builder, called Agent Builder, that opens right there in the chat pane. If your leave-policy agent is nothing more than a description and a document, that is enough: you describe what you want in a few sentences, point it at a source, and it is live in minutes without leaving the chat you already work in.

Copilot Studio is the fuller product, its own app, and it is where you go once an agent needs more than that: several structured topics rather than one description, a Power Automate flow it can trigger to actually do something, connectors to other data, or the analytics and lifecycle management a widely used agent needs. The leave-policy agent from the opening example could reasonably start in either place, but the moment it needs to log a request rather than just answer a question, that is a Copilot Studio job.

A rule of thumb worth keeping: if you can describe the whole agent in a few sentences and it only needs to read a document, start with Agent Builder in chat. If you are reaching for steps, actions, or connectors, that is your signal to open Copilot Studio instead. The rest of this lesson, and the build in the next one, use the full Copilot Studio, because agents that take action are where its extra depth earns its keep.

cards.body: Opens inside Copilot Chat, no separate app. Describe the agent in a few sentences, point it at a document or two, and it is live in minutes. Right-sized for a simple, read-and-answer agent.
cards.title: Agent Builder (in chat)

cards.body: A separate app for agents that need more: multiple topics, actions via Power Automate, connectors, analytics, and lifecycle management. Where you go once an agent has to do something, not just answer.
cards.title: Copilot Studio (the full product)

content_blocks.text: The word "agent" means two things here

In the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do" you met an agent as an AI that plans and takes several steps towards a goal with some autonomy. A Copilot Studio agent is usually a narrower thing. Most of the time it is a custom chatbot you have configured: it answers within the sources you gave it and follows the steps you laid out. It waits for someone to ask, then responds inside the boundaries you set. It is not off planning a multi-step task on its own.

The reason to be careful is that Copilot Studio can also build the autonomous kind, agents that trigger on an event and act without a person starting the conversation. That is a newer, more advanced capability. When a colleague says "we built an agent in Copilot Studio", they almost always mean the configured chatbot, not the autonomous planner. Work out which one is actually on the table before you agree to build it.
When a question deserves a built agent

Back to the leave-policy question. Not every recurring question earns an agent. It is worth building one when the same question comes up often, the answer lives in a source you can point the agent at, and someone keeps that source up to date. It is not worth it when the answer shifts case by case, when nobody maintains the underlying document, or when a pinned Teams message would do the job just as well.

cards.body: The question recurs across many people, the answer sits in a maintained source like a current SharePoint policy, and a self-serve answer would save real time. The leave-policy case fits when the documentation is genuinely kept current.
cards.title: Worth building

cards.body: The answer depends on individual judgement, the source is out of date or owned by nobody, or the volume is so low that a short email or a pinned message already covers it. Building an agent here adds friction rather than removing it.
cards.title: Not worth it

content_blocks.text: A grounded agent is only as good as the documents behind it. If the leave policy on SharePoint is outdated or contradicts itself, the agent will answer confidently from the wrong version. A fluent answer is not evidence that it is correct, so keep a named person accountable for the source content before anyone relies on the agent.
Where it fits, and where it does not

Copilot Studio is not the general-purpose Copilot you use through the day. An agent knows only what you configure it to know and does only what you set it up to do. That focus is the point: a purpose-built agent for leave questions is more reliable than a broad assistant precisely because its scope is narrow. It is also not a contact-centre platform, and it is not free. Message volume and premium connectors carry licensing cost, which is why an external-facing agent needs its likely traffic estimated before you commit to it.

questions.q: A colleague says the team built an agent in Copilot Studio. What is the most likely meaning?
options: An autonomous AI that plans and runs multi-step tasks on its own
A configured chatbot that answers within the sources and steps you gave it
A general-purpose assistant that can handle any question across the business
A background service that monitors systems and acts with no human involvement
questions.explanation: Most Copilot Studio agents are configured chatbots that respond inside boundaries you set, unlike the autonomous multi-step agent from the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do." The platform can build the autonomous kind, but that is rarely what people mean.

questions.q: Which situation is the strongest case for building a Copilot Studio agent for HR leave questions?
options: The rules change on a case-by-case basis and rarely repeat
The same questions recur often and the answers live in a maintained SharePoint policy
Nobody currently owns or updates the leave documentation
A single pinned Teams message would answer every version of the question
questions.explanation: An agent earns its place when the question recurs and points at a source that is kept current. If the source is unmaintained or the question never repeats, the effort is not justified.

questions.q: Why should a person stay accountable for the leave-policy documents even after the agent is live?
options: The agent stops working if the documents are not opened regularly
A grounded agent answers confidently from whatever the source says, including outdated or contradictory content
Microsoft requires a named document owner for every published agent
The agent cannot read SharePoint without a manual refresh each morning
questions.explanation: The agent grounds its answers in the source you point it at. If that source is wrong, the answer will be fluently wrong. Ongoing content ownership is what keeps it trustworthy.

questions.q: A colleague wants to try building a simple agent that only reads one document and answers questions from it, nothing more. Where should they start?
options: Copilot Studio, since every agent needs its own app
Agent Builder, right there in Copilot Chat, since the description-and-a-document case does not need more than that
Power Automate, since agents are built the same way as flows
They cannot build an agent without IT provisioning a separate licence
questions.explanation: Agent Builder in Copilot Chat is the right-sized tool for a simple, description-and-a-document agent. Copilot Studio earns its extra complexity once an agent needs actions, connectors, or analytics.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can tell the two senses of agent apart, and judge whether a recurring question in your own work is worth turning into a Copilot Studio agent. The next lesson takes one such question and walks through building the agent itself.

title: What Copilot Studio is and when to build an agent

content_blocks.text:
In the previous lesson, "What Copilot Studio is and when to build an agent," you learned what makes a question worth building an agent for. Now put that to work on a different recurring question. This walkthrough takes a single realistic task from an empty canvas to a working, tested agent, so you can see the whole shape before you try it on a job of your own.

The task: an agent that answers the questions a new IT starter asks in their first week, grounded on the onboarding documentation your organisation already keeps in SharePoint.
Scope the task first

Before you open the tool, decide exactly what the agent is for. A tight scope is what makes a first build succeed.

For this one: the agent answers questions from the existing IT onboarding knowledge base. Where do I request a laptop, how do I set up MFA, who approves software installs, what is the VPN address. It reads and answers. It does not open tickets, provision accounts, or take any action. Those belong in a flow, which is the Power Platform track, not here.

Two reasons to hold that line. A read-only knowledge agent is fast to stand up when the documents already exist, and it is far easier to test and trust. Once an agent starts writing to systems, the care it needs multiplies.

Write your scope as one sentence you could say to a colleague: "It answers new-starter IT questions from the onboarding library, and nothing else." If a request does not fit that sentence, it is a change of scope, not a quick addition.
Create the agent

In Copilot Studio, start a new agent. You can describe what you want in plain language and let the tool draft a starting configuration, or fill in the fields yourself. Either way, three things matter at the start:

- A clear **name**, so people know what they are talking to (for example, "IT Onboarding Assistant").
- A short **description** of what the agent is for.
- **Instructions**: a few lines telling the agent how to behave. For this task, something like: answer new-starter IT questions using only the onboarding knowledge, keep answers short, and say when you do not know rather than guessing.

Keep the instructions plain and specific. They set the standing behaviour for every conversation, so this is where you tell the agent to stay inside its knowledge and admit gaps.

This build uses Copilot Studio rather than the in-chat Agent Builder from the previous lesson, "What Copilot Studio is and when to build an agent." That is a deliberate choice, not a default: this agent needs a properly configured knowledge source with its own description, a real test pane to work through edge cases, and a path to publish and keep the agent accurate once it is live. That is exactly the "more than a description and a document" territory Copilot Studio is for. If your own first build turns out to be simpler, a document and a few sentences, Agent Builder in chat may be all you need instead.
Connect the onboarding knowledge base

This is the step that turns a blank chatbot into something useful, and it is where the tool-specific care lives. An agent grounded on your documents is only as good as those documents and the way you point at them.

Open the agent's Knowledge section and add a knowledge source. Copilot Studio supports several source types.

cards.body: A site, library, or folder. The most common choice in a Microsoft 365 organisation, and the right one when your onboarding docs already live there.
cards.title: SharePoint

cards.body: Any publicly reachable URL. Useful for published policy pages, but content is crawled periodically, so recent edits may lag.
cards.title: Public website

cards.body: PDFs, Word, and text files you add directly. Simple to start with, but there is no automatic sync when the original changes.
cards.title: Uploaded files

cards.body: Structured records rather than documents. Better for lookups against a table than for document-style questions.
cards.title: Dataverse

content_blocks.text: For this task, add the SharePoint library that holds the onboarding documents. When you add a source, give it a clear name and a genuinely descriptive summary of what it contains. That description is not decoration. The agent uses it to decide when to draw on that source, so a vague one makes grounding less reliable.

What the agent can read depends on how access is configured. With user authentication, it only surfaces what the person chatting is already allowed to see. With a shared service account, it sees everything that account can see, which may be more than an individual should. For an internal agent, confirm this with IT before go-live. Getting it wrong can expose data. The exact setup path varies by tenant, so verify it in your own environment rather than assuming a default.
Test with real questions

Copilot Studio gives you a Test pane inside the authoring screen. Open it and hold a conversation exactly as a new starter would, before anyone else sees the agent.

Do not test with the questions you know it can answer. Test with the questions people actually ask, including the awkward ones near the edges of the documentation: the policy that is half-written, the process that changed last month, the thing two documents disagree about. That is where a grounded agent either proves itself or shows you the gap.

For each answer, check it against the source document rather than trusting how confident it sounds. A fluent, well-phrased reply can still be wrong, for the reasons the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong" covered. When the agent gets something wrong, the fix is usually one of three things: the documentation does not cover it, the documentation is outdated, or the knowledge source is scoped too narrowly to include the right file.

If the agent answers a question whose source document you updated yesterday and gives the old answer, suspect the index. Knowledge indexing is not always instant, so a recent edit may not be reflected until the next refresh rather than the moment you save.
What you can now do

You have taken one real task, scoped it deliberately, created an agent, grounded it on existing documents, and tested it against the questions that matter. That loop, scope then build then verify, is the same whichever agent you build next. The next lesson covers publishing this agent to the people who need it and keeping it accurate once it is live.

You do not need reports or a team to get value from this. If you own a process others keep asking you about, the onboarding library, a set of expense rules, a recurring how-do-I question, you can stand up an agent for it and stop answering the same message by hand.

questions.q: You add a SharePoint library as a knowledge source but give it a vague one-word description. What is the most likely effect?
options: The agent cannot read the library until the description is longer
The agent is less reliable at deciding when to draw on that source
The description only appears to administrators and has no effect on answers
The library will not be indexed
questions.explanation: The agent uses the source description to decide when that source is relevant to a question, so a vague description makes grounding less reliable.

questions.q: During testing, a new starter asks about the parking policy and the agent gives a confident answer that is not in the onboarding documents. What should you check first?
options: Whether the model needs retraining on new topics
Whether the licence tier supports parking-related questions
Whether the knowledge source actually covers parking, and verify the answer against the source
Whether the agent has been published to the correct channel
questions.explanation: A fluent answer is not evidence it is correct. The agent may be filling a gap the documents do not cover, so check the source and confirm what the knowledge base actually contains.

questions.q: Why keep this first agent read-only rather than having it also open IT tickets?
options: Copilot Studio agents cannot take actions of any kind
Read-only agents are easier to test and trust, and actions belong in a separate build
Actions are only available on external-facing agents
A read-only agent does not need a knowledge source
questions.explanation: A knowledge-only agent is faster to stand up and simpler to verify. Writing to systems adds moving parts and belongs in a flow, which is a different track.

questions.q: This lesson builds the IT onboarding agent in Copilot Studio rather than the lighter in-chat Agent Builder. Why?
options: Agent Builder cannot connect to SharePoint at all
The build needs a properly configured knowledge source, real testing, and a path to publish and maintain the agent, which is Copilot Studio's territory
Copilot Studio is required for any agent that answers more than one question
Agent Builder only works for external-facing agents
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio is the right tool once an agent needs more than a quick description and a document, such as configured knowledge sources, thorough testing, and ongoing publishing and maintenance.

title: Building your first Copilot agent

content_blocks.text: You have just built and tested the IT Onboarding Assistant, the read-only agent that answers new-starter IT questions from the onboarding library in your SharePoint. So far it only lives in the Test pane. Publishing is the step that turns that test version into the one new starters actually reach. In Copilot Studio, Publish takes the current version of the agent live across every channel it is connected to. Anything you have changed since the last publish stays in draft until you publish again.
What publishing actually does

Select Publish once and the live version updates everywhere the agent is connected. You publish before anyone can use the agent at all, and you connect any additional channels after that first publish. From then on, every edit you make, whether a reworded answer, a new knowledge source, or a tightened instruction, sits in the draft until you publish again.
Publishing to Teams for your new starters

For the IT Onboarding Assistant the natural home is Microsoft Teams, where new starters already spend their day. You connect the Teams channel and the agent appears as something they can message, with no new portal to learn.

Because this is an internal agent for staff, set it to authenticate with Microsoft. That identifies the signed-in user through Entra ID, so the agent knows who it is talking to and can respect that person's own access when it reads the onboarding sources. For an agent that lives in Teams, sign-in is then handled automatically for the logged-in user, with no separate login step.

The exact labels, and where you set the channel and its authentication, vary by tenant and shift between releases, so confirm them in your own environment rather than memorising a path.
The public-facing contrast: No authentication

The choice looks different if you instead publish a public-facing agent on a website, say a product-FAQ agent that anyone can use. There Copilot Studio generates an embed code you place on the site, and it renders a chat widget in any modern browser. For that agent you would choose No authentication, so anyone with the link can chat without signing in.

That choice carries a real trade-off. With no authentication the agent cannot use tools that rely on an individual user's credentials, and anyone who has the link can talk to it. That is fine for answering published product questions and wrong for anything that touches account-specific data. It is the mirror image of your internal case: the onboarding agent wants to know who is asking, a public FAQ agent has no need to.

Publishing applies to every connected channel at once, and only the published version is live. If you fix an answer and forget to publish, new starters keep getting the old one. Treat "publish again" as the last step of every edit, not an afterthought.
Watch which questions it starts getting wrong

An onboarding agent does not fail loudly. It keeps answering, and some answers quietly drift out of date as the IT process changes, or were never quite right to begin with. Generative answers can produce a confident response that is wrong, the reason to verify that you met in the general track's "How to verify AI output" (Using AI safely). Watching the agent after launch is part of running it, not an optional extra.

Copilot Studio gives you an Analytics page for exactly this. These are the signals that tell you where an answer has gone wrong.

cards.body: Copilot Studio groups the questions new starters actually ask into themes and scores how well each is answered. This is where an onboarding question the agent has started getting wrong, such as the VPN setup steps, shows up, often before anyone complains.
cards.title: Themes

cards.body: Resolution rate is the share of engaged sessions that ended answered. Escalation rate is the share handed to a human. A rising escalation rate on one topic, say software-install approvals, points to a gap worth fixing.
cards.title: Resolution and escalation rate

cards.body: New starters can react to any answer and add a comment. Recent reactions appear on the Analytics page, so a run of thumbs-down on the MFA question tells you where to look first.
cards.title: Thumbs up and thumbs down

cards.body: Drill into individual sessions to read the exact exchange that went wrong. Reading the real question and the real answer is usually faster than guessing why a number moved.
cards.title: Session transcripts

content_blocks.text: You do not need to own the deployment to do this. If you own the onboarding content, the Analytics page tells you which answers to fix, and fixing them is a content job, not an engineering one.
Keeping it healthy over time

Review the Analytics page often in the first few weeks after launch, then settle into a regular rhythm such as monthly. When a theme shows poor answers, the fix usually lives in the source. Update the onboarding page or document the agent draws from, then publish again.

One timing trap catches people here. Knowledge source indexing is not always instant. If you update a source document, the agent may keep serving the old answer until the index refreshes, so a fix that looks broken may just need time to take effect.

Your onboarding agent only reads, so it does not call a flow today. Keep this in view for when you extend an agent to actually do something, such as logging a laptop request: flows called synchronously from an agent have a two-minute timeout. If that step calls a slow back-end system, design it as an asynchronous step rather than making the user wait, or the conversation will break under load.

Two channel details are worth confirming before you rely on them. Adaptive cards, the structured messages with buttons and layout, render fully in Teams but can fall back to plain text on a website embed. Proactive messaging, where the agent starts the conversation, works in Teams and not on a web embed. Your onboarding agent lives in Teams, so both are available to it, but confirm how it looks if you ever add a web channel.

questions.q: You updated the onboarding source document that a poorly rated answer draws from, but the agent still gives the old answer. What is the most likely cause?
options: The knowledge index has not refreshed yet since the source content changed
The agent needs to be retrained on the new content
The generative model has drifted from its original behaviour
The agent lost access to the source when you edited it
questions.explanation: Knowledge source indexing is not always instant. Until the index refreshes, the agent keeps serving the previous answer, so the fix may simply need time.

questions.q: You are publishing the IT Onboarding Assistant to Teams for new starters, and you want it to recognise who is asking. Which authentication choice fits, and how does it differ from a public web agent?
options: Authenticate with Microsoft, which identifies the signed-in user through Entra ID; a public web agent would instead use No authentication, which cannot use tools needing the credentials of the individual user
No authentication, so anyone with the link can use it, the same choice you would make for a public web agent
Manual authentication for internal agents, and Authenticate with Microsoft for public web agents
Authenticate with Microsoft for both, since a web agent also requires every visitor to sign in first
questions.explanation: An internal Teams agent uses Authenticate with Microsoft so Entra ID identifies each signed-in user. A public web agent uses No authentication, which lets anyone with the link chat but cannot use tools that need the credentials of the individual user.

questions.q: You edited several answers to fix a poorly rated onboarding topic and saved your work, but new starters still see the old answers. What did you most likely miss?
options: You did not publish the agent again after making the edits
You did not clear the analytics cache for the topic
You edited the draft in the wrong environment
You need to reconnect the Teams channel before edits appear
questions.explanation: Only the published version is live. Edits stay in the draft until you publish, which pushes the changes to every connected channel at once.

title: Publishing and maintaining an agent

content_blocks.text:
Every week you prepare for the same recurring review, and every week you open the same handful of tabs: last time's notes, the thread where a blocker was raised, the file with the latest figures, the invite to see who is actually coming. It eats the front of your morning. This capstone is different from the last few lessons. Instead of building one more agent, you compose several Copilot surfaces on this one job, so each does the part it is best at.

That is the tool-specific challenge here. The skill is not building another chatbot. It is choosing the right Copilot surface for each part of a repeating job and making the pieces work together, all while staying inside the permissions you already hold. Getting that orchestration right is most of the work, so that is where this lesson spends its words. It follows the same five steps every capstone in this path uses: pick a real task, scope it, build it, verify it, reflect on it.
Pick: choose one recurring review

Do not build a general assistant. Pick one recurring internal review you personally sit in. Your team stand-up, a sprint review, the weekly sync with another team. It could be an external client call, but it does not have to be, and the pattern fits you whether or not you have reports or clients.

A good candidate has three traits. The prep repeats, so the payoff repeats. The source material already lives in M365, in Outlook, in shared files, on the calendar, so Copilot can reach it. And the output is a briefing you read, not a decision the tool makes for you, so a wrong answer costs you a re-read rather than a mistake sent to the room.
Scope: decide what "done" looks like, and which surface owns which part

This is where the capstone diverges from building a single agent. Rather than one tool doing everything, you split the job across surfaces and write down which surface owns which part before you touch anything.

cards.body: The parts that repeat every time: what did we agree last, what is still open, what is the current goal. Best answered by Copilot chat grounded on your M365 data, or a small Studio agent in the IT Onboarding Assistant pattern if the question set is fixed enough to be worth it. This surface retrieves across your permissioned sources.
cards.title: The standing questions

cards.body: The parts anchored to one place: the thread where a blocker was raised, and the briefing you actually write. Best served by Copilot inside Outlook or Word, which acts on the item you already have open.
cards.title: The live thread and the draft

cards.body: Which exact places hold the material: the specific SharePoint site, the specific shared folder, the specific channel or thread. Name them. Do not say all my files.
cards.title: The named sources

cards.body: What stays out of scope: it does not send the briefing, it does not email anyone, it does not touch data outside the named sources. Preparing is the whole job.
cards.title: The stop line
