content_blocks.text: The split is the point. Copilot chat grounded on your data is strong when the question repeats and the answer is scattered across many M365 files, because it searches your permissioned content. Copilot inside an app is strong when the work is anchored to one thread or one document you are composing, because it acts on what is open. Ask each surface to do the thing it is good at rather than forcing one to do both.
Build: compose the surfaces

Now assemble the pieces, and stay clear about which surface does which and why.

First, the standing questions. Use Copilot chat grounded on your M365 data, and name the exact sources: the specific SharePoint site for this team, the specific shared folder, the specific channel. Not "all my files". If the question set is genuinely fixed, this is where a small Studio agent, built the way you built the onboarding assistant earlier, can own that repeatable Q and A instead. This surface retrieves.

Second, the live thread. Open Copilot inside Outlook on the exact thread where the blocker was raised and have it summarise what changed and what is expected of you. It is already looking at that thread, so you hand it nothing.

Third, the briefing itself. Open Copilot inside Word and have it draft the one-page brief, bringing in the answers from the grounded chat and the thread summary from Outlook. The in-app surface assembles the retrieved pieces into the document you carry into the room. That hand-off, retrieve in one surface, assemble in another, is the composition this whole lesson is about.

If you have the Power Platform track too, this is the same low-code Microsoft story from the other side. Gathering, formatting, or posting the briefing on a schedule is flow-and-app work that lives in that track. Build that part there and let a Copilot agent call the flow, so keep both surfaces in view.

Copilot answers respect the permissions each user already has, and that holds across every surface you compose here. If you build this under your own broad access and then share it, test as a colleague with narrower access, because they should only ever see through their own permissions, not yours. Confirm how each surface authenticates to its sources so you know whose access applies, and never assume it widens access.
Verify: treat the first outputs as claims, not results
A fresh set-up is a draft. Run it against a review whose real answer you already know, because that is the only way to catch a confident wrong answer before it costs you in the room.

cards.body: Prep for a review you already remember and compare. Fluent and wrong is the failure mode to hunt for, so trace each claim back to a real message or file.
cards.title: Check the facts

cards.body: Can you open the exact thread or document each point came from? A point with no traceable source is one you do not yet trust.
cards.title: Check the sources

cards.body: Ask for something out of scope: another team, a personal file. Each surface should decline or come up empty rather than improvise. If it answers, tighten the sources.
cards.title: Check the fences

cards.body: Have a colleague with narrower access run it and confirm they see only what their permissions allow. This is the test people skip and regret.
cards.title: Check as someone else

content_blocks.text: If it invents an action item or pulls in the wrong thread, the fix is almost always the grounding, not the wording. Narrow the sources, be more specific about which review and which folder, and run it again.
Reflect: what you actually built

You did not build another agent. You orchestrated the surfaces you already have so each did the part it is best at, inside the permissions you already hold. The grounded chat or agent answered the standing questions, Outlook pulled the live thread, Word assembled the briefing. What you get back is the scramble at the front of your morning, perhaps ten minutes, perhaps more, that you no longer do by hand before each of these reviews.

The two skills that carried this build transfer to every Copilot job you compose next: choosing the right surface for each part, and grounding on named sources rather than everything. Get those right and the rest is arrangement. Get them wrong and no single clever agent rescues it.

questions.q: Your briefing needs to answer the same standing questions every week (what did we agree, what is still open) from documents spread across several SharePoint sites. Which Copilot surface is the natural fit for that part?
options: Copilot chat grounded on your M365 data, or a small Studio agent, because it retrieves across your permissioned sources
Copilot inside a single Word document, because it drafts text well
A public web chat, because it answers general questions quickly
None, because standing questions cannot be grounded on your own data
questions.explanation: The repeating, spread-out question set is a retrieval job. Grounded Copilot chat, or a small Studio agent, searches across the sources you can already open, which is exactly what that part needs.

questions.q: You built the prep under your own broad access, and a colleague with narrower access runs it. What should you expect, and what should you do?
options: They should see only what their own permissions allow across every surface, so test as a colleague with narrower access before relying on it
They see exactly what you see, because you are the person who built it
They see nothing at all, because a composed set of surfaces cannot be shared
They see more than you, because sharing widens each users access
questions.explanation: Copilot answers do not widen access. Each person sees through their own permissions on every surface, which is why you test as a colleague with narrower access.

questions.q: Why point the grounded part at the specific SharePoint site and folder rather than at everything you can open?
options: Naming the exact sources gives sharper answers and a smaller surface to get wrong than grounding on everything
Copilot can only read one file at a time, so a folder must be reduced to a single document
Broad grounding is blocked by default and has to be requested from an administrator
Naming sources is a cosmetic label that has no effect on the answers
questions.explanation: Tight, named grounding produces sharper answers and less to verify. Grounding on everything invites the wrong document to surface with the same confidence as the right one.

title: Build a real Copilot solution, guided build

content_blocks.text:
Think about the last time something in the building needed fixing: a broken monitor arm, a meeting room with a dead screen, a tap that would not stop dripping. Someone filled in a form or fired off an email, it landed in the wrong inbox, and it sat there. The Power Platform is Microsoft's low-code kit for closing gaps like that. You could build a small app that logs each maintenance request, and a flow that reads every new request and sends it straight to the team that handles it. No developer, no new system to buy, built on the Microsoft 365 your organisation already runs.

This lesson is about knowing what the kit lets you build and when it is the right thing to reach for. From here on you are thinking as a builder, not a spectator.
The three building blocks

The Power Platform is not one tool. It is a connected set of building blocks, and each one solves a different kind of problem. You will rarely use all three at once, but they are designed to click together when you do.

cards.body: Automates a process that repeats. If something happens and then something else should happen, a flow handles it: a request arrives, and the right people get notified or a record gets updated. No code, no server to run.
cards.title: Power Automate

cards.body: Builds a lightweight app when the form or tracker you need does not exist yet. A screen your team fills in on a phone or a laptop, connected to real data, without writing application code.
cards.title: Power Apps

cards.body: Builds a chatbot or conversational agent you publish for others. You define what it handles, connect it to your data, and deploy it where people already work, such as a Teams channel. Good for a helpdesk answering the same questions every day.
cards.title: Copilot Studio

content_blocks.text: What ties them together

All three sit on top of the same ecosystem: Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Dataverse, Teams, Outlook, and hundreds of outside services reached through connectors, Power Platform's own term and a different thing from the MCP connector from the general track. That shared library is the whole point. In the maintenance example, the app that logs the request and the flow that routes it are talking to the same SharePoint list, and the Teams message to the facilities team is just one more connector doing its job. You are not wiring systems together from scratch. The connections already exist, which is why something like this can be standing up in days rather than a project quarter.

Standard connectors cover the everyday Microsoft 365 services most people already have. Premium connectors, including Dataverse, SAP, and Salesforce, need a Power Apps or Power Automate premium licence. Check what your organisation actually holds before you design around a connector you turn out not to be licensed for.
When to reach for it, and when not

The Power Platform is low-code, and that shapes what it is good at. It shines on business logic, process automation, and data-connected screens: approvals, request routing, trackers, internal tools. It is not built for complex algorithms, heavy data processing, applications facing thousands of concurrent users, custom authentication, or a polished consumer front-end. Knowing that ceiling is what stops you promising a "simple app" that quietly turns into a development project.

A useful signal: if a Power Platform solution would need a pile of awkward workarounds just to meet the requirements, ask whether real custom development is the more honest answer. A job that needs human judgment or language rather than fixed rules points the same way, and is often better handed to an AI assistant than a flow.

Speed is the reason to reach for it. A flow that would take a developer days to write in code can often be running the same afternoon, and that changes the economics of what is worth automating. The recurring task that eats twenty minutes of your own week, the request you keep re-typing by hand, is exactly the size of problem this kit was made for. You do not need a team or a mandate to begin. You need one process that annoys you.
What you can do now

You can now tell the three building blocks apart, name the one that fits a given problem, and spot when the honest answer is something outside the Power Platform entirely. The next lesson takes the maintenance idea and shows what a first build actually looks like, with no code involved.

questions.q: A new maintenance request needs to trigger a Teams message to the facilities team the moment it is logged. Which building block is built for that step?
options: Power Apps, because it holds the form
Power Automate, because one event should trigger another action
Copilot Studio, because it talks to people
A connector working on its own
questions.explanation: When something happens and then something else should happen automatically, that is event-driven automation, which is exactly what a Power Automate flow does.

questions.q: Your team wants an application for 8000 external customers, with complex pricing calculations and a fully offline mobile mode. How should you read this against the Power Platform?
options: It fits well, since Power Apps supports all of this natively
It fits once you add the right premium connectors
Several of these requirements sit at or beyond the low-code ceiling, so custom development deserves serious consideration
The right answer is Copilot Studio rather than Power Apps
questions.explanation: External scale, complex calculations, and reliable offline mode are all places where low-code struggles. When multiple requirements crowd the ceiling, that is the signal to weigh custom development.

questions.q: Field staff need a simple screen on their phones to log equipment checks, and no developer is available. Which building block is the natural starting point?
options: A Power Automate flow with a manual trigger
A Copilot Studio bot that asks about each check
A Power Apps app built for a mobile screen
A shared spreadsheet on OneDrive
questions.explanation: A custom mobile screen for structured data entry, built without code, is what Power Apps is for. A flow moves data but does not give people an interface to fill in.

title: What the Power Platform enables and when to reach for it

content_blocks.text:
Somewhere on your team there is a spreadsheet that tracks who has the loan laptop, the spare monitor, the demo kit for client visits. It works until two people edit it at once, or someone takes an item and forgets to update the row, and then nobody quite trusts what it says. That is the kind of small, shared problem Power Apps is built for, and it makes a good first build because you can get a working version running in an afternoon without writing any code.

This lesson walks you through that build end to end: pick the task, decide where the data lives, generate the app, and check it holds up. Keep the target modest. This first build is about seeing the shape of a no-code build once, so the next one is faster.
Scope it small first

The most common mistake on a first build is adding features. Resist it. For the kit tracker, the whole thing is one list of items, who currently has each one, when it went out, and when it is due back. No approvals, no reminders, no reporting yet. You can add those later once the core works.

Write the fields down before you touch the tool: item name, borrower, date out, due back, status. That short list is your whole data model.
Decide where the data lives
A Power App is a front end. It needs somewhere to store the records behind it, and that choice matters more than any screen you design. For a first build you have two sensible options.

cards.body: Good enough for a small team and a few hundred records with simple logic. It is the fastest backend to start with, and your team may already have a SharePoint site to put it on. This is the right choice for the kit tracker.
cards.title: A SharePoint list

cards.body: The stronger foundation when the tool needs relationships between tables, role-based access, or an audit trail of who changed what. Reach for it when the solution has to grow beyond one team or hold sensitive data.
cards.title: Dataverse

content_blocks.text: For a shared kit tracker, a SharePoint list is enough. Create the list first, with the five columns you wrote down, before you open Power Apps. The app is easier to generate when the data structure already exists.
Build the app

You do not have to start on a blank canvas. Power Apps can generate a working app directly from your SharePoint list: a screen to browse all items, a screen to view one record, and a form to add or edit. That gives you something functional in minutes, which you then open in the visual editor and adjust by dragging controls around. There is no code, though more advanced behaviour uses spreadsheet-style formulas.

The exact menu path to generate an app from a list shifts between updates, so follow the current on-screen option rather than a remembered click sequence. The starting point is your SharePoint list, not a blank Power Apps project.

Once the starter app is open, keep your edits light for this first pass. Rename the screens so they read clearly, make sure the form shows the five fields you care about, and set the status field to a simple choice like Out or Returned. That is a complete tool.

There's a second way to get that starting app, and it's worth knowing even if you don't reach for it on this particular build. Instead of generating from your SharePoint list and then dragging controls, you can open a blank canvas and describe the app to Copilot in Power Apps in a sentence or two, something like "an app to track loaned equipment: item name, borrower, date out, due back, status", and it drafts a working app for you, table and all. You can keep talking to it afterwards too: ask it to add a screen, adjust a layout, or add a field, and it edits the app rather than you finding the right control and dragging it into place by hand.

This is Copilot in Power Apps, the assistant built into the app builder itself, not the Microsoft 365 Copilot you meet elsewhere in this hub's Copilot track. Same basic idea, describe what you want and let it draft something, but a different product living inside a different tool, worth naming precisely so the two don't blur together.
Check it actually works

A build is not done when it opens. It is done when someone other than you can use it. Add two or three test records, then hand a colleague a phone, since a kit tracker is something people will reach for on the move. Ask them to loan an item out and mark another one returned, and confirm those changes land back in the SharePoint list where you expect them.

This is also where the one real trap of a no-code build shows up.

Power Apps does not always pull your whole list. When a filter or search cannot be handed to the data source, it works on only the first slice of records, commonly 500 and configurable up to around 2000. This is called delegation. Past that limit, searches can quietly return incomplete results with no error message. A kit tracker sits well under it, so you are fine here. Just know the ceiling exists before you ever point an app at a large list.
A note on where it lives

A new app usually lands in your tenant default environment, which everyone shares. That is fine for trying something out with your team. Before anything beyond your team comes to depend on it, it is worth asking who owns the app after you and whether it belongs in a dedicated environment. Governance has its own lesson later in this track, "Governed, safe use, DLP and connectors"; for a first build, just know the question exists.
What you can do now

You have built a real, shared tool without code, and you have seen the method: scope it small, sort the data first, generate rather than start blank, then test it as a user would. The next lesson takes the automation half of the platform, using Power Automate to handle the steps that should happen on their own, like a reminder when kit is overdue.

questions.q: For the kit tracker (one small team, a single list, a few hundred records), which backend is the best starting point for a first build?
options: Dataverse, to future-proof it from day one
A SharePoint list
SQL Server
A shared Excel file on OneDrive
questions.explanation: For a small, simple, shared tracker a SharePoint list is the fastest backend and entirely enough. Dataverse becomes worth the extra setup when the solution needs relationships, roles, or an audit trail.

questions.q: Six months on, the tracker has grown to 8000 items and users report that search returns incomplete results with no error. What is the most likely cause?
options: SharePoint cannot store that many records
The app has hit the delegation limit and is filtering only a capped local slice of the data
Power Apps needs a premium licence before search works
The list has to be rebuilt in Excel
questions.explanation: When a filter cannot be delegated to the data source, Power Apps works on only the first few hundred records and returns incomplete results silently. This is the delegation limit, and it appears once a list grows large.

questions.q: Which of these is a poor fit for a Power Apps first build?
options: Replacing a shared Excel tracker for a team
A mobile form for staff to log equipment returns
A customer-facing portal for thousands of external users that must work fully offline
An internal tool for logging IT requests
questions.explanation: Large external user scale and reliable offline use sit at or beyond the Power Apps ceiling. The other three are exactly the lightweight, internal, shared scenarios it handles well.

title: Your first build, what's possible without code

content_blocks.text: Kit gets forgotten. It goes out, the due-back date passes, and unless someone happens to notice, it just does not come back. In this lesson you build a flow that watches the kit tracker for anything overdue and chases it automatically: it checks the list once a day, emails the borrower on anything overdue, and tells the kit owner too if a reminder gets ignored.
Scope it before you open the designer

Get three things concrete first. What counts as overdue? How often should the flow check? And what happens if a reminder gets ignored?

For this build: an item is overdue when its Due back date has passed and its Status is still Out (the five columns from your first build). The flow checks once a day. And if the borrower has not returned the item within a week of the first reminder, the kit owner gets looped in too, so this does not rely on the borrower alone.

This is the same shape as a lot of quiet admin you already own: a licence nearing renewal, an invoice sitting unpaid, a review nobody has booked. Build this once and you can rebuild it for any of those.
Set the trigger

Sign in at make.powerautomate.com and create a new scheduled cloud flow from blank. Choose the Recurrence trigger, set it to run once a day, and pick a sensible time, for example 8am.

This is a scheduled flow rather than one that reacts to a single item changing. Nothing has to happen for it to fire; it just checks the whole list on its own timetable, which is exactly right for a question like "what is overdue today" that depends on the current date, not on one record being edited.

The flow runs under the account whose connection it uses. If you build it under your personal login and later change teams, it stops working the day your access changes. For anything the team depends on, set the connection up under a shared or service account.
Find what's overdue

Add a Get items action (SharePoint) pointed at your kit tracker list, and use its Filter Query to ask for exactly the rows you care about: Status eq 'Out' and DueBack lt '@{utcNow()}'. That single query does the checking for you; the flow never has to loop over items that are not overdue.

Everything after this step runs once per row the filter returns, using an Apply to each.
Send the reminder

Inside the Apply to each, add a Send an email action (Office 365 Outlook). Address it to the Borrower field from the current item, and use the item name and due-back date in the message so the email is specific rather than a generic nag: "The demo kit was due back on 4 March and is still showing as out. Please return it or let the team know."

If Due back is ever left blank when an item goes out, the filter has nothing to compare and that item never surfaces as overdue. Make setting the date part of checking an item out, not an optional extra.
Escalate when it stays overdue

A single reminder is easy to ignore. Still inside the loop, add a Condition that compares Due back against a week ago: Due back is less than @{addDays(utcNow(), -7)}. When that is true, send a second email, this time to the kit owner, naming the item, the borrower, and how many days overdue it is. A borrower gets nudged straight away; a genuinely stuck item gets a second set of eyes on it without you checking the list by hand.

cards.body: Recurrence, once a day. Fires on a schedule rather than reacting to one item changing.
cards.title: Trigger

cards.body: Get items with a filter query for Status eq 'Out' and an overdue Due back. Returns exactly the rows that need attention.
cards.title: Find overdue

cards.body: Apply to each overdue row: email the borrower, and add the kit owner once it has been overdue more than a week.
cards.title: Remind and escalate

cards.body: SharePoint and Office 365 Outlook. Both standard, so this build needs no premium licence.
cards.title: Connectors used

content_blocks.text: Keep the cadence sane

This flow runs every day and will happily email the same borrower every single day an item stays overdue. For a kit tracker that is usually fine, a daily nudge is the point, but if you reuse this pattern somewhere a daily email would be too much, add a Last reminded column and only send when it is empty or old enough, so people are not trained to ignore their own reminders.

A scheduled flow that fails silently is worse than no flow at all, because everyone assumes overdue kit is being chased when it is not. Add a failure notification to yourself before you switch this on, not after the first overdue item goes unnoticed for a month.
Catch failures, not just overdue items

Everything so far handles overdue kit. It says nothing about what happens if the flow itself has a bad day, say the Send an email action fails because a mailbox is full or a connection has expired. By default, each action only runs after the one before it succeeds, so a failure like that just stops the run silently partway through; nobody gets the reminder, and nothing tells you it didn't go out.

Every action has a Configure run after option, in its three-dot menu, that lets you add a step for what happens when the previous action is skipped, fails, or times out, not just when it succeeds. Add a second Send an email action after your reminder email, configure it to run only when that email "has failed," address it to yourself, and put the item and borrower in the message. Now a failure surfaces the same day, instead of you finding out a month later that nobody had been chased at all.

Configure run after is easy to miss because the option only appears once an action already exists to attach it to, and it is off by default for every action you add. Power Automate's own analytics view, in the flow's run history, is the other place to check; it shows pass/fail counts over time, which is worth a glance now and then even once you've wired up failure emails.
Verify before you switch it on

Use the Test option and run the flow manually rather than waiting for tomorrow's recurrence. Before you do, edit one test record in the kit tracker so its Due back date is in the past and its Status is still Out, then run the flow and confirm the borrower's email arrives.

Then push that same test record's due-back date more than a week into the past, run the flow again, and confirm the kit owner's escalation email also arrives. Check the run history for both runs so you can see exactly which rows the filter matched.
What you built

You now have the shape every scheduled flow reuses: a recurring trigger, a filtered query for the records that qualify, and an action for each one that matches, with an escalation path for the ones that do not resolve themselves. Swap the overdue kit for a licence nearing renewal, an invoice sitting unpaid, or a review nobody has booked, and the skeleton is the same.

Think about one thing on your own list that quietly goes stale if nobody checks it. What counts as overdue, how often should it be checked, and who needs to know if it stays that way? That is the flow you build next.
A faster way to start next time

You built every piece of this flow by hand: the trigger, the filter, the loop, the escalation. That was worth doing once so you know what each part is actually for. Next time you need something in this shape, you don't have to start from a blank canvas either. Open a new flow and describe it to Copilot in Power Automate instead, something like "check a SharePoint list once a day for items that are overdue, email the borrower, and email the owner too if it's been more than a week", and it drafts a first version of the trigger, filter, and actions for you to check over and adjust.

It won't always get every condition exactly right, particularly anything as specific as the escalation window, so read through what it builds the way you would check anyone else's work before you trust it, but it's a legitimate way to get from nothing to something testable in minutes instead of an hour of clicking through the designer.

This is Copilot in Power Automate, a flow-building assistant, not the Microsoft 365 Copilot from this hub's Copilot track and not Copilot Studio either. It only drafts and edits flows inside Power Automate.

questions.q: Why use a Recurrence trigger instead of a trigger that fires when an item is created or changed?
options: Whether an item is overdue depends on today's date, not on one record being edited, so the flow needs to check the whole list on its own schedule
Recurrence triggers are the only ones that support SharePoint lists
A trigger on item creation cannot read the Due back column
Scheduled flows do not need a connection to run under
questions.explanation: Overdue status changes with the calendar, not with an edit event, so a scheduled check of the whole list is the right shape, unlike a trigger tied to one item changing.

questions.q: Where does the Get items filter query 'Status eq 'Out' and DueBack lt utcNow()' do its work?
options: It returns only the overdue rows up front, so the rest of the flow only has to act on items that actually need a reminder
It deletes items from the list once they are returned
It sends the reminder email directly, without an Apply to each
It only works if the list has fewer than ten items
questions.explanation: The filter query does the checking. Everything downstream, the Apply to each and the escalation condition, only ever sees rows that are genuinely overdue.

questions.q: Why send the escalation email to the kit owner only after an item has been overdue for more than a week, rather than on every run?
options: A single missed reminder is not yet a problem; escalating only once it persists avoids looping in the owner on every ordinary late return
Power Automate cannot send two different emails from the same flow
The kit owner's email address is only available a week after the item goes out
Escalation is required by the connector licence after seven days
questions.explanation: The condition on how long an item has been overdue is what separates a borrower who is a day late from one who has genuinely gone quiet, so the owner only gets pulled in when it is actually worth their attention.

title: Automating a process with Power Automate

content_blocks.text: A flow earns its value by reaching across systems. That same reach is the risk this lesson is about. The moment a flow can read a SharePoint list and write to a personal cloud-storage account in the same run, it can carry data across a boundary your organisation never agreed to. Data policies, still widely called DLP (data loss prevention), are the guardrail that decides which connectors are allowed to touch each other in the first place.
How a data policy draws the line

A data policy sorts every connector into one of three groups: Business, Non-Business, or Blocked. The rule is short. A flow may combine connectors from within a single group, but it cannot mix a Business connector with a Non-Business one in the same flow. A Blocked connector cannot be used at all where the policy applies.

The group names carry no built-in meaning. What matters is the boundary they draw. An administrator places the connectors that handle trusted work data (SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, Dataverse) in one group, and the connectors that reach personal or unvetted services in another. Because the two groups cannot be used together, a flow simply cannot pull customer records from SharePoint and push them out through a personal Dropbox or consumer OneDrive account. The two connectors sit on opposite sides of the line, so the designer will not let them run together.

New connectors are added to the Non-Business group by default when a policy is created. A few core Microsoft connectors, including most standard M365 ones, cannot be placed in the Blocked group at all. This is why the boundary is usually drawn by promoting trusted connectors up into Business. Trying to block everything else outright is rarely practical.
What happens when a flow crosses the line

If a maker builds a flow that combines connectors from two different groups, the flow does not run. It is flagged as a policy violation and suspended until the offending connector is removed. That is the containment working as designed: the data is stopped before it moves, rather than discovered in a log afterwards.

A policy change is retroactive. If an administrator moves a connector into a different group, flows that were already live and combined it across the new boundary stop running and are suspended. Before tightening a policy, check which existing flows use the affected connectors, or you can break working automation with no warning to the people who depend on it.
Where policies are set, and who sets them

Data policies are an administrator control. They are configured in the Power Platform admin center and applied either at the tenant level, across everything, or scoped to specific environments. You cannot set a policy for one individual user. Where several policies apply to the same environment, the most restrictive combination wins, and an environment-level policy cannot loosen a tenant-wide one.

For a manager, this is the lever worth understanding. You do not have to inspect every flow your team builds. You set the boundary once, and the platform enforces it on every flow and app in scope, including ones built after the policy is in place, since new connectors land in the default group automatically. The judgement is in deciding which services count as trusted for which kind of data, and that decision is worth making deliberately.
Before you publish a flow

You do not need to be an administrator to work with this. Anyone building a flow can see which policy applies to their environment and design inside it from the start, which is far cheaper than discovering a violation the day you try to go live. Before you publish, run through these checks.

cards.body: List every destination connector in the flow. Confirm each one is a place your organisation has approved for that kind of data, not just somewhere convenient.
cards.title: Where does the data go

cards.body: If the flow mixes a trusted work connector with an external or personal one, expect it to be blocked. Check the data policy before you build, not after the flow is finished.
cards.title: Will it survive the policy

cards.body: A flow runs with the access of the connection owner, so it can reach everything that account can. A shared service account with scoped access keeps the blast radius small if something goes wrong.
cards.title: What identity runs it

cards.body: Add a failure notification so a suspended or broken flow is noticed by a person, rather than stalling quietly while the process it supports grinds to a halt.
cards.title: Does it fail loudly

questions.q: A flow reads customer data from SharePoint (classified Business) and tries to write it to a personal cloud-storage connector (classified Non-Business). The policy applies to this environment. What happens?
options: The flow is flagged as a policy violation and suspended until the personal storage connector is removed
The flow runs but records a warning in the run history for the administrator to review
The flow runs normally because SharePoint is a standard connector
The flow runs only if the maker has a Power Automate Premium licence
questions.explanation: A Business connector cannot be combined with a Non-Business connector in the same flow. The designer blocks the flow and suspends it before any data moves.

questions.q: An administrator moves a connector into the Blocked group. Some flows already in production use that connector. What is the most likely result?
options: Those flows continue running until each one is next edited
Those flows stop running and are suspended as policy violations
Those flows automatically switch to an approved connector
Nothing changes, because the policy only affects flows built after the change
questions.explanation: Policy changes are retroactive. Live flows that now violate the policy are suspended, which is why the affected flows should be checked before a policy is tightened.

questions.q: Where can a data policy be applied in Power Platform?
options: At the tenant level or scoped to specific environments, but not per individual user
At the level of each individual maker so different people get different rules
Only on premium connectors, since standard connectors carry no data risk
Only inside a single flow, set by whoever built it
questions.explanation: Data policies are set by administrators at the tenant or environment level. They cannot be scoped to one user, and when several apply the most restrictive combination wins.

title: Governed, safe use, DLP and connectors

content_blocks.text: Your kit tracker already works, but right now the only way to flag a damaged or lost item is a stray comment to whoever is nearby. This lesson extends the app you already generated with a phone-friendly screen: whoever has an item can flag it as damaged or lost, add a note, and attach a photo, so the kit owner finds out properly instead of by accident. It is a good next canvas-app skill: extending a generated app with a new screen, not starting from a blank one.
Pick and scope before you open the tool

A well-scoped addition to a canvas app touches one new screen and one or two new columns, not a rebuild. This one fits comfortably: a Flag issue screen reached from an item's details, a note field, a photo, and two new Status options.

Write down the fields before you touch anything. On top of the five columns from your first build, you need a Condition note (what's wrong) and a Photo. Those become new columns on the same list, not a new list.

Resist the urge to redesign the whole tracker while you are in there. This lesson adds one capability: flagging an issue with a photo. A bigger rework, approval routing, reporting, is its own project. Ship the small addition first.
Extend the list first, then the app

The data comes before the interface, same as your first build. Open the kit tracker SharePoint list and add two columns: Condition note (single line of text) and Photo. While you are there, add Damaged and Lost as two more options on the Status choice column, alongside Out and Returned.

Then open the app Power Apps generated from this list back in your first build. You are extending an existing app, not generating a new one, so open it in Power Apps Studio and add a new, blank screen. Name it Flag issue.

cards.body: The gallery of every item, already built in your first build. Add a button on each row that opens the details screen.
cards.title: Browse screen (already built)

cards.body: One item shown in full, already built. Add a Flag an issue button here that navigates to your new screen.
cards.title: Details screen (already built)

cards.body: The new screen. A short form: condition note, a photo, and buttons for Mark as damaged or Mark as lost, each setting Status accordingly on submit.
cards.title: Flag issue screen (new)

content_blocks.text: You are shaping an app that already works rather than building from nothing, which is most of what makes this fast. The new screen is the only genuinely new surface.
Shape the new screen for a phone

Two things make the Flag issue screen genuinely usable on site. First, add photo capture. Power Apps has an Add picture control that lets someone take a photo with the phone camera or choose an existing one; drop it onto the new screen and bind it to the Photo column so the image saves with the item's record.

Second, keep the two buttons doing one job each. Mark as damaged and Mark as lost should each write the Condition note text, the photo, and the matching Status value back to the same list item, then navigate back to the details screen so the person can see it took effect.

Confirm the exact camera or image control and how it writes back to your list against current Power Apps documentation before you rely on it. Saving photos to SharePoint has specific handling, and the control names and behaviour shift between releases. Do not assume a click-path you have not seen on screen.

Setting Status, the note, and the photo on the correct list item when a button is pressed needs a small Power Fx formula on each button's OnSelect, along the lines of Patch(KitTracker, ThisItem, {Status: "Damaged", ConditionNote: TextInput1.Text, Photo: AddPicture1.Photo}). It is a few lines, not a program, and it is the first formula this track has asked you to write directly rather than relying on a generated default.
Verify it, and watch for the trap

Preview the app inside the studio, flag a test item as damaged, and check the record actually updates in your SharePoint list: Status, Condition note, and Photo all present. Then open it on a phone through the Power Apps mobile app and flag one for real, photo and all. Testing on the device it will be used on is not optional for a mobile screen.

Here is the tool-specific trap, and you met its name in your first build: delegation. Your browse screen will look perfect in testing with a dozen items and then quietly return incomplete results once the tracker grows to thousands. For large lists, Power Apps only processes records up to a set limit unless your filter and sort functions are ones the data source can handle itself, and when a formula is not delegable it shows a yellow warning icon on it.

Treat that yellow delegation warning as a real signal, not a cosmetic one. On a list that stays small it rarely bites. On one that grows, it means records past the limit are silently dropped from what your app shows, and nobody notices until a genuinely damaged item goes missing from the view.
For a kit tracker that could grow well past a single team, keep your gallery filters simple and delegable, or plan to move to a data source with broader delegation support if the volume climbs.
Publish, share, reflect

When it works, save and republish from the studio, so the whole team gets the new screen without you sending a new link. It already sits wherever you shared the original app, including a Teams tab if you embedded it there.

Then reflect on the loop you just ran: you extended a real, working app with one new capability, scoped to a single screen and two columns, and verified it on the actual device before trusting it. That loop, extend rather than rebuild, is usually the faster and safer one once an app is already in use.

questions.q: Your kit tracker's browse screen works perfectly in testing with 15 items. Months later, some flagged items are missing from the view, and the list now holds about 4,000 items. What is the most likely cause?
options: The SharePoint list has hit its maximum row limit
A non-delegable filter is only processing records up to the app limit, so the rest are excluded
The connection to SharePoint has expired and needs re-authenticating
The Power Apps mobile app cannot display more than a few hundred records
questions.explanation: This is the classic delegation problem: a filter the data source cannot handle itself only processes records up to the app limit, and anything past that is silently dropped.

questions.q: The Flag issue screen only writes to your existing SharePoint kit tracker and is shared with internal staff. What licensing does it require?
options: Power Apps Premium for every user, because it captures photos
Only the Microsoft 365 licence most staff already have, because SharePoint is a standard connector
A per-app plan for each person who flags an item
Dataverse capacity, because the app writes updates
questions.explanation: SharePoint is a standard connector included with Microsoft 365, so a canvas app built on it and shared internally needs no premium licence, whether it creates records or updates existing ones.

questions.q: Why does setting Status, the note, and the photo on a button press need a Power Fx formula here, when the rest of the app so far has not?
options: A generated form saves its own fields automatically, but a custom action on a button, updating a specific item from a specific screen, has to be written explicitly
Power Apps cannot save photos without a formula anywhere in the app
Formulas are only needed once a list passes the delegation limit
The generated screens do not support any user input
questions.explanation: The generated browse, details, and edit screens save through their own built-in logic. A custom screen and button you added yourself needs its action written out, which is where a short Patch formula comes in.

content_blocks.text: This still leaves a gap. Anyone can check out any item right now, including the ones you can now flag as high-value or repeatedly damaged. The next lesson adds one more layer: certain items need a manager's sign-off before they leave the building, and that sign-off is a Power Automate flow working together with this app for the first time in this track.

title: Building a no-code app with Power Apps

content_blocks.text:
Until now you have built the pieces of the kit tracker apart. In Band 2 you made a flow that ran on its own, in "Automating a process with Power Automate," chasing overdue items on a schedule. In the last lesson, "Building a no-code app with Power Apps," you extended the app to flag damaged or lost items. This capstone joins app and flow for the first time: the app captures a request, and the automation decides what happens to it.

The task: certain items, the demo kit, anything above a value you set, need a manager's sign-off before they can leave the building. Someone requests to check one out through the app: which item, why, how long. The moment they submit, if the item needs sign-off, a flow routes it to their manager for approval and emails them the outcome. No one copies anything from one place to another. This is what separates owning two tools from running a platform.
Pick a task where the handoff is the point

Choose something in your own work that has a capture step and a routing step. A checkout sign-off works because it has both: a person supplies information, then that information needs to travel to someone else and come back with a decision. Expense pre-approval, equipment loans, and access requests all share the shape.

Avoid anything where the decision has real legal or financial weight for a first build. You want a process where a wrong route or a missed notification is an annoyance, not an incident. A kit sign-off sits comfortably there.
Scope it: extend the shared table first

Here is the part that separates a platform from two disconnected toys. The app and the flow do not talk to each other directly. They meet in a data source, and that data source is the contract between them. Get it right before you touch either half.

Rather than building a new table from scratch, extend the kit tracker list itself, the same one from your first build. Add a Sign-off status column (choice: Not required, Pending, Approved, Rejected) and a Requested by column. The status field is the channel: the app sets it to Pending on submit for an item that needs sign-off, the flow changes it to Approved or Rejected, and the app reads it back so the borrower can see where things stand.

Design Sign-off status as a fixed choice set (Not required, Pending, Approved, Rejected), not free text. Both halves read and write it, and a typo like "Aproved" that the flow never matches is the kind of bug that only shows up in front of a real borrower.

Add the columns to the same kit tracker list before you open Power Apps or Power Automate, because both will point at it. This is the payoff of having kept everything in one table from the start: there is nothing new to wire up, only two columns to add to something that already works.
Build the app half

Add a Request checkout screen to the same app you extended in the previous lesson, "Building a no-code app with Power Apps." Let the borrower pick an item, state why and for how long, and submit. On submit, the screen sets Sign-off status to Pending if the item is flagged as needing sign-off, or leaves it Not required and marks the item straight out otherwise. The borrower should never see or set their own sign-off status.

Keep the app honest about what it does not control. Once a request is Pending, the borrower waits; the app cannot show a decision that has not happened yet. A simple read-only view of their own requests with the current status is enough, and it is the payoff for wiring Sign-off status through both halves.
Build the automation half

Now the flow. Because you are extending the same list rather than writing to a fresh table, the trigger has to watch for changes, not new rows: use "When an item is created or modified" pointed at the kit tracker, then add a Condition that only continues when Sign-off status equals Pending. That condition is what stops the flow reacting to every ordinary edit, including its own.

The middle of the flow is an approval. Power Automate has a built-in approval action that sends a request to a named person and waits for their response before continuing. Feed it the manager for this borrower. When the response comes back, the flow writes Approved or Rejected to Sign-off status, sets the item's own Status to Out and fills in Date out on an approval, and emails the borrower the result.

A flow that triggers on any change to a row and also writes back to that same row can trigger itself in a loop, and here you are triggering on modified rows deliberately, so the guard matters even more than usual. The Sign-off status condition is what prevents that: once the flow's own write sets the status away from Pending, the next trigger for that row finds the condition false and stops. Test this before you leave it running; a loop can fire a lot of approvals fast.
Verify the two halves as one system

Do not test the app and the flow separately and call it done. The whole reason you built this is the handoff, so verify the handoff. Submit a real checkout request through the app for an item flagged as needing sign-off, using a test account, then watch the flow run history to confirm it triggered, check the approval actually reached the manager, respond to it, and confirm both the email arrived and the item's Status and Sign-off status updated back in the app.

Run the rejection path too, not just the happy one. A system that only works when everyone says yes is half-tested. Reject a request and confirm the borrower is told clearly, and that the item stays available rather than sitting on Pending. Also request an item that does not need sign-off and confirm it checks straight out with no approval step at all.

Approvals route to real inboxes and Teams. During testing, point the manager field at yourself or a test account so you are not sending live approval requests to a colleague who has no idea what your capstone is.

cards.body: Borrower submits the request. The app sets Sign-off status to Pending for flagged items. It never sets the outcome itself.
cards.title: App writes

cards.body: A row modified to Pending starts the flow. It reads the manager and sends the approval, then waits for a response.
cards.title: Flow triggers

cards.body: On response, the flow sets Sign-off status to Approved or Rejected, updates Status and Date out on approval, and emails the borrower.
cards.title: Flow writes back

cards.body: The borrower sees the updated status in their view. Nobody copied anything between the two tools.
cards.title: App reads back

content_blocks.text: Package it as one thing

The lesson title calls this a combined solution for a reason. In Power Platform a solution is a container that holds the app and the flow together, along with the table if you built it in Dataverse, so they move and deploy as a unit rather than loose pieces someone has to reassemble. Building your capstone inside one solution from here on means you can hand the whole system to someone else, or promote it from a test environment to a live one, without leaving a half behind.
Share it, and keep it maintained

Packaging the app and flow into one solution answers how you move this system somewhere else. A separate question is who else can touch it once it's live, and what you do when a change breaks something. Both halves need an answer before this capstone is really done.

For the flow: right now, you are its only owner, and it runs under the connection you built it with. Add a co-owner, someone else on the team who understands what it does, so it survives you changing roles or being on leave; a co-owner can see the run history and edit the flow the same way you can. If someone just needs to trigger it manually without touching the logic, run-only access is the better fit: they can start it and see whether it succeeded, and nothing more.

For the app: every time you publish, Power Apps keeps the version you're replacing. If a change breaks something, a renamed field a formula still expects, a control reference that no longer resolves, open the app's version history and restore the last version that worked, rather than trying to unpick the change by hand with people already unable to check kit out.

Restoring an app version only rolls back the app. It doesn't touch the kit tracker list or the flow, so if the actual break was in your data or your flow logic, rolling back the app will look like it fixed things and won't have. Check all three parts, app, list, flow, before you assume a version restore is the whole answer.
Reflect

Step back and notice what the integration actually required. The hard part was not building an app or building a flow; you could already do both. It was extending one shared table so the two halves spoke the same language, and being disciplined about which half owns which field. The app owns what the borrower asks for. The flow owns the decision. Sign-off status is where they meet.

That pattern travels. Any time a capture step needs to trigger a routed decision and report back, it is the same three moves: a shared table, a trigger on the write, and a status the automation owns and the app reads. You started this track with a flat list of who has what. You are finishing it with a kit tracker that flags problems, chases the overdue, and gates the items that need a decision before they go out the door, all as one system.

questions.q: What actually makes the app and the flow work as one system?
options: They share a single data source, and the flow triggers on what the app writes
The app calls the flow directly through a button-to-flow API
They must use the same premium connector licence
They run inside the same browser tab at the same time
questions.explanation: The two tools do not call each other. They meet at a shared table: the app writes Sign-off status to Pending, and that write is what starts the flow.

questions.q: Why design Sign-off status as a fixed choice set before building either half?
options: Both halves read and write it, so a mismatched value silently breaks the handoff
Fixed choices make the app load faster
Power Automate cannot read text fields at all
It is the only field type approvals accept
questions.explanation: The status is the channel between the app and the flow. If the values do not match exactly, the flow never recognises them and the borrower is left on Pending.

questions.q: The flow triggers on "created or modified" and also writes back to the same row. What stops it looping?
options: The condition that only continues when Sign-off status equals Pending, so the flow's own write (setting it away from Pending) stops the next trigger from re-entering
The app will refuse to open the table
The approval email will be sent in plain text only
Sign-off status resets to blank each night
questions.explanation: A trigger that fires on any change and also writes back can re-trigger itself. The Pending-only condition is what breaks the loop, since the flow's own write moves the row out of the state the condition checks for.

questions.q: Why build the checkout sign-off app and flow inside one Power Platform solution from here on, rather than as two separate pieces?
options: A solution packages the app, flow, and table together so the whole system moves and deploys as one unit
Solutions are required before Power Automate allows an approval action
Building outside a solution disables premium connectors
A solution automatically tests the app and flow before you publish them
questions.explanation: A solution is a container that holds the app, flow, and table together, so the system can be handed off or promoted to a live environment without reassembling loose pieces.

content_blocks.text: You have now built the two things this track teaches, working together as a platform rather than side by side, on the same kit tracker you started with. That is the capstone.

title: Combined solution build (app + automation together), guided build

content_blocks.text:
Most of the tools you have met so far help you think, write, or find things faster. Lovable is a different kind of tool: you describe the app you want in plain language, and it builds working software you can open in a browser and share with other people.

That is the shift worth holding onto. You describe an outcome in plain words and get back something that actually runs, without writing code or filling in a template.
Where Lovable fits

You already know the difference between a job that needs a document and a job that needs a small tool other people will use. Lovable is for the second kind. When the thing you need is not a summary or a draft but a place where a few colleagues enter information and see it laid out, that is when Lovable earns its place.

Take the internal tool you keep meaning to build. Say the quarterly objectives your team sets each cycle live in a spreadsheet nobody enjoys opening, and half the entries have gone stale by week three. What you actually want is a simple page where each person adds their objectives and everyone can see them together. Historically that meant a developer, a backlog, and a wait. Lovable lets you describe that page and have a working version in front of you the same afternoon.

Lovable produces real software, which means it carries real consequences. Before you share an app that collects anything sensitive, or point colleagues at it as the source of truth, treat it the way you would any tool going live: check what it stores, who can see it, and whether it does what you claimed. A confident-looking app can still be wrong.
When to reach for it, and when not

cards.body: A small, well-scoped tool a handful of people will use: collecting inputs, showing them back, a light internal workflow. You can describe what it should do in a few plain sentences.
cards.title: A good fit

cards.body: A one-off answer, a document, or analysis you need once. If nobody has to use it as software afterwards, a chat assistant or a spreadsheet gets you there faster than building an app.
cards.title: Reach for something else

content_blocks.text: If you lead a team, the same instinct covers the small tools you would never get budget to commission. If you do not, it covers the ones you would otherwise build by hand in a spreadsheet and maintain forever. Either way the judgement is the same: has this job quietly turned into a tool other people will use?

The skill this module builds is not learning to drive every button. It is recognising the moment a job has become a tool, and knowing you can now build that tool yourself. The next lesson takes the objectives page from idea to something running.

questions.q: When is Lovable the right tool to reach for?
options: When you need a small app that several people will use to enter and view information
When you need a quick answer to a one-off question
When you want to summarise a long document
When you need last quarter numbers pulled from a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Lovable builds working software for a group to use, not one-off answers a chat assistant handles faster.

questions.q: What does Lovable actually produce?
options: A working app you can open in a browser and share
A written plan describing how to build the app
A spreadsheet template you fill in by hand
Source code you must compile yourself before anyone can use it
questions.explanation: You describe the app in plain language and get back software that runs, not just a plan or a template.

questions.q: You have built an internal app in Lovable that will hold the objectives your colleagues enter. What should you do before sharing it widely?
options: Check what it stores, who can access it, and that it behaves as you claimed
Nothing further, since an app that runs is an app that is correct
Rewrite it in a traditional programming language first
questions.explanation: A confident-looking app can still be wrong or expose data, so verify behaviour and access before it goes live.

title: What Lovable is and when to use it

content_blocks.text: In Lovable you build by describing. That makes the first sentence you write matter more than any button you press, so a few minutes spent scoping pays off fast.

You met Lovable in the previous lesson, "What Lovable is and when to use it," as the tool for turning a described idea into a working web app. This lesson walks you through doing it once, end to end, with a small real task: a lending tracker for your team library, the shelf of books and kit that people borrow and keep forgetting to return.
Pick a task worth building

Choose something small, real, and yours. The lending tracker works well as a first build because you already know exactly how it should behave: someone picks an item, records who took it and when, and the list shows what is currently out. You do not need anyone else to sign off, and you will know within a minute whether the result is right. That fast, personal feedback loop is what makes it a good first build, whether or not you manage a team.
Scope it before you type
Lovable builds roughly what you describe, so decide the shape of version one first. Keep it to what the tracker genuinely needs on day one, and hold everything else back.

cards.body: A list of items, each with a title, a type such as book or device, and a status of available or out.
cards.title: What it holds

cards.body: Borrow and return: record who took an item, then mark it back in later.
cards.title: The main action

cards.body: Your team, on a shared link. No logins for a first version.
cards.title: Who uses it

cards.body: Reminders, overdue chasing, and reports can wait. Keep version one small.
cards.title: What to leave out

content_blocks.text: Describe your first version

Open Lovable and start a new project. In the prompt box, describe the app in plain language, working straight from your scope above. There is no code to write and no database to choose. You are telling Lovable what the app is for and how it should behave, and it builds from there. Writing a clear prompt is a skill the general track's "How to write a good prompt" (How to prompt well) already covered, so here you are just applying it to a build.

A description for the tracker might read: build a lending tracker for a team library. Show a list of items, each with a title, a type of book or device, and a status of available or out. Let someone borrow an item by entering their name, which marks it out and records the date. Let anyone mark an item as returned.
Watch it come together

Lovable generates a first version and shows it in a live preview. This is the moment the tool is built around: you describe, and something runnable appears. Click through it the way a colleague would. Add an item, borrow it, and mark it returned.
Verify it does the job

Test against your scope, not against how polished it looks. Run the one path that matters: can you borrow an item and watch it change to out, then return it and watch it change back? Check the smaller things against your scope note too, such as whether the type field offers book and device. If the model produced something plausible but wrong, you will only catch it by trying the real path, because a confident-looking screen is no proof that it works.

Before you share the link, check what happens to your data. A first generated version may reset when the page reloads, or may save entries somewhere everyone with the link can read. Confirm where entries are stored and who can reach the app before you put any real names into it.
Reflect

Notice where the app did something you did not ask for, or missed something you assumed it would know. That gap between your description and what appeared is the raw material for the next lesson, where you refine the app by describing the changes you want. Keep your scope note as well. It is the checklist that tells you when version one is actually done, rather than when it merely looks finished.

questions.q: Why does scoping the tracker matter before you describe it in Lovable?
options: Because Lovable cannot build anything until you have listed every future feature
Because Lovable builds roughly what you describe, so a clear scope leads to a closer first version
Because the tool charges more for longer descriptions
questions.explanation: Lovable builds from your description, so deciding the shape of version one first gives it something concrete to build.

questions.q: What is the right way to check the first generated version?
options: Confirm it looks polished and professional
Count how many features it included
Run the core path against your scope, such as borrowing an item and returning it
questions.explanation: A confident-looking screen is no proof it works; testing the real path against your scope is.

questions.q: What should you confirm before sharing the app link with your team?
options: Where entries are stored and who can reach the link
Whether the colours match your brand
How fast the preview loaded
questions.explanation: A first version may not persist data or may expose it to anyone with the link, so check storage and access before adding real names.

title: Building your first app

content_blocks.text:
Your first version of the app exists. It runs, it roughly does the job, and now you can see everything about it that is not quite right: a field in the wrong place, a list that should be filterable, a layout that looks fine on your laptop and breaks on a phone. Iterating is how you close that gap. In Lovable you do it the same way you built the first version, by describing what you want in the chat panel, except now each request is a small correction rather than the whole app.

You already know the describe, check, refine loop from the general track's "Working iteratively" (How to prompt well). This lesson is about how that loop behaves inside Lovable specifically, where every request you type can regenerate part of a working app you would rather not break.

The tool-specific catch: a broad instruction gets a broad rewrite. Ask Lovable to "make the tracker better" and you cannot predict what it changes. Ask it to "add a dropdown to filter the item list by type, book or device" and you can check exactly one thing afterwards.
Three ways to make a change

Lovable gives you three distinct modes for this kind of work, and reaching for the right one is what actually keeps a small change small. Plan mode is for thinking before you touch anything: sketch out an approach, ask questions about how the lending tracker currently works, or work out how a fix should land before you commit to it. Agent mode is the one that actually rewrites the app based on what you type in chat, and it is what you have been using for every prompt so far. Visual Edits lets you click directly on an element in the preview, the item title, a button, a spacing gap, and adjust it on the spot, without writing a prompt at all.

For something as small as changing the form heading from "Log an item" to "Borrow or return," Visual Edits is usually faster and safer than describing it in words. Save Agent mode for anything that touches behaviour or layout logic, like the type filter, and reach for Plan mode when a change is big enough that you want to think it through before you commit to a direction.

Picking the wrong mode costs more than it saves. Describing a one-word heading change in a full sentence to Agent mode risks it touching more than the heading, when Visual Edits would only ever change what you clicked.
Change one thing at a time

The habit that makes iteration manageable is scoping each request to a single change. Type one clear instruction, let the app rebuild, then look at the preview before you type the next one. This is slower than listing five fixes in one message, and it is worth it: when something goes wrong, you know which request caused it, because only one thing changed.

Take the lending tracker from the previous lesson, "Building your first app." You have a running list of items and a borrow-and-return form. You want three improvements: a filter by item type, a fix for the title that wraps badly on a phone, and a confirmation message after someone borrows or returns an item. Resist the urge to ask for all three at once. Do the filter, check it, then move on.
Describe the change, and where it goes
When you request a change, say what you want and where it belongs. Lovable is editing a real interface, so location matters as much as behaviour.

cards.body: Add a dropdown above the item list that filters by type: book or device.
cards.title: Add a feature

cards.body: After someone borrows or returns an item, show a confirmation message instead of reloading the page.
cards.title: Change behaviour

cards.body: On narrow screens the item title overlaps the status badge. Stack them vertically below a certain width.
cards.title: Fix layout

cards.body: Change the form heading from Log an item to Borrow or return.
cards.title: Adjust content

content_blocks.text: Notice that each of these names a specific element and what it should do. That is the tool mechanic. How to write a clear instruction in general is covered in the general track's "How to write a good prompt" (How to prompt well); here the point is simply to keep each Lovable request narrow and anchored to a part of the screen you can point at.
When a change makes it worse

Sometimes a request does the wrong thing, or fixes one part and breaks another. This is normal, and it is why you change one thing at a time. Lovable keeps a history of versions as you go, so a bad change is not permanent. You can go back to the version before your last request and try describing it differently.

Do not keep piling new instructions on top of a broken state, hoping the next one will sort it out. That tends to compound the mess. When a change goes wrong, revert to the last good version first, then re-describe the change more precisely.

If a request half-worked, it is often better to revert and rephrase than to patch the patch. "The filter appeared but it is below the list, move it above" is a fine follow-up. But if the whole page has scrambled, going back a step is faster than talking the tool out of a state it should never have entered.

Revert handles one bad step. But sometimes it is not one broken request, it is the whole project that has drifted somewhere you do not want it, after a long session of small compromises stacked on top of each other and nothing single to point at and undo. For that, remix the project instead: Lovable clones the app at a version you choose into a fresh copy, so the working history stays intact and you can try a different direction from there without risking the version you already have. Use revert for "that last change broke it." Reach for remix when the build itself feels tangled and what you want is a clean copy to continue from, not one more patch on top of the mess.
Remixing is also how you safely try something risky: clone the lending tracker before a change you are unsure about, and experiment on the copy instead of the version people are already using.
Fixing layout and mobile issues

Layout problems are the ones you are most likely to miss, because you build on a wide screen and the break only shows on a narrow one. In the lending tracker, the item title and its available/out status might sit side by side comfortably on a laptop and then collide on a phone.

Check the app at a narrow width. Lovable shows a live preview, and there is usually a way to view it at a phone-sized width or open it on your actual phone. When you find a problem, describe it in terms of what should happen at that size: "on narrow screens, stack the title above the status instead of side by side". Describing the symptom and the screen size gives the tool something concrete to correct.

Verify visually, do not assume. A fluent "Done, the layout is now responsive" in the chat is not proof. Look at the preview at the width where it was breaking. This is the same reason you check any AI output: confident wording is not evidence that it worked.
Knowing when to stop

Iteration ends when the app is usable, not when it is perfect. Before each new request, ask whether the thing you are about to change would actually stop someone using the app, or whether it is polish you can leave. For an internal lending-tracker tool, "people can find an item, filter it by type, and borrow or return it without the page looking broken on a phone" is usually the finish line.

A practical way to converge: keep a short list of what still bothers you, fix the ones that block use, and consciously decide to stop on the rest. The loop can run forever if you let it. Deciding it is good enough is part of the skill, whether you are shipping this to a team or just using it yourself.

questions.q: You want to add a filter by item type, fix a mobile layout bug, and change a heading in your lending-tracker app. What is the most reliable way to make these changes in Lovable?
options: Describe all three changes in one message so the app rebuilds once
Make one change, check the preview, then request the next
Rebuild the app from scratch with all three included in the original description
Request the two visual changes together and the filter separately
questions.explanation: Changing one thing at a time means that if something breaks, you know which request caused it.

questions.q: A change you requested has scrambled the whole page. What should you do first?
options: Type more instructions to talk the tool back into shape
Revert to the last good version, then re-describe the change
Accept the new version and fix the pieces one by one
Start a completely new app
questions.explanation: Reverting to a known-good version is faster and cleaner than patching a broken state with more requests.

questions.q: The chat says the layout is now responsive. What confirms it actually is?
options: The confident wording in the chat reply
A second request asking it to double-check
Viewing the preview at the narrow width where it was breaking
The fact that no error appeared
questions.explanation: Fluent output is not proof; you check the app at the width where the problem showed.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can take a rough first app and steer it toward something usable: scoping each request to one change, saying where on the screen it belongs, reverting when a change goes wrong, and checking the result at the size where it matters. The next lesson takes this loop further, using it to build a real app from a description end to end.

title: Iterating on your app

content_blocks.text: You have already watched Lovable respond to your descriptions and reshape an app as you talk to it. This lesson names what you were doing and turns it into a repeatable method. You will build one real app end to end, from a plain description to something you could put in front of people, by directing a machine that writes the code for you.
What vibe coding is

Vibe coding is building real, working software by describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI write the code. The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025, and it captures something new: someone with no coding background can go from an idea to a working app in an afternoon, without touching syntax.

The roles are worth stating plainly. You describe the intent, the model writes the implementation, and you check whether it did what you meant. You are the product owner and the tester. The model is the developer. You do not need to understand every line it produces. You need to understand what the app is supposed to do and whether it does it.

Vibe coding is not AI doing everything. It is you staying in charge while the model handles the code. The moment you stop steering and just accept whatever appears, you have stopped vibe coding and started gambling.

For a manager, this is the real payoff: you can validate an idea yourself before you ask anyone to build it properly. It is also a foothold if you have no team at all. A recurring manual task that ends in a file or a form can often become a small tool you direct into existence in an hour.
Pick a task worth building

The build for this lesson is a conference session-feedback collector: a short form an attendee fills in after a session, plus a simple way to read what came back. It is a good candidate for a reason. The scope is small, the group of users is defined, and if it has a rough edge nobody is harmed. Anyone who runs a workshop, a training session, or an internal talk has this exact need, so it is a real job rather than a toy.

Not everything belongs here. A quick internal tool with a handful of users and low stakes is the sweet spot. Something that will handle sensitive data, serve hundreds of people, or need to keep running for years is a different kind of project, and pushing a described-in-an-afternoon build into that role creates problems someone else has to clean up. Keep your first builds firmly in the small-and-internal zone.
Scope before you describe

Here is the specific challenge of vibe coding, the one that separates a clean build from a frustrating one. The model is quick to start typing. If your description is vague, it will fill every gap with a reasonable guess, and reasonable guesses are often wrong for your situation. By the time you notice, the app is built on the wrong assumption.

So the work happens before the first prompt. You do not need diagrams. You need to answer four questions about the thing you are building.

cards.body: The inputs a person gives. For the collector: the session name, a rating out of five, and a written comment. Name these first so the model does not invent its own fields.
cards.title: What goes in

cards.body: The result you want back. Here it is a saved response and a simple view of average ratings and comments you can read at a glance.
cards.title: What comes out

cards.body: The steps in the middle. A person submits the form, the app stores the response, and it shows a confirmation. Each step is something the model has to get right.
cards.title: What happens between

cards.body: The edge cases. Someone submits an empty form, or sends the same rating twice. Decide now what should happen, or the model will decide for you.
cards.title: What could go wrong

content_blocks.text: Ten minutes answering these gives you a brief. That brief is the thing you describe to Lovable, and it is worth keeping in a note so you can refer back to it and stay consistent as the build grows.
