The most common vibe coding mistake is describing a feature you have not scoped. "Add a way to see the results" gives the model nothing to aim at. "Show a page listing every comment with the average rating at the top" gives it a target you can actually check against.
Describe the first version

Do not describe the whole app at once. Build the smallest version that does the one thing that matters, confirm it works, then add the rest. This is the minimum viable product idea applied to a build: get the core flow right before you polish anything.

For the collector, the core flow is submit a response and store it. Your first description to Lovable might be:

Build a simple web app for collecting feedback after a conference session. Show a form with the session name, a rating from one to five, and a comment box. When someone submits, save the response and show a short thank-you message.

Lovable builds a working version and shows it in the preview. Once that flow holds up, you layer on the next piece as its own request: a results view that lists the comments and shows the average rating. After that, perhaps a way to choose which session the feedback is for. One request, one thing to check, every time.

This rhythm is what keeps a build recoverable. When you add a feature and something breaks, you know which change caused it, because you only made one. A single giant prompt that produces a tangle gives you no such handle.
Check it does what you meant

A preview that looks right is not proof that it works. This is the same reason you learned to verify any AI output in the general track's "How to verify AI output" (Using AI safely): fluency is not evidence. A confident-looking app can still do the wrong thing.

So test it as a real attendee would. Open the preview, fill in the form, and submit. Did the thank-you message appear? Now try the edge case you scoped: submit an empty form and see whether it behaves the way you decided it should. Check the results view against what you actually entered. You are not reading the code. You are driving the app and comparing what it does to the brief you wrote.

When something is off, describe the gap, do not just say "fix it". "The rating saved as text instead of a number, so the average is wrong" points the model straight at the problem. Vague reports get vague fixes.

Making those responses persist for real attendees, and getting the app to a shareable link, is its own step. The next lesson covers it: deploying, sharing, and connecting your app to data. For now, verify the behaviour and shape in the preview.
What you can now do

You can take a real, small need and turn it into a working app by describing it, scoping before you build, and checking each step against what you meant. That is the whole method, and it is the same one whether you are collecting session feedback or sorting a folder of files.

The judgment matters more than the speed. Knowing what to build, scoping it clearly, and staying honest about when a job has outgrown a described-in-an-afternoon tool is what makes this a skill rather than a party trick.

questions.q: Before you describe your feedback collector to Lovable, you spend ten minutes writing down what goes in, what comes out, and what should happen if someone submits an empty form. Why is this worth doing?
options: It is not; the model builds better apps when you let it make these decisions itself
A clear brief means the model fills fewer gaps with its own guesses, so you get closer to what you meant on the first build
Lovable cannot start a build until you upload a written specification
It lets you skip testing the app afterwards
questions.explanation: Vague descriptions get filled in with reasonable-sounding guesses that may not match your situation. Scoping first gives the model a target you can check against.

questions.q: You want the collector to store responses, show a results view, let you filter by session, and email you a weekly summary. What is the best way to build it?
options: Describe all four features in one detailed prompt so the model builds them together
Get the core flow working first, storing a submitted response, then add each further feature as its own step and check it
Build the weekly email first because it is the hardest part
Skip the results view, since a no-code tool cannot display data back to you
questions.explanation: Getting the smallest working version right first, then layering features one at a time, keeps each change testable and easy to trace if it breaks something.

questions.q: A colleague with no coding background wants to build the session-feedback collector for an internal workshop of about thirty people. Is this a reasonable thing to vibe code?
options: No, any app with a form needs a professional developer
Yes; a small internal tool with limited users and low stakes is a good fit, and directing the build takes clear description rather than coding skill
Only if the colleague learns a programming language first
Yes, but only if it is going to become the company-wide standard feedback system
questions.explanation: Small, internal, low-stakes tools are the sweet spot for vibe coding, and describing intent clearly is the skill that matters, not writing code.

title: Vibecoding, build a real app by describing it

content_blocks.text: From working preview to a live link

In the last lesson, "Vibecoding, build a real app by describing it," you built the feedback collector by describing it, and it ran in the preview. The preview is only visible to you inside the editor. To let anyone else open it, you publish the app, which gives it a real web address you can share. This lesson walks through publishing, sharing that link, and connecting the app to a store so the responses people submit are actually kept.

Publishing and saving data are two separate steps. A published app can look finished and still be throwing away every response, because a form needs somewhere to write to before it keeps anything. Do the data connection before you send the link out.
Step 1: Publish the app

Open your project in Lovable and use the publish control in the editor. Publishing builds the current version of your app and puts it on a public web address. The first time, you will get a default address provided by Lovable; you can attach your own custom domain later if you need the link to sit under your organisation.

Give it a moment to build. When it finishes, you have a live URL that loads the same app you saw in the preview, now reachable by anyone who has the link.

A published Lovable link is public to anyone who opens it. There is no sign-in wall unless you build one. Do not use a plain published form to collect anything sensitive, and assume the address can be forwarded on.
Add a sign-in wall, if you need one

You do not have to leave it open. If the feedback you are collecting is sensitive, or you only want your own team submitting responses, ask Lovable directly for it: a prompt like "add email and Google sign-in, and require someone to be signed in before they can open the feedback form" is enough. Lovable wires up a sign-in screen and gates that one route, while anything else you have published, a public landing page, for instance, stays reachable without it. You do not have to protect the whole app to protect the part that matters.

Lovable's sign-in runs on the same backend you just connected the data to, so identities and responses live in one place. If you want to see exactly what gets created before you ask for it on something you plan to send to a wide audience, Lovable's "Add Authentication" page in its Go Deeper section and the official Supabase-auth walkthrough video both step through it end to end.
Step 2: Connect a place to keep the responses

A form on its own does not remember anything. When someone submits the feedback collector, that response has to be written somewhere, or it is gone the moment the page closes. Lovable connects to a hosted data store for exactly this, so your app can save each submission as a row and you can read them back later.

In the editor, open the data or backend integration option and connect a data store. You will be asked to authorise the connection and, for the feedback collector, to have a table that holds each response: who submitted it, the rating or comment, and the time it came in. Once the app is wired to that table, every submission from the live link lands there as a new record.

Describe the data step the same way you described the app. A prompt like "save each submitted response to the connected database and show me a confirmation message" lets Lovable wire the form to the table for you, rather than you configuring it by hand.
Step 3: Verify before you share

This is the step people skip, and it is the one that saves you. Open the live URL yourself, in a private browser window so you are not signed in as the builder, and submit a test response the way an attendee would. Then check that the response actually appears in your connected data store.

If the submission shows up as a new row, the whole chain works: live link, form, and storage. If it does not, the form is not connected to the table yet, and you have caught it before anyone real hit a dead form.

cards.body: Build the current version and get a public web address for the app.
cards.title: Publish

cards.body: Wire the form to a hosted store so each submission is saved as a record.
cards.title: Connect data

cards.body: Submit a test response on the live link and confirm it lands in the store.
cards.title: Verify

cards.body: Send the confirmed link to attendees, with any custom domain attached.
cards.title: Share

content_blocks.text: Step 4: Share the link

Now send the URL to your attendees. Because it is a normal web address, you can drop it into an email, a calendar invite, a chat message, or a QR code on a slide. Anyone who opens it gets the current published version.

One thing to know about updates: changes you make in the editor do not go live until you publish again. You can keep editing safely, because attendees stay on the last published version until you push a new one. When you are happy with a change, publish again and the same link updates for everyone.
Republishing reuses the same address, so a link you have already shared keeps working after an update. You do not need to send a new URL each time you change the app.
If you are an individual contributor

None of this needs a team or a budget. If you are the one running a workshop, a retro, or a sign-up sheet, you can publish a small collector, connect it to a store, and have real responses arriving in minutes, without filing a ticket or waiting on a platform team. The verify step is where you earn trust in it: once you have watched your own test response land in the table, you can send the link out knowing it holds.

questions.q: Why should you connect a data store before sharing a published feedback form?
options: A published form discards every submission until it is wired to a place that keeps the responses
Publishing is slower once data is connected, so it must be done first
The link will not load at all without a connected store
questions.explanation: Publishing makes the app reachable, but a form only keeps submissions once it is connected to a store to write them to.

questions.q: You edit the app after sharing the link. What do attendees see?
options: The last published version, until you publish again
Your unpublished edits immediately
A broken link until you republish under a new address
questions.explanation: Edits stay in the editor until you publish; attendees remain on the last published version, and republishing updates the same link.

questions.q: What is the point of submitting a test response in a private browser window before sharing?
options: It checks the live public link and the storage the way a real attendee would experience them
It publishes the app for you
It hides the app from search engines
questions.explanation: A private window is not signed in as the builder, so it mirrors what an attendee hits and confirms the response reaches the store.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can take an app from a private preview to a live link, give it somewhere to keep the data people send, confirm the whole chain works, and share it. That is the full loop for a builder-tool app: describe, build, publish, connect, verify, share. From here, the same steps scale from a one-off feedback collector to any small tool your team keeps asking for.

title: Deploying, sharing, and connecting your app to data

content_blocks.text: You already know the general landscape: a handful of AI tools, each better at some jobs than others. This lesson is narrower. It is about one of them, Claude, and the honest question of when it earns a place in your day and when it does not.
The kind of work Claude is for

Claude is at its best when a job needs reading, reasoning, and writing held together at once. Picture forty pages of customer feedback landing in your inbox before a planning meeting. You do not need every quote. You need to know what people are actually asking for, which complaints repeat, and which two or three themes should shape next quarter. That is the work: judgement over a large, messy pile of text that no single glance can hold.

Hand that to Claude and you are using it for what it does well. You paste or upload the feedback, ask for the recurring themes with examples, and then push back where the summary feels thin. The read that only you can give, the call on what matters for your team, stays yours. The slog of getting from forty pages to a shaped starting point is what you have offloaded.

A useful test before you reach for Claude: would this take you real thinking time to do by hand? If yes, it is probably worth handing over. If you could answer it in ten seconds by opening one file, you do not need an assistant for it.
When you did not need it

The counter-case matters just as much. If you just need last week's revenue figure, the office address, or a date you already have written down somewhere, opening Claude is the slow path. You will type a request, wait for a reply, and then verify it anyway, when the answer was a lookup you could have done yourself in less time and with more certainty.

This is the trap worth naming. Because Claude is fluent and quick to answer, it is tempting to route everything through it, including the questions that have a single correct answer sitting in a system you trust. For those, go to the source. Fluency is not evidence, and a confident sentence is not the same as a checked fact.
Where it sits next to the rest

Claude is one assistant among the tools you met in the general track's "You're ready: here's what comes next" (From foundation to tools), not a replacement for all of them. It will not run your spreadsheets or query your database of record. What it gives you is a strong general reasoner for language-heavy work: drafting, summarising, comparing, turning something long and shapeless into something you can act on.

You do not need a team to get value here. An individual contributor with no reports still meets this work constantly: a long thread to catch up on, a policy document to make sense of, three overlapping drafts to reconcile into one. Those are Claude jobs whether or not anyone reports to you.

cards.body: You are working through a lot of text and need reasoning, comparison, or a first draft. The answer needs judgement, not just retrieval.
cards.title: Reach for Claude when

cards.body: The answer is a single fact in a system you already trust. A lookup is faster and more certain than asking, waiting, and verifying.
cards.title: Skip it when

cards.body: You use it and the output feeds a decision. Confident wording is not proof, so check anything that matters against the source.
cards.title: Still verify when

content_blocks.text: Whatever Claude produces from your material, treat it as a strong draft, not a verified result. Before a summary or a figure leaves your hands, check the claims that carry weight against the original.
What you can now do

You can now tell the two situations apart: the language-heavy, judgement-shaped jobs where Claude saves you real time, and the quick lookups where it just adds a step. That call, made before you start typing, is what keeps the tool useful rather than a habit. The next lesson gets you set up and into your first real task.

questions.q: Which task is the clearest fit for Claude?
options: Pulling last quarters exact revenue figure from your finance system
Turning forty pages of customer feedback into the three themes that should shape planning
Confirming a meeting date already written in your calendar
questions.explanation: Claude is strongest on language-heavy work that needs reasoning over a large pile of text, not single-fact lookups from a trusted system.

questions.q: Why is asking Claude for a single known fact often the slow path?
options: Shorter questions tend to get slower replies from the model
You type, wait, and then verify anyway, when the source would answer faster and more certainly
Simple factual questions usually produce lower quality answers
questions.explanation: For a lookup with one correct answer in a system you trust, going to the source is quicker and more reliable than asking and then checking.

questions.q: What should you do with a summary Claude produces before it feeds a real decision?
options: Publish it as final since the wording is confident
Check the claims that carry weight against the original material
Delete the source so only the summary remains
questions.explanation: Fluent output is not proof, so verify the load-bearing claims against the source before acting on them.

title: Where Claude fits and when to use it

content_blocks.text: Claude opens as a single conversation window. There is a box to type in, a space above it where responses appear, and not much else to learn before you start. This lesson gets you through a first useful session: what the screen gives you, how a conversation actually works, and one real task you can finish in a few minutes.
What you are looking at

You reach Claude in a browser at claude.ai, or through the desktop and mobile apps. However you open it, the layout is the same. You type a message at the bottom, Claude replies above it, and the exchange builds down the screen as you go.

cards.body: Where you type. Press send and Claude responds. This is the main thing you interact with.
cards.title: The message box

cards.body: Claude replies just above the box. Longer answers stream in as they are written, so you can start reading before the response finishes.
cards.title: The response area

cards.body: Starts a fresh conversation with no memory of the last one. Use it when you switch to an unrelated task.
cards.title: New chat

cards.body: You can add a file or paste a large block of text into the message rather than typing it all out.
cards.title: Attachments

content_blocks.text: There is usually a model picker somewhere near the message box that lets you choose a faster or a more capable model. You can ignore it for your first session. The default is a sensible starting point, and you can experiment once you know what you are doing.
How a conversation works

Claude remembers what you said earlier in the same conversation. That is the part people miss at first. You do not have to pack everything into one perfect message. You can send something, read the reply, and then send a follow-up that refers back to it. Claude has the earlier exchange in view.

That memory stops at the edge of the conversation. Start a new chat and Claude knows nothing about the last one. So keep related work in the same conversation, and open a new one when you genuinely move on.

Two things Claude does not do on its own. It does not know today's news or live data unless you give it that information, and it does not act in your other systems. It works on what is in front of it in the conversation.
Your first useful task

Here is a task worth trying first, because it plays to what Claude is good at and you can check the result yourself: turning a long, tangled email thread into a short list of what was decided and what is still open.

Pick a real thread from your inbox, ideally one that ran to a dozen replies and left you unsure where things landed. Copy the whole thread and paste it into the message box. Then ask for what you want out of it: a list of decisions that were actually made, and a separate list of questions still open. Send it.

Claude will read the thread and give you back the two lists. Now read them against the thread. Did it catch the decision buried in the third reply? Did it invent an agreement that nobody actually made? This checking step is the point. Claude can produce a confident, fluent summary that is wrong in a detail, and the only way to trust it is to verify it against the source, as the general track's "How to verify AI output" (Using AI safely) covered.

If something is off, say so in your next message. "You missed the deadline change in the last email" or "the budget was not agreed, that is still open". Claude revises using the correction, and you do not re-paste the thread. That back and forth is the normal way of working, not a sign you got it wrong the first time.

Before you paste anything into Claude, check that the content is something you are allowed to put into an external tool under your organisation's rules. An email thread can contain personal data or confidential terms. When in doubt, leave it out or ask.
What you have done

If you got a messy thread down to two clean lists and checked them, you have run a complete Claude session: paste in the material, ask for a specific output, verify it, refine it. That loop is most of what day-to-day use looks like. The next lesson goes deeper into the interface and the controls that shape how Claude responds.

questions.q: You paste an email thread into Claude and get a summary. Claude confidently lists a decision that, reading back, nobody actually agreed to. What does this tell you?
options: Claude has malfunctioned and should be restarted
A fluent, confident response can still be wrong, so you verify the output against the source
The email thread was too long for Claude to read
You need a more capable model for this task
questions.explanation: Fluency is not evidence of accuracy. Checking the output against the original thread is the step that lets you trust it.

questions.q: Halfway through a conversation about your email thread, you want Claude to add a point it missed. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Start a new chat and paste the whole thread in again
Send a follow-up message telling Claude what it missed, without re-pasting the thread
Rewrite your first message from scratch and resend it
Switch to a different model and try again
questions.explanation: Claude keeps the earlier exchange in view within the same conversation, so a short correction is enough. You do not need to re-supply the thread.

questions.q: A colleague asks Claude for the latest figures from a report published this morning that they have not shared with it. What is the accurate expectation?
options: Claude will fetch the report from the web automatically
Claude only works from what is in the conversation, so it cannot know figures it was not given
Claude updates its knowledge every night, so it should have the report
Claude can read any file saved on that computer
questions.explanation: By default Claude works from what you provide in the conversation. It does not pull live data or read your systems unless that has been set up separately.

title: Getting started with Claude

content_blocks.text: Getting your bearings

Before you lean on Claude for real work, it helps to know where the few controls live and what each one changes. The interface is deliberately sparse: a message box, a place to attach files, a model selector, and a small set of response controls. This lesson is a tour of those surfaces and nothing more. How to write the instruction itself belongs to the prompting work you did in the general track's "How to write a good prompt" (How to prompt well), so here you are just learning which dial does what.
Everything below is a mechanic, not a technique. Knowing where the style control sits is separate from knowing what to ask for. You already have the second part.
The message box

The message box is the wide field at the bottom of the screen. You type or paste your request there and send it. You can send a long paste, several paragraphs, or a single line, and you can keep replying in the same thread to build on what came before. A new chat starts a clean slate with none of the earlier conversation in view.

That distinction matters more than it looks. Staying in one thread keeps the earlier exchange available to Claude; opening a new chat drops it. When to do which was covered in the general track's "Working iteratively" (How to prompt well), so treat this as just the button that does it.
Response length and style

This is the control you will reach for most, so it is worth grounding in a real task. Say you have a dense internal policy paragraph full of clauses and defined terms, and you want a short version in plain language a new starter could follow.

You paste the paragraph and ask for a plain-language rewrite. If the first result is longer or more formal than you wanted, you do not need to re-argue the request. Claude exposes a small set of response style presets, typically including a shorter or more concise setting and a plainer register, alongside the default. Switching the style and asking again gives you a tighter, simpler version without rewriting your instruction from scratch.

A shorter or plainer style changes how Claude writes, not whether it is right. A concise rewrite of a policy can still drop a condition or soften a rule. Read the output against the source before you circulate it.

You can also just say what you want in the message itself, for example "keep it under five sentences" or "no jargon". The style presets and the plain instruction do the same kind of job; the preset saves you repeating yourself across several messages.
Attaching files

Rather than pasting a long document into the message box, you can attach it. There is an upload control near the message box for adding files such as a PDF, a spreadsheet, or an image, and once attached you can ask questions about the contents in the same thread. For the policy example, you might upload the full policy document and ask for the plain-language version of one section rather than pasting the raw text.

How Claude handles large or multiple documents, and where its limits sit, is its own lesson later in this track, "Working with documents in Claude." Here the point is only that the upload control exists and sits beside the message box.
Choosing a model

Claude offers more than one model, and you select which one a chat uses from a model selector, usually shown near the top of the conversation or beside the message box. Different models trade speed against depth: a faster one turns around quick, well-scoped jobs, and a more capable one is worth the extra wait on longer reasoning or a large document.

You met what a model is in the general track's "LLMs and models" (What AI is), so you do not need that again. The only new thing here is that the picker exists and that switching it changes the trade-off, not the interface around it.

cards.body: Where you type or paste a request. Same thread keeps context in view; a new chat starts clean.

cards.body: Presets and plain instructions that change length and register, such as a shorter or plainer rewrite.
cards.title: Response style

cards.body: Upload control beside the message box for documents, sheets, and images to ask about in the thread.
cards.title: Attach files

cards.body: Pick a faster or a more capable model per chat, trading speed against depth.
cards.title: Model selector

content_blocks.text: Where Projects live

You will also see an entry point for Projects, a separate area from a normal one-off chat. A Project is where you keep material Claude should have in view across many conversations, so you are not re-pasting the same background each time. Setting one up and deciding what to put in it is the next lesson, so for now just note where the entry point sits and carry on.
Rule of thumb for an individual contributor: use a plain chat for a one-off ask, and a Project when you keep returning to the same body of material, like a policy set you rewrite from often.
Quiz

questions.q: You asked for a plain-language rewrite of a policy paragraph and the result is too long and too formal. What is the quickest fix using the response controls?
options: Switch to a shorter or plainer response style and ask again
Open a brand new chat and paste the paragraph again with no other change
Switch to a different model and hope the tone changes
questions.explanation: The style presets change length and register without you rewriting the whole request.

questions.q: What does staying in the same chat thread do, compared with starting a new chat?
options: It keeps the earlier conversation in view so Claude can build on it
It permanently saves the conversation as a Project
It changes which model the conversation uses
questions.explanation: One thread keeps prior context available; a new chat starts with none of it.

questions.q: You switched to a shorter response style for a policy rewrite. What still needs doing before you share it?
options: Check the shorter version against the source for any dropped condition
Nothing, a concise style guarantees the rewrite is accurate
Re-upload the document to confirm the style took effect
questions.explanation: A shorter or plainer style changes wording, not correctness, so verify against the original.

title: Claude's interface and response controls

content_blocks.text: When a Project earns its place

Say you send a monthly team newsletter. Every time you sit down to draft it, you find yourself re-pasting the same things into a fresh chat: the tone you want, the format you settled on, the last couple of issues so the new one carries on from where you left off. That repetition is the signal. When you keep re-explaining the same background to Claude, a Project holds it for you so you do not have to.

By default, each new chat starts blank. Claude carries nothing over from your last conversation. That is fine for one-off tasks. It becomes friction the moment you are working on something that comes back round every week or month. A Project fixes that by giving you a container where the background is already loaded before you type.
What a Project holds

A Project is a named workspace that holds two things: a set of files you upload, and a standing instruction Claude reads at the start of every conversation inside it (often labelled the Project Instructions). Open a chat inside the Project and Claude already has both in view. You are not re-pasting the tone guide, and you are not hunting for last month's issue to remind it how the newsletter reads.

For the monthly newsletter, that means the tone guide and the last few issues live in the Project once. Every draft you start there begins from that shared context instead of a cold prompt.

A Project is where you set the persistent context for a whole line of work. The general track's "How models read your input" (How AI works) covered why re-pasting the same background eats into your context window every session. A Project is where you stop paying that cost by hand.
Writing the Project Instructions

The Project Instructions are a short brief. Treat them like the onboarding you would give a capable colleague taking over the newsletter: enough to get it right, not a manual.

For the newsletter, a useful brief covers what the newsletter is and who reads it, the role you want Claude to take (a drafting partner for a monthly internal update), the constraints that always apply (warm but concise, British English, no more than one page), and your output preferences (lead with the single most important update, then the rest as short sections).

Keep it tight. A wall of instructions is harder for Claude to follow than a focused brief, because the constraints that matter get buried. If something is really reference material rather than a rule, upload it as a file instead of pasting it into the instructions.
What to upload
Upload the files Claude should be able to draw on in any conversation inside the Project. For the newsletter, three kinds pull their weight.

cards.body: Your standing reference for voice, length, and house style, so each issue sounds like the last one without you re-describing the tone every time.
cards.title: The tone guide

cards.body: Recent newsletters give Claude a concrete pattern to match and let it pick up threads, so a follow-up on last month can actually follow up.
cards.title: The last few issues

cards.body: The rough notes, wins, and updates for the issue you are drafting now. Upload the current version so Claude is working from where you actually are.
cards.title: Working material for this issue

content_blocks.text: One Project per ongoing job, or one per type of work

How you organise Projects depends on how you work. Two patterns hold up.

One Project per ongoing thing. The newsletter gets its own Project, with everything about it in one place. This works when the context is bounded and applies to all your work on it.

One Project per type of work. A single Project for internal communications, with instructions about tone and format that you reuse across the newsletter, the town-hall recap, and the quarterly update. This works when the way you write matters more than which specific piece you are on.

You do not have to commit permanently. Start with whichever matches your current biggest friction point, and split later if one Project starts trying to do too much.
What Projects do not do

Two limits are worth knowing before you rely on one.

First, files in a Project are static. If you revise the tone guide or want last month's issue in the mix, you re-upload it. Claude does not track changes to the original.

A Project does not remember what you said in a chat and carry it forward on its own. If a useful decision comes up mid-conversation and you want it to hold for next month, put it into the Project Instructions or upload the relevant file. Otherwise it stays in that one chat.

Second, a Project does not reach into your other systems. It will not pull the latest figures from a shared drive or read your inbox. Bringing Claude live data from the tools you work in is a separate feature, covered when you look at connecting Claude to your tools.
Check your understanding

questions.q: You open a new chat inside your newsletter Project. What does Claude already have in view before you type anything?
options: Nothing, because each chat inside a Project still starts from a blank slate
The Project Instructions and any files you have uploaded to the Project
Every message from your previous newsletter chats in that Project
Your inbox and shared drive, so it can pull the latest updates itself
questions.explanation: Claude reads the Project Instructions and uploaded files at the start of every conversation inside the Project. It does not carry chat history forward on its own, and it does not reach into external systems unless a connector is set up.

questions.q: You have rewritten your tone guide. It is uploaded to the newsletter Project. What do you need to do so Claude uses the new version?
options: Nothing, because Claude syncs automatically when the original file changes
Add a note about the change to the Project Instructions
Re-upload the updated tone guide to replace the old one
Create a fresh Project and move everything across
questions.explanation: Files in a Project are static uploads. Claude does not track edits to the source, so you re-upload the new version to replace the old one.

questions.q: Which Project Instructions setup is most likely to help with the monthly newsletter?
options: A 2000-word description of the whole team, its history, and every past campaign
A tight brief: who reads it, the role Claude plays, the tone and length rules, and how to order the sections
No instructions at all, since Claude works better without direction
The full company style manual pasted straight into the instructions box
questions.explanation: Instructions work best as a focused brief, like onboarding a capable colleague. Too much text buries the constraints that matter. Long reference material belongs in an uploaded file, not in the instructions.

content_blocks.text: Try it now

Take the one piece of work you come back to most often, whether that is the newsletter, a weekly report, or a recurring update. Create a Project for it, write a five-sentence brief as the Project Instructions, and upload one relevant file. Then start a chat inside it and notice how different it feels from a blank one.

title: Projects and persistent context

content_blocks.text: If you keep pasting the same instructions into Claude week after week, that is a Skill waiting to be written. You write it once and invoke it whenever you need it.

Projects, from the last lesson, hold the context for one body of work. Skills are the other half of making Claude your own: a saved instruction set for a task you do again and again, that travels with you wherever you work. You learned to write strong prompts in the general track's "How to write a good prompt" (How to prompt well). A Skill is one of those prompts, saved under a name so you never type it out again.
What a Skill is

A Skill is a short, named set of instructions that Claude follows when you invoke it. You create it once in Claude settings, under the Skills section, and after that you call it by name or with a slash command, or Claude reaches for it when a task clearly matches. A Skill lives at the account level rather than inside one Project, so once it is enabled you can use it in any chat, inside any Project, and in Cowork.

Think of it as a standing procedure you have handed Claude. Instead of re-describing the shape of your weekly update every Monday, you invoke the update Skill and Claude already knows the format you want.
What makes a good Skill
Skills earn their place on tasks that repeat, have a format you care about, and carry preferences Claude could not guess from a one-line prompt.

cards.body: Turn a call transcript into decisions made, actions with owners, and open questions, always in that order and always short.
cards.title: Meeting summary

cards.body: Turn rough notes into the exact status format your team reads, with the same sections in the same order every week.
cards.title: Weekly status update

cards.body: Review a draft the way a doubtful reader would, flagging gaps, weak claims, and anything that needs evidence before it goes out.
cards.title: A sceptical second read

content_blocks.text: Writing one

A Skill is really just a precise prompt, saved. A useful one names the trigger, so Claude knows when to use it, the role it should take, the steps in plain terms, the output format you want, and the things to avoid. A status-update Skill might say: when I share rough notes, produce an update with these sections in this order, keep the tone factual, hold it to one page, and never invent a number that is not in the notes. Short and specific enough that the output comes back the same every time.
Skills or Project Instructions

They are easy to confuse, because both save you from repeating yourself. The difference is when each one applies. Project Instructions are always on for every chat inside a Project: who Claude is here, the background it needs, the standing tone. A Skill is invoked for a specific task, wherever you happen to be. They work together, a Project setting the context and a Skill handling a recurring job inside it.

A Skill only helps if it matches how you actually want the output. Write one for a single weekly task, use it a few times, and keep it only if it earns its place. A vague Skill produces vague work, the same as a vague prompt does.
Sharing with your team

If a team agrees on one structure for something like a status update, a shared Skill gives everyone the same output without each person inventing their own version. On team and enterprise plans you can share a Skill with named people or the whole organisation from the same settings, once an owner turns sharing on. On personal plans there is no built-in sharing, so you copy the text into a shared document. Either way a Skill is plain text, so it moves around easily. If you manage people, a small shared library of Skills is a quiet way to set a standard for what good output looks like. If you manage no one, that same library keeps your own recurring work consistent from week to week.
Check your understanding

questions.q: You create a Skill in Claude settings and enable it. Where can you then use it?
options: Only in the Project that was open when you created it
Anywhere you use Claude, including any chat, any Project, and Cowork
Only in new chats you start after creating it
Only after you copy it into each Project by hand
questions.explanation: A Skill lives at the account level, not inside one Project. Once it is enabled, Claude can draw on it across chats, Projects, and Cowork without you copying it anywhere.

questions.q: What is the main difference between Project Instructions and a Skill?
options: Project Instructions are for short tasks and Skills are for long ones
Project Instructions are always active in every chat in a Project, while a Skill is invoked for a specific task
Project Instructions are written in code and Skills in plain text
There is no real difference between them
questions.explanation: Project Instructions are always-on context that Claude reads at the start of every chat in a Project. A Skill is a task-specific set of instructions you call on when you need it. Both can live in the same Project and complement each other.

questions.q: Which task is the best candidate for a Skill?
options: A one-off analysis you will not need to repeat
A quick question about a term you do not understand
A weekly update that always follows the same structure
An open brainstorm with no particular format in mind
questions.explanation: Skills pay off on recurring tasks with a format you care about. A weekly update fits perfectly: it happens often, the structure is fixed, and writing the Skill once saves effort every single week.

content_blocks.text: Try it now

Pick one task you do with Claude more than once a week. Write a Skill for it in under two hundred words: the trigger, the format you want, and one or two things to avoid. Invoke it the next time the task comes up, and compare the result with what you were getting before.

title: Skills, teaching Claude your way of working

content_blocks.text:
You have three vendor contracts open in three tabs, and someone needs to know by this afternoon where their payment terms and notice periods actually differ. You could read all three end to end and build the comparison by hand. Or you could hand the PDFs to Claude and let it do the first pass while you check the parts that matter. This lesson is about the second option: getting documents into a conversation, working with long ones, and reasoning across a whole set at once.

A couple of lessons back, "Projects and persistent context" set up context that persists. This one is narrower and more practical. It is about the documents themselves, and the tool-specific challenge is real: a single PDF is easy, but a set of them, some long, is where people either save an afternoon or quietly give up and go back to reading by hand.
Getting a document into Claude

To bring a document into a conversation, use the attachment control in the message box, or drag the file straight onto the chat. Claude reads common formats directly: PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, plain text, and images. You do not convert anything first. Attach the file, then write your instruction in the same message.

For the three contracts, that means attaching all three to one message rather than pasting their text in one at a time. Claude can then see the full set together, which is the whole reason this works better than copy and paste.

Attaching a file and asking your question in the same message tends to work better than attaching first and asking in a follow-up. Claude reads the document with your instruction already in view, so it knows what to look for while it reads.
Working with a large PDF

Claude reads a long PDF in full, including tables and, in many cases, scanned pages rather than clean digital text. So a forty-page contract is not a problem you have to break up in advance. You attach it and ask.

The limit to keep in mind is the one you already met in the general track's "How models read your input" (How AI works): everything in a conversation has to fit within the context window Claude can hold at once. A single large PDF usually fits comfortably. Several very large ones together may not. If Claude starts missing things in a genuinely huge document, point it at the sections that matter ("focus on the payment and termination clauses") or split the file, rather than asking it to hold everything at maximum detail.
Reasoning across a document set

This is the part worth slowing down for. With all three contracts attached, you are no longer asking Claude to summarise one thing. You are asking it to compare, and comparison needs structure in the instruction.

A weak request is "compare these contracts". A useful one names the dimensions and the shape you want back: "Compare the payment terms and notice periods across these three contracts. Give me a table with one row per contract, and note where any of them differ from the other two." Ask Claude to say which document each point came from, so you can trace anything surprising back to its source. That single instruction is what makes the output checkable instead of a wall of confident prose.

Verify the numbers against the source before you act on them. Claude can state a notice period or a payment term fluently and still get it wrong, or attribute a clause to the wrong contract. This is the same reason to check any AI output that you met earlier in the path, in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong." For contract terms specifically, open the PDF and confirm the figure that matters before it reaches a decision.
One chat, or a Project
Where you put the documents depends on whether this is a one-off or something you will return to.

cards.body: Best for a one-off job like this contract comparison. The files live in that conversation. When the work is done, you are done, and nothing lingers in your setup.
cards.title: Attach to a single chat

cards.body: Best when the same documents come up again and again. Every chat in the Project starts with them already in view, so you are not re-attaching each time. If a source file changes, re-upload it: uploads do not update themselves.
cards.title: Add to a Project

content_blocks.text: For the three contracts, a single chat is usually right. If they are part of a supplier review you will keep revisiting for weeks, a Project earns its place.
What this does not do

Claude reads the documents you give it. It does not reach into a folder and pull related files on its own, and it does not write changes back to the original. If you want it to draft a revised clause, it produces the text for you to paste in; it will not edit the PDF. Connecting Claude to a live source so it can fetch files itself is a separate step, covered later in this track, in "Connecting Cowork to your tools (MCP in practice)."

questions.q: You need to compare payment terms and notice periods across three contract PDFs. What is the most effective way to set this up?
options: Paste the text of each contract into three separate messages, one after another
Attach all three PDFs to one message and ask for a comparison table that notes which document each point comes from
Start three separate chats, one per contract, then merge the summaries yourself
Attach the three PDFs and ask Claude to compare them without naming any dimensions
questions.explanation: Attaching the full set to one message lets Claude reason across all three at once, and naming the dimensions plus asking for the source document makes the output checkable.

questions.q: You attach one genuinely enormous PDF and Claude starts missing clauses that you know are in it. What is the sensible response?
options: Assume Claude cannot read PDFs of that type and give up on the file
Point Claude at the specific sections that matter, or split the file, so the relevant part fits comfortably
Attach the same file several more times so Claude sees it repeatedly
Switch to a different format and hope the content survives the conversion
questions.explanation: Everything in a conversation shares one context window. Narrowing Claude to the sections that matter, or splitting a very large file, keeps the relevant content in full view.

questions.q: Claude reports that one contract has a 30-day notice period. Before this figure goes into a decision, what should you do?
options: Accept it, because Claude read the actual PDF rather than working from memory
Open the source PDF and confirm the notice period yourself
Ask Claude the same question again and trust it if the answer matches
Assume it is correct as long as the output was formatted as a clean table
questions.explanation: A fluent, well-formatted answer can still be wrong or misattributed. For a figure that drives a decision, confirm it against the source document.

content_blocks.text: Try it now

Take two or three documents that describe the same kind of thing (contracts, policies, product specs, or reports) and attach them all to one chat. Ask Claude to compare them on two specific points and to name which document each answer comes from. Then open one of the source files and check a single figure. Notice how much faster the first pass was, and where you still had to look yourself.

title: Working with documents in Claude

content_blocks.text:
When Claude gives you a short answer, it stays in the chat. When it produces something bigger, like a full report or a checklist you plan to reuse, it can open that output in its own panel beside the conversation. That panel is an Artifact. It is not just tidier formatting. It changes what you can do with the output next, because you can edit it, revise it, and copy it out without scrolling back through the chat to find the latest version.

This lesson covers what an Artifact is, when Claude creates one, and how to turn a back-and-forth conversation into a reusable structured output.
What an Artifact is

An Artifact is a separate pane that opens alongside the conversation when Claude produces a substantial piece of content. You read and steer in the chat on one side, and the finished output sits on the other, updating as you refine it.

Claude creates one when the content is substantial enough to work with on its own, rather than for every reply.

cards.body: Reports, process descriptions, templates, communication drafts, checklists. Content you will read as a finished piece rather than a chat message.
cards.title: Documents and structured text

cards.body: Formatted content with headings, tables, and lists. Useful for structured notes or anything destined for a markdown-based tool.
cards.title: Markdown

cards.body: Scripts, queries, formulas, HTML pages, simple visualisations. Some can be previewed live in the pane, so you see the result and not only the code.
cards.title: Code and interactive content

content_blocks.text: For a one-line answer or a quick clarification, Claude just responds in the chat. Artifacts are for outputs long enough to stand alone.
Turning a conversation into a reusable checklist

Suppose you are putting together an onboarding checklist for a new starter on your team. You do not have to write the whole thing up front. Work it out in conversation, then ask Claude to produce the result as an Artifact.

1. **Talk it through first.** Describe the role, the first week, the accounts and access they need, who they should meet. Let Claude ask questions and fill gaps. This is where the thinking happens.
2. **Ask for the output as an Artifact.** Once the content is roughly right, say what you want and what it should look like: "Produce this as a structured onboarding checklist with sections for week one, first month, and access requests, using checkboxes." Being specific about the shape gives Claude more to work with than "write a checklist."
3. **Read it in the pane.** The checklist opens as an Artifact beside the chat. From here you refine it in place rather than regenerating it from scratch.
Ask for what the output should look like, not only what it should contain. Naming the structure, the sections, and the format up front usually saves you an editing round later.
Iterating on the Artifact

Once the Artifact exists, you change it by asking, in the chat, for the specific edit you want. Claude updates the Artifact in place. You might say:

- "Add a section at the end for the 30-day check-in."
- "Turn the access list into a table with the owner for each system."
- "Remove the parts about the office badge, we are fully remote."

If an edit takes the checklist in the wrong direction, Claude keeps a version history on the Artifact, so you can go back to an earlier state rather than trying to undo the change by hand.

Artifacts live inside the conversation, and they are outputs in Claude rather than saved files on your systems. To keep the checklist, copy the content out into wherever it needs to live, or keep the conversation somewhere you can find it again. Do not treat the pane as permanent storage.
Verify before you circulate

Because Claude generates the content, treat the checklist as a strong draft, not a finished source of truth. This is the same reason to check any AI output that you met in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong": fluent and confident is not the same as correct. Before it goes to a new starter, confirm the access requests, the named owners, and any dates are actually right for how your team works. That final read is the part only you can give, whether or not you manage anyone.

questions.q: You ask Claude to produce a two-page onboarding checklist and it opens an Artifact. What is the main practical benefit over a normal inline reply?
options: The checklist is automatically saved to your shared drive
It opens in a separate pane, is easy to copy out, and can be updated in place as you refine it
It is delivered as a finished document file ready to send on
Claude switches to a more capable model for Artifacts
questions.explanation: An Artifact sits in its own pane beside the chat, so it is easy to read, copy, and revise in place without scrolling back through the conversation. It is not saved to external systems on its own.

questions.q: Your checklist Artifact has three sections and you want to add a 30-day check-in and shorten the intro. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Start a fresh conversation and regenerate the whole checklist with the changes
Copy the Artifact out, paste it back into the chat, and ask for a rewrite
Ask Claude in the chat to update the Artifact directly: add the check-in section and shorten the intro
Download it and make the edits by hand
questions.explanation: You can ask Claude to modify an existing Artifact in place. It applies your changes without you regenerating the whole thing or pasting the content back in.

questions.q: A colleague says Artifacts are purely cosmetic and a normal chat reply works just as well. When are they clearly wrong?
options: When the output is a single sentence
When you expect to iterate on a structured output several times
When you are asking a quick one-off question
When the reply is a short list of bullets
questions.explanation: For repeated work on a structured output, an Artifact keeps the working version separate from the chat, supports version history, and makes copying out straightforward. For short or one-off replies the difference is minimal.

title: Artifacts and structured output

content_blocks.text: What actually happens to what you type

Every time you paste something into Claude, you are handing it to a system that runs outside your own machine. It helps to have a clear picture of what that means. Claude is a chat assistant: it reads what you give it, responds, and does not go looking through your files or your inbox on its own. The risk here is lighter than with tools that plug directly into your live company data. But lighter is not none, and the one decision that matters is the same every time: what you choose to put in the box.

The general track's "How to verify AI output" (Using AI safely) already covered why you verify AI output and never treat fluent text as fact. This lesson is narrower. It is about the input side: what you share with Claude before it ever responds.
The one judgement call: is this yours to share

Most of what you would naturally bring to Claude is fine. A public product description, a blog draft, a meeting agenda, a chunk of text you wrote and would happily forward to a colleague: paste it and get on with the work. The question only gets sharp when the content is not yet public and not yet yours to move around freely.

Take a concrete pair. You want Claude to tighten the wording of two documents. One is next quarter's results memo, still under embargo, full of numbers the market has not seen. The other is the public description of the same product on your website. The second one is safe to paste without a second thought. The first is exactly the kind of thing to hold back, or strip down, until you know your organisation is comfortable with it going to an external tool.

Treat an external AI tool the way you treat any system outside your company walls. If a document would need approval before you emailed it to someone outside the organisation, it needs the same approval before you paste it into Claude.
A quick test before you paste

You do not need a policy memorised to make this call. Ask yourself one thing: if this text ended up somewhere I did not intend, would that be a problem. If the honest answer is yes, do not paste it as-is. Usually you have a cleaner option anyway: give Claude the shape of the problem without the sensitive specifics.

For the results memo, that might mean pasting the structure and the wording you want help with while replacing the actual figures with placeholders. Claude can improve the phrasing of a sentence without knowing whether the number is nine or ninety. You keep the confidential part on your side and still get the help.

cards.body: Public or already-shared material: product descriptions, published docs, your own drafts, anything you could forward externally without approval.
cards.title: Safe to paste

cards.body: Unreleased financials, customer records, personal data, credentials, anything under embargo or NDA. Remove or mask the sensitive specifics, then ask for help on what remains.
cards.title: Pause and strip first

cards.body: Secrets that would cause real harm if exposed: passwords, API keys, security details. There is no version of these that belongs in a chat box.
cards.title: Do not paste

content_blocks.text: Where the individual contributor stands

This is not only a management concern. You do not need a team or a title to be the person holding a sensitive document at the moment it matters. The colleague drafting the embargoed memo, the analyst with the raw customer list, the developer with a config file full of keys: each of them makes this call alone, at their own keyboard. Knowing where the line sits is part of doing the work well, not a rule handed down from above.

Your organisation may run Claude under a business or enterprise agreement with its own data-handling terms, which can differ from the consumer version. Confirm which one you are using and what its terms say before deciding what is acceptable to share.
What you can now do

You can tell at a glance which documents are safe to hand Claude and which need masking or approval first. You can get real help on sensitive material by sharing its shape without its secrets. And you know to check your own organisation's terms rather than assume. Next you will meet Claude Cowork, where Claude connects to your actual tools and data, and this input-side judgement matters more, not less.

questions.q: You want Claude to improve the wording of next quarters results memo, which is still under embargo. What is the best move?
options: Paste the full memo, since Claude does not publish anything
Replace the confidential figures with placeholders, then ask for help on the phrasing
Wait until the memo is public before using Claude at all
Paste only the first half of the memo
questions.explanation: You get the phrasing help you need while keeping the embargoed numbers on your side.

questions.q: Which of these is genuinely safe to paste into Claude without extra thought?
options: A customer contact list
The public product description from your website
A config file containing API keys
An internal document marked confidential
questions.explanation: Public material you could share externally without approval carries no added risk when pasted.

questions.q: What is a reliable test for whether something is safe to share with Claude?
options: Whether the text is longer than a page
Whether it contains any numbers
Whether it would need approval before you emailed it outside the organisation
Whether you personally wrote it
questions.explanation: The external-email test maps directly onto whether content is yours to send to an outside tool.

title: Using Claude safely, what you share and where it goes

content_blocks.text: You have 200 survey files sitting in one folder, exported one at a time, each named something like "export_final_v2 (3).csv". They need renaming to a consistent scheme and sorting into subfolders by region and quarter. By hand, that is a lost afternoon and at least three quiet mistakes. This is the shape of work Claude Code is built for: not a single answer to a single question, but a multi-step job carried out over real files on your machine.
Where Claude Code fits

In the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do" you met the idea of an agent: an AI that plans and takes several steps towards a goal with some autonomy, rather than answering once and stopping. Claude Code is that idea made concrete and pointed at operational work. It runs on your computer, reads the files in front of it, and carries out a task step by step until the job is done.

That is what separates it from the Claude you have used in a browser. Claude chat is where you think, draft, and analyse: you bring the text, it gives text back, and nothing on your machine changes. Claude Code acts. On the survey folder, it renames the files, moves them into the right subfolders, and shows you exactly what it changed.

Claude Code opens in whatever folder you point it at, and that folder becomes its workspace. You do not need to be a command-line expert to use it. You need to know which folder holds the files you want worked on.

You reach that workspace through more than one door. The Desktop app is the fastest way in: install it, open it, and point it at a folder, nothing else to configure first. If you already spend your day in VS Code, the Claude Code extension puts the same agent in a panel next to your files instead of a separate window; its own setup guide covers installing and connecting it, worth reading before your first session there. Either door gets you to the same place: once it is open, everything below works the same.
The agent loop

Hand Claude Code the survey folder and it does not fire off one command and hope. It works a loop: it reads what is actually there, proposes a plan, carries out the steps, checks the results, and then either finishes or comes back to you with a question. On these files that means it spots the three different naming patterns you did not know were mixed in, tells you before it touches anything, and asks how you want the odd ones handled.

You are the director here. You decide what the task is, you approve the plan, and you judge whether the result is right. Claude Code does the work; the judgement stays with you.

Before it runs anything that changes your files, Claude Code shows you what it intends to do and waits for your approval. That checkpoint is where you catch a confident but wrong plan, for the same reason the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong" drilled in: a fluent plan is not a correct one.
What this is and is not

Claude Code can also write and run software, and if shipping an application is your goal, the developer track is where that lives. The frame worth holding here is narrower and fits far more people: an automation and operations assistant. The jobs it earns its place on are the repetitive, multi-file, multi-step ones you currently grind through by hand.

cards.body: Rename and sort hundreds of exports into one consistent scheme, in a single run.
cards.title: Reorganise a file set

cards.body: Merge a folder of spreadsheets, clean the columns, and produce one summary file.
cards.title: Consolidate data

cards.body: Read through a set of reports and compile the key points into one structured list.
cards.title: Extract from documents

cards.body: Convert a folder of files from one format to another, applying the same rule to every file.
cards.title: Reformat in bulk

content_blocks.text: If you manage a team, the payoff is obvious: the afternoon this task would have cost someone is handed back. If you are the one who currently does it, that afternoon is handed back to you. Either way, the skill is spotting which tasks are worth handing over, so your attention goes to the work only you can do.
What it cannot do

It makes mistakes. It will occasionally misread a pattern or misunderstand what you asked, which is why you verify the output rather than trust it. By default it works only on what is in the folder you opened; reaching out to a database or a SharePoint site needs a connector, the same MCP standard from the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do." Setting one up for Claude Code itself comes later in this track, in "Connecting Cowork to your tools (MCP in practice)." And it does not remember between sessions unless you give it standing context, covered later in this module, in "Advanced Claude Code patterns."

Do not point Claude Code at the only copy of files you cannot afford to lose. Work on a copy, or ask it to write results into a new folder and leave the originals untouched, until you trust how a particular task behaves.
What comes next

You now have the frame: Claude Code is the general-track agent applied to files, data, and knowledge work, with you directing and verifying at each step. The next lesson gets hands-on with that survey folder and the everyday file and data tasks like it, so the loop stops being a description and becomes something you have run yourself.

questions.q: You have 200 exported survey files that need renaming to a consistent scheme and sorting into subfolders. Which tool fits the job?
options: Claude chat, because it reads file contents faster
Claude Code, because it can carry out the renaming and sorting directly on your machine
Either one, since both understand file names equally
Neither, because renaming files is not something AI can help with
questions.explanation: Claude chat returns text and changes nothing on your machine. Claude Code reads the folder, plans the work, and carries out the renaming and sorting itself.

questions.q: What makes Claude Code an agent rather than a chatbot?
options: It runs on a more capable model than Claude chat
It works in a loop: reading, planning, acting, and checking results until the task is done
It runs on remote servers instead of your own machine
It permanently stores everything you tell it
questions.explanation: The loop of reading, planning, acting, and checking is what makes it an agent. It takes actions and observes the consequences rather than only producing text.

questions.q: Claude Code shows you a plan and waits for approval before it renames any files. Why does this step matter most?
options: It is a legal requirement for automation tools
It is your checkpoint to catch a confident but wrong plan before it changes real files
It slows the tool down so you have time to take notes
It signals that the task has failed and must be restarted
questions.explanation: The approval step is where you verify that Claude Code understood the task, because a plan that reads well can still be wrong. Catching it here is far cheaper than undoing changes afterwards.

title: What Claude Code is, an agentic assistant beyond chat

content_blocks.text: You have twelve monthly CSV exports sitting in one folder. Each is a slightly different shape, a few of them repeat rows, and you need them combined into a single clean summary table with the duplicates stripped out. That is exactly the kind of job Claude Code handles well, and it is also the kind where rushing straight to a result tends to cost more time than it saves. This lesson walks through the working loop that keeps you in control of a file or data task: look before acting, agree a plan, let it run, then verify and save.
The working loop, applied to files and data

The loop has four phases. In software work they are usually called explore, plan, code, and commit. For file and data work the code step is really a build step, and the commit step is really about saving a verified result, so the four become explore, plan, build, and verify. The order is what matters. Each phase is a checkpoint before Claude Code does anything you would have to undo.

cards.body: Ask Claude Code to read the files and describe what it finds before it changes anything. This is where a mismatched format or an unexpected column shows up early.
cards.title: Explore

cards.body: Get an ordered list of steps before any script runs. Read it and push back in plain language if a step touches files you did not want touched.
cards.title: Plan

cards.body: Approve the plan and watch it work. Claude Code asks permission before each command that changes files, so you stay the checkpoint.
cards.title: Build

cards.body: Open the result and check it against what you asked for. When it is right, save the output where it will not be overwritten, and leave the originals untouched.
cards.title: Verify and save

content_blocks.text: Run the explore phase first

There is no special command for this. You tell Claude Code to look before it acts. For the CSV folder, that sounds like:

*"Before you change anything, read through the CSV files in this folder and tell me what you find: how many there are, what columns each one has, and whether the structure is consistent. Do not write any code yet."*

Claude Code reports back the file names, the columns it sees, any patterns, and anything that looks off, such as three files that use a different date format or one that has an extra column. Now you know it is working from the real state of your data, not an assumption about it.
Agree the plan before anything runs

Once Claude Code understands the folder, ask for the approach:

*"Based on what you found, how would you merge these into one summary table and remove the duplicate rows? List the steps before you start."*

Read the plan with three questions in mind. Does it plan to modify any files you wanted left alone? Does it understand the output you need, down to the format and which columns to keep? Does the sequence make sense to you even at a high level? If something looks wrong, say so plainly. You do not need to know how to fix it. Describing the problem is enough, and Claude Code will revise the plan.

The plan is your cheapest correction point. A column mapped the wrong way or a hardcoded file path is a two-minute fix here, and a much longer one once it is buried in a finished output you have already started using.
Build, then verify and save

With the plan agreed, approve it and let Claude Code work. It writes the script, runs it, and checks the result, pausing to ask permission before each command that changes files. You can watch each step and interrupt if it heads somewhere you did not intend.

When the run finishes, do not assume it is done. This is the verify step. In software work this final step is a git commit, a saved snapshot with a note on what changed. For file and data work you may have no repository at all, so the step is simpler: confirm the output is correct, then save it somewhere it will not get overwritten. The principle is identical. You check before you move on.

Reviewing the output as a non-developer means checking what you can actually see, not reading the code. Does the summary match what you asked for? Open the table and confirm the columns are the ones you wanted, in the format you specified. Are the duplicates gone? Spot-check a value you know appeared twice across the monthly files. Did the edge cases survive? Blank fields, an odd delimiter, a month with no data are where a clean-looking script quietly drops rows, so test those on purpose.

One more check pays off every time: ask Claude Code to explain what it did. A prompt like *"walk me through what this script does, step by step, in plain language"* is the most underused review technique there is. If the explanation does not match your intent, you have caught the problem before it reached real data.

If Claude Code was meant to write a new summary file, confirm the twelve original exports are untouched before you close the session. Mistakes here are rare, but an overwritten source file is not something a fresh run can recover.
Keeping a long session from drifting

Claude Code holds the session in a context window, the same limit you met in the general track's "How models read your input" (How AI works). The longer a session runs, the more of that window fills with history, and at some point the earliest decisions get pushed out. You notice it before Claude Code does: it contradicts something you agreed an hour ago (you asked for a semicolon delimiter and it starts using commas), it seems to forget a file it already processed, or its answers turn vague and generic.

The most effective habit is the plainest one. Keep sessions focused: one task per session where you can, and start fresh for the next. If you do need to carry decisions forward, ask Claude Code to summarise what was built and decided before you reset, and open the next session with that summary at the top. Setting up standing context that loads automatically every session is the next step up, and the next lesson covers it.
Quiz

questions.q: You point Claude Code at a folder of twelve monthly CSV exports and ask it to build one summary table straight away. It returns a table but notes it skipped three files it could not read. Which step would most likely have caught this first?
options: Running the task again until all twelve files are included
Asking Claude Code to explore and describe the files before building anything
Writing a longer prompt that lists every column name in advance
Splitting the job across several sessions
questions.explanation: The explore phase is where format differences surface. Had Claude Code described the files first, the three odd exports would have shown up before it built its approach.

questions.q: Early in a long session you asked for the summary as a CSV with a semicolon delimiter. An hour later Claude Code starts producing comma-delimited output instead. What is the most likely cause?
options: Claude Code defaults to commas for large tables
The context window has filled up and the earlier instruction is being dropped
The source CSV files changed format partway through
A permission prompt was declined earlier in the session
questions.explanation: Drift like this is a classic sign of context pressure. Restate the constraint, or start a fresh, focused session with the requirement stated at the top.

questions.q: Claude Code writes a script you cannot read, and it produces your summary table. What is the most reliable way to review it as a non-developer?
options: Assume it is correct because it ran without an error
Ask Claude Code to explain step by step in plain language what the script does, then check the output against your requirements
Read the code line by line until you understand every part
Ask a developer to sign off before you look at the result yourself
questions.explanation: A plain-language walkthrough surfaces wrong assumptions before they matter, and checking the real output against what you asked for confirms the result. You do not need to read the code to do either.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can take a messy folder of exports and drive Claude Code through the full loop: have it look at the files, agree a plan you have actually read, let it run under your eye, and confirm the result before you save it. That sequence adds a few minutes at the start and saves the longer debugging session that skipping it invites.

title: Working with Claude Code, files, data, and automation

content_blocks.text: Once the explore-plan-code-commit loop feels natural, the next gain comes from not repeating yourself. This lesson covers the patterns that let Claude Code arrive already briefed: standing project context, a reusable instruction you invoke by name, connections to the tools where your data already lives, and guardrails that hold no matter what you type. All of it stays on the non-developer side of Claude Code. Where the work tips into writing actual software, this lesson points you on.
Standing context with CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.md is a plain text file in your project folder. Claude Code reads it at the start of every session and treats it as ground truth for that project. Anything that is always true about the work goes here: what the project is, the folder structure, the output format you need, what must never be deleted, and how you want Claude Code to behave (show a plan first, keep answers short, ask before creating files).

You do not write it from scratch. Start a session, describe the project, and ask Claude Code to generate a CLAUDE.md from what it finds and what you tell it. Then read it back and fix the one or two things that are not quite right.

The rule of thumb is simple. If you type the same thing at the start of every session, it belongs in CLAUDE.md. Instructions that only matter for today stay in the conversation.

In-session instructions override CLAUDE.md. Something you say mid-session that contradicts a standing rule wins for that session. If a constraint keeps getting missed, check whether a stray in-session instruction is quietly overriding it before you rewrite the file.
Clearing and compacting a session

CLAUDE.md is what Claude Code reads before a session starts. What happens once the session is under way is a separate problem.
