A long working session accumulates the same way any long conversation does: files it has read, drafts it produced, dead ends already ruled out, and the general track's "Providing context, and what never to include" (How to prompt well) already covers why a context window that has gone noisy starts producing answers that drift or repeat themselves. Claude Code gives you three commands to act on that directly instead of just noticing it too late. /context shows you what is currently loaded, so you can tell a session has gotten heavy before it shows up in the answers. /compact summarises everything so far and keeps going on a lighter load, useful mid-task when you still need the decisions that were made but not the full path that got you there. /clear wipes the session and starts clean, best once a task is genuinely finished and nothing from it needs to carry forward.

Reach for /compact when you are still mid-task and want to lighten the load without losing it, and /clear once the task is actually done. Compacting a session you are about to abandon anyway just costs a moment for nothing.
The weekly data-tidy, saved once

Say every Monday you tidy the same export: drop the cancelled rows, rename three columns, and write a clean CSV to an outputs folder. In an ordinary session you re-brief those steps each time. A reusable instruction lets you save them once and invoke them by name. In Claude Code, that reusable instruction is a custom slash command: a short file of steps saved under a name, which you trigger by typing a slash and that name. It is a different feature from the Skills you met in the chat module, which are a separate, more involved capability built around their own file format; a slash command is the lighter tool built for exactly this kind of repeatable briefing.

This is where it differs from CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md is tied to one project folder. A slash command travels with you, so you can run the same tidy across any folder that holds one of those exports. You give it a name and the steps, and next Monday you type the slash command and Claude Code loads those steps before you type anything else. A job that used to need a paragraph of briefing now needs one command.

Keep the saved steps to things that genuinely stay the same week to week. Anything that changes with each run, like which week you are reporting on, you still say in the session.
Connecting Claude Code to your other tools

By default Claude Code only sees the folder you opened it in. To let it reach data that lives elsewhere, you connect it through MCP, the same open standard you met in the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do," and the same kind of connection you may have already set up for Claude Cowork. A connector configured once lets Claude Code query a database, read and update records in a tool like Airtable, or search a document store from the same session, with no manual export in the middle.

Because it is the same standard, a connector your team sets up for Cowork generally works in Claude Code too. One setup, both tools.

A connector only reaches what the account behind it can already reach, and now Claude Code can act on live systems, not a local copy. Before you point it at anything sensitive, confirm what the connection can read and write, and keep the verify habit from the core loop: check what it changed before you trust the run.
Hooks: guardrails that hold

Hooks are automatic triggers that run before or after Claude Code acts. You set them in its settings file: you name the event to watch for and the command to run, and Claude Code fires it every time.

Because a hook runs below the conversation, nothing said in-session can talk it out of firing. That is the whole reason to use one. A hook that blocks writes to your raw-data folder is a stronger guarantee than the same rule in CLAUDE.md, which an in-session instruction can override. Put the constraints you cannot afford to get wrong into hooks, and keep the softer preferences in CLAUDE.md.

Hooks also carry other lightweight jobs: back up a file before it is overwritten, log every command for an audit trail, copy a session summary to a shared folder when you finish.
When a job is too big for one session

For most tasks a single session is plenty. When a job is large enough that running it in parallel batches would save real time, extracting themes from fifty transcripts, say, Claude Code can split the work across subagents and pull the results back together. Reach for this only when sequential processing is the actual bottleneck, not by default.
Where coding use goes

Everything above serves data and automation work: context, reusable instructions, connections, and guardrails, all directed by someone who does not write code for a living. If your use starts tipping into building and shipping software (working in a real codebase, version control, tests), that is the developer track's territory. It covers this same tool with the coding-specific workflow, so cross over when the work does and come back here for the operational patterns.

cards.body: Project-level context that loads every session. Best for what is always true about one project and for soft preferences.
cards.title: CLAUDE.md

cards.body: /context to check what's loaded, /compact to lighten a long session without losing it, /clear to wipe it and start over.
cards.title: Context commands

cards.body: A named set of steps you invoke across any project by typing a slash command. Best for a job you repeat, like the weekly data-tidy.
cards.title: Reusable instruction (slash command)

cards.body: Reaches data outside your folder: a database, Airtable, a document store. Configured once, shared with Cowork.
cards.title: Connector (MCP)

cards.body: An automatic trigger below the conversation. Best for a guardrail that must not be overridden in-session.
cards.title: Hook

questions.q: You work across three different data projects and keep typing the same output-format brief at the start of every session. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Add the brief to a CLAUDE.md in each of the three project folders
Save the brief as a reusable instruction and invoke it by name in any project
Keep a text file of the brief and paste it in each time
Ask Claude Code to memorise your preferences across all sessions
questions.explanation: A reusable instruction travels across projects, so you invoke one saved set of steps anywhere. CLAUDE.md is per-project, which means maintaining the same brief in three separate files.

questions.q: You need a strong guarantee that Claude Code never writes to your raw-data folder. Which approach holds up best?
options: Write the rule into CLAUDE.md
Repeat the rule at the start of every session
Configure a hook that blocks writes to that folder
Rename the folder so it is harder to find
questions.explanation: A hook runs below the conversation and cannot be overridden by anything said in-session. CLAUDE.md and spoken instructions are softer and can be contradicted mid-session.

questions.q: A teammate wants to pull data from a company database and update Airtable from Claude Code without exporting files by hand. What makes that possible?
options: Installing a more capable version of Claude Code
Splitting the work across subagents
Connecting both systems through MCP connectors so Claude Code reaches them directly
Adding the database schema to CLAUDE.md
questions.explanation: MCP connectors let Claude Code reach systems outside the local folder. Once configured, it can query the database and write to Airtable in the same session, with no manual export.

questions.q: A colleague wants to extract themes from fifty interview transcripts and asks whether subagents would speed this up. When is that actually worth reaching for?
options: Always, since running everything in parallel is faster by default
Only when a job is large enough that sequential processing is the actual bottleneck, not as a default habit
Never, because Claude Code cannot split work across subagents
Only when the transcripts are stored in Airtable rather than local files
questions.explanation: Subagents pay off when a job is large enough that parallel batches save real time. Reaching for them by default on ordinary tasks adds complexity without a real benefit.

questions.q: A colleague says the weekly data-tidy slash command must just be Claude Code's name for the Skills you use in Claude chat. Is that right?
options: Yes, they are the same feature with two different names
No, a slash command is a distinct feature from Skills, which are a separate, more involved capability
No, because slash commands only exist in Claude chat, not Claude Code
Yes, but only for tasks involving file and data work
questions.explanation: Claude Code's custom slash commands and Claude chat's Skills solve a similar problem (not repeating yourself) but are separate, distinct features — conflating them, as this lesson used to, was a factual mix-up worth catching.

title: Advanced Claude Code patterns

content_blocks.text: You have a grant application due Friday, and the pieces already exist. A previous submission to work from, a budget spreadsheet, the programme write-up, a page of impact figures, and the funder's guidelines. Assembling them into one coherent bid is the actual job. In plain browser chat, that job starts with a chore: open each file, copy it, paste it into the conversation, then do the same for the next one before Claude can even see the full set. A spreadsheet often will not paste cleanly at all. Claude Cowork removes that opening chore. It reads the files where they already sit.
What Cowork actually is

Claude Cowork is Claude with reach beyond the conversation. It started as a desktop application and has since expanded to the browser and to mobile, so you are not tied to one device to use it. On desktop, you bring it up with a keyboard shortcut from wherever you happen to be working, and it can read the files and folders on your machine that you give it access to, and look at what is on your screen when you ask it to. The model underneath is the same Claude you have used in the browser. What changes is its reach. It can work with what is already in front of you, without you copying anything in.

That reach is the reason the previous lesson, "Using Claude safely, what you share and where it goes," matters here. Because Cowork can read your screen and open local files, it can pick up far more than you meant to hand over in one go. Invoke it deliberately, and keep it pointed at only the files the task actually needs.
Where it beats plain chat

Go back to the grant application. In the browser, the friction is not the writing, it is the ferrying: every source document has to be copied in before Claude can use it. With Cowork, you gather the documents together, point it at them, and ask it to draft the bid from the whole set. It reads all of them in place. The minutes you would otherwise spend shuttling content between windows simply go away.

The same pattern holds for any task where the material is spread across several files or already open on your screen. Reconciling three versions of a report, pulling figures out of a spreadsheet into a summary, drafting a reply to the message you are looking at. Whenever the work is really about combining things you already have, rather than one clean question, Cowork is the version that fits.
How it sits alongside Claude.ai

Cowork does not replace Claude.ai. They share a model, and both keep your Projects and your history. Cowork now runs on desktop, in the browser, and on mobile (the browser and mobile versions are in beta), so the real difference is not which device you are on. It is what each one can reach.

cards.body: You upload or paste in whatever Claude should see. It is well suited to long, focused sessions and holds a full conversation and your Projects.
cards.title: Claude.ai, plain chat

cards.body: Reaches beyond the conversation: on desktop it works with local files you give it access to and can look at what is on your screen when you ask. It fits quick, in-context jobs across the tools you already have open, rather than ones you copy in.
cards.title: Claude Cowork

content_blocks.text: When to stay in the browser

Not every job wants screen access. A long, focused session, structuring a proposal from a blank page or thinking through a decision over many turns, is still served well by the browser and its full conversation history. Cowork earns its place on the quick, in-between jobs that touch what is already open: summarise this, draft that, tell me what I am looking at.

If you lead a team, the tasks worth pointing people at Cowork first are the repetitive assembly jobs that quietly eat afternoons: the monthly report stitched together from five exports, the bid built from last cycle's documents. If you have no reports, the same test works on your own week. The next time you catch yourself copying a third file into a chat, that is the moment Cowork was built for.

questions.q: You need to assemble a grant application from five separate files already saved on your laptop: a previous submission, a budget spreadsheet, and three supporting documents. You would rather not copy each one into a chat by hand. Which tool fits best?
options: Claude.ai in a browser tab, with each file pasted in one at a time
Claude Cowork on the desktop
A fresh browser conversation for each document
The browser, because a spreadsheet cannot be read either way
questions.explanation: Cowork can read the files where they sit, so you point it at them rather than pasting each document in turn.

questions.q: What is the main thing that distinguishes Claude Cowork from a plain Claude.ai chat?
options: It runs on a more capable model
It reads your screen and local files without copy-pasting
It is the only version that keeps Projects and history
It works with no internet connection
questions.explanation: The model is the same. Cowork differs by reading what is already in front of you, which removes the copy-paste step.

questions.q: When does a long piece of work still belong in Claude.ai in the browser rather than in Cowork?
options: Summarising the PDF you currently have open
Drafting a reply to the email in front of you
A long, focused session structuring a proposal from a blank page
Reading a spreadsheet stored on your laptop
questions.explanation: Cowork shines on quick, in-context jobs. A long, deep working session is still well served by the browser and its full conversation history.

content_blocks.text: Now that you know which jobs are worth handing to Cowork, the next lesson turns to working with it in practice, and how to keep it a genuine collaborator rather than a black box.

title: What Claude Cowork is and when to use it

content_blocks.text:
Most of the value in Cowork shows up in the back-and-forth, not in the first reply. You rarely get the final version of anything on the first attempt, and you are not meant to. This lesson is about running a working session well: keeping one thread going as you refine, giving Claude the context once so it carries across, and moving the finished work into whatever application it needs to live in.

The running example throughout is a half-day workshop agenda you are shaping and reshaping until it holds together.
Keep one thread going

The most useful habit in a working session is to stay in the same conversation while you refine, rather than starting fresh for each change.

Say you ask Claude for a first draft of the agenda. You read it back and react: the morning is too dense, the group is senior so the introductions can go, and there should be a working break before lunch. Because you are still in the same thread, you do not re-paste the agenda to make those changes. Claude already has the current version in view and edits from there. Each round builds on the last, so by the fourth or fifth pass you are adjusting timings and wording, not re-explaining the whole thing.

How to phrase that feedback well is prompting craft, and the general track's "How to write a good prompt" (How to prompt well) already covers it. What matters here is the mechanic: one continuous thread is what lets your earlier decisions accumulate instead of evaporating.

A long thread can also turn against you. If you switch to a genuinely different task, the old context becomes noise and can pull answers off course. The general track's "Working iteratively" (How to prompt well) is the guide here. A good rule: one thread per thing you are shaping.
Give Claude the context once

For work you return to across several sessions, load the shared context once instead of rebuilding it every time you open a chat. Two features do most of this work.

A Project holds the material Claude should always have in view for a body of work. For the workshop, you might create a Project and add the objectives, the list of who is attending and their roles, and last quarter's agenda for reference. From then on, every conversation you start inside that Project already has that background, so a new thread does not mean a cold start.

Global instructions are the standing preferences that apply everywhere: your role, the kind of output you want, the language to default to. You write them once and Claude carries them into every session. Keep them to what you actually need. They are persistent context, not a biography.

If you notice yourself giving Claude the same shaping instructions on task after task, that repeated instruction is worth saving as a Skill, the named instruction set you met earlier in the track, in "Skills, teaching Claude your way of working." Skills work in Cowork too, so keep noticing the candidates as they come up and save the ones that recur.
Encoding it for the whole team: Plugins

A Skill you have tuned until it works is still only yours until someone copies your files or you walk them through it in person. Plugins are Cowork's answer to that: a packaged bundle of Skills, ready for a teammate to install rather than rebuild. Once your events team finally agrees on what a good workshop agenda looks like, wrapping that agreement into a Plugin means the next person who runs it starts from the structure and phrasing you spent five rounds getting right, instead of relearning it from scratch.

A Plugin is still just instructions someone wrote, shared instead of kept private. Before your team relies on one, especially one built outside your own group, read what it actually does the same way you would check a Skill: confirm it does not reach further, or assume more, than you expect.

The habit worth building alongside Plugins is simpler and applies even when nothing gets packaged up formally: once a working session lands on something genuinely good, whether that is a Skill, a Plugin, or just the agenda itself once it is finished, share it with your team rather than leaving it in your own history. The five rounds of refinement in this lesson's example are exactly the kind of work worth handing over, not just using once and forgetting.
Iterating together across surfaces
Cowork is not only the desktop window. Claude can work inside the tools where the work already lives, so you can refine in place rather than copying text back and forth.

cards.body: The main Cowork window. Invoke it with a keyboard shortcut from anywhere, and it works with the files on your machine you give it access to and can look at what is on your screen when you ask. Best for the longer shaping sessions where you want everything in one place, like building the agenda from scratch.
cards.title: Desktop app

cards.body: A browser extension that brings Claude onto the page you are reading. Useful when the work lives in a web tool: an online document, a portal, or the web versions of Outlook and Teams. It reads the current page and uses it as context.
cards.title: Claude in Chrome

cards.body: Claude is available directly inside some Microsoft 365 apps as an add-in, separate from Microsoft Copilot. Where your organisation has enabled it, you can work with Claude on a document without leaving the app. The list of supported apps changes over time, so check what is available to you. Claude can also reach Microsoft data through an MCP connector.
cards.title: Claude in Microsoft 365

content_blocks.text: For the agenda, this means you can draft and refine in the desktop app, then move the finished version into a Word document and keep tidying it there, or drop it into an Outlook invite and ask Claude to write the covering note without switching windows.

The Chrome extension reads the content of whatever page is open, and the Microsoft 365 integration works with what is in front of you. Before you invoke either on sensitive material, check that it is covered by your organisation's AI data policy. The safe-use section of "Connecting Cowork to your tools (MCP in practice)," later in this module, goes into this properly.
Where Claude sits next to Copilot in M365

If your organisation also runs Microsoft Copilot, the two are not interchangeable, and the Copilot track covers when to reach for which in depth. In short, Copilot has deep access to your Microsoft 365 data and is stronger when the task needs it to search across your inbox, calendar, or files. Claude is stronger when you want a specific output format or the skills and instructions you have already set up. For shaping the agenda, where the value is in the iteration and the format, Claude is the natural fit.
What you can now do

You can run a proper working session in Cowork: hold one thread while you iterate, set up a Project and global instructions so context persists instead of being retyped, and carry the same work across the desktop app, Chrome, and Microsoft 365. That is the difference between using Claude for one-off answers and using it as something you actually work alongside.

questions.q: You are refining the workshop agenda over five or six rounds of feedback. What is the most effective way to work?
options: Start a new conversation for each revision so every version stays focused
Stay in one thread so the current draft and your earlier feedback remain in view
Paste the full agenda back at the top of every message
Move to a different application between each revision
questions.explanation: Keeping one continuous thread lets your earlier decisions accumulate, so Claude edits from the current version rather than starting cold each round.

questions.q: You want Claude to always know your role and preferred output format without repeating it in every session. Which feature fits?
options: A separate Project for each task
Global instructions
The Chrome extension
A skill you invoke by name
questions.explanation: Global instructions are standing preferences that apply to every conversation. A Project holds context for one body of work, and a skill applies a specific treatment when invoked.

questions.q: You are reading a long report inside a web portal and want a quick summary without copying the text into another window. Which surface is the best fit?
options: The desktop app with the report downloaded and attached
Claude in Chrome
Claude in Word via the Microsoft 365 integration
A browser tab with the text pasted into Claude.ai
questions.explanation: The Chrome extension reads the page you already have open and uses it as context, so you can summarise in place without moving the content anywhere.

questions.q: Your events team wants everyone who plans a workshop to start from the same agenda structure you finally landed on, not their own version of it. What Cowork feature is built for that?
options: A private Skill that only you can invoke
A Plugin that packages the Skill so the whole team can install and use it
A new Project shared with the whole team
Global instructions copied into each teammate's account
questions.explanation: Plugins package Skills (and the setup around them) so a team shares one standard treatment, instead of each person rebuilding or copying the same instructions individually.

title: Working collaboratively with Claude

content_blocks.text: MCP is the standard you met in the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do": the open protocol that lets an assistant reach your other tools and data directly, instead of waiting for you to paste things in. Cowork is where you put it to work. On its own, Cowork works with the files you point it at and can look at what is on your screen when you ask. Connect it to a tool such as your calendar or a shared folder, and it can go and fetch what it needs by itself. This lesson shows how to make those connections, what one connection unlocks, and where to be careful.
What a connection adds

Take a job you probably repeat every week: pulling together a stand-up brief for your team. Normally you open the calendar to see who is in and what is scheduled, glance at the shared project folder for the latest status notes, and stitch the two into a short summary. Connect Cowork to that calendar and that folder once, and you can ask for the brief directly. It reads the coming week from the calendar, pulls the recent files from the folder, and drafts the summary. You check it and send it.

If you do not run the stand-up yourself, the same two connections still earn their place. Point them at your own week and the group you sit in, and Cowork assembles your personal brief the same way.
The saving is not the drafting, which Cowork could already do from pasted text. It is removing the gather step: the tabs you open and the copying you do before you can even ask.
Making a connection

Open the connections settings in Cowork and choose the tool you want to add. Sign in to that tool when prompted, and confirm the access it requests. Once authorised, the connection stays available across your sessions, so this is a one-time setup rather than something you repeat each morning.

Connections vary in what they grant. Some are read-only: Cowork can see the calendar or the folder but change nothing. Others can also act, such as sending a message or editing a file. Note which kind you are enabling, because the second kind is doing things on your behalf.
Check before you connect
A connection is a standing grant of access, so it is worth a moment of thought before you confirm it. Three questions cover most of the risk.

cards.body: A connector scoped to one shared folder has far less reach than one that can see your whole drive or mailbox. Prefer the narrower scope when the task allows it.
cards.title: What can it read?

cards.body: Read-only connectors are lower risk than ones that can send, edit, or delete. Know which you are granting before you confirm.
cards.title: What can it do?

cards.body: Connectors from Anthropic or a vendor already in your approved stack are safer than an unknown or community one. If the source is unclear, do not connect it to work data.
cards.title: Who built it?

content_blocks.text: The same care applies to what you feed a connection over time. Keep a connected project scoped to one piece of work, and when that work ends, remove connections and files that no longer belong there so context does not carry over into the next thing.

A connector can pull in client data, personal data, or commercially sensitive material without you copying it in by hand. That convenience is exactly why you check your organisation's AI data policy covers the source before you connect it, not after.
Verify what it assembles

Because a connection lets Cowork gather inputs on its own, you are no longer watching every piece go in. That is the point of it, but it also means the output deserves a read before it leaves you. Skim the stand-up brief against the calendar and the folder: did it catch the meeting that moved, and use the latest status note rather than last week's?

This is the same reason you met in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong" for checking any AI output. Fluent text is not evidence that it is right or complete, and a connection that fetches its own data does not change that. It just makes the quick check the last step rather than an optional one.
What you can now do

You can connect Cowork to a tool, judge whether that connection is safe to grant, and use it to remove the gathering work from a recurring task. The stand-up brief is one example; any job where you assemble the same few sources into the same short output is a candidate for the same setup.

questions.q: You want Cowork to pull next week meetings and the recent status notes into a stand-up brief without you pasting anything. What makes that possible?
options: Connecting Cowork to your calendar and the shared folder through a connector
Raising the response length setting
Opening each file on screen one at a time
Switching to the browser version of Claude
questions.explanation: A connector lets Cowork reach the calendar and folder itself, so it can gather the inputs rather than wait for you to paste them.

questions.q: Before adding a connector that can read your local files, which check matters most?
options: Whether it has a polished setup screen
What data it reads, what actions it can take, and whether the source is trusted
How many colleagues have already installed it
Whether it responds faster than the browser
questions.explanation: Reach, actions, and source are the three things that decide the risk of a connector before you grant it access.

questions.q: A connector lets Cowork assemble the brief on its own. Why still read it before sending?
options: Connectors slow down the more you use them
The output can be fluent and still wrong or incomplete, so you confirm it against the calendar and folder
Cowork deletes the source files once it has read them
The brief cannot be edited after it is generated
questions.explanation: A connector does not remove the need to verify. Fluent output is not proof it is correct, so check it against the sources it drew from.

title: Connecting Cowork to your tools (MCP in practice)

content_blocks.text:
This is the last stop in the track, so make it a real one. Pick a task you actually do, open Claude, and take it from raw mess to something you would send. The example running through this lesson is event-feedback triage: a few hundred free-text responses from a workshop or webinar, the kind you normally skim, half-tag, and abandon. By the end you will have sorted them into recurring themes and pulled the outliers worth a second look, and you will have done it in a way you can repeat next month.

The method is the same one every guided build in this path uses: pick, scope, build, verify, reflect. What changes is the tool. Claude is genuinely good at reading a large pile of text and telling you what is in it, which is exactly why it can hand you a summary that reads beautifully and is quietly wrong. Keeping a long session on track, and catching the fluent-but-wrong result, is the real work here.
Pick a task worth the session

Good candidates share three traits: the work recurs, so the setup pays off; the input is text-heavy, so reading is the bottleneck; and the output is a judgement you own, so you can tell when it is off. Event feedback fits all three. So does a monthly stack of support tickets, a channel of user requests, or your own weekly inbox triage. You do not need a team for this to be worth it. If the task is yours and it comes back every few weeks, it qualifies.
Scope it before you open Claude

Decide what a good result looks like before you type anything. Vague inputs get fluent, shapeless answers, and with a few hundred responses you will not notice the drift until late.

For the feedback triage, write down four things: the source (the exported responses), the output you want (a short list of themes, each with a count and two or three verbatim quotes), the outliers you care about (strong complaints, unusual requests, anything that does not fit a theme), and what you will do with it (a follow-up note, a fix list, a decision). That last one matters most. It tells you when the result is good enough to stop.

Keep the scope somewhere Claude can see it every time. If this is a monthly job, put the instructions and a sample of last month's output in a Project so each new session starts already loaded, instead of you re-explaining the task from scratch.
Build in passes, not one giant ask

The temptation is to paste everything and ask for the themes in one go. Resist it. A single sweeping prompt over hundreds of responses is where a long Claude session drifts: it invents a tidy category that was not really there, or folds two different complaints into one clean-sounding theme.

Work in passes instead. First, ask Claude to read the responses and propose candidate themes without forcing a count, so you see its raw read. Second, review those themes yourself and tell it which to merge, split, or drop. Third, ask it to assign every response to a theme and give you the counts plus real quotes. Each pass is small enough that you can check it before the next one builds on it.

Watch for the session losing the thread. After several long turns, Claude can start answering the theme it named three messages ago rather than the responses in front of it. If the output stops matching the source, do not keep patching it. Start a fresh chat, bring the agreed theme list with you, and re-anchor on the raw responses.
Verify against the source, not against how it reads

The goal is not a tidy list. It is a list you can trust. A theme summary is the kind of output that sounds authoritative and can still misrepresent what people wrote, so fluency is not your evidence here. The raw responses are.

Run a few concrete checks rather than a general re-read.

cards.body: Pick three quotes Claude attributed to a theme and find them in the source. Confirm they say what the theme claims they say.
cards.title: Spot-check the quotes

cards.body: If a theme is tagged as forty responses, that is a big share. Ask to see all forty, or a clear sample, and skim for ones that do not belong.
cards.title: Sanity-check the counts

cards.body: Ask what did not fit any theme. A triage that files every single response into a neat bucket is usually hiding the outliers you most wanted to find.
cards.title: Hunt the residual

cards.body: The strong complaints and unusual requests are the point of the exercise. Read those in full, in the original words, before you act on them.
cards.title: Re-read the flags yourself

content_blocks.text: If a check fails, the process is doing its job. Correct the theme list and re-run the assignment pass.
Reflect, then make it repeatable

When the output holds up, stop and note what you had to correct and where you had to intervene. If Claude kept collapsing two distinct themes, add that instruction to your Project so next month it does not. If the counts drifted after a long session, that tells you to break the job into shorter chats sooner.

That reflection is what turns a one-off into a routine you trust. You have now taken a real, recurring task from raw text to a verified result, and you have done it with your judgement in the loop at every pass. That is the same working relationship with Claude that the rest of this track has been building towards.

questions.q: Why build the triage in several small passes instead of one prompt over all the responses?
options: Smaller prompts are cheaper to run, which is the point
Each pass stays small enough to check before the next one builds on it, which limits how far a wrong theme can spread
Claude cannot read more than a few responses at once
A single prompt is against the tool guidelines
questions.explanation: Passes let you catch a bad theme early, before later steps assign hundreds of responses to it.

questions.q: A theme summary reads clearly and confidently. What does that tell you about its accuracy?
options: It is reliable, because a confident summary reflects the underlying data
Very little on its own, so you verify the quotes and counts against the raw responses
It is probably wrong, since confident output is usually invented
It is accurate as long as the counts add up
questions.explanation: Fluency is not evidence. The check is whether the quotes and counts match the source responses.

questions.q: During a long session, the output starts matching a theme named several turns ago rather than the actual responses. What is the better move?
options: Keep correcting it turn by turn until it recovers
Start a fresh chat, carry the agreed theme list over, and re-anchor on the raw responses
Reduce the number of themes so there is less to track
Ask it to summarise its own previous answers
questions.explanation: When a session drifts, a fresh chat that re-grounds on the source beats patching a conversation that has lost the thread.

title: Solve a real problem with Claude, guided build

content_blocks.text: What Obsidian is and when it helps

Say you have been tracking a competitor for months. Every earnings call, every quiet pricing change, every product launch you noticed went into a note. Six months in, that running scan is worth more than any single entry in it. The real question is whether anything can read the whole pile back to you when a planning meeting lands on your calendar. That gap is what Obsidian is built for.
A different kind of note tool

Obsidian stores each note as a plain text file on your own computer, written in a lightweight format called markdown. There is no proprietary database behind it and no cloud account you have to depend on. A note is just a `.md` file you can open, move, back up, or hand to another tool. Most note apps you have used do not work this way. OneNote keeps its notes in a format only Microsoft can read, and Notion keeps everything on its own servers.

That sounds like a small technical detail. It is the reason the rest of this matters.
Why plain files matter now

Because your notes are ordinary files, anything that can read files can read them, including the AI assistants you met earlier in this path, in the general track's "You're ready: here's what comes next" (From foundation to tools). Point one at your competitive scan and it can search every note at once, pull together what you know about a rival before a strategy session, or surface the pricing moves you logged back in January and had half forgotten. No export step, no copy-paste, no reformatting. The prediction engine works on text, and your vault is text.

Connecting an assistant to your vault uses the same connection standard covered in the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do" (How AI works). For now, the point is simpler: the format your notes are in decides whether an AI tool can help you with them at all.

Connecting an assistant to a folder does not quietly upload it. You choose which folder to open for a given task, and nothing leaves your machine until you do. Apply the same judgement you would give any sensitive document before you point a tool at your notes.
The part that compounds

One good note is a reminder to yourself. A vault you have added to for months is context. The scan you started in spring can answer a question in autumn that you did not think to ask when you wrote it. Every note you add raises the quality of the next question you put to an assistant.
When Obsidian is not the answer

Obsidian is a personal thinking space, not a collaboration tool. Anything a team needs to edit together belongs in SharePoint or Teams, and Obsidian does not replace them. It is not a project manager and not your company knowledge base. What it takes over is the notebook nobody else ever opened, the notes you were keeping only for yourself. If your competitive scan is really a shared team document, keep it where the team can reach it. If it is your own read on the market, that is the work Obsidian is for.

cards.body: Personal, local, plain text. Best for your own knowledge, long-term thinking, and giving an AI assistant context. Not built for shared documents.
cards.title: Obsidian

cards.body: Sits inside the Microsoft ecosystem. Fine for M365 meeting notes and shared notebooks. Hard for an AI tool to read across your whole history.
cards.title: OneNote

cards.body: Shared, official, and real-time. Keep them for team documents, compliance, and quick coordination. Neither is a personal thinking space.
cards.title: SharePoint and Teams

cards.body: Cloud databases and pages. Good for team wikis. Your data lives on its servers, and an AI tool cannot read it without a connector you build and maintain.
cards.title: Notion

questions.q: You want an assistant to brief you from six months of competitor notes before a strategy meeting, with the least manual work. Which setup makes that easiest?
options: Notes in OneNote, copied into the chat when you need them
Notes in an Obsidian vault of plain markdown files the assistant can read directly
Notes in a shared SharePoint folder the whole team edits
Notes in a Word document you export to PDF first
questions.explanation: Plain files can be read directly, so there is no export or copy-paste step. The other options add manual work or depend on a format an AI tool cannot read across.

questions.q: When is Obsidian the wrong choice?
options: When you want to capture your own read on a competitor over time
When you want an assistant to find patterns across your past notes
When a team needs to edit a shared document together
When you want to link related ideas across projects
questions.explanation: Obsidian is a personal tool. Collaborative editing belongs in SharePoint or Teams. It shines at personal capture and AI-assisted retrieval.

questions.q: What is the core reason plain markdown files are more AI-friendly than OneNote notes?
options: Markdown files are smaller and faster to open
Any tool with file access can read plain text, including AI assistants, while a proprietary format cannot be read the same way
Markdown supports richer formatting than OneNote
OneNote needs a paid subscription to open
questions.explanation: The advantage is access, not formatting. Plain files can be read by any tool that reaches your file system, whereas a proprietary format shuts most tools out.

content_blocks.text: Obsidian is worth reaching for when the notes are yours to think with and you want an AI assistant to help you use them later. If that describes your competitive scan, or any body of notes you return to over time, the next lesson shows how to start one.

title: What Obsidian is and when it helps

content_blocks.text: You just came out of a project meeting with a page of scribbled decisions and a short list of things someone now has to do. This lesson takes you from nothing installed to that meeting captured as a clean note in Obsidian, with headings for each section and a tickable checklist for the actions. By the end you will have a working vault and know the handful of markdown that fills it.
Install and open your first vault

Obsidian is free to download from obsidian.md and installs like any other application on Windows or Mac. You do not need to create an account to start.

The first time you open it, Obsidian asks you to create or open a vault. A vault is just a folder on your computer that Obsidian treats as your knowledge base, so this step is really about choosing where your notes will live. Pick a location that is easy to find and gets backed up. Your Documents folder synced through OneDrive works well. Avoid burying the vault in a deeply nested, IT-managed path. The folder name is only a name, and you can rename it later.

Obsidian does not back up your vault for you on the free version. Because the vault is just a folder of files, put it somewhere your normal backup already covers, like OneDrive. The built-in Obsidian Sync is a paid add-on you do not need for this.
Find your way around

With a vault open, you are looking at three areas: a file list on the left, the editor in the middle where you write, and a side panel on the right you can ignore for now. That is the whole interface you need today.
Capture the meeting as a note

Create a new note (Ctrl+N on Windows, Cmd+N on Mac). The title you type becomes the filename, so name it something you will recognise later, such as `Project kickoff 2026-07-02`. Consistent, dated titles make notes easy to sort now and easy for an AI assistant to filter when you point one at your vault in a later lesson, "Using Obsidian with an AI assistant."

Then type the meeting straight into the editor. A note is a plain markdown file, which means you format it with a few text symbols instead of a toolbar.
The markdown you actually need

You met markdown in the general track's "Markdown" (How to prompt well), so here is only how it behaves inside Obsidian, using the meeting note as the example.

A single `#` at the start of a line gives you the note title. Two, `##`, marks each section, so you might have `## Decisions` and `## Action items`. A hyphen at the start of a line, `- like this`, makes a bullet. Wrapping text in double asterisks, `**like this**`, makes it bold.

For the action items, write each one as a task rather than a plain bullet: `- [ ] confirm the vendor pricing with Sara`. Obsidian turns `- [ ]` into a checkbox you can click to tick off, and it shows as `- [x]` once done. That is the piece worth remembering here, because it turns a list of things to do into something you can actually work through after the meeting.

You will also see links written as `[[Note name]]`. Those are how notes connect to each other, and the next lesson on linking and structure is where that belongs, so leave it aside for now.
What to skip for now

Obsidian has a large plugin ecosystem, a graph view, and deep customisation. Almost none of it matters in your first week. The graph view, community plugins, templates, and the paid Sync feature can all wait. The tool rewards writing notes, not configuring them, and the real trap is spending more time tuning the setup than using it.

cards.body: Download Obsidian free from obsidian.md, no account needed. On first launch, create a vault by choosing a folder. That folder is your knowledge base.
cards.title: Install and open

cards.body: Put the vault where it is easy to find and already backed up, such as Documents synced through OneDrive. Avoid deep IT-managed paths.
cards.title: Save it somewhere backed up

cards.body: A hash for a heading, two hashes for a subheading, a hyphen for a bullet, double asterisks for bold, and hyphen bracket space bracket for a tickable checkbox.
cards.title: Markdown you need

cards.body: Graph view, community plugins, templates, and paid Sync can all wait. Writing notes matters more than configuring the tool.
cards.title: Skip for now

questions.q: You are setting up Obsidian on your work laptop. Where should you put the vault?
options: Inside a shared SharePoint site so colleagues can open it too
In a folder that is easy to find and gets backed up, such as Documents synced through OneDrive
In the deepest IT-managed system folder for maximum security
It does not matter, because Obsidian stores the vault in its own cloud by default
questions.explanation: A vault is just a folder on your computer, so choose one that is easy to reach and already backed up. Obsidian does not store it in the cloud unless you pay for Sync.

questions.q: In your meeting note you want action items you can tick off as they are done. Which markdown gives you a checkbox?
options: A single hyphen followed by the task
A hyphen, then an open and closed square bracket with a space between them, then the task
A hash followed by the task
Double asterisks around the task
questions.explanation: Writing hyphen bracket space bracket turns the line into a checkbox in Obsidian, and marking it with an x shows it as done. A plain hyphen makes an ordinary bullet.

questions.q: A colleague spends their first afternoon installing plugins and designing a template system before writing any notes. What is the main risk?
options: Obsidian limits how many plugins you can add in the first session
A setup built before you have real notes is likely to be wrong, and the upkeep discourages you from actually writing notes
Plugins can corrupt the vault if they are added too early
Template systems require the paid version of Obsidian
questions.explanation: The common mistake is over-configuring before you know what you need. Start by writing notes, and add structure only when you feel its absence.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can install Obsidian, create a vault in a sensible location, and capture a real meeting as a structured note with headings and a working checklist. That is a complete note-taking loop. The next lesson shows how to connect notes to each other so your vault becomes more than a folder of separate files.

title: Getting started, notes and markdown

content_blocks.text: You have a folder of notes now. This lesson turns that folder into something you can actually move through: notes that point to each other, and just enough structure that the right context is one click away when you come back to it weeks later.
Linking one note to another

The core move in Obsidian is the link. Inside any note, type two square brackets and start typing a note title: `[[`. Obsidian shows a list of your existing notes as you type. Pick one, close the brackets, and you have a clickable link between the two notes.

Take a live example. You keep a note for a project you are running. During the project you make a call about which vendor to use, and you write that up in its own note. You also have a note for each person involved. From the project note, link out to all of them:

`See [[March vendor decision]] and the owners [[Priya Shah]] and [[Tom Green]].`

Now the project note is a hub. When you open it in three months to brief someone or write a summary, you do not have to remember where the decision lives or who signed off. You follow the links.

If you link to a note that does not exist yet, Obsidian keeps the link as a placeholder and creates the note the moment you click it. So you can link to `[[March vendor decision]]` before you have written it, then fill it in later. The connection is already in place.
Links go one way as you type them, but Obsidian tracks them both ways. On the decision note you can see everything that points to it, so you do not have to add the link twice.
Tags for the things that cut across notes

A link connects two specific notes. A tag labels a note as belonging to a group, wherever that note happens to sit. You add one by writing a hash and a word anywhere in the note: `#decision`, `#meeting`, `#project/atlas`.

The point of tags is that one note can carry several, and a tag never moves the file. Your vendor decision note can be tagged `#decision` and `#project/atlas` at the same time. Later, when you want every decision you have made across all projects, you filter on `#decision` and they all surface, no matter which folder they live in.

Keep the set small at first. A handful of tags you actually reuse beats twenty you invent once and forget. Add a new one only when you notice yourself wanting it.

Links and tags work inside a single vault. A `[[link]]` resolves to a note in the same vault and will not reach a note in a different one. If you keep separate vaults for separate parts of your life, treat each as its own self-contained set.
Just enough structure

You do not need an elaborate folder tree, and building one before you have many notes usually means rebuilding it later. A light structure is enough: a folder or two for the areas you work in, and one note you treat as your way in.

That entry note, often called `Home` or `Index`, is the one note you open first. It links out to the things that matter: your active projects, your key reference notes. Without it, a growing vault becomes a flat pile you search through every time. With it, you have one starting point that you, or an AI assistant reading your vault later, can follow to reach everything else.

The order to remember is simple. The vault holds folders, folders hold notes, and links and tags run across all of them regardless of which folder a note sits in. Structure groups your notes; links and tags connect them.

cards.body: Type [[ and a note title to connect two specific notes. Obsidian tracks the connection both ways, so each note shows what points to it.
cards.title: Link

cards.body: Write a hash and a word anywhere in a note to label it. A note can carry several tags, and a tag never moves the file.
cards.title: Tag

cards.body: A couple of folders plus one Home note as your way in. Keep it light and add folders only when you feel the absence of one.
cards.title: Structure

content_blocks.text: Why this pays off later

None of this is busywork for its own sake. The next lesson connects an AI assistant to your vault, and a linked, lightly tagged vault is exactly what makes that useful. When notes point to each other and share consistent tags, an assistant reading the vault can follow the same trails you would: from a project to its decisions to the people involved. A pile of disconnected files gives it far less to work with.

questions.q: You want your project note to reach the related decision note and the two people involved in one click each. What is the most direct way to set this up in Obsidian?
options: Copy the full text of the other three notes into the project note
Add a link to each of the other notes using the double-bracket syntax
Move all four notes into the same folder and rename them with a shared prefix
Add the same tag to all four notes and filter on it each time
questions.explanation: A double-bracket link is a clickable connection to a specific note. Linking out from the project note to the decision and the two people notes puts each of them one click away.

questions.q: When is a tag a better fit than a link?
options: When you want to connect two specific notes to each other
When you want to group notes that share a theme, wherever they sit in your folders
When you want to move a note into a different folder automatically
When you want the connection to work across two separate vaults
questions.explanation: Tags label notes as part of a group regardless of folder, so filtering on one tag surfaces every note that carries it. Links are for connecting two specific notes.

questions.q: What is the risk of designing an elaborate folder hierarchy before you have written many notes?
options: Obsidian limits how many folders a new vault can contain
Folders and tags cannot be combined in the same vault
The structure you guessed at is likely wrong, so you end up rebuilding it once real notes reveal what you actually need
Deep folders stop links from resolving
questions.explanation: The structure that fits your work emerges from use. Starting light and adding folders only when you feel the need avoids rebuilding a system you designed before you understood the shape of your notes.

title: Linking and structure

content_blocks.text: Picture asking a plain question out loud: what did we actually decide about the supplier change back in spring? If your notes are scattered across chat threads and half-finished pages, you answer that by scrolling and guessing. If those same notes sit in a vault an AI assistant can read, you ask the assistant and it reads the relevant notes back to you. This lesson is about that shift, from searching your own memory to querying your own writing, and what it asks of the way you take notes.
How an assistant reads your vault

Your vault is a folder of plain text files. That is the whole mechanism. Any AI assistant that can reach your file system can open those files, search them, and reason over them, without you pasting anything into a chat. There is no special Obsidian integration to buy, no plugin to install, no API key to wire up.

You already met how an assistant gets that kind of access in the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do" (How AI works). The point specific to Obsidian is smaller and more useful: because a vault is just files, making it readable to AI takes no extra work. If your notes exist as text, they are already in the format an assistant wants.

This is the quiet advantage of plain text. Notes locked in a proprietary format have to be exported or shared one page at a time before an assistant can use them. A vault skips that step entirely, which is why the readability question moves from "can it read this at all" to "is what I wrote clear enough to be worth reading".
What this changes about note-taking

The value of a note stops being only in writing it down. It becomes the ability to use it later, at speed, with help. A single note read back to you is a small convenience. Six months of notes an assistant can search across is a different kind of asset: a store of your decisions, your open questions, and your reasoning that any future question can draw on.

That effect compounds. The question you ask today benefits from the note you wrote in January, as long as January's note still makes sense out of context. This is where note-taking habits start to matter in a way they never did when you were the only reader who could fill in the gaps.
Writing notes an assistant can actually use

Here is the catch that the supplier-change question exposes. If the only trace of that decision is a note that reads "supplier change, maybe Q3?", an assistant reading your vault is as stuck as a colleague would be. It cannot tell whether that was decided, proposed, or dismissed. A chaotic scribble with abbreviations only you understand confuses an assistant for the same reason it confuses everyone else.

A few habits make your notes hold their meaning when they are read cold, months later, by something that was not in the room.

cards.body: A fragment like "supplier change maybe Q3" loses its meaning fast. "Decision: we move to the new supplier from Q3, pending a final price review" still answers the question in six months.
cards.title: Full sentences for the key points

cards.body: Title similar notes the same way every time, such as a fixed pattern for meeting notes with the date. Predictable titles let an assistant sort and filter them reliably instead of guessing.
cards.title: Consistent naming

cards.body: Two lines saying what the note is about help an assistant place it before it reads the whole thing. This matters most when it is scanning dozens of notes to answer one question.
cards.title: A short summary at the top

cards.body: Write "Decision:" and then the decision in full. The word makes the note findable, and the full sentence survives being pulled out of its original context.
cards.title: Be explicit about decisions

content_blocks.text: None of this means writing polished prose. The barrier to capturing a note should stay near zero, or you will stop capturing. It means spending the extra few words on the points you will want to retrieve, so the version of you asking the question later, and the assistant helping you, both get a clean answer.

content_blocks.prompt: Two versions of the same note about a supplier decision. Predict which one an assistant can actually answer from, months later.

options.label: "supplier change, maybe Q3?"
options.reason: A fragment like this loses its meaning fast. The assistant is as stuck as a colleague who was not in the room.

options.label: "Considering a supplier change, still weighing options"
options.reason: This reads clearly but never states whether the change was actually decided. An assistant still could not confirm the decision from this alone.

options.label: "Decision: we move to the new supplier from Q3, pending a final price review"
options.reason: A full sentence with explicit context still answers the question when read cold, months later.

content_blocks.text: A note on judgement

Your vault lives on your machine, and local files are not sent anywhere on their own. When you point an assistant at your vault, you are choosing to share specific notes for a specific task, and you decide what is in scope.

Apply the same judgement you would to any sensitive document. If a note holds confidential or personal information, think before you hand the folder that contains it to an external assistant. Readable does not mean everything should be read by everything. You control what you share and when, so use that control on purpose.
Where this leaves you

You do not have to manage a team to feel this. If you take notes only for yourself, the payoff is direct: the effort of writing one clear sentence today is repaid every time an assistant answers a question from it later without you digging. If you do lead a team, the same habits make your own record something you can query in seconds before a decision, rather than a place you avoid because you cannot find anything in it.

questions.q: You want an assistant to answer "what did we decide about the supplier change" from your vault. What actually has to be in place?
options: The notes must first be exported to PDF and attached to the conversation
The assistant must have access to your vault folder, and the decision must be written clearly enough to read out of context
You need a paid Obsidian plugin that exposes your vault to AI
The relevant notes must all sit in a single file
questions.explanation: A vault is plain text, so no export or plugin is needed. The two real requirements are access to the folder and a note whose meaning survives being read cold.

questions.q: Because a vault is just plain text files, what does that change about the real question you need to ask before AI can help with your notes?
options: The question moves from whether an assistant can read your notes at all to whether what you wrote is clear enough to be worth reading
It means you must convert your notes to PDF before an assistant can read them
It means only some of your notes will ever be visible to an assistant
questions.explanation: Plain text skips the export/access problem entirely, so the real bottleneck becomes clarity of what you wrote, not whether the format is readable.

questions.q: Why does note-taking quality matter more once an assistant can read your vault?
options: Because AI cannot process markdown formatting reliably
Because the assistant reads notes cold, so anything only you could decode stays useless to it
Because unclear notes will be automatically deleted from the vault
Because assistants can only read notes written in full paragraphs
questions.explanation: An assistant was not in the room and cannot fill gaps from memory. A fragment only you understand is as opaque to it as it would be to a colleague.

title: Using Obsidian with an AI assistant

content_blocks.text: Your vault is a folder of plain markdown files on your own machine. That is what makes Obsidian private by default, and it is also what you hand over to any sync service or plugin you switch on.

Two ordinary choices quietly move your notes beyond your own device: how you sync a vault across machines, and which community plugins you let read it. Neither is risky by nature. Both are worth a moment of thought once the vault holds sensitive material such as client notes, HR records, or unreleased plans.
Where your notes go when you sync

Obsidian keeps everything local until you decide otherwise. To read the same vault on your laptop and your phone, you either use Obsidian's own Sync service or point a general cloud tool such as iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive, or Google Drive at the vault folder.

The difference that matters for sensitive work is who can read the files once they leave your device. Obsidian Sync is designed so that only you hold the key and the provider stores encrypted data it cannot open. A general cloud folder is different: the files sit there in a form readable by whoever administers that account, including your IT team and the provider, under that service's own terms.

Before you put sensitive notes in any synced vault, check where that provider actually stores the data and whether that storage is allowed under your confidentiality agreements and your data policy. A vault syncing to a personal cloud account is often the exact thing those agreements forbid.
Community plugins can read the whole vault

Obsidian ships with community plugins switched off behind Restricted Mode. When you turn that off to install one, you are running third-party code inside your vault.

A plugin runs with the same reach you have. It can read every note in the vault, and many legitimately need to. It can also make network requests, which means a plugin is technically able to send vault content elsewhere. Most community plugins are open source and well behaved, but "most" is the operative word.

So treat installing a plugin as a small trust decision rather than a convenience click. A few checks before you enable one:

cards.body: Prefer plugins that are open source and widely used, so the code can be inspected and problems get caught by others.
cards.title: Check who made it

cards.body: A plugin that only restyles your notes is lower risk than one that syncs, uploads, or calls an external service.
cards.title: Read what it does

cards.body: Any plugin that talks to an outside server can in principle send vault content there. Ask whether it actually needs to.
cards.title: Notice network access

cards.body: For a vault of sensitive notes, install only the plugins you genuinely need rather than everything that looks useful.
cards.title: Keep sensitive vaults lean

content_blocks.text: You do not need to own the security policy to make these calls well. Whatever your role, you are the one deciding what goes into a synced vault and which plugins get to touch it, note by note.

questions.q: You turn off Restricted Mode to install a community plugin. Why does that deserve a moment of thought?
options: The plugin runs as third-party code that can read every note in your vault and make network requests
Community plugins are known to be malicious
Plugins noticeably slow Obsidian down
questions.explanation: A plugin has the same reach you do, so it can read the whole vault and, in principle, send content out over the network.

questions.q: You keep sensitive notes in a vault and want it on your phone too. What is the key question before syncing it through a general cloud service?
options: Whether storing that data in that location is permitted under your confidentiality agreements and data policy
Whether the sync will be fast enough across devices
Whether the service can handle markdown files
questions.explanation: A general cloud folder is readable by whoever administers the account, so the first question is whether that storage is allowed at all.

questions.q: For sensitive notes, what distinguishes Obsidian Sync from pointing Dropbox at your vault folder?
options: Obsidian Sync is designed so only you hold the key and the provider stores data it cannot read
Obsidian Sync keeps your notes in a more secure file format
Obsidian Sync never leaves your notes on any server
questions.explanation: Both services hold your data on their servers, but Obsidian Sync encrypts it so the provider cannot read the contents.

title: Using Obsidian safely, vault sync and plugins

content_blocks.text:
You have set Obsidian up and learned to run it safely. Now you build something real with it, end to end. The task for this guided build is a vault for a professional certification you are studying for: the months-long kind of effort where notes pile up from courses, practice exams, and your own working-out, and where the whole pile is worthless if you cannot find the one thing you need the night before the test.

The shape is the same one every build in this path follows. You pick a real task, scope it, build it, verify it, and reflect. What makes this build its own thing is the last quality you will design for: a vault that an AI assistant can actually read and reason over. Getting there is less about clever plugins than about how you write.

If you manage a team studying for the same certification, the vault you build here is also a template you can hand them. The habits scale from one person revising alone to a group building shared knowledge.
Scope it before you touch a folder

Before you make a single folder, decide what you want to be able to do at the end. Not "organise my notes", which is a chore with no finish line, but something you can test. For a certification effort it might be: revise a weak exam domain in twenty minutes, or ask an AI assistant to quiz you on the areas you keep getting wrong.

Scope is what keeps you from building an elaborate system you abandon in a fortnight. Write the one or two outcomes down. Everything you build should serve them, and anything that does not is decoration.
Build the folder skeleton

Start with a flat top level and a clear logic behind each folder. A hybrid model works well here: one place for raw capture, one for the live material organised by exam domain, one for the concepts that outlast any single study session, and one for reusable resources. A simple log for daily study notes rounds it off.

cards.body: Where everything lands first when you are moving fast. You process it later, so you never have to make a filing decision mid-lecture. The most important folder in the vault.
cards.title: Inbox

cards.body: The exam areas, one folder each. Practice-test reviews, worked problems, and notes tied to a specific part of the syllabus live here while you are actively revising.
cards.title: Domains

cards.body: Evergreen explanations in your own words. This is the knowledge that stays useful after the exam and the folder worth investing your best writing in.
cards.title: Concepts

cards.body: Things you reference but do not rewrite: templates, a formula sheet, links to source material. Keep it separate from the notes you actively edit.
cards.title: Resources

content_blocks.text: Prefix folders with two-digit numbers and gaps, such as 00 Inbox, 10 Domains, 20 Concepts, 30 Resources, so Obsidian sorts them in the order you work rather than alphabetically, and you can slot new folders in later without renaming everything. And do not create a folder until you have at least three notes that belong in it. If you hesitate for more than a few seconds about where a note goes, the structure has a gap or an overlap. Fix that before it compounds.
Capture notes that survive to exam night

The easiest thing to do is paste: copy the lecture transcript, drop in the slide export, screenshot the practice question. It feels productive and it saves you nothing. You still have to read the whole transcript later to find the one idea that mattered.

Ask a sharper question before writing a note: what would I want to find here the week before the exam? If the honest answer is the three concepts you got wrong on the mock test and why, write a note on those three. Three habits make the capture worth keeping.

Write in complete sentences for anything that matters. "Subnet mask thing, revisit" is meaningless in a month. "I keep confusing the broadcast address with the network address; the network address is the first in the range, the broadcast is the last" is still useful when you have forgotten you ever struggled with it. Date the note, so you can tell early confusion from a genuine gap that persisted. And state the so-what in one line: what this means for how you will answer that kind of question.

Capture is easy; processing is the actual work. Set aside a short window, ten minutes at the end of a study session, to turn raw captures into one or two clean notes. One good note pulled from a week of scribbles beats a hundred you never revisit.
Link concepts so revision compounds

Folders tell you where a note lives. Links tell you how ideas connect, and for exam revision that connection is where the value sits. Obsidian uses double square brackets for internal links, so writing the name of another note inside `[[...]]` creates a live link to it.

The move that pays off: when a practice-exam review exposes a weakness, link it to the concept note behind it. Over a few weeks, the concept notes that collect the most incoming links are exactly your recurring blind spots. That pattern is invisible in a folder list and obvious once the links are there.

Link with intent. A link is a claim that two ideas are related, so make it when the connection saves you a future search or reveals a pattern, and skip it when two notes merely share a word. Tags are the better tool for broad grouping such as a status of revised or shaky; links are for the specific relationships between ideas.
Templates for the notes you write again and again

If you are typing the same headings for the third time, template them. For a certification vault, two templates earn their keep almost immediately: a practice-exam review and a concept note. Keep each one lean, just the sections you always want, because a template you skip fields in is one you will stop using.

A practice-exam review template might be nothing more than a date line and headings for Score, What I got wrong, Why, and What to revise. The headings act as a checklist that stops you writing a vague "did okay" and moving on.

Obsidian has a built-in Templates feature, and the community plugin Templater does more. Templater can run small snippets so a note fills its own date on creation, for example `<% tp.date.now("YYYY-MM-DD") %>`, and place your cursor where you want to start typing. You do not need to write any code to benefit; the date and cursor features alone cover most of the need.

Templater is a community plugin, so it runs third-party code. Install it from the community plugins area only after the safe-use checks you learned in the previous lesson, "Using Obsidian safely, vault sync and plugins," and point its template folder at your Resources folder. Verify the current plugin name and settings against Obsidian before you rely on a specific menu path.
Make it readable to an AI assistant

This is the part specific to Obsidian, and it puts to work what the earlier lesson on using Obsidian with an AI assistant showed you. It is the reason the writing habits above are not just tidiness. Because every note is a plain markdown file on your own machine, an AI assistant that can read your files (through the file access covered in the general track's "Beyond chat: agents, connectors, and what they can do") can work directly with your vault. It can quiz you, summarise your weak domains, or draft a revision plan from your notes.

But readable is not the same as useful. An assistant reading your vault has no memory of anything outside the text you give it. It cannot guess what a cryptic abbreviation meant or which exam domain a loose note belongs to. It reads what is there, the way a stranger would. The way you write is what closes that gap.

Use clear headings, so the assistant can tell a decision from background. Name things with a brief clarifier the first time, so "CIDR (the notation for IP address ranges)" carries its own meaning. Make relationships explicit in words, not only links, because "this follows from the routing rules in my Networking concept note" travels with the text even when the assistant is reading one file. And add a date and a status line to the notes you lean on, so it can tell current understanding from something you have since superseded.

For the handful of notes you will query most, a small block of structured metadata at the very top helps. Between two lines of three dashes, add a few fields such as date, domain, and status. An assistant can read that block and answer a request like "summarise my shaky topics in the networking domain" with precision.

An AI assistant can only hold so much text in view at once, the context window from the general track's "How models read your input" (How AI works). Do not point it at your whole vault and hope. Ask it to read one folder, such as your networking domain, and it will do far better. This is why curated concept notes beat a hundred raw transcripts: you are handing over knowledge, not a haystack.
Verify the build

You scoped this vault around one or two outcomes. Now test them against reality rather than assuming the build worked.

Take the coldest test first. Open one concept note and read it as if you had never seen it, with no memory of the study session behind it. If a reference is opaque or you cannot tell when you wrote it, that is the note failing the AI test too, because the assistant sees the same thing you just saw. Fix the missing context.

Then run the real thing. Ask your assistant a genuine question against one folder: "read my networking domain notes and quiz me on what I get wrong most." If the answer is sharp and specific, your notes are. If it is vague and generic, the notes are vague, and no prompt will rescue them. The quality of the output tracks the quality of what you wrote.
Reflect

You have built a vault that holds up under pressure and hands clean context to an AI. The deeper takeaway is that writing for your future self and writing for an assistant turned out to be the same discipline: dated notes, named things, explicit connections, curated rather than dumped.

Think about the last exam or deadline you prepared for. What did you wish you had written down at the start but did not? Picture the note that would have held it, and write your next one that way.

questions.q: You keep pasting full lecture transcripts into your vault so you do not lose anything. Why does this undermine both your revision and an AI assistant working on the vault?
options: Transcripts take up too much storage on a local vault
Pasted content still has to be read to find what matters, and it buries the few ideas worth keeping
Obsidian cannot index long transcripts
An AI assistant refuses to read files above a certain length
questions.explanation: Passive capture just moves the work to later. The assistant, like you, has to wade through the transcript to find the decisions and concepts, and a curated note would have handed those over directly.

questions.q: You want to ask an AI assistant to summarise your weak areas across five months of study. Which vault condition makes that request work best?
options: Having every note in one folder so the assistant can find them
Having several hundred notes so there is enough material
Having clean, dated concept notes that distil your patterns, with a folder you can point the assistant at
Having structured metadata on every single note in the vault
questions.explanation: The output tracks the input. Curated concept notes with clear context and a scoped folder give a precise answer, whereas volume alone and a vague dump produce noise.

questions.q: When does adding a small block of structured metadata at the top of a note earn its place?
options: On every note, so the vault stays consistent
Only on notes longer than a page
On the notes you expect to query or filter, such as concept notes you will ask the assistant about by domain or status
Only when you have the Templater plugin installed
questions.explanation: Metadata carries a maintenance cost, so it pays off on the notes you actually query by field. Inbox items and rough captures do not need it.

questions.q: You keep retyping the same five headings every time you write up a practice-exam review. What is the templating habit worth building for this?
options: A lean template with just the sections you always want, such as Score, What I got wrong, Why, and What to revise
A single giant template that covers every possible note type in the vault
No template at all, since Templater requires writing code
