A template that includes every field you might conceivably need
questions.explanation: A template only earns its place if you actually keep using it. A lean template stays in use; one with fields you skip most of the time gets abandoned.

title: Build a structured vault, guided build

content_blocks.text: Every team space in Confluence grows the same way. Someone creates it for a project, pages pile up, meeting notes and decisions and half-written specs accumulate, and a few months later nobody can tell you what state the work is actually in without reading twenty pages. The AI features in Confluence are aimed at that problem. They sit on top of the pages you already have and help you find them, summarise them, and draft against them, so what your team wrote down stays findable and usable.

The exact name keeps moving. Atlassian has been folding these capabilities into Rovo and Atlassian Intelligence, so the label in your instance may differ from a colleague's. What matters is the behaviour described here, not the wording on the button.
It reads your space, not the open web

The thing that makes these features useful is where they look. A general chatbot answers from its training. The AI in Confluence answers from your content: the pages, spaces, and comments you already have permission to see. This is the grounding idea you met in the general track's "How to verify AI output" (Using AI safely), applied to a knowledge base. When you ask for a summary of a project space, you get a summary of your project, not a plausible-sounding guess about projects in general.

That also sets the boundary. If something was never written down, or lives in a space you cannot open, the AI cannot see it either. It works with the knowledge your team captured.

items.text: Turn 40 scattered pages into a two-paragraph status digest
items.reason: This is exactly the summarise job the lesson describes, drafted from pages that already exist.

items.text: Find the onboarding runbook you cannot remember the title of
items.reason: Plain-language search over pages you already have permission to see.

items.text: Recall a decision that was only ever discussed out loud, never written up
items.reason: It only works from what was captured. Nothing written down means nothing to draw on.

items.text: Summarise a space you do not have permission to open
items.reason: It only draws on content within your existing access, never the open web or restricted spaces.

content_blocks.prompt: Sort each scenario into what the AI can help with, and what it cannot.

content_blocks.text: The example worth holding onto

Picture a project space that has been running for two quarters. Forty-odd pages, several contributors, decisions scattered across meeting notes and comment threads. Your steering group does not read any of it. They want to know where things stand.

This is the job these features are built for. You point the AI at the space and ask for a short status digest: what has shipped, what is blocked, what changed since last month. Instead of one person spending an afternoon reading and rewriting, you get a first draft of that digest in a paragraph or two, pulled from the pages themselves. You still read it and fix it, but now you are editing a draft rather than starting from a blank page and a wall of notes.
The shape of the jobs

cards.body: Locate a page or answer buried in a space by asking a plain-language question about what it contains.
cards.title: Find

cards.body: Turn a long page, or a whole sprawling space, into a short read for people who will not open it.
cards.title: Summarise

cards.body: Start a new page from material that already exists, such as turning a set of notes into a written-up decision record.
cards.title: Draft

content_blocks.text: The next lesson shows how you trigger each of these. For now the point is the pattern. Every one of these jobs is the AI reading what your team wrote and handing you a head start from material that already exists.
What it does not do

Grounding on your own pages makes the output more trustworthy than a generic chatbot. It does not make it correct. The AI can still misread a table, miss a caveat in a comment, or report a blocker as resolved when the page saying so is out of date. Confident wording is not evidence the summary is right, for the same reason you learned in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong" (How AI works).

So the digest is a draft you sign off, never a fact you forward unread. The next lesson pairs each feature with that safe-use habit.

You do not need to own a space to get value here. If you maintain a single runbook or one team page, the same features help you keep it current and let a colleague get the gist without reading all of it.

Treat AI-generated summaries as unverified until you check them against the source pages. A summary that reads cleanly can still carry a wrong date or a dropped dependency, and it now looks authoritative.
Check yourself

questions.q: A colleague forwards you an AI-generated summary. It reads cleanly and looks polished. What should you do before relying on it?
options: Check it against the source pages, since fluent wording is not evidence it is correct
Trust it, since a clean summary is unlikely to contain errors
Forward it on as-is to save time, since it already looks authoritative
questions.explanation: A clean, confident-sounding summary can still carry a wrong date or a dropped dependency, so checking it against the source pages is the habit that catches it.

questions.q: A steering group wants the state of a busy project space without reading it. What is the AI a good fit for here?
options: Producing a first-draft status digest from the pages that you then check and correct
Deciding on its own which blockers matter and sending the update for you
Guaranteeing a fully accurate summary that needs no review
questions.explanation: Summarising a sprawling space into a digest is the core use case, but the output is a draft you verify, not a finished fact.

questions.q: Something important was discussed verbally and never written on any page. Can the AI include it in a summary?
options: No, because it can only work from content that was captured and that you can access
Yes, it infers the missing context from similar projects
Yes, as long as the space is large enough
questions.explanation: The features work from what your team wrote down and what your permissions allow, so knowledge that was never recorded stays invisible to them.

title: What Confluence AI does

content_blocks.text: You met what Confluence's AI features are for in the last lesson, "What Confluence AI does." This one is hands-on: how to actually run a search, summarise a long page, draft a new one, and polish text that's already there, using a single real task as the thread. Say you have just come out of a project kickoff, you need to write up the notes, and you half-remember there is an onboarding runbook buried somewhere in the space but you cannot recall where anyone filed it.

The AI features may appear under Atlassian's own branding (Rovo or Atlassian Intelligence) rather than the word "AI", and exactly where each control sits depends on your plan and your admin's settings. Look for an AI or sparkle icon near the search bar or in the editor toolbar. If you cannot see it at all, it has most likely not been switched on for your instance yet, which is a matter of admin configuration rather than a fault at your end.
Search: finding the buried runbook

Ordinary Confluence search matches keywords. The AI-assisted search lets you ask in plain language, so instead of guessing the exact title someone gave the runbook, you can type what you actually want: "where is the new-hire onboarding runbook for the delivery team". It reads across the pages you have access to and returns a direct answer with links to the source pages, rather than a raw list you then have to sift.

Two habits make this reliable. Name the team or space if you know it, because it narrows the field. And always open the linked source page before you act on the answer, because the summary is a pointer to the truth, not the truth itself.
Summarise: getting the gist without reading it all

Once you have the runbook open, or any long page, use the summarise action to get its shape before you read every line. On a single page the control usually sits near the top of the page or in the AI panel. You ask for a summary, and it returns the key points, which is enough to decide whether this is the right document and which section you need.

The more useful move is summarising across several pages at once, for example asking for the current state of a project that spans a dozen pages. That is powerful, and it is also where the one real risk of these features lives.

A cross-page summary is built from pages you already have permission to see. Confluence will not surface anything from a page or a space you cannot open yourself, so a summary cannot leak restricted content the way the raw idea of "reading across pages" might suggest. The real risk is different: a summary strips away each page's own context, so a stale figure, a superseded decision, or a dropped caveat can end up sitting in one confident paragraph with nothing to flag that it has gone out of date. Before you paste an AI summary somewhere wider, such as an open page or a chat, check the claims that carry weight against the source pages, not just whether the content is shareable.

content_blocks.prompt: This cross-page status summary is about to be pasted into a company-wide update. Spot the planted problem.
content_blocks.example: Project Atlas is on track for its Q3 release. The vendor procurement blocker was resolved last sprint, and the new onboarding flow is in final QA.

candidates.text: Project Atlas is on track for its Q3 release
candidates.reason: General project status, easy to check against the space.

candidates.text: The vendor procurement blocker was resolved last sprint
candidates.reason: The page reporting this was last updated before the blocker actually cleared. A cross-page summary strips away each page's own context, including how current it is, so a stale status can read as settled fact. This is the real risk the lesson warns about, not a permissions leak.

candidates.text: The new onboarding flow is in final QA
candidates.reason: General project status, nothing to flag.

content_blocks.text: Draft: writing the meeting-notes page

Now write the notes up. Create a new page and use the draft or AI writing action in the editor. Give it the raw material, such as your rough bullet points from the kickoff, and tell it what you want, for example "turn these into a structured meeting-notes page with decisions, owners, and next steps". It returns a formatted draft directly in the editor that you can then edit like any other content.

Treat the draft as a first pass, never the final page. The AI does not know who actually owns an action unless you told it, and it will happily write a confident, tidy sentence around a detail it invented. You are the one who was in the room, so the facts, the names, and the decisions are yours to confirm.
Enhance: polishing the words you already have

Search, summarise, and draft all work with what's missing: finding a page, condensing several, writing a new one. Enhance is different. It works on text that already exists and is basically fine, just not quite right for the reader in front of you. Select a paragraph, a section, or a whole page, and ask the AI to change its tone, tighten the writing, fix spelling and grammar, or translate it into another language, without changing what it says.

Back to the onboarding runbook you tracked down earlier: it was written by an engineer, for engineers, and reads like it. Your new starter on the client side keeps asking someone to translate the jargon in person. Instead, highlight the dense section and ask the AI to make the tone friendlier and simpler. Or say the same runbook now needs to go to a partner team in Antwerp who works in Dutch day to day — select it and ask for a translation, rather than finding someone free to do it by hand.

Enhance changes the wording, not the meaning underneath it. A tone rewrite or a translation can still drift on a term that matters, especially a technical name or an internal acronym that does not translate cleanly. Read the result against the original before you publish it, the same way you check a summary or a draft — polished wording is not proof the meaning survived intact.

cards.body: Ask in plain language across pages you can access. Returns a direct answer with links. Open the source before acting on it.
cards.title: Search

cards.body: Condense one long page or a set of pages. Fast for triage. Watch what a cross-page summary surfaces before sharing it wider.
cards.title: Summarise

cards.body: Turn rough notes into a structured page in the editor. Always a first pass. You confirm the facts, names, and decisions.
cards.title: Draft

cards.body: Select text you already have and ask for a different tone, tighter writing, or another language. It changes the wording, not the facts inside it — check the result against the original.
cards.title: Enhance

content_blocks.text: The one rule that ties all four together

Every one of these features can be wrong while sounding completely sure of itself, for the same reason you covered in the general track's "Why the same prompt gives different answers, and why it can be confidently wrong": fluency is not evidence. So the workflow is the same each time. Let the AI do the fetching, condensing, drafting, or polishing, then verify against the source before you rely on it. That is the difference between the tool saving you time and the tool quietly introducing a mistake into a page other people will trust.

questions.q: The AI-assisted search returns a confident, direct answer with a link to a source page. What should you do before acting on it?
options: Open the linked source page and confirm it actually says that
Act on the answer immediately, since it already cites a source
Ignore the source link, since the summary already did the reading for you
questions.explanation: The answer is a pointer to the truth, not the truth itself, so opening the source page before acting on it is the habit that catches a misread.

questions.q: The draft feature produces a clean meeting-notes page listing an action owner you do not recognise. What is the right response?
options: Publish it, since the AI formatted it confidently
Assume the name is correct because it read your notes
Check it against what actually happened in the meeting before publishing
Delete the whole draft and start again by hand
questions.explanation: A draft is a first pass. The AI can invent a plausible owner it was never given, so you confirm names and decisions against the real event.

questions.q: You cannot find the AI search or summarise controls anywhere in your Confluence. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The features have been removed from Confluence entirely
Your account is too new to use them
The features are not enabled for your instance, which is an admin setting
You need to summarise a page before search will appear
questions.explanation: Availability of the AI features depends on your plan and admin configuration, so a missing icon usually means they are not switched on rather than a fault with your account.

questions.q: You ask the enhance feature to translate a runbook section into Dutch for a partner team. The result reads fluently. What should you still do before sharing it?
options: Check that technical terms and specifics kept their meaning in translation, since fluent wording is not proof of that
Nothing, since a fluent translation is unlikely to have drifted
Ask the partner team to translate it themselves instead
Re-run the translation a second time to be sure
questions.explanation: Enhance changes wording, not meaning, and translation is exactly where a technical term can drift while still reading smoothly. The same source-check habit from search, summarise, and draft applies here.

title: Using AI features in Confluence (search, summarise, draft), with a safe-use callout

content_blocks.text: Search, summarise, draft, and enhance all cover one clean, bounded action: ask a question, get an answer; select some text, get it improved. Most weeks in a real project space are messier than that. You do not just want a single answer, you want to keep asking. And some jobs, like writing up a meeting nobody wrote notes for, happen the same way every single week — worth a purpose-built assistant rather than a fresh prompt each time. That is what Rovo Chat and Rovo Agents are for.
Rovo Chat: an ongoing conversation, not a one-off action

Rovo Chat opens the same three ways wherever you are in Confluence: the "Ask Rovo" icon in the nav bar, typing /rovo inside the editor, or the app switcher. Unlike a single search query, once it is open you keep talking to it. Ask about the vendor procurement blocker in your project space, then follow up with who owns it, then ask it to draft a two-line Slack update out of the answer — each question builds on the last, the way it would asking a colleague who has actually read every page in the space, rather than starting a new search from scratch each time.

It can run in a side panel next to the page you are working on, so you keep your place, or expand to full screen for a longer back-and-forth when you need the whole window. Same assistant either way, just how much room it takes up.

Rovo Chat still only answers from spaces and pages you have permission to see, and it can still be confidently wrong about something that reads correctly — chat does not relax either rule from the earlier lessons, it just changes how many questions you get to ask in one sitting.
Rovo Agents: built-in specialists for the jobs that repeat

Chat is general-purpose — you can ask it almost anything about your space. Agents are the opposite: pre-built, task-specific AI teammates, each built for one recurring job, that you use directly inside Confluence without writing a careful prompt every time. Two are worth knowing by name.

cards.body: Turns a meeting into notes for you — AI-generated summaries and action items, built for catching up on a discussion you weren't in or half-followed.
cards.title: Meeting Insights Reporter

cards.body: Assists and elevates a brainstorming session — a standing helper for the kind of loose, idea-generating meeting that never produces a tidy page on its own.
cards.title: Brainstorm Facilitator

content_blocks.text: Back to your project space: that Tuesday stand-up you keep half-missing because you're at a client site is exactly the Meeting Insights Reporter's job — point it at the meeting and get the notes and action items you would otherwise have chased down individually. And when the team sits down next quarter to brainstorm what the space should tackle next, that is a Brainstorm Facilitator session, not a blank page and a facilitator hoping everyone speaks up.

content_blocks.prompt: You missed Tuesday's stand-up again and just want to know what you missed, fast. Which is the better fit?

options.label: Meeting Insights Reporter
options.reason: Correct — it's built for exactly this: catching up on a discussion you weren't in, notes and action items included.

options.label: Rovo Chat, starting from a blank question
options.reason: Would get there eventually, but you'd be asking Chat to reconstruct piece by piece something Meeting Insights Reporter already does end to end.

options.label: Brainstorm Facilitator
options.reason: Built for generating ideas in a live session, not summarising one that already happened.

questions.q: What's the real difference between Rovo Chat and the search/summarise/draft/enhance actions from the last lesson?
options: Chat is an ongoing conversation you keep building on, not a single request-and-answer action
Chat is only available to Confluence admins
Chat cannot see anything in your Confluence spaces
Chat replaces the need to check sources against the original pages
questions.explanation: The earlier lesson's actions are each one bounded request; Chat is a back-and-forth where each question can build on the last, the way a conversation with a colleague would.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Rovo Chat's entry points?
options: The "Ask Rovo" icon in the nav bar
Typing /rovo inside the editor
The app switcher
A dedicated Chat tab in space settings

questions.q: Your team is about to run a session to generate ideas for next quarter's project scope. Which named agent fits?
options: Meeting Insights Reporter
Brainstorm Facilitator
Rovo Search
Rovo Studio
questions.explanation: Brainstorm Facilitator is built to assist and elevate exactly this kind of idea-generating session. Meeting Insights Reporter is for catching up on meetings that already happened.

title: Rovo Chat and Agents: beyond single actions

content_blocks.text: Your steering group has asked for the same thing every sprint for two quarters: a short recap of your project space in their exact format — shipped, blocked, changed since last time, plus a line on morale. Search won't draft that unprompted. Meeting Insights Reporter gets you meeting notes, not a sprint recap. Brainstorm Facilitator doesn't fit either. Across this track you've picked up four single actions (search, summarise, draft, enhance), an ongoing conversation, and two named specialists — between them, every job Atlassian already anticipated you'd need. This one, a specific, repeating, house-style report nobody else was going to guess, is what Rovo Studio is for: building your own agent, tailored to your space, instead of waiting for Atlassian to ship one that fits.

Treat what follows as the concept and the questions worth answering before you open Studio, not a click-by-click tour of its screens — the real interface may lay things out a little differently. Read this first, then go open Studio yourself and see how closely it matches; that comparison will teach you more than a screenshot ever would.
Why build one, instead of using what's already there

Rovo Studio is described as a no-code, low-code builder for creating custom agents and automations tailored to a team's specific knowledge or actions — distinct from ready-made agents like Meeting Insights Reporter or Brainstorm Facilitator. Where those two are built for a job Atlassian assumed most teams have, Studio is for the job only your team has: that exact sprint-recap format, a checklist unique to how your space runs, a recurring cleanup task nobody enjoys doing by hand. The steering-group recap above is exactly this kind of Studio candidate: specific, repeating, and shaped by house style rather than anything a general-purpose agent could guess.
What a custom agent is actually built from

Atlassian describes creating a custom Rovo Agent as starting from one of two places — duplicating and modifying an existing agent that's already close to what you need, or building one from scratch — and then giving it three ingredients.

cards.body: What the agent should actually do each time it runs — the job description you'd give a new team member covering this task.
cards.title: Instructions

cards.body: The prompts that kick it off, so you and your team don't have to remember the right phrasing each time.
cards.title: Conversation starters

cards.body: Where it's allowed to pull from — for a space-specific agent, that's most likely this project space itself.
cards.title: Knowledge sources

content_blocks.text: For the sprint-recap agent, that might look like: instructions telling it to pull shipped/blocked/changed items from the space and write them in your steering group's format; a conversation starter like "generate this sprint's recap"; and the project space itself as the one knowledge source it draws from.
Duplicate an existing agent, or start from scratch?

Worth deciding before you open Studio: if a prebuilt agent already gets you most of the way there, Atlassian's own path is to duplicate and modify it rather than start blank, reusing whatever machinery already exists. Meeting Insights Reporter is closer to a sprint recap than a blank page is, so it's worth reviewing before committing to a from-scratch build.

options: Studio builds a custom agent tailored to your team's own knowledge and jobs, where prebuilt agents cover jobs Atlassian anticipated for everyone
Studio only works for Confluence administrators

questions.explanation: The documented path to a custom agent is duplicate-and-modify an existing one, or build from scratch — checking whether an existing agent is close enough avoids rebuilding something that already exists.

title: Guided build: your own Rovo agent, made in Studio

content_blocks.text: It's your first Monday on the platform team, and the ticket at the top of your queue is small: add a purchase-order number field to invoice-parser, the internal FastAPI service that turns scanned vendor invoices into structured JSON. Your onboarding buddy Marcus points at the small Copilot icon already sitting in your VS Code status bar. "It's on by default here, just start typing and see what it suggests." You've used Microsoft 365 Copilot before, to draft an email and summarize a meeting recap last week, and you've heard two developers a few desks over talk about "running Claude Code" on their laptops like it's some separate thing entirely. Are all of these the same assistant wearing different name tags? They are not, and untangling that now saves you from aiming your first good question at the wrong tool.
Same word, three different tools

This hub already covers two of the three elsewhere, and it's worth being precise about which is which before you write a line of code. Microsoft 365 Copilot, the one you used for that meeting recap, lives in the Copilot track and works on office content: documents, email threads, meeting transcripts, slides. Claude Code, the one your neighbours were running, lives later in this same Developer track, in Module 3. It's a general-purpose coding agent you point at a whole project from a terminal or editor, and it plans, edits multiple files, and reports back with real autonomy. GitHub Copilot, the subject of this entire module, is neither of those. It lives directly inside your editor and inside GitHub itself, and right now it is reading the exact function you have open.

cards.body: Lives inside Word, Outlook, Teams, PowerPoint, Excel. Works on office content: drafts, summarizes, and rewrites documents and conversations. Covered in the Copilot track, not here.
cards.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot

cards.body: Runs from your terminal or editor as an autonomous coding agent. You hand it a task across a whole project and it plans, edits, and checks its own work with real independence. Covered later in this same track, Module 3.
cards.title: Claude Code

cards.body: Lives inline in your editor and on GitHub.com, watching the exact file and function in front of you. It completes code as you type and chats about what's on your screen right now, closer to a pair programmer sitting beside you than an agent you send off with a task. This module.
cards.title: GitHub Copilot

content_blocks.text: Don't take these boundaries as fixed law. GitHub Copilot also ships an agent mode that can work across several files with real autonomy (Module 2 covers it), and Claude Code is perfectly happy answering a single quick question. Read the split above as "where each tool earns its keep first," not as a wall between them.
Where you'll actually meet GitHub Copilot

Open invoice-parser in VS Code and you'll find GitHub Copilot in three places before you've done anything deliberate: grey "ghost text" completions appearing as you type, a chat panel you can open from the sidebar or a keyboard shortcut, and a small Copilot icon at the top of any file offering inline actions. None of it requires you to describe your whole task up front the way Claude Code does. You start typing the po_number field, and it's already guessing the next few lines from the code already in the file.
Why an editor-native assistant is a different shape of tool

The thing that makes GitHub Copilot worth a whole module of its own, rather than a paragraph tucked into an existing one, is that its usefulness compounds with how much of your day already happens inside code and GitHub: the file you're editing, the pull request you're opening, the issue someone just filed, the terminal command you're about to run wrong. The next lesson walks through all four of those surfaces on this exact po_number ticket.

GitHub Copilot writes fluent code, not necessarily correct code. It has no idea invoice-parser validates purchase-order numbers against a specific vendor whitelist unless that logic is visible nearby, so a suggestion that compiles cleanly can still be quietly wrong. Read what it gives you the way you'd read a new teammate's first pull request: with real scrutiny, every time.
What's ahead in this track

This module stays inside GitHub Copilot itself: where you meet it (this lesson), how you use it day to day (next), how to prompt it well, and how to give it durable context with Copilot Spaces. Module 2 moves from assistant to agent, the same shift you'll notice again in Module 3, when Claude Code gets a much deeper treatment than the light version already sitting in the Claude track.

questions.q: Marcus tells you Copilot is "already on" in your VS Code status bar, completing code as you type in invoice-parser. Which tool is he talking about?
options: Microsoft 365 Copilot
Claude Code
GitHub Copilot
All three behave identically here, so it doesn't matter
questions.explanation: GitHub Copilot is the assistant that lives inline in the editor, watching the exact file you have open. M365 Copilot lives in Office apps and Claude Code runs as a separate agent from a terminal or editor session you start deliberately.

questions.q: You want to turn a rough set of meeting notes into a written recap for your manager. Which of the three tools is actually built for that job?
options: GitHub Copilot
Microsoft 365 Copilot
Claude Code
Any of them, since they all read plain text equally well
questions.explanation: M365 Copilot works on office content like meeting transcripts and documents. GitHub Copilot is scoped to code and GitHub, and Claude Code is built for multi-step work on files in a project, not drafting a meeting recap.

questions.q: What's the clearest way to describe the difference between GitHub Copilot and Claude Code?
options: GitHub Copilot is simply a weaker, older version of Claude Code
GitHub Copilot completes and chats about what's directly in front of you in the editor; Claude Code is an autonomous agent you point at a whole project
They are the same product with two different names depending on which company sells it
Claude Code only works in a browser, while GitHub Copilot only works in a terminal
questions.explanation: GitHub Copilot is editor- and GitHub-native, reacting to the file, selection, or PR in front of you. Claude Code is a general-purpose agent you hand a whole task to, which then plans and acts across a project with more autonomy.

title: What GitHub Copilot is, and how it fits alongside Claude Code and M365 Copilot in this hub

content_blocks.text: Back to the po_number ticket. Shipping it means: adding a field to the invoice model, writing the extraction logic, adding a test, opening a pull request, and getting it reviewed, and at some point along the way you'll probably run a git command you don't fully remember the flags for. GitHub Copilot follows you through every one of those steps, but it shows up differently depending on where you are: ghost text in the model file, a conversation in the chat panel, a suggested first-pass review on the pull request itself, and a plain-English translator sitting in your terminal.
Code completion: the ghost text you already saw

This is the surface you met on day one. As you type the new po_number field into the Pydantic model, Copilot proposes a full line, or several lines, as pale grey "ghost text" ahead of your cursor. Press Tab to accept it whole, or accept it word by word if only part of it is right. If the first suggestion isn't quite it, Copilot usually has more than one candidate queued up in a suggestions pane you can cycle through rather than retyping from scratch. It also adapts to what's already in the file: match the docstring style and naming convention already used in models.py, and the suggestions it offers you will follow the same pattern.

Ghost text is easiest to accept when you're moving fast, which is exactly when you're least likely to notice it quietly reusing a currency-rounding convention from elsewhere in the file that has nothing to do with a purchase-order number. Read the whole suggestion before you hit Tab, not just the first line of it.
Copilot Chat: the conversation about your code

Once the field exists, you need extraction logic that pulls a PO number out of a scanned invoice's text, and that's a conversation, not a completion. The Chat view holds a running back-and-forth scoped to your workspace: ask it to explain an approach, sketch a regex, or reason about an edge case. Highlight the regex you've drafted and open inline chat right there in the file to ask a question about that exact selection without losing your place. For a single quick question, quick chat pops up a small input box without opening the full panel. And smart actions, the right-click menu, give you one-click versions of common asks like "explain" or "generate tests" on whatever you've selected. You highlight your new regex and ask, in plain language, why it might fail on a PO number that includes a dash, and Copilot Chat walks through the pattern with you.
GitHub Copilot on GitHub.com: help on the pull request itself

Once your branch is ready, Copilot follows you to GitHub.com too. It can draft a pull request description that actually summarizes your diff instead of the placeholder template, and, if you ask for one, act as an automatic first-pass reviewer, commenting inline on specific lines. It's also useful before you've written anything: ask it questions about an unfamiliar part of the repo, or let it help triage and label an incoming issue. You open your po_number pull request, request a Copilot review before pinging a human, and it flags that your new field has no validation for an empty string, a real catch you hadn't gotten to yet.

Treat a Copilot review the way you'd treat a very fast, very literal junior reviewer: good at catching what's plainly there, like a missing validation check, but not going to notice that the vendor whitelist logic changed last quarter. Request the human review anyway.
GitHub Copilot in the CLI: when the terminal is the part you don't trust

Somewhere in shipping this ticket, a teammate pastes you a git command in Slack to fix a messy branch, and you don't want to run it blind. `gh copilot explain` takes an intimidating shell command and translates it into plain English before you run it. The reverse direction works too: describe the outcome you want in plain language and `gh copilot suggest` proposes a candidate command, for instance "undo my last commit but keep the changes staged." Read the explanation, or the suggested command, before you run it, especially anything that touches history or deletes files. The CLI is the one surface here where a confidently wrong suggestion can do real, hard-to-undo damage.

cards.body: Ghost text as you type in the file, adapting to the code already around it. Fastest surface, least context of the four; verify before accepting.
cards.title: IDE completion

cards.body: Chat view, inline chat on a selection, quick chat for a one-off, and smart actions for common asks. Best for anything that needs explanation or reasoning, not just completion.
cards.title: Copilot Chat

cards.body: PR description drafting, a requestable first-pass review, inline PR comments, and issue triage help. Lives where the review and history of the work already lives.
cards.title: GitHub.com

cards.body: `gh copilot explain` and `gh copilot suggest` translate between plain English and shell commands. The surface for when the terminal itself is the risky part.
cards.title: CLI

content_blocks.text: One thread, four places to pull it

It's the same underlying assistant in all four places, reading whatever surface you're currently standing in: a file, a conversation, a pull request, a terminal command. The skill worth building here isn't memorizing four separate tools, it's noticing which surface actually matches the question you have, instead of defaulting to chat for everything or bailing out to a browser search when the answer was one keystroke away.

questions.q: A teammate pastes a `git` command into Slack and asks you to run it on your branch. You don't fully recognize the flags. Which Copilot surface is built for checking it first?
options: IDE code completion
Copilot Chat's inline chat on a code selection
The GitHub Copilot CLI (`gh copilot explain`)
A Copilot review request on GitHub.com
questions.explanation: The CLI's `explain` mode is built exactly for this: translating an unfamiliar shell command into plain English before you run it, which matters most for commands that touch history or delete things.

questions.q: You've just opened your po_number pull request and want a fast first pass before you ask a human teammate to review it. Which surface do you reach for?
options: IDE code completion on the diff
A requested Copilot review on GitHub.com
Quick chat in the editor
`gh copilot suggest` in the terminal
questions.explanation: GitHub.com is where Copilot can review a pull request directly, commenting inline on specific lines. It's a fast first pass, not a substitute for the human review that follows.

questions.q: What's actually true about GitHub Copilot across these four surfaces?
options: Each surface is a separate, unrelated product that happens to share a name
It's the same underlying assistant, adapting to whatever context you're currently in: a file, a chat, a PR, or a terminal
Only the IDE version can see any of your code
The CLI and GitHub.com versions require a different subscription from the editor version
questions.explanation: One assistant, four contexts. The value is in recognizing which surface matches the question in front of you, not in treating them as four different tools to learn separately.

title: Copilot across your workflow: IDE, Chat, GitHub.com, and CLI

content_blocks.text: A bug report comes in on invoice-parser: an invoice with one line item in EUR, nested inside an otherwise all-USD invoice, gets parsed with the wrong amount. You could open Copilot Chat and type "fix this bug." You already know, from How to prompt well in the general track, exactly what happens next: a vague ask gets a vague answer, because the model fills every gap you left with the most generic plausible guess. That instinct doesn't change inside an editor. What does change is the vocabulary available to you for handing Copilot the right piece of context in the first place, because a code editor gives you tools a plain chat window doesn't: comments Copilot reads as instructions, and a set of chat mechanics, participants, slash commands, and variables, built specifically to scope a request to the right file, symbol, or piece of output.
This lesson assumes you can already write a good prompt

Specificity, naming your audience, deciding a format, setting constraints, giving the context that's actually relevant and leaving the rest out, iterating instead of expecting one perfect shot on the first try: all of that is covered already in the general track's How to prompt well module, and none of it gets repeated here. What follows is specific to Copilot: the mechanics unique to writing prompts inside an editor and a real repository, layered on top of the general skill you already have.
Comment-driven prompting: the prompt lives in the code

The most Copilot-specific habit is prompting through a comment. Write a comment or docstring above where your cursor sits describing exactly what the function beneath it should do, then let Copilot complete from there. "# validate a currency line" gets you a generic, unhelpful stab. "# reject a currency line if its symbol doesn't match the invoice's declared currency, unless it's an intra-EU conversion line" gives Copilot the actual edge case your bug report is about, and the completion that follows is aimed at your real problem instead of a plausible-sounding average one. This is the same specificity lever from the general prompting lessons, just expressed as a line of code above a function instead of a message in a chat box.

A vague comment gets a vague completion for exactly the reason a vague chat prompt gets a vague reply. The fix is the same fix you already know: name the actual case, in the comment, instead of describing the feature in the abstract.
Chat participants: pointing chat past the one open file

By default, Copilot Chat mostly sees what's open in front of you. Chat participants widen that. `@workspace` scopes a question across the whole repository, useful for something like "where else in invoice-parser do we validate a currency code?" instead of hoping the one file you happen to have open contains the answer. `@vscode` answers questions about the editor and its settings rather than your code. `@terminal` can reason about the integrated terminal's recent output, handy when a stack trace scrolled past faster than you could read it. `@github` reaches for GitHub-hosted context, like searching issues or pull requests for a prior discussion of the same bug. For a real codebase question, `@workspace` is the one you'll reach for most.
Slash commands: naming the job instead of describing it

Slash commands are shortcuts for jobs Copilot already knows how to do, so you don't have to spell them out in prose every time. Highlight the currency-parsing function and type `/explain` for a walkthrough of what it currently does, `/tests` to generate a test case for the EUR-nested-in-USD scenario your bug report describes, `/doc` to draft the docstring you've been putting off, or `/fix` once you've actually pinned down what's wrong. `/new` scaffolds a new file or project when you're starting from nothing. Each one is a named job, not a sentence you have to construct fresh each time.
Chat variables: naming exactly what Copilot should look at

Chat variables attach precise material to your question instead of leaving Copilot to guess what "this" refers to. `#selection` points at exactly the block of code you've highlighted. `#file` points at a specific file, even one you don't currently have open. `#codebase` searches broadly across the repo, similar in spirit to `@workspace`. `#terminalLastCommand` pulls in the last thing you ran in the terminal, useful when a command just failed and you want Copilot reasoning about that actual output. "#selection explain why this fails on a line with two currency symbols" gets you a sharper answer than a bare "explain this," for the same reason a scoped prompt always beats an unscoped one: you've removed a guess Copilot would otherwise have to make.

cards.body: @workspace (whole repo), @vscode (editor/settings), @terminal (recent terminal output), @github (issues/PRs). Widen a question past the one file you have open.
cards.title: Chat participants

cards.body: /explain, /fix, /tests, /doc, /new. Name a job Copilot already knows how to do, instead of describing it in a full sentence each time.
cards.title: Slash commands

cards.body: #selection, #file, #codebase, #terminalLastCommand. Attach precisely the material the question is actually about, so Copilot isn't guessing what "this" means.
cards.title: Chat variables

questions.q: You want Copilot Chat to answer a question about a validation pattern used somewhere else in invoice-parser, not just the file you currently have open. What do you reach for?
options: The /explain slash command
The @workspace chat participant
The #selection chat variable
A plain, unscoped question in quick chat

questions.q: You've highlighted the currency-parsing function and want Copilot to generate a test case for it without typing out a full description of what you want tested. What's the fastest route?
options: Type a detailed paragraph describing the exact test case you want
Use the /tests slash command on the selection

questions.q: A teammate says their comment-driven prompt above a function keeps producing a generic, unhelpful completion. What's the most likely fix?
options: Switch to a different, more capable model
Make the comment name the actual case or edge case they want handled, instead of describing the feature abstractly
Abandon comment-driven prompting and only use chat from now on
Add more blank lines above the function so Copilot has more room to think
questions.explanation: A vague comment produces a vague completion for the same reason a vague chat prompt produces a vague reply: the model fills every gap you left generically. Naming the specific case is the fix, same as it is anywhere else in prompting.

title: Prompting Copilot well

content_blocks.text: Every time someone opens Copilot Chat and asks about invoice-parser's currency-validation rules, they get an answer built from whatever happens to be open in their editor at that moment, because the actual rule lives in a one-page design doc almost nobody keeps open, plus a style guide two folders away that most people have never opened at all. Dana, the newest hire on the team, has now asked a version of the same currency-validation question three times this week and gotten a slightly different half-answer each time. A Copilot Space fixes this by giving Copilot a fixed, curated set of material to draw on every single time, instead of only whatever's on screen in the moment.
What a Space actually is

A Space is a persistent, curated bundle of context: repositories, individual files, pasted text, links, plus custom instructions for how Copilot should use them. Once it exists, every chat conversation you open inside that Space draws on the same material, instead of only the open editor. That's a real difference from `@workspace`, which you met in the previous lesson: `@workspace` searches your actual repo live, right now, whatever state it happens to be in. A Space is something you build once, deliberately, and it can include things that live outside the repo entirely, like a design doc or a style guide, without anyone needing to have those files open.
Creating your first Space

Name the Space, then add sources: point it at the invoice-parser repository, attach the design doc and the style guide as individual files, and write a short custom instruction for how Copilot should behave inside this Space specifically, something like "when asked about currency handling, always mention the intra-EU exception." Call it "invoice-parser context." From then on, anyone asking a question inside that Space, Dana included, gets an answer grounded in the actual rule, not a guess reconstructed from whatever file happened to be open.
Sharing, discoverability, and governance

A Space can stay personal, or be shared with your team or org, at which point it shows up for others to find and reuse without rebuilding it themselves. That's the real payoff for Dana's situation: one person builds the Space once, and everyone after her benefits without repeating the setup. It's also a small governance decision the moment you share it. A shared Space starts to function as a quasi-official answer source for whatever it covers, so who can edit it versus who can only use it, and how much people trust what it says, matters more once other people are actually relying on it.

A Space is only as good as its last update. If invoice-parser's currency rule changes next quarter and nobody touches the Space, Copilot will confidently keep repeating the old rule to Dana and to everyone who joins after her. Treat a shared Space like real documentation that needs upkeep, not a one-time setup task you check off and forget.
Do's and don'ts of working in a Space
The instinct to make a Space more useful by adding more to it works against you, the same way it does with context in a single prompt.

cards.body: "invoice-parser context" is a Space. "Everything our whole org has ever written" is not. A focused Space gives Copilot a clear, relevant set of material to draw on.
cards.title: Do: scope it to one real subject

cards.body: The same specificity that makes a single prompt good applies here, just aimed at the Space as a whole instead of one message: name the exact behavior you want, like always flagging the intra-EU exception.
cards.title: Do: write specific custom instructions

cards.body: More material sitting in a Space is not automatically better, for the same reason a 60-page contract pasted whole is worse than the one relevant clause. Add what the subject actually needs.
cards.title: Don't: dump everything in "for completeness"

cards.body: A Space is living material, not a snapshot. Revisit and prune it as the underlying code, docs, and rules actually change, or it quietly starts lying.
cards.title: Don't: treat it as a one-time archive

content_blocks.text: When a Space beats @workspace or a plain chat

Reach for a Space when the material Copilot needs lives outside the repo entirely, like a design decision or a business rule no amount of code-reading could infer, or when you want the same grounded context to stay stable across an entire team's conversations rather than depending on whatever any one person happens to have open that day. Reach for `@workspace` when the question is really about the live state of the code itself, right now, today.

questions.q: Dana keeps getting inconsistent answers about invoice-parser's currency-validation rule because it lives in a design doc almost nobody keeps open. What actually fixes this?
options: Tell Dana to always keep the design doc open in a second editor tab
Build a Copilot Space that bundles the design doc, the style guide, and custom instructions, so every chat draws on the same material
Ask Dana to stop using Copilot Chat for questions about business rules
Rename the design doc so it's easier to find in the file tree
questions.explanation: A Space gives Copilot a fixed, curated bundle of context that doesn't depend on what happens to be open. It solves exactly this kind of recurring, inconsistent-answer problem.

questions.q: Your team's invoice-parser Space hasn't been updated since the currency-validation rule changed last quarter. What's the actual risk?
options: The Space will slow down noticeably for every user
Copilot will confidently keep repeating the outdated rule to anyone who asks, including new hires
The Space will automatically delete itself after a few months of inactivity
Nothing; Spaces always reflect the live state of the repository automatically
questions.explanation: A Space only knows what it was given. If the underlying rule changes and nobody updates the Space, it becomes a confident, stale answer source rather than a helpful one.

questions.q: What's the real difference between asking @workspace a question and asking the same question inside a Copilot Space?
options: There is no real difference; Space is just a rebrand of @workspace
@workspace searches the live repository you have open right now; a Space is a curated, stable bundle you build once, which can include material that lives outside the repo entirely
A Space can only contain code files, never documents
@workspace is for teams and Spaces are only ever personal

title: Copilot Spaces: giving Copilot durable context

content_blocks.text: This module starts on new ground: a different team and a different repo from Module 1's invoice-parser, because the shift this module covers — from an editor-bound assistant to an agent that owns a whole task — deserves its own codebase to play out against, not a continuation of the last one. Someone files an issue against your team's billing-service repo: "Add CSV export to the invoices dashboard — finance keeps asking for it." A year ago you'd either pick it up yourself or hand it to whoever has bandwidth, and either way a person types every line. Today you have another option: assign the issue directly to an agent. It reads the issue and the codebase, proposes a plan, writes the code, runs the tests, and opens a pull request — without you typing a single line. This lesson is about what changed to make that possible, and what your job becomes once an agent, not a person, opens that PR.
Assistant, or agent?

You already know the assistant shape from GitHub Copilot's inline suggestions and chat: you're in the editor, you ask a question or accept a completion, and it responds to exactly what's in front of you. It has no memory of the issue tracker, no opinion about what to do next, and no ability to act once the conversation ends. That's an assistant — bounded to the moment you're in, and entirely reactive.

An agent is given a goal, not a keystroke. Point it at "Add CSV export to the invoices dashboard" and it decides what files to touch, what order to do the work in, and when it's done — the same way a competent new hire would work through a ticket. The shift isn't a smarter model. It's that the tool now owns a multi-step task end to end, and you've moved from typing alongside it to reviewing after it.
The loop: plan, act, evaluate

Every agent task in billing-service runs the same three-phase loop, whether the task is small or large:

Plan — the agent reads the issue, the relevant code, and any linked context, then writes out what it intends to do before touching anything: which files it'll change, what the new CSV export function looks like, which existing tests it expects to affect.

Act — it executes that plan: writes the code, adds or updates tests, runs the test suite and linter locally, and pushes a branch.

Evaluate — it checks its own work against the plan and the issue (did the tests pass? does the export match what finance asked for?), then opens a pull request summarizing what it did and why.

The loop doesn't end there — evaluation continues once a human opens the PR. That's the next section.

The plan is only as good as the issue. "Add CSV export to the invoices dashboard" is workable because it names the feature and the audience. "Make the dashboard better" gives an agent nothing to plan against, and it will fill the gap with its own guess about what "better" means — often not the guess you'd have made.
GitHub as the system of record

Notice where all of this happened: the issue, the branch, the commits, the PR, the test run — every step lived inside GitHub, not in a chat transcript that vanishes when you close the window. That's deliberate, and it's what makes agent work trustworthy at all. GitHub is acting as the system of record and the control plane: the place where the task was defined, the place where the work is visible mid-flight, and the place where the result gets checked before it goes anywhere near production.

If an agent instead worked silently on someone's laptop and dropped a finished zip file on you, you'd have no way to audit what it tried, what it discarded, or why. Because the agent operates through issues, branches, and PRs like any contributor would, its entire trail is inspectable after the fact — by you, by a teammate, or by whoever's on call when something in the export breaks three weeks from now.
Reviewing the agent's PR: the contributor model

Here's the mental model that keeps this safe: treat a PR from an agent exactly like a PR from a new external contributor. You wouldn't merge a stranger's PR because it "looked confident" — you'd read the diff, check that the tests actually exercise the new behavior, and confirm it does what the issue asked, not just something plausible. An agent deserves precisely that same scrutiny, no more trusting and no less.

Concretely, that means: the PR is attributed to the agent's own identity, not silently merged as if you wrote it; required status checks still have to pass; and a human — you — still approves before it merges. The agent did the typing. The judgment about whether the result is correct and appropriate to ship is still entirely yours, same as it would be for any other contributor's PR.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can tell the difference between an assistant answering you in the moment and an agent carrying a whole task from issue to pull request, and you know why the plan → act → evaluate loop and GitHub's role as system of record are what make handing over that much responsibility safe rather than reckless. Reviewing an agent's PR with a contributor's skepticism — not a rubber stamp — is the habit that carries through the rest of this module: governance, spec-driven development, and multi-agent work all build on this same one idea, that GitHub-native trails plus human review are what make agent output trustworthy.

questions.q: Finance asks for a CSV export on the invoices dashboard. You assign the GitHub issue directly to a coding agent instead of picking it up yourself. What makes this agent behavior rather than assistant behavior?
options: It uses a more advanced language model than Copilot's inline suggestions
It takes the whole task from issue to opened pull request on its own, deciding what to do and in what order, rather than responding only to what you type in the moment
It runs somewhere other than your laptop
It cannot be reviewed once it starts working
questions.explanation: The model isn't what makes something an agent — it's that the tool owns a multi-step task end to end (plan, act, evaluate) rather than only reacting to a single prompt or keystroke.

questions.q: An agent opens a PR for the CSV export feature. The PR description says the tests pass and the feature is complete. What should you do before merging?
options: Merge it — a clean plan → act → evaluate cycle means the work is already verified
Read the diff, check what the tests actually assert, and confirm the change matches the issue — the same scrutiny you'd give any new contributor's PR
Only check it if the PR looks unusually large
Ask the agent to re-run the loop a second time as proof
questions.explanation: The contributor model means an agent's PR earns the same review as a human contributor's — a confident-sounding summary is not evidence the change is correct or appropriately scoped.

questions.q: Why does it matter that the agent's plan, branch, commits, and PR all live inside GitHub rather than in a private chat session?
options: GitHub is simply where the code has to end up eventually
It makes GitHub the system of record and control plane — every step the agent took is visible and auditable after the fact, not just the final result
It's required for the agent's model to function
It prevents the agent from making any mistakes
questions.explanation: Because the work happens through issues, branches, and PRs, anyone can inspect what the agent tried and why — that traceability is what makes trusting agent output different from trusting a black box.

title: From assistant to agent: the plan -> act -> evaluate loop

content_blocks.text: The CSV export shipped cleanly — the agent's PR was easy to review, tests were solid, low stakes if something had been slightly off. Now leadership wants to hand agents more of the backlog, including a ticket that touches how invoice totals are calculated before they're sent to customers. That one is not the same kind of task. A bug in CSV formatting is an annoyance; a bug in a total calculation is money going out wrong. Before billing-service hands agents anything else, the team needs to decide, explicitly, which kinds of changes an agent can make on its own and which ones need a human standing in the way first.
Not every task deserves the same trust

The instinct to treat every agent task the same way — full autonomy or full suspicion — doesn't hold up once the stakes vary this much. What billing-service needs instead is risk-based autonomy: define, ahead of time, which categories of change an agent can carry out with light review, which need a human to authorize before anything executes, and which are off-limits to agents entirely for now.

For this team, that split looks roughly like: fixing a typo, adding a test, or extending a report format is low-risk — an agent can do it and a normal PR review is enough. Refactoring the invoice-total calculation, touching anything that talks to the payment provider, or changing what a webhook sends externally is high-risk — those need a human to explicitly sign off on the plan before the agent is allowed to act, not just review the PR afterward.
GitHub-native controls that enforce it

Deciding on autonomy tiers only matters if something actually enforces them, and the enforcement billing-service uses is built into GitHub rather than bolted on:

CODEOWNERS marks the billing-calculation files so any PR touching them — agent-authored or not — automatically requires review from a specific senior engineer, no exceptions.

Rulesets on the main branch require passing status checks and at least one human approval before merge, and can block certain file paths from being touched without that approval regardless of who or what opened the PR.

Environments gate the deploy step itself: pushing to the production environment requires a named human to click approve in the Actions run, even if every check upstream already passed.

Together these mean the boundary isn't a suggestion the agent is trusted to respect — it's a rule GitHub enforces the same way it would for a careless human contributor.

Don't confuse telling an agent what it shouldn't do with actually preventing it. An instruction like "never modify the payment webhook" in a prompt or a project-instructions file is a reasonable first layer, but it can be misunderstood, overridden by a later instruction, or simply missed. CODEOWNERS and branch rulesets don't rely on the agent remembering or agreeing — they're enforced by GitHub regardless of what the agent intended.
Human-in-the-loop for high-risk actions

For the invoice-total ticket, human-in-the-loop means more than "someone reviews the PR eventually." It means a person authorizes the plan before the agent starts acting — reading the proposed approach the same way you'd sanity-check a colleague's plan before they touched a live billing calculation — and a different gate (the environment approval) before anything the agent built reaches production. Two checkpoints, at the two moments the cost of a mistake is highest: before the work starts, and before it ships.
Keeping a trail: observability and audit

Every one of these controls also leaves a record. The Actions run log shows exactly which workflow ran, what it did, and who approved which gate. The PR history shows the plan the agent proposed, what changed between review comments and the final version, and who approved it. If the invoice-total logic is wrong three weeks after it ships, this trail is how you find out whether it was the agent's plan, a reviewer's oversight, or a requirement nobody stated clearly — rather than everyone guessing.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can set risk-based autonomy boundaries instead of treating every agent task as equally trustworthy, and translate those boundaries into GitHub-native controls — CODEOWNERS, rulesets, environments — that enforce themselves rather than depending on an agent remembering an instruction. You also know why the trail those controls leave behind (audit logs, approval history) matters just as much as the boundary itself: it's what lets you reconstruct what happened when something eventually goes wrong. The next lesson, spec-driven development, tackles a related problem from the other end — giving an agent clear enough intent up front that it needs less correcting in the first place.

questions.q: Billing-service wants an agent to refactor the function that calculates invoice totals — code that directly affects what customers are charged. What's the appropriate autonomy level for this task?
options: Full autonomy — the same as any other refactor, since the agent already passed its own test suite
A human authorizes the plan before the agent acts, and a separate approval gate before anything reaches production
No autonomy at all — this task should never involve an agent
Autonomy depends only on how confident the agent's PR description sounds
questions.explanation: Risk-based autonomy means high-stakes changes get human sign-off at more than one point — before the agent starts acting and before the result ships — not just a single after-the-fact PR review.

questions.q: Why does billing-service rely on CODEOWNERS and branch rulesets instead of just instructing the agent not to touch the payment webhook code?
options: Instructions in a prompt are actually more reliable than repository-level controls
GitHub-native controls are enforced regardless of what the agent intended or misunderstood, while a prompt instruction can be overridden or missed
CODEOWNERS is required for any repository to function
Rulesets make the agent work faster
questions.explanation: A guardrail that depends on the agent remembering or agreeing isn't really a guardrail. CODEOWNERS and rulesets enforce the boundary at the platform level, independent of the agent's behavior.

questions.q: Three weeks after an agent-assisted change ships, the invoice-total calculation turns out to be subtly wrong. What lets the team reconstruct what happened?
options: Asking the agent to explain itself again from memory
The Actions run logs, PR history, and approval trail that recorded the plan, the changes, and who signed off at each gate
There's no way to know after the fact — that's an accepted risk of using agents
Checking whether the same bug exists in a staging environment
questions.explanation: Observability and audit trails are the point of running this work through GitHub's controls — they let you trace a problem back to the plan, the review, or the approval, rather than starting from zero.

title: Governance for agentic engineering

content_blocks.text: Finance's next ask is bigger: a whole new notifications service that emails customers when an invoice is overdue — nothing like it exists in billing-service today. Filing a single issue and assigning it to an agent, the way you did for the CSV export, won't work here. There's no existing code for the agent to anchor a plan to, and "build a notifications service" is vague enough that ten different agents would build ten different things. This is the greenfield problem, and it's what GitHub Spec Kit and spec-driven development are for.
The problem spec-driven development solves

You saw in the first lesson that a vague issue produces a plan built on guesses. On an existing codebase, the agent at least has real files, existing patterns, and current tests to anchor those guesses to. On a blank slate, it has nothing — "build a notifications service" could mean an in-app banner, a Slack message, or the overdue-invoice emails finance actually wants, and the agent has no way to know which one you meant beyond a coin flip dressed up as confidence.

Spec-driven development (SDD) fixes this by forcing intent onto the page before any code exists — not as documentation you write afterward to justify what got built, but as the actual first step, in an order that can't be skipped.
Constitution, spec, plan, tasks

GitHub Spec Kit structures that intent into four artifacts, built in sequence, each one narrowing from the last:

constitution.md comes first and rarely changes between features — it's billing-service's standing engineering principles: use the existing auth library, log to the existing observability stack, never write directly to the invoices table from a new service. Every later artifact has to respect it.

spec.md is what the notifications service should do, in plain terms: who receives what, when an invoice counts as overdue, what happens if the email fails to send. No implementation detail yet — just intent and edge cases, the same scoping questions the habit of "what goes in, what comes out, what could go wrong" already trains you to ask.

plan.md is the technical answer: which language and framework, how the new service talks to billing-service's existing invoice data, where it's deployed.

tasks.md breaks the plan into a concrete, ordered checklist an agent can work through one item at a time — each one small enough to review on its own, the same discipline as reviewing one agent PR at a time rather than one giant one.

The order is load-bearing. It's tempting to jump straight to tasks.md once you know roughly what you want — but tasks written without an approved spec just relocate the vague-issue problem one level down. Read and adjust each artifact before moving to the next; that's the whole value of the greenfield approach, not a formality to click through.
Where this differs from just filing a good issue

A well-scoped GitHub issue works fine for a bounded change to code that already exists, like the CSV export. It's disposable — once the PR merges, the issue's job is done. The four Spec Kit artifacts are meant to persist: constitution.md keeps governing every future feature in this service, and spec.md and plan.md stay in the repo as the living record of what the notifications service is supposed to do and why, for the next engineer or agent who touches it — not a one-off conversation that evaporates once the first version ships.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can recognize when a task is greenfield enough that a single issue won't give an agent the intent it needs, and you know the sequence — constitution, spec, plan, tasks — that GitHub Spec Kit uses to fix that, plus why skipping ahead to tasks defeats the purpose. Where lesson 1 was about trusting an agent's output on a bounded, existing-code task, this lesson is about setting up trust on a blank one, by writing the intent down before anything gets built.

questions.q: Finance wants an entirely new notifications service and there's no existing code to anchor an agent's plan to. Why won't a single well-written GitHub issue work as well here as it did for the CSV export?
options: Issues can only be used for bug fixes, not new features
On a greenfield project the agent has no existing code or patterns to ground its guesses in, so even a decent issue leaves too much genuinely undefined
GitHub Spec Kit requires disabling the issue tracker
New services can only be built manually, without any agent involvement
questions.explanation: A good issue works when there's an existing codebase to anchor interpretation. On a blank slate there's nothing to anchor to, so intent has to be established more formally before implementation starts.

questions.q: In GitHub Spec Kit's workflow, what does spec.md capture that plan.md does not?
options: The specific programming language and framework to use
What the feature should do and for whom, including edge cases — without implementation detail
The ordered checklist of tasks an agent will execute
The engineering principles that apply to every feature in the repo
questions.explanation: spec.md is intent: behavior, audience, and edge cases in plain language. The technical how — architecture and stack — is plan.md's job, one step later.

questions.q: A teammate suggests skipping straight to tasks.md for a new greenfield feature since "we already roughly know what we want." What's the risk?
options: There's no risk — tasks.md is the only artifact that actually matters
Tasks written without an approved spec just relocate the vague-issue problem to a different document, instead of actually resolving it
GitHub Spec Kit technically requires all four files to exist, so this is a compliance issue only
It would make the constitution.md file redundant
questions.explanation: The sequence is load-bearing: each artifact narrows the last. Skipping to tasks without a real spec just means the ambiguity that was supposed to get resolved shows up later, in code, instead of on paper where it's cheap to fix.

title: Spec-driven development

content_blocks.text: While the notifications service is in progress, one of billing-service's engineers wants something much smaller and faster: an internal ops console where support staff can retry a failed invoice webhook with one click, instead of paging an engineer every time a payment provider's callback fails silently. It doesn't need a spec, a constitution, or a formal review cycle to get started — it needs someone to describe it to an AI coding agent and iterate until it works. That is vibe coding, and if you've been through the Lovable track, you've already met the term.
You've met this term before

The Lovable track's "Vibecoding, build a real app by describing it" defines vibe coding as building real, working software by describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI write the code, while you stay in charge as the product owner and tester rather than the one typing syntax. That definition is exactly right, and it isn't specific to Lovable — it's the same thing happening here, with a coding agent like GitHub Copilot's agent mode instead of a hosted app builder.

What carries over completely: scope before you describe, change one thing at a time, and check behavior rather than trust confident-sounding output. If you've done the Lovable lesson, you already have the instincts this lesson needs — what's different is the terrain those instincts now apply to.
The same discipline, sharper stakes

In Lovable, a vague description gets filled with a reasonable-looking guess inside a hosted preview you can revert with one click. Here, that same vague description becomes a guess written as real code, committed to a real git history, in a repo other engineers — and other agents, per the earlier lessons in this module — will read and build on next. The underlying failure mode hasn't changed: an under-scoped ask gets filled with assumptions you didn't make. What's changed is that the result is now a permanent, reviewable, mergeable artifact rather than a disposable preview, so the cost of an unscoped guess landing wrong is higher, not different in kind.

"It was quick to build" is not a review exemption. A retry-webhook button that lets support staff resend a request to a payment provider is exactly the kind of change that should go through the same PR review — and, per the governance lesson, the same autonomy-tier thinking — as anything else touching billing-service. Vibe coding changes how fast the first draft appears. It changes nothing about who has to check it before it ships.
Generating requirements and a wireframe before you generate code

The Lovable lesson's "scope before you describe" step — what goes in, what comes out, what happens in between, what could go wrong — has a direct, more formal equivalent here: ask the coding agent to draft a short product-requirements note and a rough text wireframe of the console screen before either of you writes a line of implementation. For the retry-webhook console: inputs are the failed webhook's ID and a support agent's decision to retry; output is a status message and an updated retry count; the edge case worth deciding now is what happens if someone clicks retry twice in the same minute.

Getting the agent to produce that requirements note and wireframe as an actual saved artifact — not just a mental note — means you're reviewing intent before code exists, the same habit the previous lesson built around spec.md, just lighter-weight and appropriate for a task this small.
Effective prompts for a codebase, not a blank canvas

Inside a real repo, an effective vibe-coding prompt references what's actually there: "add a retry button to WebhookDetail.tsx that calls the existing retryWebhook function in webhooks.ts" gives the agent a target inside a codebase it can check itself against, the same way "show a page listing every comment with the average rating at the top" gave Lovable something concrete to aim for. And the one-change-at-a-time rhythm from that lesson still applies, maybe more so: get the retry button working and reviewed, then add the confirmation message, then the double-click guard, each as its own request and its own small PR — not one prompt that tries to build the whole console at once.
