content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can connect this deeper version of vibe coding back to the term you may already know from the Lovable track, and you know exactly what carries over unchanged (scoping, one change at a time, verifying behavior) versus what's higher-stakes here (a permanent codebase instead of a disposable preview, and the same PR/governance discipline from earlier in this module applying regardless of how fast the first draft appeared). The next lesson takes this further still: what happens when more than one agent is working on billing-service at the same time.

questions.q: An engineer wants to quickly build an internal console where support staff can retry a failed invoice webhook, by describing it to a coding agent and iterating. Which Lovable-track habit carries over unchanged to this technical setting?
options: None of it — vibe coding for engineers is a completely different practice
Scoping before you describe, changing one thing at a time, and verifying behavior instead of trusting confident-sounding output
Only the term itself carries over; the actual method is unrelated
The habit of reverting with one click, since that's unique to hosted app builders
questions.explanation: The core discipline — scope first, one change at a time, verify rather than trust — is the same skill whether you're directing Lovable or a coding agent in a real repo. What changes is the terrain it's applied to, not the method.

questions.q: What makes an under-scoped vibe-coding prompt riskier in a real engineering repo than in a hosted app builder like Lovable?
options: Coding agents are less capable than Lovable's builder
The resulting guess becomes a permanent, committed artifact that other engineers and agents will read and build on, not a disposable preview you can revert instantly
Real repos don't allow any form of undo
It isn't riskier — the stakes are identical in both settings
questions.explanation: The failure mode (a vague ask gets filled with the model's own assumption) is the same in both settings. What's different is the cost: a real repo's history is permanent and shared, unlike a hosted preview one click away from reverting.

questions.q: The retry-webhook console "was quick to build" using vibe coding. Does that change whether it needs PR review before merging?
options: Yes — vibe-coded changes are informal by nature and can skip review
No — it should go through the same PR review and autonomy-tier thinking as any other change touching billing-service, regardless of how fast the first draft appeared
Only if the console is used by more than ten people
Review is optional as long as the agent's summary says the tests passed
questions.explanation: Vibe coding changes how quickly a first draft appears, not who has to check it before it ships. A webhook-retry feature touching a payment provider still gets the same review discipline as any other billing-service change.

title: Vibe coding, the deeper version

content_blocks.text: Leadership wants the CSV export, the notifications service, and the webhook-retry console all shipped together in one release, plus a handful of smaller fixes — more independent work than one agent should reasonably do in sequence. Instead, the team splits it: one agent scaffolds the notifications service, another wires up the admin console's remaining polish, a third handles the export edge cases finance flagged late. Three agents, working at once, on branches of the same repo, all supposed to land in the same release. That's the coordination problem this lesson is about.
One agent, then many

Every lesson so far in this module dealt with a single agent running its own plan → act → evaluate loop, reviewed by a human afterward. That model doesn't disappear here — each of the three agents on this release still runs that same loop individually. What's new is the layer above it: something has to decide how the big release-sized task splits into three agent-sized ones, hand each agent its slice, and reconcile the results into something that ships together without the three pieces stepping on each other.
The conductor pattern

That coordinating role is the conductor pattern, and the name is deliberately literal: a conductor doesn't play an instrument, they decide who plays when. In billing-service's release, the conductor's job is to break "ship the export, the notifications service, and the console fixes together" into three well-scoped subtasks, open a tracking issue for each, assign one to each worker agent, and watch for all three to report back — without writing a line of the export, service, or console code itself. It's the same judgment a lead engineer uses splitting a big ticket across a team, just automated: the conductor's only output is good task breakdown and coordination, not implementation.
Coordinating agents via GitHub Actions events

The hand-offs between the conductor and the three worker agents run on GitHub Actions events rather than anyone watching a dashboard: a workflow triggers when the conductor's tracking issue is labeled ready, which assigns and kicks off a worker agent; that agent's PR opening triggers another workflow that runs checks; the checks completing successfully is the event that tells the conductor "this piece is done, here's the artifact." No agent polls another agent directly — each one reacts to something GitHub already tracks natively (an issue label, a PR, a check run), which means the entire coordination trail is visible in the Actions log the same way a single agent's work was in lesson 1, just with three threads instead of one.
Isolation: keeping agents out of each other's way

Three agents working at once only stays safe if none of them can quietly step on what another is doing. Each worker agent gets its own branch, so nobody's uncommitted changes leak into anyone else's. Permissions are scoped tightly enough that the notifications-service agent can't push directly to files the export agent owns. And concurrency controls in the Actions workflows stop two agents from triggering the same deploy or the same shared migration step at the same moment — a rule enforced by GitHub, not by hoping the agents coordinate politely on their own.
When agents collide

Isolation reduces collisions; it doesn't eliminate them. The console-fixes agent and the export agent both end up touching a shared formatting utility, and their branches produce a real merge conflict. This gets resolved exactly the way lesson 1 said any agent's work gets evaluated: through GitHub-native review and checks, not through the agents negotiating with each other. The conductor flags the conflict, a human (or a designated resolver agent with narrower scope) reviews both changes side by side, and one branch rebases onto the other before either merges. If one agent's task fails outright — the notifications-service tests won't pass — the recovery pattern is the same as for a single agent: retry with a clearer task description, roll back that piece without blocking the other two, or escalate to a human, rather than letting a stuck agent silently hold up the whole release.

The riskiest multi-agent design isn't too little autonomy — it's skipping isolation to move faster. Letting two agents push directly to main, or letting the conductor merge every worker's PR the moment it opens instead of waiting for each one's checks, trades a manageable single conflict now for a much harder one to unwind once everything's tangled together on the same branch.

As soon as any worker agent opens its PR, the conductor merges it into main immediately, so the release branch always has the latest code from all three agents ready to go.

content_blocks.text: What you can now do

You can describe why a large, splittable release benefits from a conductor coordinating several worker agents rather than one agent working serially, how GitHub Actions events (issue labels, PR opens, completed checks) let those agents hand off work without polling each other directly, and what isolation and conflict-recovery patterns keep three agents working at once from quietly corrupting each other's output. This closes out the module: from recognizing a single agent's loop, to governing what it's allowed to do, to giving it clear intent up front, to directing it conversationally, to coordinating several of them at once — all resting on the same foundation this module opened with, GitHub as the system of record that makes any of this auditable.

questions.q: Billing-service splits a release into three subtasks and assigns one to each of three worker agents. What is the conductor's job in this pattern?
options: To write the trickiest of the three pieces of code itself, since it has the most context
To break the release into well-scoped subtasks, assign and coordinate the worker agents, and reconcile their results — without implementing any of the feature code itself
To replace the human reviewer for all three agents' PRs
To run continuously in the background merging every PR the moment it appears
questions.explanation: The conductor pattern is coordination, not implementation — like a lead engineer splitting and tracking a big ticket across a team, its output is task breakdown and hand-offs, not code.

questions.q: Why do the worker agents in billing-service's release hand off work to each other through GitHub Actions events (issue labels, PR opens, completed checks) instead of messaging each other directly?
options: Direct agent-to-agent messaging isn't technically possible on any platform
Routing hand-offs through events GitHub already tracks keeps the whole coordination trail visible and auditable, the same way a single agent's work was traceable through issues and PRs
It's faster than any other coordination method
It removes the need for any human review of the release
questions.explanation: Using GitHub-native events as triggers means every hand-off is visible in the Actions log and PR history — extending the same system-of-record principle from a single agent's work to several agents working at once.

questions.q: Two worker agents' branches both modify a shared formatting utility, producing a real merge conflict. What's the appropriate way to resolve it?
options: Let whichever agent's PR was opened first win automatically, since first-come is a simple rule
Route the conflict through the same GitHub-native review and checks any single agent's PR would face, with a human or a narrowly scoped resolver deciding, then rebase before merging
Have the two agents negotiate the conflict directly with each other, without human or review involvement
Cancel both agents' work and restart the release from scratch
questions.explanation: Conflicts between agents get resolved the same way any agent's individual output gets evaluated — through review and checks, not by letting agents settle it between themselves or applying an arbitrary tie-break rule.

title: Multi-agent workflows and orchestration

content_blocks.text: This module starts on new ground again: a different team and repo from Module 2's billing-service, because a deep dive into Claude Code itself deserves a codebase of its own to work against, not a hand-off from the last module's agentic-engineering scenario. Three weeks into the invoice-service team, you're handed a bug ticket: partial refunds are returning a 500 instead of a partial credit. Before you touch a single line, you need to decide how you're actually going to run Claude Code against this repo — a Node/TypeScript API with a Postgres database, six other engineers pushing to it daily, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that will reject anything that doesn't pass. Claude Code isn't one piece of software with one way in. It's the same engine reachable from five different doors, and which one you pick changes what a session actually looks like.
Five entry points, one engine

Terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, the Claude Desktop app, and the web all run the same underlying agent — same model, same tools, same permission model. What changes is where the conversation lives and what it can see. A terminal session lives in your shell, in whatever directory you launched it from. An IDE session lives inside a project you already have open, with diffs rendered next to the file instead of as a text block. The Desktop app and the web version exist so a session can start without you opening a terminal or an editor at all. None of these is "more powerful" than another — for invoice-service, you'll likely end up using at least two of them, for different moments in the same day.
Terminal: the reference environment

Terminal is where every Claude Code feature lands first, and it's the version most documentation assumes. Install it once with `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then run `claude` from inside the invoice-service checkout. It opens a conversation scoped to that folder: it can read every file under it, run shell commands there, and nothing outside it unless you explicitly point it elsewhere. For day-to-day repo work — the refund bug, a migration, a CI failure — this is the version to reach for, because everything downstream in this module (Plan Mode, hooks, MCP servers, custom subagents) is configured through it.

Claude Code authenticates two different ways: signing in with a Claude.ai account (Pro, Max, or Enterprise) or using an Anthropic Console API key billed separately by usage. They draw from different limits. If a teammate says Claude Code is running slow or capped and you aren't, check which one of you is on the API key — it's easy to assume everyone authenticated the same way when they didn't.
VS Code and JetBrains: Claude Code inside your editor

The Claude track's light Claude Code module already pointed you to the Desktop app and gave a passing mention of VS Code. The IDE story is bigger than that mention: install the Claude Code extension for VS Code, or the equivalent plugin for JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ, WebStorm, PyCharm, and the rest of the family), and a Claude Code panel opens alongside your editor rather than in a separate terminal window. The underlying session is identical to the terminal one, but proposed changes render as an inline diff in the file you're already looking at, and you can add a file to context by clicking it instead of typing its path. For reviewing what Claude Code changed in `refund-handler.ts` before you approve it, the inline diff view is noticeably easier to read than a terminal diff.
The Desktop app and the web: no terminal required

The Claude Desktop app now has three tabs — Chat, Cowork, and Code — so a Code session is one click away with nothing to install beyond the app itself. It's the natural choice on a machine where you don't want a dev environment set up at all, or for a quick look at a repo you don't normally work in.

Claude Code on the web goes a step further: the session runs in a cloud sandbox rather than on your machine, connected to a repository you authorize from GitHub. You describe the task from a browser tab, it works against a checkout of your repo in the cloud, and it opens a pull request when it's done rather than leaving changes on a local disk. For invoice-service specifically, this is the option worth knowing about for the afternoon you're on a locked-down laptop or someone else's machine and still need a small fix to go out.

The web version only sees what's pushed to GitHub — uncommitted local changes and anything in your `.gitignore` are invisible to it, because there is no local disk in the loop. Don't reach for it mid-way through a local session you haven't pushed; start it fresh from the branch you actually want it working against.
Picking a starting point for invoice-service

There's no single right answer, but a reasonable default: terminal for the actual repo work — the refund bug, the migration, anything this module covers from here — because every configuration file (CLAUDE.md, hooks, MCP servers, custom subagents) lives in the repo and terminal is where you'll set them up. Add the VS Code or JetBrains extension once you're doing this daily, so review happens inline instead of a context switch to a separate window. Keep the Desktop app and the web version in your back pocket for the moments terminal isn't available at all.

title: Installing and running Claude Code

content_blocks.text: Back to the refund bug: partial refunds on invoice-service return a 500 instead of issuing a partial credit. You already know the shape of the loop Claude Code runs — the Claude track's light Claude Code module walked you through it as explore, plan, build, and verify, on a folder of CSV exports with no git history and no tests. Here the same four checkpoints apply to a real codebase, and three mechanics specific to Claude Code make each one sharper: Plan Mode as an actual read-only mode rather than just an instruction, permission modes that decide how much Claude Code does without asking, and a visible task list for anything with more than one step.
From explore-plan-build-verify to Explore → Plan → Code → Commit

The four phases are the same four phases — what changes is what "build" and "verify" mean once there's a git history and a test suite behind the work. Build becomes Code: actual source changes, tracked by git, reviewable as a diff. Verify becomes Commit: not just checking the output looks right, but running the real test suite, and only then recording a commit with a message that explains why, not just what. If you're coming from the light module's CSV-folder example, that lesson's "save the output somewhere it won't get overwritten" becomes, here, an actual `git commit` — the same principle, expressed in the vocabulary a codebase already has for it.
Explore: let Plan Mode do the reading

Press Shift+Tab to cycle Claude Code's permission modes, and one of them is Plan Mode: a mode where Claude Code can read files and run read-only commands, but cannot edit anything or run anything that changes state, no matter what you ask it to do. For the refund bug, that's exactly the tool for explore: *"Look at how refunds are handled in this codebase — trace the request from the route through to the database write, and tell me where a partial refund diverges from a full one. Don't change anything yet."* Because edits are physically disabled in this mode, not just discouraged, you get an honest exploration pass with zero risk of Claude Code jumping ahead to a fix before you've agreed there's a plan worth having.

Plan Mode is a genuine mode change, not a polite request. Anything that would write a file or run a mutating command is blocked at the tool level while it's active — a stronger guarantee than just asking Claude Code nicely to "not change anything yet," which an ambiguous follow-up could still override.
Plan: read it, then exit Plan Mode to approve it

Once the exploration is done, ask for the plan: *"Based on what you found, what's the smallest change that fixes partial refunds without touching how full refunds work?"* Claude Code proposes a plan while still inside Plan Mode — still no edits possible. Read it the same way the light module already taught: does it touch files it shouldn't, does it match the fix you actually want, does the sequence make sense even at a glance. When you're satisfied, exiting Plan Mode (Shift+Tab again, or approving directly) is the moment it's allowed to start writing code — which is why this is the cheap correction point the light module called it, just enforced by the tool instead of by good manners.
Code: watch the todo list, not just the diff

On anything more than a one-file change, Claude Code keeps a running task list visible in the terminal as it works — each step marked pending, in progress, or done. For the refund fix that list might read: locate the refund handler, add the partial-amount branch, update the corresponding test fixture, run the suite. It's worth glancing at for the same reason the plan was worth reading: if a step appears that you didn't agree to, or a step you expected never shows up, that's your signal to interrupt before the diff even lands, not after.
Commit: run the real tests, then write a commit that explains why

Verify, in a repo with an actual test suite, means running it: *"run the test suite and fix anything that fails because of this change."* Watch for the difference between a test failing because your fix is wrong and a test failing because it encoded the old, buggy behaviour on purpose — Claude Code can tell you which is which if you ask, but it can also guess wrong, so read the failure before accepting either explanation.

Once it's green, the commit itself is the last checkpoint. Ask Claude Code to write the message, but read it before it lands: a good one names the bug and the fix (`fix: issue partial credit instead of 500 on partial refunds`), not just `update refund-handler.ts`. From there, *"open a PR against main with a description of what changed and why"* gets the change in front of the rest of the team — the equivalent of the light module's "save the output where it won't get overwritten," expressed as the actual git and GitHub mechanics a codebase gives you.
The loop, side by side

title: The agentic loop, in practice

content_blocks.text: invoice-service has grown a CLAUDE.md already — a previous engineer's half-finished attempt, three lines about the folder structure and nothing else. You're two hours into a session refactoring the credit-note feature across a dozen files, and Claude Code starts asking you where the Postgres connection string lives, something it correctly identified in the first ten minutes. The light Claude Code module already taught you why this happens — the context window fills up and old decisions get pushed out — and named the fix in the abstract as "standing context." This lesson names the actual three commands for managing it, and turns that half-finished CLAUDE.md into one that actually holds.
Three commands, three different fixes
/context, /compact, and /clear all address context pressure, but they're not interchangeable, and reaching for the wrong one costs you the wrong thing.
/context: see what's actually filling the window before you act

Run `/context` and Claude Code shows a breakdown of what's consuming the current context window — the system prompt, tool definitions, any MCP servers you've connected, the files it's read, and the conversation itself. On the credit-note session, this is where you'd notice that three large migration files got pulled in early and are still sitting in context long after you stopped needing them, quietly taking up room the actual work now needs. Check it before you decide whether to compact or clear — the fix depends on what's actually eating the space.
/compact: keep working, shed the history

`/compact` summarises everything so far into a condensed form and keeps the conversation going — you don't lose the thread of the credit-note work, but the verbose back-and-forth that got you there collapses into a paragraph. Use it mid-task, when you want to keep going but the session has accumulated more history than substance. You can also steer what it keeps: *"/compact, keep the details about the migration schema and the naming convention we agreed, drop the rest"* is a legitimate way to bias the summary toward what actually matters for what's left to do.
/clear: start over, on purpose

`/clear` wipes the context entirely — no summary, no carryover. Reach for it when you're switching to an unrelated task in the same terminal window: finishing the credit-note refactor and moving on to an unrelated CI flake, say. Carrying the credit-note context into that conversation would only add noise Claude Code has to sift through to find what's relevant to the new task. If there's anything from the finished task worth keeping, ask for a summary first and paste it into the new session's opening message — the same "summarise before you reset" habit the light module already taught, just with a command that makes the reset itself clean.

/compact and /clear look similar in that both free up space, but only one of them preserves anything. Reaching for /clear when you meant /compact loses the entire session's history — including decisions you might still need.
Writing a CLAUDE.md that actually holds

A CLAUDE.md worth having for invoice-service is more than three lines about folder structure. It's ground truth that would otherwise get re-explained every session: the commands that actually build and test the project (`npm run build`, `npm test`, `npm run lint`), the parts of the repo with a rule attached (migrations under `db/migrations/` are append-only — never edit a migration that's already merged), the conventions a new file should follow (errors are thrown as typed `AppError` subclasses, not raw `Error`), and how to get a local environment running at all (`docker compose up db` before anything else will connect). None of this is exotic — it's exactly what you'd tell a new hire in their first hour, written down once instead of repeated in every session.

Don't hand-write it from scratch. Open a session in the repo and ask Claude Code to draft one from what it can already see — the package.json scripts, the folder layout, the lint config — then correct the two or three things it guessed at or got wrong. That's usually faster and more accurate than writing it unassisted, and it's the same "describe the project, let Claude Code propose" pattern the light module described.
One CLAUDE.md, or several

A single project-root CLAUDE.md is the right amount of structure for most of invoice-service. Once a subtree has its own rules — the billing package has a stricter error-handling convention than the rest of the repo, say — a nested CLAUDE.md inside `packages/billing/` loads automatically only when Claude Code is working in that subtree, on top of the root one rather than instead of it. There's also a personal CLAUDE.md at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` for preferences that follow you across every project you touch, regardless of repo — commit message style, or how verbose you want explanations. Keep the boundary clean: what's true about this specific project goes in the repo's CLAUDE.md, what's true about how you like to work goes in the personal one.

CLAUDE.md is still only a strong default, not an enforced rule — an in-session instruction that contradicts it wins for that session, exactly as the light module warned. If a constraint in CLAUDE.md keeps getting quietly overridden, that's not a reason to restate it more forcefully; it's a sign you actually need a hook, which the MCP-and-hooks lesson later in this module covers.

title: Context management and CLAUDE.md

content_blocks.text: Every PR the invoice-service team opens is supposed to follow the same description template — what changed, why, how it was tested, a rollback note — and almost none of them actually do, because remembering the template is the part everyone forgets under deadline pressure. Separately, the team keeps running the full test suite by hand after every Claude Code session and eyeballing the output, which is exactly the kind of repetitive verification step worth delegating. Both problems point at the same part of Claude Code's customisation system, and this lesson is where it finally gets a precise treatment — including a correction to something you may have read elsewhere in this hub.
The correction, stated plainly

If you came through the Claude track, its "Advanced Claude Code patterns" lesson describes a reusable, named set of steps you invoke by typing a command, and calls that "the counterpart of the Skills you met in the chat module." That's describing a custom slash command — and a slash command is not a Skill. They're two different features with two different mechanics, and the rest of this lesson is the accurate version of both, plus subagents, which are a third thing again.
Slash commands: a fixed prompt you invoke by name

A custom slash command is a markdown file under `.claude/commands/` in the repo (or `~/.claude/commands/` for one that follows you everywhere). It has no frontmatter, no trigger logic, and no judgment involved: you type `/open-pr`, and its contents get pasted into the conversation as if you'd typed them yourself. For invoice-service, `.claude/commands/open-pr.md` could contain the team's PR description template verbatim, so typing `/open-pr` after a fix is briefed and ready always produces a PR with the changed/why/tested/rollback structure in it, because the template is now guaranteed rather than remembered.
Skills: instructions Claude decides to use, not instructions you invoke

A Skill is a different mechanism entirely: a `SKILL.md` file with YAML frontmatter — at minimum a `name` and a `description` — that Claude reads and decides for itself whether to apply, based on whether your request matches the description. You never type `/pr-description-writer`; you just ask for a PR the way you normally would, and if the Skill's description says something like "use when opening a pull request against this repo, to enforce the team's PR description format," Claude recognises the match and pulls the Skill in on its own.

The other structural difference is progressive disclosure. `SKILL.md` itself stays short — just enough for Claude to decide whether the skill applies and what to do first — and can point to additional files (a longer reference doc, an example, a script) that only get loaded into context if the skill actually needs them partway through. A CLAUDE.md-sized file loaded on every single session is expensive if most sessions don't need it; a Skill only costs context on the sessions where it's actually relevant.

The frontmatter field `allowed-tools` can restrict what a Skill is permitted to do while it's active — a skill for drafting a PR description has no reason to run Bash, so restricting it to read-only tools means even if the instructions inside it were ever wrong, the blast radius is capped.
Where CLAUDE.md and hooks sit relative to Skills

Four mechanisms, four different answers to "when does this apply": CLAUDE.md loads on every session in its scope, unconditionally — it's always-on project memory. A Skill loads only when Claude judges your request matches its description — on-demand, and it can defer most of its content until needed. A hook (covered in full in the next lesson) fires on a fixed event — before or after a tool runs, say — with no model judgment involved at all; it's deterministic, not discretionary. A slash command does nothing until you type its name; it's the only one of the four that's entirely under your explicit control rather than triggered automatically.
Sort it out: which mechanism is which

items.text: Enforce the team's PR description template, filled in exactly the same way every single time it's invoked by name.
items.reason: No judgment needed and always identical — a fixed template you invoke explicitly is a slash command, not something that should require Claude to decide when to use it.

items.text: Automatically apply the team's PR description conventions whenever a PR is being opened, without anyone remembering to type a command.
items.reason: Judgment-based, on-demand application from a description match is exactly what a Skill does — no explicit invocation needed.

items.text: Block any write to the db/migrations/ folder no matter what's said in the conversation.
items.reason: A hard, deterministic guardrail that can't be talked out of firing belongs in a hook, not a Skill or CLAUDE.md, both of which a later instruction can override.

items.text: Always know the project's build/test commands and folder conventions in every single session in this repo.
items.reason: Always-on project memory loaded every session is CLAUDE.md's job.

items.text: Run the full test suite in an isolated context and report back only which tests failed and why, without being able to edit any code itself.
items.reason: An isolated context window, a narrow tool allowance, and a summary returned to the parent conversation describe a subagent, not a Skill (which shares the current context).

content_blocks.prompt: invoice-service is picking a mechanism for each of these needs. Sort each one into the feature that actually fits.

content_blocks.text: Subagents: isolated context, delegated work

A subagent is a separate assistant with its own context window, created with the `/agents` command: you give it a name, a description of when it should be used (its trigger condition), a system prompt, and — critically — its own restricted set of allowed tools. Once defined, Claude Code can delegate to it automatically when a task matches its description, or you can invoke it by name. The parent conversation never sees the subagent's full working process, only whatever it returns — which keeps your own context window free of a test run's verbose output.

For invoice-service, a `test-runner` subagent makes the case well: allow it Bash and Read only, deny Write and Edit entirely, and its system prompt tells it to run the suite and report failures with a summary of cause, not to attempt fixes. Even if its instructions were somehow wrong, it structurally cannot modify a file — the tool restriction is the actual guarantee, not the wording of its prompt.
Design patterns worth building in from the start

A few habits make subagents (and Skills, to a lesser extent) noticeably more reliable in practice. Ask for structured output — a fixed format like a bullet list of failing tests with file and line, rather than free-form prose — so the parent conversation can parse and act on the result without re-reading a wall of text. Ask for obstacle reporting explicitly: a subagent instructed to say what it couldn't do, and why, is far more useful than one that either silently gives up or guesses past a blocker and reports success anyway. And default to the narrowest tool allowance the job needs, the same instinct behind the test-runner's Bash-and-Read-only scope — it's easier to loosen a restriction later than to discover after the fact what an overly broad one let happen.

cards.body: A fixed prompt you invoke explicitly by name. No frontmatter, no judgment — what you typed is what runs, every time.
cards.title: Slash command

cards.body: A SKILL.md file Claude applies on its own when your request matches its description. Progressive disclosure keeps most of its content out of context until it's actually needed.
cards.title: Skill

cards.body: Always-on project memory, loaded every session in its scope. The default home for what's always true.
cards.title: CLAUDE.md

cards.body: A deterministic trigger on a fixed event, immune to being overridden in-conversation. Covered in full next lesson.
cards.title: Hook

cards.body: An isolated assistant with its own context and its own restricted tools, delegated to automatically or by name, returning only a summary to the parent.
cards.title: Subagent

title: Skills and subagents for engineering work

content_blocks.text: Two separate asks land on the invoice-service backlog in the same week: someone wants Claude Code to open and update real GitHub issues instead of you copy-pasting between the terminal and the browser, and someone else wants an automatic e2e check that clicks through the refund flow in a browser after any change to it, without a human triggering it by hand. The first is a job for MCP — connecting Claude Code to a tool it doesn't already have. The second is closer to a hook — something that should happen automatically, no request needed, every time a certain kind of change lands.
MCP: giving Claude Code a new tool, not a new fact

Model Context Protocol connects Claude Code to an external server that exposes tools of its own — a GitHub server that can open issues and read PR threads, a browser-automation server (built on Playwright) that can click through a real page, a database server that can run read-only queries against a copy of the schema. Add one with `claude mcp add`, pointing it at the server's command or a remote URL, and its tools show up in Claude Code's tool list the same way its built-in ones do — the difference is invisible once it's connected.

For invoice-service, a GitHub MCP server means "open an issue for this and link it to the PR" becomes something Claude Code can just do, rather than a step you do yourself after the session ends. A browser-automation MCP server means "click through the refund flow with a $12 partial refund and confirm the credit note shows up" is a real, observed check — not Claude Code reading the code and guessing it probably works.

MCP servers can be scoped locally to your own machine, to the project (checked into the repo so the whole team gets the same connections), or to your user account across every project you touch. A server configured only for you personally won't be available to a teammate running the same repo — check the scope before assuming a connection you set up is shared.
GitHub integration: two different doors, easy to conflate

A GitHub MCP server is Claude Code reaching out to GitHub from inside a session you started. The Claude Code GitHub App is the reverse door: install it on the invoice-service repo, and tagging `@claude` in an issue or a PR comment triggers a Claude Code session inside GitHub's own infrastructure, without you opening a terminal at all. One is a tool Claude Code uses when you ask; the other is a bot that responds when your team asks, from wherever they already are — a PR comment thread, not a terminal. The code review setup in this module's last lesson is built on this second door.
Hooks: rules that fire without being asked

A hook is a shell command Claude Code runs automatically on a specific event, defined in `.claude/settings.json` (or the personal `~/.claude/settings.json`). You name the event — `PreToolUse` before a tool call, `PostToolUse` after one, `UserPromptSubmit` when you submit a message, `Stop` when a session ends, among others — and a matcher narrowing which tool or file it applies to, and Claude Code runs the command every time that event fires, with zero model judgment involved. That's the entire difference from a Skill: a Skill is Claude deciding whether to apply something; a hook fires regardless of what Claude thinks, every time, because the harness runs it, not the model.
A hook worth having on invoice-service

A `PostToolUse` hook matching file edits under `src/` that runs `npm run lint -- --fix` after every write keeps formatting consistent without anyone remembering to run it — the CI pipeline stops catching lint failures that a hook would have silently fixed a minute earlier. A stricter one: a `PreToolUse` hook matching any write under `db/migrations/` that checks whether the target file already exists and, if so, exits with a non-zero code — which blocks the write outright and returns its stderr to Claude Code as the reason. That second one is the sharper example, because it's the actual enforcement mechanism for "migrations are append-only," the rule you already put in CLAUDE.md in the previous lesson but which, as that lesson noted, a stray in-session instruction can still talk its way around. A hook can't be talked out of anything.

Gotchas worth knowing before you write one: a hook runs as a real subprocess with its own timeout, so a slow script stalls the whole session, not just itself. A PreToolUse hook that exits non-zero blocks the tool call — powerful, but a matcher that's broader than intended can end up blocking far more than you meant to. And a hook that always exits 0 without doing anything useful is a false sense of security; test it against the exact case it's meant to catch, not just against a happy path.
Spot the flaw

content_blocks.prompt: Here's a hook someone on the invoice-service team wrote to block edits to db/migrations/ once a file is merged. One part of it undermines the whole point. Find it.

candidates.reason: PreToolUse is correct here — you want to block the write before it happens, not clean up after it's already landed.

candidates.reason: Naming is a style preference, not a functional flaw — it doesn't change whether the hook actually blocks anything.

candidates.text: The hook is defined in project settings rather than personal settings.
candidates.reason: Project scope is the right choice for a rule the whole team should be bound by, not just one person's local setup.

content_blocks.text: The invoice-service team has been shipping the refund fix, the credit-note feature, and a growing pile of smaller PRs, and human review is starting to lag — not because reviewers are careless, but because there are more PRs than reviewer-hours in a day. Someone proposes automating a first pass: not to replace a human sign-off, but to catch the mechanical stuff — a missed test, an inconsistency with what CLAUDE.md already says about error handling — before a person's attention is needed at all.
Setting up automated review on the repo

This rides on the same GitHub App door from the previous lesson. With it installed on invoice-service, a PR can trigger an automatic review comment — either on every PR, or only when someone tags `@claude` on one — without a person kicking it off from a terminal. The review reads the diff against the codebase's own conventions: does this match what CLAUDE.md says about error handling, is there a test for the new branch, does anything here look like the same class of bug the refund fix addressed last week. It leaves its findings as a normal PR comment, in the same thread a human reviewer would use.

Automated review is a first pass, not a substitute for a human approving the merge. It's well suited to catching the mechanical, checklist-shaped issues — a missing test, an inconsistency with a stated convention — and poorly suited to judging whether the change is the right one to make at all. Keep a human required reviewer on the branch protection rule regardless of what the automated pass says.
Going further: the Claude Code SDK, briefly

Everything covered so far in this track runs through the interactive CLI, the IDE extensions, or the GitHub App — you or a teammate trigger a session, and a conversation happens. The Claude Code SDK is the option one level down from that: a Python and TypeScript package that lets you build your own program on top of the same agent, running headlessly, with no conversation and no human watching it in real time.

The kind of thing it's for: a nightly job that runs Claude Code over every PR opened that day rather than waiting for someone to tag it, or an internal tool specific enough to invoice-service's own workflow that neither the CLI nor the GitHub App quite fits. This is genuinely a different scope of work — you're writing and operating a program, not configuring a hook or a Skill — and it's a pointer for when you're ready to go there, not a workflow this lesson is trying to teach in depth.

content_blocks.text: Northwind Metrics' support inbox gets roughly 400 tickets a day, and right now a human reads every single one before deciding who handles it. You've been asked to build a small internal service that reads an incoming ticket, drafts a first-pass reply, and flags how urgent it is — no chat window, no copy-pasting into Claude.ai, just your code calling Claude directly. This lesson is where that starts.

Everything you've done with Claude so far, in this hub or elsewhere, has gone through some app's chat interface. The API strips that away: you send a request, you get a response, and every part of the conversation — including whether there even is one — is something your code manages. That is both the appeal and the catch. Nothing is hidden from you, but nothing is handled for you either. This lesson covers the pieces you need before you can send Claude a single ticket and get something useful back: authentication, the shape of a request, picking a model, and getting output your code can actually use.
Getting a key, and making your first call

An API key is how the Anthropic API knows which account, and which bill, a request belongs to. You generate one in the Anthropic Console, and from there every request carries it, typically read from an environment variable rather than typed into your code. A first call, sending one ticket's text to Claude and asking for a one-line summary, looks roughly like this:

```python
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

response = client.messages.create(
    model='claude-sonnet-5',
    max_tokens=200,
    messages=[
        {'role': 'user', 'content': 'Summarize this ticket in one sentence: My export keeps failing at 90% with no error message.'}
    ]
)
print(response.content[0].text)
```

That's the whole shape of an API call: a model, a cap on how long the reply can be, and a list of messages. Everything else in this lesson is refining pieces of that call.

An API key is a bearer credential — anyone who has it can spend against your account. Never hardcode it into a script, and never commit a .env file that holds one. Read it from the environment, and check your .gitignore before your first commit, not after.
Multi-turn conversations, and what the system prompt actually does

The API has no memory of its own. Claude.ai feels like an ongoing conversation because the app resends the whole history with every message; the API does exactly the same, except your code is the app now. A multi-turn exchange is just a growing messages list, alternating user and assistant roles, that you pass in full every time:

```python
messages = [
    {'role': 'user', 'content': 'A customer says their export fails at 90%.'},
    {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'Ask them whether the export is large. Timeouts are the usual cause past a few thousand rows.'},
    {'role': 'user', 'content': 'They confirmed it is about 40,000 rows. What should the reply say?'}
]
```

Separate from that list is system, a top-level parameter that sets standing instructions for the whole conversation rather than one turn in it — the persona and ground rules, not the back-and-forth. For the triage tool, the system prompt is where you'd put something like: you triage incoming support tickets for Northwind Metrics, always identify the likely cause before suggesting a fix, and never promise a refund. That instruction applies to every ticket the service ever processes, so it belongs in system, not repeated inside every user message.
Choosing a model: Opus, Sonnet, Haiku

Claude comes in a few sizes, and picking one is a real engineering decision, not a formality. The three you'll choose between are Opus, the most capable and most expensive, best kept for the judgment calls; Sonnet, the balanced default for most production work; and Haiku, the fastest and cheapest, built for high-volume, well-defined tasks. The triage tool actually needs two different models for two different jobs inside it: classifying each of those 400 daily tickets into a category and urgency level is simple, repetitive, and needs to be cheap and fast — that's Haiku. Drafting the actual reply to a ticket that's been flagged as a genuinely tricky complaint is worth spending more on — that's Sonnet, or Opus if the case escalates further. Using Opus for every one of the 400 tickets would work, but you'd be paying premium prices for a decision Haiku makes just as well.

cards.body: The most capable model, and the slowest and most expensive of the three. Reach for it on the judgment calls: an escalated complaint, a decision with real consequences if it's wrong, a task where getting it right matters more than getting it fast.
cards.title: Opus

cards.body: The balanced default. Strong reasoning at a fraction of Opus's cost and latency — the right starting point for most production tasks, including drafting a real reply to a customer.
cards.title: Sonnet

cards.body: The fastest and cheapest of the three. Built for high-volume, well-scoped work like classifying a ticket's category and urgency, where speed and cost matter more than depth.
cards.title: Haiku

content_blocks.text: Streaming: showing progress instead of a spinner

By default, an API call waits until Claude has generated the entire response before handing any of it back — fine for a one-line urgency tag, less fine for a full draft reply that might take several seconds to generate. Streaming changes that: instead of one response, you get a sequence of small events as each piece of text is produced, so you can display the reply as it's written rather than staring at a blank field. For the triage tool's dashboard, streaming is what lets a support agent watch the drafted reply appear word by word instead of waiting on a spinner with no sense of whether anything is happening. It's a stream=True argument on the same call, and a loop over the events it returns instead of a single return value.
Getting structured data back

Classifying a ticket only helps your code if the result comes back in a shape your code can read — a category and an urgency level, not a paragraph explaining Claude's reasoning. The direct way to get this is to ask for it explicitly and be specific about the shape:

```python
response = client.messages.create(
    model='claude-haiku-4-5-20251001',
    max_tokens=100,
    system='Classify support tickets. Respond with only a JSON object, no other text.',
    messages=[
        {'role': 'user', 'content': 'Ticket: My export keeps failing at 90% with no error message. Return JSON with keys category and urgency (low, medium, high).'}
    ]
)
```

Your code then parses response.content[0].text as JSON and reads result['category'] and result['urgency'] directly, no regex or string-scraping involved.

Asking for JSON is a strong instruction, not a guarantee. Claude will occasionally wrap the JSON in a sentence of preamble, or add a trailing note, especially if the prompt leaves any room for it. Parse defensively, and know that the more reliable fix, giving Claude a tool with an enforced schema instead of asking nicely, is exactly where the next lesson on tool use is headed.
What you can build with just this

title: Calling Claude directly: the API fundamentals

content_blocks.text: The classification prompt from the previous lesson works on the dozen tickets you tried by hand in the console. It has never seen the other 399 tickets that will hit it today, or the 400 tomorrow. Before this goes anywhere near production, you need a way to know it still works, not a feeling that it probably does.

This lesson assumes you can already write a good prompt. The general track's "How to write a good prompt" and "Specific levers for better output" (How to prompt well) already cover audience, format, constraints, examples, and role framing, and none of that changes just because the prompt now runs inside an API call instead of a chat window. What does change, once a prompt is a piece of running software rather than something you personally read and judge, are two things: your code needs to reliably pull a specific piece out of Claude's answer, and you need a way to know a prompt edit made things better instead of quietly worse, across cases you didn't happen to check by hand. Those two problems, structure for parsing and evaluation at scale, are what this lesson adds.
XML tags: structure for programs, not just readability

You met format specs in the general track as a lever for getting a cleaner response. There's a sharper, API-specific reason to reach for XML tags in particular: Claude has been trained to respect XML boundaries with real precision, which makes them a reliable place for your code to look. Instead of asking for loose JSON and hoping nothing wraps it in prose, you can ask Claude to place each field inside its own named tag:

```
Classify the ticket below.

<ticket>My export keeps failing at 90% with no error message.</ticket>

Respond in this exact form:
<category>...</category>
<urgency>low|medium|high</urgency>
```

Your code then looks for <category> and <urgency> specifically, rather than parsing the whole reply as one blob and hoping the structure holds.

An XML tag in a prompt is a contract between your prompt and your parsing code, not just a formatting nicety. If you rename urgency to priority in the prompt, your parser breaks until you update it to match. The two live together, and a change to one is a change to both.
Example-based prompting, at volume

Showing Claude a worked example is already a lever you know. At the volume this tool runs at, it earns its keep more than almost anything else, because a written rule is looser than it feels. Mark it urgent if it mentions data loss sounds precise until Northwind's ticket queue produces the edge case: a customer joking that they'll lose their mind if the export isn't fixed today. Three or four real labeled tickets, including one deliberately ambiguous one, pin down the boundary a plain-English rule leaves fuzzy, and at 400 tickets a day, that fuzzy boundary is not a hypothetical, it is Tuesday.
Building an eval harness: stop eyeballing outputs

An eval, in this context, is unglamorous: a set of real or realistic tickets with a known correct answer for each, run through your prompt automatically, graded, and scored as a percentage. Pull 50 real historical tickets Northwind's team already triaged correctly by hand, keep their human-assigned category and urgency as the answer key, and write a short script that sends each ticket through your classification prompt and checks whether Claude's answer matches. That one script is the difference between "I tried a few tickets and it seemed fine" and "this prompt scores 47 out of 50, and here are the 3 it gets wrong."

cards.body: Compare Claude's answer to a known-correct value directly in code: does category equal 'billing', does urgency equal 'high'. Fast, cheap, and exact; use it for anything with one right answer, which covers most of the triage fields.
cards.title: Code-based grading

cards.body: Use Claude itself as the grader for anything with no single right answer, like whether a drafted reply's tone matches the ticket's urgency. You give the grading model the ticket, the draft, and a rubric, and it scores the result. Slower and less exact than code-based grading, but the only option once 'correct' is a judgment call.
cards.title: Model-based grading

content_blocks.text: Put together, the harness is one loop: for each of the 50 tickets, call the API with your current prompt, grade the result against the answer key (code-based for category and urgency, model-based if you're also scoring the drafted reply's tone), and print a pass rate at the end. When you add the ambiguous-ticket example from the section above, you rerun the same 50 and check the score moved the direction you wanted, instead of trusting that it probably did.

An eval harness for something this narrow takes an afternoon to build and keeps paying for itself every time you touch the prompt afterward. Skipping it doesn't save that afternoon, it just moves the cost to whichever customer's ticket gets silently misclassified after your next 'small' prompt tweak.
What this adds to what you already know

cards.body: Audience, format, constraints, examples, role, self-critique. The general track's prompting module covers all of this, and it applies exactly the same whether the prompt runs in a chat window or an API call.
cards.title: Fundamentals (already covered)

cards.body: A parsing contract, not just a format spec: precise tags your code can reliably extract, load-bearing wherever a downstream system reads a specific field out of Claude's answer.
cards.title: XML structuring

cards.body: A test dataset, an answer key, and automatic grading, so a prompt change is judged by a score across every case you've collected, not by rereading a handful of examples yourself.
cards.title: The eval harness

questions.q: Your ticket classifier's prompt asks Claude to place the urgency inside an <urgency> tag, and your parser looks for that exact tag. A teammate renames it to <priority> in the prompt, without telling you. What breaks?
options: Nothing — Claude infers the intent either way
Your parser stops finding the field, because the tag name is a contract shared between the prompt and the code that reads it
The API call fails outright with an error
Claude automatically updates the parser to match
questions.explanation: An XML tag used for parsing is a contract between the prompt and the code reading the output. Renaming it in one place without the other breaks the link even though the prompt itself still 'reads fine.'

questions.q: You want to know whether adding one more worked example to your classification prompt actually improved accuracy, not just on the 3 tickets you tried by hand, but across the ones you didn't check. What's the right move?
options: Ship it and watch for complaints
Rerun your eval harness's full test set and compare the score before and after the change
Ask Claude whether the new version is better
Assume it helped, since worked examples generally do
questions.explanation: An eval harness turns 'did this change help' into a number measured across your whole test set, rather than a guess based on the handful of cases you happened to glance at.

questions.q: Which grading approach fits checking whether a drafted customer reply's tone actually matches the ticket's urgency level?
options: Code-based grading, since tone is a simple string match
Model-based grading, since tone is a judgment call with no single correct string to compare against
Neither — tone can't be evaluated automatically
Code-based grading, but only if the reply is under 50 words
questions.explanation: Tone has no exact right answer to match against in code, so it needs a grader that can make a judgment call — that's what model-based grading is for. Code-based grading fits hard fields like category or urgency better, where there's one correct value.

title: Prompt engineering and evaluation for production

content_blocks.text: The triage tool drafts a reply that sounds confident and is wrong: it tells a customer they're on the Standard plan when they upgraded to Pro last month. Claude isn't lying, it's guessing. Nothing in the prompt gave it the customer's actual account data, so it filled the gap with the most plausible-sounding answer. What it needs is a way to ask for that data itself, mid-conversation, instead of you trying to paste in every customer's full history up front.

Tool use is how you give Claude the ability to ask for something instead of guessing at it. You describe a function to Claude, a name, a description of what it does, and the shape of the arguments it takes, and Claude can decide, mid-response, to call it. Nothing about that function actually runs on Anthropic's servers. Claude only ever produces a request to call it; your code is the one that executes it, and hands the result back. That division, Claude decides, your code executes, is the whole idea, and it's also exactly what an MCP server formalizes in the next lesson, so it's worth understanding by hand once first.
Defining a tool schema

The description field isn't documentation for a human reading your code later. It's most of what Claude uses to decide whether and when to call the tool at all. A vague description ('gets customer stuff') produces the same unreliable, sometimes-it-calls-it-sometimes-it-doesn't behavior as a vague prompt. Write it the way you'd brief a new team member on what the function does and when to reach for it.
The turn Claude asks for a tool, and the turn you answer it

When Claude decides to use a tool, the response comes back with stop_reason set to tool_use and a content block naming the tool and the arguments it wants to call it with, instead of a finished answer. Your code reads that block, actually runs the function (a real database lookup, in Northwind's case), and sends the result back as a new message with a tool_result block tagged to the same tool-call ID:

```python
# Claude's response included a tool_use block requesting look_up_customer('NM-40231')
tool_result = look_up_customer('NM-40231')  # your actual function, runs in your code

messages.append({'role': 'assistant', 'content': response.content})
messages.append({
    'role': 'user',
    'content': [{
        'type': 'tool_result',
        'tool_use_id': response.content[-1].id,
        'content': str(tool_result)
    }]
})
```

You call the API again with this longer messages list, and this time Claude answers using the real account data instead of guessing at it.
Building the loop by hand

Put those two turns in a while loop and you have an agent: call the API, check stop_reason, and if it's tool_use, execute the tool and call again; if it's end_turn, you have Claude's final answer and you're done. That loop, checking, executing, and calling again until the model is satisfied, is genuinely the whole mechanism behind every 'agent' framework you'll come across. Frameworks add convenience around it, a registry of tools, retries, logging, but there's no hidden trick past this loop, and building it by hand once is worth more than reading about it.

Always cap how many times the loop can go around. Five or so is a sane default for something like ticket triage. Nothing stops a confused prompt or a flaky tool from producing a Claude that keeps calling the same lookup forever, and an uncapped loop turns a bug into an open-ended API bill.
Extended thinking, for the harder judgment calls

Extended thinking gives Claude a visible scratchpad to reason in before it answers, separate from the reply itself, useful for exactly the kind of call that's hardest to get right in one pass, like whether an angry, ambiguous ticket should escalate to a human or get a standard reply. It isn't something you'd turn on for the simple classification pass from the first lesson; the cost and latency aren't worth it there. Reserve it for the branch of the loop that actually carries judgment, and keep the thinking content separate from what you show the customer. It's Claude's reasoning, not a customer-facing message.
What you can now build

questions.q: Claude's response comes back with stop_reason set to tool_use and a block requesting look_up_customer('NM-40231'). What actually looks up that customer's data?

Your own code executes the real lookup function and sends the result back as a tool_result
The Anthropic API runs the function on its servers automatically
The loop ends immediately, since tool_use means the task failed

questions.q: Why cap the number of iterations in a hand-built agent loop?
options: The API rejects any call past a fixed iteration count
Without a cap, a confused agent or a flaky tool can keep looping indefinitely, running up API cost with no natural stopping point
Extended thinking requires a fixed number of loop iterations to activate

questions.explanation: Nothing about the loop itself guarantees it terminates. A cap is a deliberate safety net against a stuck or confused agent looping forever.

questions.q: Where does extended thinking earn its cost and latency in the triage tool?
options: On every single ticket, including the routine category/urgency classification pass
On the harder judgment calls, like deciding whether an ambiguous ticket needs to escalate to a human
Only when the tool schema includes more than one required field
Never — extended thinking is only useful for tasks with no tool use involved
questions.explanation: Extended thinking is worth its added cost and latency on genuinely hard judgment calls. Routine, well-scoped steps like the classification pass don't need it and shouldn't pay for it.

title: Tool use and agent loops, built by hand

content_blocks.text: The look_up_customer function from the last lesson is hardcoded straight into the triage script. Now a second internal tool, a small Slack bot the account team wants for checking a customer's plan without opening the dashboard, needs the exact same lookup. Copy-pasting the function into a second codebase means fixing the same bug twice the next time the customer schema changes. Time to pull it out into something both tools can share.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is what that sharing looks like formalized: a standard client-server protocol so any MCP-aware application can plug into a set of tools, without writing bespoke integration code for each one. Where the tool in the last lesson lived entirely inside your one script's tools list, an MCP server exposes the same kind of tool over a standard interface, so the triage script, the Slack bot, and even a teammate poking around from Claude Desktop can all reach it without any of them owning a private copy of the lookup code.
Three primitives: tools, resources, prompts

MCP defines exactly three kinds of things a server can offer. Tools are actions your code executes on request; look_up_customer, network-exposed now instead of hardcoded into one script, is exactly this. Resources are read-only data a client can fetch or attach, like a specific customer record or the day's ticket queue as a file the client can pull in in full. Prompts are reusable prompt templates the server hands out, so a client can request the server's own draft_reply template with the ticket and customer data filled in, instead of every client reinventing that prompt from scratch.

cards.body: Actions the server executes on request, like look_up_customer. The client asks; the server's code runs and returns a result — the same tool-use idea from the last lesson, now reachable by more than one client.
cards.title: Tools

cards.body: Read-only data a client can fetch, like a customer record or today's ticket queue. No execution involved, just data the client can pull in as context.
cards.title: Resources

cards.body: Reusable prompt templates the server offers, like a standard draft_reply template. Any client can request it pre-filled, instead of every integration rewriting the same prompt.
cards.title: Prompts

content_blocks.text: Writing a server with the Python SDK

The type hints and docstring aren't just style here. The SDK turns them directly into the schema Claude sees when deciding whether to call this tool. A vague docstring ('does customer stuff') produces exactly the same unreliable calling behavior the last lesson warned about with hand-written descriptions, just one layer further removed from where you'd think to look for the cause.
Testing with the Inspector before anyone connects

Before wiring your new server up to the triage script, the Slack bot, or anything else, the Server Inspector lets you run it standalone and poke at it from a browser: list the tools it exposes, invoke look_up_customer with a real ID, and see the raw JSON that comes back. It's worth the five minutes it takes, every time. Confirming the server behaves correctly in isolation is a much smaller problem to debug than confirming it once three different clients are all talking to it at once.
Defining a client

A client is the other half: code that connects to your MCP server, asks it what tools, resources, and prompts it exposes, and wires the answers into a Claude conversation. Under the hood, this is the same tool_use loop from the last lesson. Claude still asks to call a tool, your code still executes it and returns a result, except now 'your code' is a thin client talking to the server over a standard transport, and the tool's actual implementation lives in one shared place instead of being copied into the triage script and the Slack bot separately.

This lesson covers building and connecting to a server on your own machine. Running one in production, multiple clients connecting concurrently, choosing between the stdio transport used here and Streamable HTTP, scaling behind a load balancer, is real depth of its own, covered in "Model Context Protocol: Advanced Topics" (sampling, transports, production scaling). Worth knowing that course exists once this server needs to run somewhere real; not needed to get the local version working today.

cards.body: The three things a server can expose: tools execute, resources are read-only data, prompts are reusable templates.

questions.q: Both the ticket-triage script and a new Slack bot need the same customer lookup. What does pulling it into an MCP server solve that hardcoding it into both scripts wouldn't?
options: It makes the lookup run faster
It means both clients share one implementation, instead of maintaining and fixing the same logic in two places
It removes the need for a tool schema entirely

questions.q: In the Python SDK's decorator style, where does the tool's schema actually come from?
options: You still write a separate input_schema dictionary by hand, same as calling the API directly
The function's type hints and docstring, which the SDK reads to generate the schema automatically
A configuration file you maintain separately from the function
The Server Inspector generates it the first time you run the tool

Deploy it to production and monitor for errors
Run it standalone with the Server Inspector and invoke its tools directly in the browser
Skip testing — the SDK guarantees correctness from the type hints alone
questions.explanation: The Inspector lets you test a server in isolation before any real client depends on it, which is a much smaller problem to debug than troubleshooting multiple clients at once.

title: Building MCP servers and clients

content_blocks.text: The triage agent works beautifully on your laptop: you run the script, it processes a batch of tickets, you watch the output. Northwind Metrics needs it running continuously against the live ticket queue, day and night, without someone's terminal window staying open forever, and their infrastructure team, who already run everything else on AWS, has a question before they'll sign off: does this have to be a raw Anthropic API key, or can it go through Bedrock like everything else does?

A managed agent is Anthropic's answer to the first half of that problem: instead of you hosting the always-on process that keeps calling the API, executing tools, and looping, you hand over the agent's definition, its tools, its instructions, its loop, and it runs continuously on Anthropic's infrastructure. You stop owning the uptime and scaling of the loop itself, and focus on the tool logic and the business rules that make it Northwind's triage agent rather than a generic one.
What a managed agent actually replaces

Run the loop yourself, the way the hand-built version from earlier in this module works, and you own everything around it: a server that stays up, a way to restart it if it crashes, and a way to scale it if 400 tickets a day becomes 4,000. A managed agent takes over exactly that layer. It doesn't change what the agent does, the same tools, the same system prompt, the same judgment calls, it changes who's responsible for keeping it running.
Event streaming: watching the agent work

This is the agent-level version of the response streaming from the first lesson. Instead of streaming just the words of one reply, a managed agent streams events for the whole loop as it happens: a tool call starting, its result coming back, a thinking step, the final answer. For Northwind's support team, that's the difference between a dashboard that shows nothing until triage finishes and one that shows 'looking up customer NM-40231' in real time, the same way you'd want visibility into any process working on your behalf rather than a black box.
Same model, different door: Bedrock and Vertex AI

To answer the infrastructure team's question directly: Claude is also available through Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud's Vertex AI, and it's genuinely the same models, not a lighter or different version, reached through that cloud provider's own SDK and identity and access setup instead of an Anthropic API key. If Northwind's infrastructure is already standardized on AWS, wiring the triage agent through Bedrock means the tool schemas, the loop, and everything else in this module carry over unchanged; only the plumbing that authenticates and sends the request differs. The same is true of Vertex AI on Google Cloud.

This is worth knowing exists, not worth building deep expertise in unless a client's infrastructure actually requires it. If a client's cloud platform is already decided by factors well outside this project, that's a real constraint to respect, not a battle to fight. Wire the same tools and the same loop through whichever door their infrastructure team already has open.

cards.body: Hand over the agent's definition — tools, instructions, loop — and Anthropic hosts the always-on process, so you're no longer responsible for the loop's uptime and scaling.
