content_blocks.text: Your team's PR queue has fourteen open pull requests right now, and this morning's stand-up ran the same way it always does: nobody could say off the top of their head which ones were actually waiting on a review and which had just gone quiet. Your manager's ask lands directly on you: "Can you build us something that tells us when a PR's gone stale, before it costs us a release?" No existing codebase to inherit, no ticket half-written for you, just a Monday and a blank repo. This is the capstone, and it's built that way on purpose: everything this track has taught you so far, GitHub Copilot in Module 1, the agentic-engineering habits in Module 2, Claude Code in Module 3, comes together here, on one build, from the first line to the merged PR.
The build: PR Watchdog

Call it PR Watchdog. It's a small scheduled job, not a product: once a weekday morning, it asks GitHub for every open pull request across your team's repos, flags anything that's been open more than five business days with no review activity at all, and posts a short digest to the team's Slack channel. Small enough to build in a day or two, real enough that if you get the stale-PR rule wrong, someone will tell you within a week.
Stage 1 — Write the spec before you write a script

The habit from "Spec-driven development" earlier in this track was built for a much bigger greenfield job, a whole notifications service, and it's tempting to think a tool this small doesn't need any of that ceremony. It doesn't need the full four-file ritual. It does need the same underlying discipline: decide what PR Watchdog is and isn't allowed to do before you write a single line, because a vague idea in your head produces exactly the same vague, guessed-at implementation from an AI tool that a vague issue produces from an agent.

Two short paragraphs cover it. The constitution: PR Watchdog only ever reads from GitHub, it never comments, approves, or merges anything itself, and it posts to exactly one Slack channel, never DMs. The spec: "stale" means open more than five business days with zero review activity, and the digest lists each stale PR's title, age, and author, sorted oldest first. Nothing about implementation yet, just the two things worth being precise about before Copilot or Claude Code writes a line: what the tool is trusted to touch, and what counts as the case you're actually solving.

Skipping the ceremony is fine for something this size. Skipping the discipline isn't. "Build a tool that flags stale PRs" still leaves "stale" undefined, and whichever tool you hand that sentence to will guess at a threshold, same as an agent guesses at an unscoped issue. Write the two paragraphs first, even if you never save them as separate files.
Stage 2 — Draft the polling logic with GitHub Copilot

The part of this that's genuinely quick is the part GitHub Copilot is built for: reading through GitHub's REST API docs isn't the job, writing the function that calls it is. Open a new github.py and write the comment first, the same comment-driven habit from "Prompting Copilot well": "# fetch every open PR across a list of repos, using a GitHub token from the environment, and return title, author, created date, and whether it has any reviews". Let Copilot complete from there, and you'll have a working get_open_prs() in under a minute.

Before you trust it, widen the question the same way that lesson taught: highlight the function, ask @workspace whether anything else in the (still mostly empty) repo already handles GitHub auth, then ask #selection what happens if a team has more than 30 open PRs at once. That question catches something the first minute's excitement would have missed: GitHub's API pages results at 30 per call by default, and Copilot's first draft only ever reads page one. A team comfortably under 30 open PRs would never notice; a team having a genuinely bad week would silently lose every stale PR past the thirtieth.

This is the exact gotcha from Module 1: code that compiles cleanly and runs without error can still be quietly wrong, because Copilot has no idea your team's real PR volume unless you tell it. Read the whole suggestion, and specifically ask about the boundary cases a first draft is least likely to have considered, the same instinct that caught the missing pagination here.
Stage 3 — Hand the real build to Claude Code

github.py is one file, one function, easy to hold in your head. The rest of PR Watchdog, staleness scoring, Slack formatting, the scheduling entrypoint, tying it together into something that actually runs unattended, is exactly the kind of multi-file job this track's Module 3 built for Claude Code rather than Copilot's inline completions. Start with a short CLAUDE.md: the repo's one real command (python -m prwatch.run), the constraint from your Stage 1 spec (never comment, approve, or merge, read and post only), and where the Slack webhook and GitHub token live (environment variables, never hardcoded). Then run the loop that lesson taught: Plan Mode first, to have Claude Code trace what github.py already returns and propose the shape of scorer.py and slack.py before it writes either; read the plan; then let it code, watching the task list the same way you would on any real bug fix.

One rule from your Stage 1 constitution is worth enforcing at the tool level, not just writing down: PR Watchdog's GitHub token and Slack webhook live in a .env file that should never once reach git history. A CLAUDE.md line saying so is a good first layer, per "Context management and CLAUDE.md", but it's still just an instruction. The enforced version is a PreToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json, matched against file writes, that checks whether the target path is .env and exits non-zero if it is, blocking the write outright regardless of how the request was phrased.

This is the same principle from Module 4's very first lesson, that an API key is a bearer credential nobody should ever commit, enforced the Module 3 way instead of the API-fundamentals way: a hook that can't be talked out of firing beats a comment or a CLAUDE.md line that a later instruction could still override.

content_blocks.prompt: Someone on your team wires up the .env-blocking hook for PR Watchdog. One part of it leaves a real gap. Find it.
content_blocks.example: A PreToolUse hook, matcher "Write", running a script that exits non-zero only if the exact target path equals ".env", intended to stop the GitHub token and Slack webhook secrets from ever being committed.

candidates.text: The check only matches a path that exactly equals ".env", so a secrets file saved as .env.local or nested under config/.env would slip through untouched.
candidates.reason: A check narrower than the real set of paths that could hold secrets leaves exactly the gap it was built to close — anything named slightly differently gets through free.

candidates.text: The hook runs before the tool call rather than after.
candidates.reason: PreToolUse is correct here — you want to stop the write before it lands, not clean up a secret that's already been committed.

candidates.text: The hook is defined in the project's .claude/settings.json rather than a personal one.
candidates.reason: Project scope is right here — this is a rule the whole team building PR Watchdog should be bound by, not one person's local preference.

content_blocks.text: Stage 4 — optional: give each flagged PR a plain-English nudge

PR Watchdog's digest works fine as a bare list of titles and ages. If you want to go one step further, the way Module 4 covered calling Claude directly from your own code applies here in miniature: for each stale PR, send its title and the files it touches to the API and ask for one plain sentence explaining why it's worth a look today, something like "touches the checkout flow and has sat untouched for 8 days." This is exactly the high-volume, well-scoped, cheap-and-fast job Module 4's model-choice lesson described Haiku for, not Opus or Sonnet: a one-line classification-shaped task running against however many PRs are stale that morning, never anything requiring deep judgment.

Treat the nudge as a caption, not the fact. The digest should still show the objective numbers, age and reviewer count, next to whatever one-liner Claude drafts, the same reason Module 1 taught you to verify a Copilot suggestion instead of trusting confident phrasing: a fluent sentence is not the same thing as a correct one, and the raw age-in-days is what actually caught someone's attention first.
Ship it: review it like anyone else's PR

PR Watchdog now reaches into every repo your team owns and posts to a channel the whole team reads, which makes it exactly the kind of thing Module 2's contributor model was built for. Whether Claude Code wrote most of scorer.py and slack.py or you typed every line yourself doesn't change the review: read the diff, confirm the tests actually call get_open_prs() and exercise scorer.py's staleness rule rather than just passing, and check nothing touches the .env file or logs a token or webhook URL in plain text anywhere. Put the repo behind the same kind of guardrail Module 2's governance lesson described for billing-service, a required review before merging to main, even though you might be the only engineer on this. The point isn't distrust of your own work; it's that a tool with write access to Slack and read access to every repo deserves the habit of scrutiny regardless of who or what wrote it.

cards.title: Stage 1 — Spec it

content_blocks.text: Reflect

Notice what actually made this a capstone rather than four separate exercises: no single stage did all the work. Copilot was fastest exactly where the task was small and self-contained; Claude Code earned its place exactly where the job spanned several files and needed a plan checked before it ran; the spec-driven habit and the contributor-model review weren't optional extras, they were what kept both tools honest at the two moments that mattered most, before anything was built and before anything shipped. That's the pattern worth carrying past PR Watchdog itself: pick the tool for the shape of the task in front of you, and keep the review discipline constant regardless of which tool did the typing.

content_blocks.task: Build a smaller version of PR Watchdog, or adapt the idea, against a real repo you actually have access to.

steps.text: Write your own constitution and spec before opening an editor: what your version is allowed to touch (read-only against GitHub is the safe default), and exactly what condition should trigger a flag.
steps.label: Spec it in two paragraphs

steps.text: Use Copilot to write the single function that calls the GitHub API and returns the data your rule needs. Ask a scoped question about a boundary case (pagination, rate limits, a repo with zero PRs) before you trust the first draft.
steps.label: Draft the small part

steps.text: Use Claude Code, with a short CLAUDE.md and Plan Mode, to build the scoring and output logic. Add one hook enforcing the one rule you actually care about, not a long list of them.
steps.label: Hand off the rest

steps.text: Before you let it run on a schedule, read the diff the way you would a new contributor's: does it match your two-paragraph spec, and can you explain what it does back in one sentence.
steps.label: Review it like a stranger's PR

content_blocks.material: A repo you can create a GitHub personal access token for, and either GitHub Copilot or Claude Code (or both) available in your editor.
content_blocks.whatToNotice: How naturally the task splits itself between the two tools once you're looking for it, and how much of the actual risk in a build like this lives in the review step at the end, not in which tool wrote which line.

questions.q: PR Watchdog's stale-PR rule and its no-comment, no-merge, read-only constraint get written down as two short paragraphs before any code exists. What is this actually doing?
options: Slowing the project down for no real benefit, since the tool is small
Applying spec-driven development's discipline at a scale that fits the build, so both Copilot and Claude Code are working from a defined intent instead of a guess
Replacing the need to review any code the tools produce later
A GitHub-specific requirement that only applies to greenfield services
questions.explanation: The full constitution/spec/plan/tasks ritual is overkill for something this size, but the underlying discipline, deciding intent before code exists, is the same one, just scaled down to two paragraphs instead of four files.

questions.q: PR Watchdog calls the Claude API directly to draft a one-line nudge for each stale PR. Which model fits that job, and why?
options: Opus, since a customer-facing message deserves the most capable model available
Haiku, since it's a high-volume, well-scoped, cheap-and-fast task, not a judgment call worth Opus's cost and latency
Sonnet, since it is the only model that supports single-sentence output
Whichever model is used elsewhere in the codebase, for consistency
questions.explanation: A one-line nudge generated for however many PRs are stale each morning is exactly the shape of task Haiku is built for: fast, cheap, and well-scoped, with no deep reasoning required.

questions.q: PR Watchdog's .env-blocking hook only checks whether a written file's path exactly equals ".env". What's the problem, and what should catch it before the tool ships?
options: Nothing — an exact path match is the most precise kind of check available
A file saved as .env.local or nested under a subfolder would slip past the check entirely, so the hook needs a wider check and the pre-merge review needs to look for exactly this kind of gap
The hook should be removed, since CLAUDE.md's instruction not to commit secrets is already enough
PreToolUse hooks cannot check file paths at all, only tool names
questions.explanation: A check narrower than the real set of risky paths leaves exactly the gap it was meant to close. This is also exactly the kind of thing the pre-merge review in the final stage exists to catch, whether or not the hook itself is airtight.

content_blocks.text: You've now taken a real, small idea from a stand-up complaint to a shipped tool, using GitHub Copilot for the fast, contained part, Claude Code for the multi-file build, and the spec-first, review-like-a-stranger's-PR discipline from Module 2 to keep both of them honest at the two moments that mattered. That's the capstone, and it's also just how real engineering work with these tools looks from here on.
